source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. I (Montreuil, 1896), pp. 347–353

1.title: De variis translationibus Scripturarum veteris Testamenti, et de comparatione translationum LXX interpretum ac sancti Hieronymi ad invicem, atque de his, in quibus Hieronymus et Augustinus consentire et dissentire videntur circa translationem LXX interpretum
1.title_en: On the various translations of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, on the translations of the Seventy Interpreters and of St Jerome compared with each other, and on the points in which Jerome and Augustine seem to agree and to disagree about the translation of the Seventy

paras.t: Scripturam veteris Testamenti transtulerunt diu ante Christi incarnationem Septuaginta interpretes, quorum translatione utebatur Ecclesia usque ad tempus Hieronymi. Porro, post Christi adventum alii plures transtulerunt easdem Scripturas. Primo videlicet Aquila, deinde Theodotion, postmodum Symmachus. Fuit quoque translatio alia, cujus auctor nescitur, quæ vocatur quinta editio. Hi omnes transtulerunt de Hebræo in Græcum. Fuerunt etiam alii plures, qui de Græco transtulerunt Scripturas has in Latinum. Tandem B. Hieronymus, multis rationabilibus inductus motivis, præfatas Scripturas ex Hebraico transtulit in Latinum. De hac autem materia infra magis dicetur.
paras.en: The Scripture of the Old Testament was translated, long before the incarnation of Christ, by the Seventy Interpreters, whose translation the Church used until the time of Jerome. After the coming of Christ, several others translated the same Scriptures: first Aquila, then Theodotion, afterwards Symmachus. There was also another translation, whose author is not known, which is called the fifth edition. All of these translated from Hebrew into Greek. There were many others besides who translated these Scriptures from Greek into Latin. At last Blessed Jerome, moved by many reasonable motives, translated the said Scriptures from the Hebrew into Latin. More will be said of this matter below.

paras.t: Denique de LXX interpretibus et translatione eorum ait Augustinus octavodecimo de Civitate Dei, quod dum missi fuissent ab Eleazaro tunc Judæorum pontifice, Ptolemæo regi Ægypti, ipse rex Ptolemæus tanquam vir prudens, volens explorare fidelitatem illorum interpretum, jussit ut unusquisque eorum seorsum solus transferret Scripturam eamdem: quo facto, inventi sunt omnes tam concorditer transtulisse, quod nec in aliquo verbo, neque in ordine verborum alter discreparet ab alio; sed ita omnes interpretati sunt unum et idem, quasi fuisset dumtaxat unus interpres: quod fuit revera valde mirabile et stupendum atque divinum, nec aliter fieri potuit, nisi a Deo. Vere etenim Spiritus unus erat in omnibus illis viris, et ideo tam mirabile donum acceperunt a Deo, quatenus etiam per hoc commendaretur auctoritas Scripturarum illarum tanquam veraciter divinarum, non humanarum, ad profectum gentium crediturarum: quod post Christi adventum videmus impletum. Hæc sententionaliter asserit Augustinus libro præallegato, capitulo 42.
paras.en: Now of the Seventy Interpreters and their translation Augustine says, in the eighteenth book of the City of God, that when they had been sent by Eleazar, then high priest of the Jews, to Ptolemy king of Egypt, King Ptolemy, as a prudent man wishing to test the faithfulness of those interpreters, ordered each of them to translate the same Scripture separately and alone. When this was done, they were all found to have translated so harmoniously that not one differed from another in any word, nor in the order of the words; but all rendered one and the same thing, as if there had been only one interpreter. This was truly most wonderful, astonishing and divine, and could not have come about except from God. For indeed one Spirit was in all those men, and therefore they received so wonderful a gift from God, so that by this too the authority of those Scriptures might be commended as truly divine, not human, for the profit of the nations that were to believe: and this we see fulfilled since the coming of Christ. This is the substance of what Augustine asserts in the book cited, chapter 42.

paras.t: Præterea ejusdem libri capitulo 43 scribit in hæc verba: Fuerunt et alii qui Scripturas illas transtulerunt in Græcum, translationem tamen LXX interpretum recepit Ecclesia, quasi alia non sit, et ea utuntur Græci fideles, quorum plerique ignorant aliam esse. Nostris quoque temporibus fuit Hieronymus presbyter, homo doctissimus, qui easdem Scripturas non ex Græco, sed ex Hebræo eloquio in Latinum vertit. Et quamvis Judæi fateantur translationem ejus esse veracem, LXX vero interpretes asserant in multis errasse, tamen Ecclesiæ Christi judicant, nullum translatorem esse præferendum auctoritati et translationi LXX interpretum. Nam, quamvis non apparuisset in eis unus Spiritus Dei, sed more hominum eruditorum contulissent inter se verba suæ translationis, ut id permaneret quod eis omnibus placuisset, tamen nemo unus interpres esset eis anteponendus; sed quum tantum signum deitatis in eis apparuit, quod scilicet (sicut prætactum est) omnes seorsum tam concorditer transtulerunt, constat quod quicumque alius Scripturas illas veraciter transtulit, concors est translationi illorum LXX, aut LXX illi aliter transferendo, prophetice sunt locuti. Idem quippe Spiritus, qui fuit in Prophetis quando verba Scripturarum locuti sunt, fuit in LXX dum eadem transtulerunt: qui Spiritus per LXX interpretes aliud dicere potuit, et per eosdem aliqua prætermittere et aliqua addere, ostendens utrosque, videlicet Scripturarum auctores, et LXX interpretes, fuisse prophetas. Denique, quintodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Merito creduntur LXX interpretes accepisse Spiritum Dei, ut si quid mutarent aut aliter dicerent, non dubitaretur id esse divinitus factum. Idem asserit Augustinus in aliis pluribus locis. Nam et quarto libro de Doctrina christiana fatetur, quod LXX interpretes, qui divino interpretati sunt Spiritu, idcirco nonnulla aliter transtulerunt quam in Hebræo habetur, quatenus ex hac diversitate moveretur lectoris intentio ad perscrutandum sensum spiritualem.
paras.en: Moreover, in chapter 43 of the same book he writes in these words: “There were also others who translated those Scriptures into Greek; yet the Church has received the translation of the Seventy Interpreters as if there were no other, and the Greek faithful use it, most of whom do not know that there is another. In our own times, too, there was the priest Jerome, a most learned man, who turned the same Scriptures into Latin, not from the Greek but from the Hebrew tongue.” And although the Jews acknowledge that his translation is true, and assert that the Seventy Interpreters erred in many things, yet the Churches of Christ judge that no translator is to be preferred to the authority and the translation of the Seventy Interpreters. For even if the one Spirit of God had not shown itself in them, and they had compared the words of their translation among themselves after the manner of learned men, so that what pleased them all should stand, still no single interpreter would be set above them. But since so great a sign of the Godhead appeared in them, namely (as was said before) that they all, working apart, translated so harmoniously, it is certain that whoever else has translated those Scriptures truly agrees with the translation of those Seventy; or else that the Seventy, in translating otherwise, spoke prophetically. For the same Spirit who was in the Prophets when they spoke the words of the Scriptures was in the Seventy when they translated them; and that Spirit could say something else through the Seventy Interpreters, and through them leave some things out and add others, showing that both, namely the authors of the Scriptures and the Seventy Interpreters, were prophets. Again, in the fifteenth book of the City of God Augustine says: “The Seventy Interpreters are rightly believed to have received the Spirit of God, so that if they changed anything or said it otherwise, it should not be doubted that this was done by God.” Augustine asserts the same in many other places. For in the fourth book of On Christian Doctrine he also acknowledges that the Seventy Interpreters, who translated by the divine Spirit, rendered some things otherwise than they stand in the Hebrew for this reason: that by this difference the reader's attention might be moved to search out the spiritual sense.

paras.t: Itaque, his præmissis, videndum est quid de LXX interpretibus et translatione ipsorum Hieronymus senserit. In prologo quippe proprio super Genesim, inter cetera ait: Nescio quis primus septuaginta cellulas Alexandriæ mendacio suo construxerit: in quibus (interpretes illi) divisi, eadem scripserint, quum Aristæus Ptolemæi hyperaspistes (id est protector vel custos), et Josephus, nil tale retulerint, sed quod congregati fuerint in eadem basilica, et de transferendis contulerint, non prophetaverint. Aliud est enim esse vatem, aliud interpretem. LXX illi interpretati sunt Scripturas ante Christi adventum, et quod nesciebant, dubiis protulerunt sententiis. In his verbis videtur Hieronymus discordare ab Augustino in tribus. Primo, quia affirmat confictum seu mendosum esse quod LXX dicuntur seorsum in cellulis seu cameris transtulisse. Secundo, quoniam asserit eos non esse interpretatos spiritu prophetali. Tertio, quia testatur eos nescivisse seu non intellexisse quædam verba quæ transtulerunt, ideoque ea protulisse ambigue.
paras.en: These things being set down first, we must see what Jerome thought of the Seventy Interpreters and their translation. In his own prologue to Genesis he says, among other things: “I know not who first built the seventy little cells at Alexandria by his lie, in which (those interpreters), divided from one another, are said to have written the same things; whereas Aristæus, Ptolemy's hyperaspistes (that is, protector or guard), and Josephus relate nothing of the kind, but say that they were gathered together in one hall and conferred about what was to be translated, not that they prophesied. For it is one thing to be a seer, another to be a translator. Those Seventy translated the Scriptures before the coming of Christ, and what they did not know they put forth in doubtful phrases.” In these words Jerome seems to disagree with Augustine on three points. First, because he affirms that it is invented or false that the Seventy are said to have translated separately in little cells or chambers. Secondly, because he asserts that they did not translate by the spirit of prophecy. Thirdly, because he testifies that they did not know, or did not understand, certain words that they translated, and therefore rendered them ambiguously.

paras.t: Præterea in prologo super Job: Fieri, inquit, non potest, ut quos plura intermisisse conspexerint, non eosdem etiam in aliquibus errasse fateantur, præcipue in Job. In his verbis dicit Hieronymus oportere concedi, quod LXX, qui aliqua omiserunt, in aliquibus etiam erraverunt: quod tamen prima facie non videtur bene sonare, nec etiam verbis Hieronymi alibi positis concordare, præsertim quoniam sancti Apostoli et Evangelistæ inveniuntur usi fuisse translatione LXX interpretum, imo et universalis Ecclesia usque ad tempus Hieronymi. In prologo quoque super Paralipomenon librum scribit Hieronymus: Si editio (id est translatio) LXX interpretum permaneret pura, et prout ab eis in Latinum versa est, superflue impelleres me, Chromati, ut Hebræa volumina Latino sermone tibi transferrem. Et paulo post subdit ibidem: Nunc autem germana et antiqua illa translatio, corrupta est et violata. In quibus verbis insinuat, ipsos LXX vere et sufficienter transtulisse Scripturas, sed eorum translationem postmodum esse corruptam: quod etiam in prologo super Esdram innuisse videtur.
paras.en: Moreover, in the prologue to Job he says: “It cannot be that those whom they see to have left out many things, they should not also confess to have erred in some, especially in Job.” In these words Jerome says it must be granted that the Seventy, who left some things out, also erred in some. Yet at first sight this does not seem to sound well, nor to agree with Jerome's words elsewhere, especially since the holy Apostles and Evangelists are found to have used the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, and indeed the universal Church until the time of Jerome. In the prologue to the book of Paralipomenon, too, Jerome writes: “If the edition (that is, the translation) of the Seventy Interpreters had remained pure, and as it was turned by them into Latin [so the printed text; Jerome's preface has “into Greek”], you would needlessly urge me, Chromatius, to translate the Hebrew volumes for you into the Latin tongue.” And a little after, in the same place, he adds: “But now that genuine and ancient translation is corrupted and violated.” In these words he implies that the Seventy themselves translated the Scriptures truly and adequately, but that their translation was afterwards corrupted; and he seems to have hinted the same in the prologue to Esdras.

1.title: Quid sentiendum sit circa præhabita
1.title_en: What is to be thought about the foregoing

paras.t: Circa inducta posset quæri, cujus assertioni sit magis consentiendum, Hieronymi an Augustini. Ad quod respondet Henricus de Hassia super Genesim, quod positio Hieronymi verisimilior esse videtur, eo quod ipse B. Hieronymus videatur fuisse homo majoris auctoritatis ex parte vitæ atque scientiæ et item experientiæ, præsertim circa divinas Scripturas et circa linguas atque historias. Unde et Augustinus de Hieronymo dixit, quod et in Decreto habetur: Quanquam secundum vocabula quæ usus obtinuit, episcopatus sit presbyterio major, Hieronymus tamen major est Augustino. Ad idem valent rationes, quas in prologo super Genesim introduxit Hieronymus, quæ tamen secundum præfatum Doctorem parum concludunt. Non enim sequitur: Aristæus et Josephus nil referunt de cellulis illis, ergo LXX non transtulerunt seorsum in cellis.
paras.en: About what has been brought forward it might be asked whose assertion is rather to be agreed with, Jerome's or Augustine's. To this Henry of Hesse, on Genesis, answers that Jerome's position seems the more likely, because Blessed Jerome himself seems to have been a man of greater authority in respect of life and of learning, and also of experience, especially in the divine Scriptures and in languages and histories. Hence Augustine too said of Jerome, as is also found in the Decretum: “Although, according to the titles which usage has established, the episcopate is greater than the priesthood, yet Jerome is greater than Augustine.” To the same end serve the reasons which Jerome brought forward in the prologue to Genesis, though according to the said Doctor they prove little. For it does not follow: Aristæus and Josephus relate nothing of those little cells, therefore the Seventy did not translate separately in cells.

paras.t: Verumtamen, quantum capere queo, argumentum illud Hieronymi apparentiam magnam sortitur. Quum enim factum illud, quod recitat Augustinus, de tam concordi singulorum translatione divisim peracta, fuisset mirabilissimum ac divinissimum opus, valde apparet quod Aristæus et Josephus describendo processum, quo facta est LXX translatio, nequaquam præterissent illud silentio. Porro Augustinus nihil allegat pro se, sed solum generaliter dicit: Traditur sane quod LXX in totidem cellis transtulerint, et non exprimit a quo vel quibus hoc traditum sit. Quocirca scribit Henricus de Hassia: Sed mirum est revera, si tantus Doctor absque historia aut scriptura valde credibili, tam constanter asseruit LXX interpretes transtulisse Spiritu Dei, et prophetali gratia claruisse, translationem quoque eorum esse translationi Hieronymi præferendam.
paras.en: Nevertheless, so far as I can grasp it, that argument of Jerome's carries great likelihood. For since the deed that Augustine relates, so harmonious a translation made by each man apart, would have been a most wonderful and most divine work, it seems very plain that Aristæus and Josephus, in describing how the translation of the Seventy was made, would by no means have passed it over in silence. Moreover, Augustine alleges nothing in his own support, but only says in general: “It is indeed handed down that the Seventy translated in as many cells,” and he does not state by whom this was handed down. Hence Henry of Hesse writes: “But it is truly a wonder if so great a Doctor, without any history or any very credible writing, so steadily asserted that the Seventy Interpreters translated by the Spirit of God and shone with the grace of prophecy, and that their translation is to be preferred to Jerome's.”

paras.t: Verum (ut tactum est) S. Augustinus forte sumpsit præcipue argumentum ex hoc, quod Apostoli et Evangelistæ allegaverunt frequenter Scripturas secundum translationem LXX: similiter ex hoc, quod sancti Patres primitivæ Ecclesiæ in Græcia fundaverunt fidem ex Scripturis secundum præfatam translationem. Officia quoque divini cultus ordinaverunt secundum eamdem. Et non est verisimile, quod Spiritus Sanctus qui tam copiose direxit et abundavit in Ecclesia primitiva, permiserit fidem religionemque christianam fundari super translationem erroneam. In Scholastica quoque fertur historia, quod datæ sunt LXX interpretibus cellulæ singulæ.
paras.en: But (as was touched on) St Augustine perhaps took his argument chiefly from this, that the Apostles and Evangelists often cited the Scriptures according to the translation of the Seventy; and likewise from this, that the holy Fathers of the early Church in Greece founded the faith on the Scriptures according to that translation, and also ordered the offices of divine worship according to it. And it is not likely that the Holy Ghost, who guided the early Church so richly and abounded in it, would have allowed the faith and the Christian religion to be founded on an erroneous translation. It is also told in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor, whom the margin names] that the Seventy Interpreters were each given a little cell.

paras.t: Præterea cum Augustino consentio in hoc, quod LXX translatio vera et efficax fuit, et quod Spiritus Sanctus direxit interpretes illos ad transferendum idonee: quoniam Spiritus Sanctus prævidit primitivam Ecclesiam Christi, imo et totam Ecclesiam, per longum tempus uti debere translatione virorum illorum: ideo eos direxit, etsi non propter Ptolemæum, tamen propter commune Ecclesiæ bonum.
paras.en: Further, I agree with Augustine in this: that the translation of the Seventy was true and effective, and that the Holy Ghost guided those interpreters to translate fittingly. For the Holy Ghost foresaw that the early Church of Christ, and indeed the whole Church, was to use the translation of those men for a long time; and therefore he guided them, if not for Ptolemy's sake, then for the common good of the Church.

paras.t: Denique S. Hieronymus sæpe fatetur, translationem LXX sibi non displicere, nec se in reprehensionem LXX de novo transferre. Quod vero in prologo super Job innuit eos in quibusdam errasse, exponendum est pie, ut dicantur errasse, id est aliqua omisisse: quod tamen ex certis causis fecerunt, ut infra partim tangetur.
paras.en: Again, St Jerome often declares that the translation of the Seventy does not displease him, and that he is not translating anew in reproof of the Seventy. And where in the prologue to Job he hints that they erred in some things, this is to be explained in a kindly sense: that they are said to have erred, that is, to have left some things out; which, however, they did for certain reasons, as will be partly touched on below.

paras.t: Postremo, quod Henricus de Hassia asserit, Hieronymum fuisse majoris auctoritatis ex parte vitæ atque scientiæ, quam Augustinum, non arbitror certum, quanquam constet Hieronymum fuisse vitæ rigorosioris, et magis exercitatum in linguis et historiis ac Scripturis veteris Testamenti. Nihilo minus Augustinus fuit vir singularis acuminis in considerando ea quæ fidem et Scripturas concernunt, et multi doctores comparant eum soli inter Doctores Ecclesiæ, quem et S. Bernardus vocat linguam Ecclesiæ. Imo in quibusdam arduis difficillimisque materiis, in quibus inter se dissensisse videntur Hieronymus et Augustinus, videlicet an Paulus restitit Petro ex intentione vel simulatione, et utrum qui ante Baptismum duas habuit conjuges, seu unam ante Baptismum, et aliam postmodum, reputandus sit bigamus post Baptismum, et consimilibus, doctores communiter magis sequuntur Augustinum. Unde et in Decreto habetur 26 dist. can. Acutius, et can. Una tantum: et extra de bigam. cap. A nobis, et cap. Nuper. Hæc tamen sine derogatione gloriosi Hieronymi dico.
paras.en: Lastly, what Henry of Hesse asserts, that Jerome was of greater authority than Augustine in respect of life and learning, I do not think certain, although it is clear that Jerome was of a stricter life, and more practised in languages and histories and in the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Nonetheless Augustine was a man of singular keenness in weighing the things that concern the faith and the Scriptures, and many doctors compare him to the sun among the Doctors of the Church; St Bernard too calls him the tongue of the Church. Indeed, in certain hard and most difficult matters on which Jerome and Augustine seem to have disagreed, namely whether Paul withstood Peter in earnest or by a feigned pretence, and whether one who had two wives before Baptism, or one before Baptism and another afterwards, is to be reckoned a bigamist [in canon law, a man married twice in succession, which bars him from holy orders] after Baptism, and in like questions, the doctors commonly follow Augustine rather than Jerome. Hence it is laid down in the Decretum, dist. 26, canon Acutius and canon Una tantum, and in the Extravagantes [that is, the Decretals outside Gratian's Decretum], title De bigamis, chapter A nobis and chapter Nuper. Yet I say this without detracting from the glorious Jerome.

1.title: Expositio brevissima prologi beati Hieronymi super Genesim
1.title_en: A very brief exposition of Blessed Jerome's prologue to Genesis

paras.t: Pentateuchum, id est quinque libros Moysis, transtulit Hieronymus ad magnam instantiam S. Desiderii præsulis. Ideo ait: Desiderii mei desideratas accepi epistolas, hoc est, epistolam gratam et diu affectatam seu caram, directam mihi a Desiderio, quem familiariter ac specialiter diligo, suscepi, qui Desiderius sortitus est nomen quodam præsagio futurorum cum Daniele, hoc est, ita vocatus est ad præsignandum mystice quædam futura. Quemadmodum enim Daniel vocatus est ab Angelo vir desideriorum, quoniam ardentissima desideria habuit pro communi bono populi sui, ita episcopus iste vocatus est Desiderius, ad præsignandum re ipsa quod ardentissimos habiturus esset affectus ad commune bonum totius Ecclesiæ, et quia desiderabilis fuit, carissimusque Hieronymo. Nam et libros Moysis postulavit sibi ex Hebræo pure et integre, fideliterque transferri propter magnum et generale bonum totius populi christiani.
paras.en: Jerome translated the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses, at the earnest request of St Desiderius, a bishop. Therefore he says: I have received the long-desired letters of my Desiderius; that is, I have received a welcome letter, long looked for, or dear to me, sent to me by Desiderius, whom I love as a close friend and in a special way; who, Desiderius, received his name by a kind of presage of things to come, in common with Daniel; that is, he was so called to foreshadow mystically certain things to come. For as Daniel was called by the Angel [[Dan 9:23|a man of desires|vir desideriorum]], because he had most ardent desires for the common good of his people, so this bishop was called Desiderius, to foreshadow in very fact that he would have most ardent longings for the common good of the whole Church; and also because he was desirable, and most dear to Jerome [the play on Desiderius, desideria (“desires”) and desiderabilis (“desirable”) is lost in English]. For he asked that the books of Moses be translated for him from the Hebrew purely, entirely and faithfully, for the great and general good of the whole Christian people.

paras.t: Deinde dicit Hieronymus, quod translationem talem assumere, sit opus periculosum, quia difficile fuit et arduum, in quo posset quis deficere et errare. Detractores quoque Hieronymi, asserebant eum nova pro veteribus cudere, id est, novam translationem pro antiqua efficere in suggillationem, hoc est in condemnationem et reprehensionem veterum translatorum, videlicet LXX. Ita ingenium quasi vinum probantes. Hoc aliqui sic exponunt: Ipsi detractores probantes, id est, approbantes ingenium quasi vinum, ita quod sicut vinum antiquum est melius novo, sic ipsi affirmant ingenia antiquorum perspicaciora fuisse, et melius conscripsisse ingeniis modernorum. Vel, probantes ingenium quasi vinum, quoniam sicut vinum novum est inflatione spumaque plenum, sic asserunt ingenia horum qui nunc sunt, esse repleta elatione et præsumptionis impuritate. Verumtamen videtur istud melius posse ita intelligi, Ingenium quasi vinum probantes. Quemadmodum enim qui vina probant, modicum inde gustant, et colorem ejus forinsecus intuentur: sic detractores translationem Hieronymi superficialiter atque cursorie attendebant, nec ejus valorem et efficaciam intrinsece ac perfecte scrutati sunt.
paras.en: Then Jerome says that to undertake such a translation is a perilous work, since it was hard and arduous, a work in which one could fall short and go astray. Jerome's detractors also asserted that he was forging new things in place of the old, that is, making a new translation in place of the ancient one, to the disparagement, that is, to the condemnation and reproof, of the old translators, namely the Seventy. Thus judging wit as they would wine. Some explain this as follows: these detractors judging, that is, approving, wit as they do wine, in this way: that as old wine is better than new, so they affirm that the wits of the ancients were keener, and wrote better than the wits of the moderns. Or: judging wit like wine, since as new wine is full of swelling and froth, so they assert that the wits of those now living are full of pride and the impurity of presumption. Yet it seems this can better be understood thus: Judging wit as they would wine. For as those who test wines taste a little of them and look at their colour from outside, so the detractors gave Jerome's translation a superficial and cursory look, and did not search out its worth and force within and thoroughly.

paras.t: Quod ut auderem, Origenis me studium provocavit, id est, labor et diligentia Origenis animavit me ad transferendum Scripturas, qui editioni antiquæ, videlicet translationi LXX, translationem Theodotionis miscuit, hoc est, ex translatione Theodotionis translationem LXX perfecit, addendo ex Theodotione quæ in translatione LXX erant omissa; asterisco et obelo, id est stella et veru, omne opus distinguens, hoc est, totam LXX translationem hinc inde notans ac discernens. Ubi enim addidit omissa, posuit stellam pro signo, ad insinuandum quod sua additio tanquam stella illuminavit et supplevit sensum Scripturæ. Porro, ubi invenit aliqua superflua in translatione LXX, posuit pro signo veru sive sagittam, ad innuendum quod talia transfoderet tanquam superflua seu mendosa. Verumtamen (ut patet ex verbis Augustini præhabitis) ea quæ LXX addiderunt in sua translatione supra Hebraicam veritatem, non erant absolute superflua neque mendosa, sed rationabiliter et mystica significatione apposita. Aliunde tamen per varios translatores et transcriptores corrupta fuit LXX translatio, sicut ex verbis Hieronymi jam probavi. Ex his patet sensus verborum sequentium: dum aut illucescere facit quæ minus ante fuerant, id est diminuta et ante omissa declarat, aut superflua quæque jugulat et confodit, et maxime, supple elucidat, quæ Evangelistarum et Apostolorum auctoritas promulgavit, hoc est, quæ Evangelistæ atque Apostoli ex veteri Testamento allegant, nec tamen in LXX translatione habentur. Ideo addit: in quibus, videlicet Evangelistis et Apostolis, id est in scriptis eorum, multa de veteri Testamento legimus, hoc est, multa invenimus allegari ex veteri Testamento, quæ in nostris [codicibus], id est in libris continentibus translationem LXX interpretum, non habentur, ut est illud: Ex Ægypto vocavi Filium meum, etc. Quod multi ignorantes, apocryphorum deliramenta sectantur, hoc est, latina et abusiva in libris non authenticis, imo et falsa aliqua continentibus posita sequuntur; et Iberas nenias, hoc est fabulas ab Hispanis inventas, seu apud Hispanos vulgatas, quæ in apocryphis continentur. Libris authenticis præferunt. Nam ea quæ Evangelistæ et Apostoli ex veteri Testamento allegant, nec tamen in translatione LXX habentur, isti indocti ac detractores non quærebant in Scripturis canonicis atque Hebraicis veteris Testamenti, sed potius in scripturis apocryphis. Porro Iberus est fluvius, a quo Hispania appellatur Iberia.
paras.en: That I should dare this, the zeal of Origen spurred me on; that is, the labour and diligence of Origen encouraged me to translate the Scriptures; who mixed the translation of Theodotion with the old edition, namely the translation of the Seventy; that is, he completed the translation of the Seventy from the translation of Theodotion, adding from Theodotion what had been left out in the translation of the Seventy; marking off the whole work with an asterisk and an obelus, that is, a star and a spit; that is, marking and distinguishing the whole translation of the Seventy here and there. For where he added what had been left out, he put a star as the sign, to suggest that his addition, like a star, lit up and filled out the sense of Scripture. Again, where he found anything superfluous in the translation of the Seventy, he put as the sign a spit or arrow, to intimate that he was running such things through as superfluous or faulty. Yet (as is clear from the words of Augustine given above) what the Seventy added in their translation beyond the Hebrew verity [that is, the Hebrew original] was not superfluous or faulty absolutely, but set down with reason and with a mystical meaning. On the other hand, the translation of the Seventy was corrupted by various translators and copyists, as I have already proved from the words of Jerome. From this the sense of the following words is clear: while he either makes to shine forth what before was lacking, that is, sets forth what was wanting and had before been left out, or cuts the throat of and pierces through whatever is superfluous; and especially, supply “makes plain”, what the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles has published; that is, what the Evangelists and Apostles cite from the Old Testament and yet is not found in the translation of the Seventy. Therefore he adds: in whom, namely the Evangelists and Apostles, that is, in their writings, we read many things from the Old Testament; that is, we find many things cited from the Old Testament, which are not found in our books [the word codicibus, “books”, is lost in the print and is supplied here from Jerome's prologue], that is, in the books containing the translation of the Seventy interpreters; as is that saying: [[Osee 11:1|I called my son out of Egypt|Ex Ægypto vocavi Filium meum]], etc. [the margin reference here cannot be read; the words are Osee 11:1 as quoted in Matt 2:15, and Jerome's point is that they come from the Hebrew, not from the Seventy]. Not knowing which, many follow the ravings of the apocrypha; that is, they follow the vain [the print has latina, “Latin”, apparently a slip, perhaps for inania, “vain”] and corrupt things set down in books that are not authentic, and that even contain some falsehoods; and they prefer Iberian trifles, that is, fables invented by the Spaniards, or current among the Spaniards, which are contained in the apocrypha, to the authentic books. For what the Evangelists and Apostles cite from the Old Testament, and yet is not found in the translation of the Seventy, these unlearned men and detractors did not look for in the canonical and Hebrew Scriptures of the Old Testament, but rather in the apocryphal writings. Now the Iberus is a river, from which Spain is called Iberia.

paras.t: Causas erroris non est meum exponere. Hoc aliqui referunt ad LXX, quasi Hieronymus dicat: Mihi non incumbit exprimere ex quibus causis acciderit error translationis LXX. Quod si ita accipiatur, per errorem intelligenda est omissio seu variatio, qua LXX aliqua omiserunt, quæ in Hebræo habentur, et aliqua aliter transtulerunt quam Hebraica continet veritas: quod tamen ex rationabili causa fecerunt, sicut subjungitur: Judæi prudenti consilio factum dicunt. Verumtamen particula illa, Causas erroris non est meum exponere, posset ad præfatos detractores et indoctos referri. Itaque Judæi excusant LXX interpretes de hoc quod aliqua omiserunt, et aliqua aliter transtulerunt, dicentes quod fecerunt hoc cum examinato consilio, ne Ptolemæus unius Dei cultor, etiam apud Hebræos duplicem divinitatem deprehenderet. Hoc aliqui sic exponunt, quod LXX omiserunt aut aliter transtulerunt ea loca Scripturarum veteris Testamenti, in quibus aliquid tangebatur de Patre et Filio, ne Ptolemæus (ad cujus instantiam transtulerunt Scripturas) consideraret, quod etiam ipsi Judæi ponerent duos deos, cum ipse esset cultor unius Dei. Quod idcirco maxime faciebant, quia in Platonis dogma cadere videbatur. Quidam habent, legunt et exponunt hæc verba pluraliter, quia sic habent: Quod idcirco maxime faciebant, quia in Platonis dogma cadere videbantur, ut sit sensus, quod LXX potissimum ideo talia verba Scripturarum omiserunt, aut aliter transtulerunt, quia videbantur cadere in dogma Platonis, hoc est, si talia transtulissent, sicut in Hebræo habentur, Ptolemæus rex putasset eos cadere in Platonis doctrinam. Nam Plato in libris suis invenitur locutus de summo Deo, quem nominat Patrem, et de νοῦ, per quem aliqui dicunt eum intellexisse Filium Patris: sicque Ptolemæus æstimasset Scripturam veteris Testamenti esse contrariam fidei, cultuique unius Dei, cujus oppositum percepit ac tenuit Ptolemæus, et ita fuisset scandalizatus. Hinc subditur: Denique ubicumque sacramentum aliquod Scriptura testatur de Patre et Filio et Spiritu Sancto, id est, ubicumque in Scripturis veteris Testamenti secretum aliquid legitur de superbeatissima Trinitate, aut omnino id tacuerunt, aut aliter interpretati sunt, ut et regi satisfacerent, et arcanum fidei non vulgarent.
paras.en: It is not for me to set out the causes of the error. Some refer this to the Seventy, as if Jerome said: It does not fall to me to state from what causes the error in the translation of the Seventy came about. If it is taken in this way, by error must be understood the omission or variation by which the Seventy left out some things that are in the Hebrew, and translated some things otherwise than the Hebrew verity has them: which they nevertheless did for a reasonable cause, as is added: The Jews say it was done by prudent counsel. Yet that phrase, It is not for me to set out the causes of the error, could be referred to the detractors and unlearned men mentioned above. So the Jews excuse the Seventy interpreters for having left some things out and translated some otherwise, saying that they did this on considered counsel, lest Ptolemy, a worshipper of one God, should find a twofold divinity among the Hebrews too. Some explain this thus: that the Seventy left out, or translated otherwise, those places of the Scriptures of the Old Testament in which something touched on the Father and the Son, lest Ptolemy (at whose request they translated the Scriptures) should think that the Jews themselves too held two gods, since he himself was a worshipper of one God. And this they did chiefly for this reason, because he seemed to fall in with the teaching of Plato. Some have these words, read them and explain them, in the plural, since their text runs: And this they did chiefly for this reason, because they seemed to fall in with the teaching of Plato; so that the sense is that the Seventy left out such words of the Scriptures, or translated them otherwise, chiefly because they seemed to fall in with the teaching of Plato; that is, if they had translated such things as they stand in the Hebrew, King Ptolemy would have thought that they were falling in with the doctrine of Plato. For Plato is found in his books to have spoken of the highest God, whom he calls Father, and of νοῦς [Greek, “mind”], by which some say he understood the Son of the Father: and so Ptolemy would have judged the Scripture of the Old Testament to be contrary to the faith and worship of one God, the opposite of which Ptolemy had perceived and held, and so he would have been scandalized. Hence is added: Lastly, wherever Scripture bears witness to some sacrament [that is, a hidden mystery] of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost, that is, wherever in the Scriptures of the Old Testament some secret is read concerning the superblessed Trinity, they either kept silence about it altogether, or rendered it otherwise, so as both to satisfy the king and not to make known the hidden mystery of the faith.

paras.t: Hanc expositionem sequuntur magister Adam de S. Victore, et Henricus de Hassia. Contra quam argui potest: Plato enim non posuit nisi unum summum verum Deum, sicut infra ostendam; et quidquid locutus videtur de νοῦ et anima mundi, seu quacumque vi regitiva hujus mundi, intellexit de substantiis essentialiter divisis a summo Patre et inferioribus eo, imo et puris creaturis, quemadmodum demonstrabo. Non ergo Ptolemæus putasset LXX incidere doctrinam Platonis, si locuti fuissent de divinitate Patris ac Filii, quoniam Ptolemæus cognovit quod Plato non posuit nisi unum verum Deum. Denique Ptolemæus fuit pro magna parte Platonicus, sicut ex diversis scriptis posset probari. Rursus, libri correctiores habent, secundum quod primo commemoravi, utpote: Quod maxime idcirco faciebant, quia in Platonis dogma cadere videbatur; ut sit sensus, quod Ptolemæus idcirco præcipue coluit unum Deum, quia in hoc sequebatur Platonem. Verumtamen an Ptolemæus ita coluit unum Deum, quod non etiam coluerit alios inferioresque deos, an simul cum diis aliquibus Ægyptiorum coluerit summum Deum, quemadmodum quarto Regum refertur de Samaritanis a rege Assyriorum adductis, quod coluerunt Dominum, et nihilo minus servierunt diis suis, certum non habeo. Est itaque sensus, quod LXX interpretes idcirco subticuerunt, aut aliter transtulerunt ea quæ in Scripturis de deitate Filii aut Spiritus Sancti continentur, ne Ptolemæus unius Dei cultor, putaret Judæos colere duos aut tres deos, scilicet Patrem et Filium, aut etiam Spiritum Sanctum. Non enim capere potuisset mysterium supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis in una essentia: ideo hoc arcanum fidei noluerunt pandere ei.
paras.en: This explanation is followed by Master Adam of St Victor and by Henry of Hesse. Against it one can argue: for Plato held only one highest true God, as I shall show below; and whatever he seems to have said of νοῦς and of the soul of the world, or of any power ruling this world, he understood of substances essentially distinct from the highest Father and lower than he, indeed of mere creatures, as I shall demonstrate. Ptolemy, then, would not have thought the Seventy were falling into the doctrine of Plato if they had spoken of the divinity of the Father and of the Son, since Ptolemy knew that Plato held only one true God. Moreover, Ptolemy was in great part a Platonist, as could be proved from various writings. Again, the more correct books have the reading I mentioned first, namely: And this they did chiefly for this reason, because he seemed to fall in with the teaching of Plato; so that the sense is that Ptolemy worshipped one God chiefly for this reason, that in this he followed Plato. Yet whether Ptolemy so worshipped one God that he did not also worship other and lower gods, or whether together with some gods of the Egyptians he worshipped the highest God, as is related in the fourth book of Kings of the Samaritans brought in by the king of the Assyrians, that they worshipped the Lord and none the less served their own gods, I do not know for certain. The sense, therefore, is that the Seventy interpreters kept silent about, or translated otherwise, what is contained in the Scriptures concerning the godhead of the Son or of the Holy Ghost, lest Ptolemy, a worshipper of one God, should think that the Jews worshipped two or three gods, namely the Father and the Son, or the Holy Ghost as well. For he could not have grasped the mystery of the supremely glorious Trinity in one essence: therefore they would not open this hidden mystery of the faith to him.

paras.t: Præterea, quod Plato posuerit unum solum verum ac summum Deum, universorum principium, nullam habet difficultatem apud eruditos in philosophia Platonis et Platonicorum. Augustinus quoque in pluribus locis et Boetius id affirmant. Octavo namque de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Unum summum et verum bonum Plato disseruit esse Deum. Sed et nono de Civitate Dei: Secundum Apuleium, inquit, Platonicum, summus Deus creator omnium sic a Platone laudatur, quod ipse solus non potest humano sermone vel modice comprehendi. Amplius Plato in Timæo docet, totum universum a summo Deo esse productum, et ipsum Deum altissimum, incomprehensibilem ineffabilemque consistere: Genitorem, inquiens, atque opificem universi tam difficile invenire, quam inventum impossibile digne profari. Hinc Proclus Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica contestatur: Omnia entia procedunt ab una prima causa. Et iterum: Omnium entium principium et prima causa est bonum. Et denuo ait quod sit unum […], id est ex se et per se Deus ac summum bonum, cui comparari non potest tota catena deorum. Quamvis autem Plato et ejus sequaces posuerint unum summum Deum independentem, tamen posuerunt sub eo diversos gradus ordinesque deorum, quos omnes dixerunt a summo Deo procedere, et omnem suam perfectionem ab illo participare. Præterea, quidam doctores recitant Platonem esse locutum de νοῦ et τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ et anima mundi, ita quod per νοῦν intellexit Patrem, per τὸ ἀγαθόν, paternum intellectum, seu mentem a Patre manantem, videlicet Filium: per animam vero mundi, Spiritum Sanctum, aut vim quamdam increatam mundi rectivam. Verum hæc recitatio non invenitur conveniens. Ait enim Augustinus decimo de Civitate Dei: Plotinus Platonicus disputans de tribus principalibus substantiis, ponit Deum Patrem, et mentem paternam, quam nominaverunt νοῦν, et animæ naturam. Porro per animam mundi Plato intellexit formam creatam, quoniam totum sensibilem mundum posuit animatum et animal maximum, cujus animam vocavit animam mundi, prout tertiodecimo de Civitate Dei Augustinus enarrat, et in primo Timæi, atque in Elementatione Procli habetur. De hac materia loquitur Thomas in Summa contra gentiles, libro quarto.
paras.en: Moreover, that Plato held one only true and highest God, the principle of all things, is no difficulty to those learned in the philosophy of Plato and the Platonists. Augustine too, in many places, and Boethius affirm it. For in the eighth book of the City of God Augustine asserts: Plato maintained that the one highest and true good is God. And in the ninth of the City of God: According to Apuleius the Platonist, he says, the highest God, the creator of all things, is so praised by Plato that he alone cannot be grasped even in small part by human speech. Further, Plato teaches in the Timæus that the whole universe was brought forth by the highest God, and that God himself, the most high, is incomprehensible and ineffable, saying: The begetter and maker of the universe is as hard to find as, once found, he is impossible to speak of worthily. Hence Proclus the Platonist testifies in his Elements of Theology: All beings proceed from one first cause. And again: The principle and first cause of all beings is the good. And again he says that it is the one […], that is, God from himself and through himself, and the highest good, to whom the whole chain of gods [the margin gives the reading caterva, “throng”, for catena, “chain”] cannot be compared. But although Plato and his followers held one highest God, dependent on none, they nevertheless placed beneath him various grades and orders of gods, all of whom they said proceed from the highest God and receive all their perfection by sharing in his. Moreover, certain doctors relate that Plato spoke of νοῦς, of τὸ ἀγαθόν [Greek, “the good”] and of the soul of the world, in such a way that by νοῦς he understood the Father, by τὸ ἀγαθόν the Father's intellect, or the mind flowing from the Father, namely the Son, and by the soul of the world the Holy Ghost, or some uncreated power ruling the world. But this account is not found to fit. For Augustine says in the tenth of the City of God: Plotinus the Platonist, discussing the three principal substances, puts God the Father, and the paternal mind, which they named νοῦς, and the nature of the soul. Further, by the soul of the world Plato understood a created form, since he held the whole sensible world to be animate and the greatest of animals, whose soul he called the soul of the world, as Augustine relates in the thirteenth of the City of God, and as is found in the first part of the Timæus and in the Elements of Proclus. Thomas speaks of this matter in the Summa contra Gentiles, book four.

paras.t: Insuper, qualiter ad instantiam Ptolemæi missi et interpretati sunt LXX interpretes, recitat Augustinus octavodecimo de Civitate Dei: quod etiam in Scholastica historia plenius continetur, ubi devotio et copiosæ oblationes Ptolemæi regis, quas misit ad templum Jerusalem, describuntur. De quibus etiam loquitur S. Hieronymus super Danielem. Itaque libro præallegato, capitulo 42, recitat Augustinus: Post mortem Alexandri Magni cœpit Ægyptus habere reges Ptolemæos, quorum primus Lagi filius, multos ex Judæa captivos transtulit in Ægyptum. Cui succedens Ptolemæus Philadelphus, liberos remisit Judæos, quos ille captos abduxerat. Insuper et dona regia misit in templum Dei, petens ab Eleazaro tunc Judæorum pontifice, dari sibi Scripturas, quas fama prædicante audivit esse divinas, et ideo concupivit eas habere in sua bibliotheca, quam nobilissimam fecerat. Quas quum pontifex ille misisset ei in idiomate Hebræo, postea ipse Ptolemæus postulavit interpretes, et dati sunt ei LXXII, videlicet sex de singulis duodecim tribubus, qui Hebrææ ac Græcæ erant linguæ doctissimi.
paras.en: Further, how the Seventy interpreters were sent at Ptolemy's request and made their translation, Augustine relates in the eighteenth book of the City of God; and this is set out more fully in the Scholastic History, where the devotion of King Ptolemy and the rich offerings which he sent to the temple of Jerusalem are described. Of these St Jerome too speaks, on Daniel. So in the book already cited, chapter 42, Augustine relates: After the death of Alexander the Great, Egypt began to have kings called Ptolemies, of whom the first, the son of Lagus, carried many captives from Judæa into Egypt. His successor, Ptolemy Philadelphus, sent back free the Jews whom the other had led away captive. He also sent royal gifts to the temple of God, asking Eleazar, then high priest of the Jews, that the Scriptures be given him, which he had heard by common report to be divine; and so he longed to have them in his library, which he had made most famous. When that high priest had sent them to him in the Hebrew tongue, Ptolemy afterwards asked for interpreters, and seventy-two were given him, namely six from each of the twelve tribes, men most learned in the Hebrew and the Greek tongue.

paras.t: Porro in Scholastica historia fertur: Post Ptolemæum Soterem regnavit in Ægypto Ptolemæus Philadelphus, qui studiosus, librorumque cupidus, Demetrium bibliothecæ suæ præfecit. Demetrius ergo regi dixit, sibi esse denuntiatum, apud Judæos esse legem ore Dei editam, et digito ejus scriptam. Atque ad ostendendam hujus legis sanctitatem, adjecit, quod transferri non posset nisi a cultoribus Dei viventis. Nam et Theopompus, quum voluisset eam inserere historiis quas scribebat, in amentiam versus est per dies triginta: Theotecus quoque pro eadem causa factus est cæcus: qui pœnitentes, sanati sunt. Suggessit itaque regi quatenus Judæorum pontifici scriberet, ut sibi Judæos Hebrææ et Græcæ linguæ peritos transmitteret, qui ad transferendam legem sufficerent. Quod ut impetraret, suasit munera cum epistolis esse mittenda. Aderat ibi Aristæus, qui calamitati Judæorum captorum diu compassus, opportunitate liberandi eos inventa, dixit ad regem: Quomodo quod postulas obtinebis, tot Judæis in tuo servientibus regno? Solve itaque eos, et nihil gratius erit pontifici Judæorum. Liberavit ergo rex eos, utpote centum viginti millia Judæorum, dans dominis eorum pro unoquoque capite centum viginti drachmas argenti. Tunc Ptolemæus rex scripsit Eleazaro pontifici: Gentem tuam quæ apud nos erat, libertate donavi, arbitrans hoc Deo esse jucundum, quorum quosdam assignavi militiæ, alios (quorum fidem probaveram) constitui in palatio. Legem vero tuam in bibliotheca nostra decrevi reponere. Bene ergo facies, mittendo nobis viros seniores qui eam valeant nobis interpretari. Misi quoque centum talenta argenti pro immolationibus faciendis. Et separavi quinquaginta talenta auri ad crateras et libatoria facienda, gemmasque sine numero ad artificium optionem. Tunc pontifex misit ei interpretes, quos rex coram universis principibus cum grandi honore suscepit atque magnifice honoravit. Quo facto, manserunt cum eo diebus duodecim. Interrogavitque eos præcipue de Dei cognitione et regni gubernatione. Cumque instruxissent eum de regni administratione, disputaverunt cum eo diffuse de uno Deo colendo. Postea introducti sunt in domum secretam secus mare, et datæ sunt eis singulæ cellulæ. Diluculo autem egrediebantur ad optandum regi bona, deinde interpretabantur usque ad nonam horam, deinceps transibant ad cibum et requiem corporis. Translatione completa, et ab universis Judæis peritis qui erant convocati, approbata, remisit rex interpretes muneribus honoratos, et Eleazaro munera misit. Denique, præter vasa misit in templum auream mensam gemmis impretiabilibus insignitam, cujus crassitudo seu spissitudo erat dimidii cubiti; attamen opus superavit materiam. Hæc in præfata Historia.
paras.en: Again, in the Scholastic History it is told: After Ptolemy Soter, Ptolemy Philadelphus reigned in Egypt; he, being studious and eager for books, set Demetrius over his library. Demetrius then told the king that he had been informed that the Jews had a law given forth by the mouth of God and written by his finger. And to show the holiness of this law he added that it could not be translated except by worshippers of the living God. For Theopompus, when he wished to insert it into the histories he was writing, was turned to madness for thirty days; and Theotecus too, for the same cause, was struck blind; and when they repented they were healed. So he advised the king to write to the high priest of the Jews to send him Jews skilled in the Hebrew and Greek tongues, able to translate the law. And to obtain this, he urged that gifts be sent with the letters. Aristæus was there, who had long pitied the misfortune of the captive Jews; finding an occasion to free them, he said to the king: How shalt thou obtain what thou askest, while so many Jews are in servitude in thy kingdom? Release them, then, and nothing will be more pleasing to the high priest of the Jews. So the king freed them, a hundred and twenty thousand Jews, giving their masters a hundred and twenty drachmas of silver for each head. Then King Ptolemy wrote to Eleazar the high priest: I have given freedom to thy nation which was among us, judging this to be pleasing to God; some of them I have assigned to the army, others, whose faithfulness I had proved, I have placed in the palace. Thy law I have resolved to lay up in our library. Thou wilt do well, therefore, to send us elders who are able to interpret it for us. I have sent also a hundred talents of silver for making sacrifices; and I have set apart fifty talents of gold for making bowls and vessels for libations, and gems without number for the craftsmen to choose from. Then the high priest sent him interpreters, whom the king received with great honour before all his princes, and honoured magnificently. When this was done, they stayed with him twelve days; and he questioned them above all on the knowledge of God and the government of a kingdom. And when they had instructed him on the administration of a kingdom, they discoursed with him at length on the worship of the one God. Afterwards they were brought into a secluded house by the sea, and were given a little cell each. At dawn they went out to wish the king well, then they translated until the ninth hour, and after that they went to food and the rest of the body. When the translation was completed and approved by all the learned Jews who had been called together, the king sent the interpreters back honoured with gifts, and sent gifts to Eleazar. Lastly, besides the vessels, he sent to the temple a golden table set with priceless gems, whose thickness or depth was half a cubit; yet the workmanship surpassed the material. So far the History named above.

paras.t: Ex quibus probatur, verum non esse quod aliqui dicunt, Ptolemæum ex quadam curiositate aut vanitate inductum ad postulandum legem atque interpretes. Ex his item posset videri, quod Ptolemæus factus fuerit cultor veri Dei dumtaxat. Insuper, de his scribit Hieronymus in expositione capituli 11 Danielis: Sub Ptolemæo Philadelpho LXX interpretes Alexandriæ Scripturam sanctam in Græcum dicuntur vertisse sermonem, qui Eleazaro pontifici multa Jerosolymam et in templi donaria vasa transmisit. Narrant historiæ habuisse eum ducenta millia peditum, viginti millia equitum, millia curruum, quadringentos elephantes, quos ex Æthiopia primus adduxit, naves longas mille quingentas, et alias mille ad cibaria militum deportanda. Insuper aliqui asserunt quod tantus sapientiæ fuit amator, quod omnium gentium libros in sua congregavit bibliotheca. Cancellarius quoque Parisiensis in tractatulo suo de Laude scriptorum, refert quod quinquaginta millia librorum in bibliotheca sua habuerit. Cujus studiositate, religiositate ac diligentia condemnantur carnales et negligentes principes ac prælati christiani.
paras.en: From this it is proved that what some say is not true, that Ptolemy was led by a kind of curiosity or vanity to ask for the law and the interpreters. From this, too, it might seem that Ptolemy became a worshipper of the true God alone. Furthermore, Jerome writes of these things in his exposition of chapter 11 of Daniel: Under Ptolemy Philadelphus the Seventy interpreters are said to have turned the holy Scripture into the Greek tongue at Alexandria; he sent to Eleazar the high priest at Jerusalem many vessels as gifts for the temple. The histories relate that he had two hundred thousand foot soldiers, twenty thousand horsemen, thousands of chariots, four hundred elephants, which he was the first to bring from Ethiopia, fifteen hundred long ships, and a thousand more to carry the soldiers' provisions. Further, some assert that he was so great a lover of wisdom that he gathered the books of all nations into his library. The Chancellor of Paris [Gerson, as the margin notes] also, in his little treatise On the Praise of Scribes, records that he had fifty thousand books in his library. By his zeal, devotion and diligence carnal and negligent Christian princes and prelates are condemned.

paras.t: Postremo Hieronymus ad reprobandum septuaginta cellulas, dicit quod Aristæus et Josephus nil inde conscripserunt. Ad probandum quoque quod LXX interpretes non habuerunt spiritum prophetiæ, assumit: Nisi forte putandus est Tullius Œconomicum Xenophontis, et Platonis Protagoram, et Demosthenis pro Ctesiphonte, afflatus rhetorico spiritu transtulisse. Quasi dicat: Si LXX vates fuerunt quoniam transtulerunt, ergo et Tullius fuit vates qui transtulit Œconomicum, id est librum de dispensatione domus, quem Xenophon discipulus Socratis, vir magnæ facundiæ, edidit: qui Tullius etiam transtulit librum Platonis intitulatum nomine Protagoræ sui discipuli. Plato enim libros suos intitulavit nominibus discipulorum suorum, propter quos edidit eos. Iste tamen Protagoras, Platonis discipulus fuit, non autem famosus ille Pythagoras, quemadmodum in vulgatis bibliis legitur. Qui Tullius item transtulit librum Demosthenis, quem pro defensione Ctesiphontis composuit.
paras.en: Lastly Jerome, to disprove the story of the seventy little cells, says that Aristæus and Josephus wrote nothing of them. And to prove that the Seventy interpreters did not have the spirit of prophecy, he adds: Unless perhaps Tully is to be thought to have translated the Œconomicus of Xenophon, and Plato's Protagoras, and Demosthenes' speech for Ctesiphon, inspired by a rhetorical spirit. As if he said: If the Seventy were prophets because they translated, then Tully too was a prophet, who translated the Œconomicus, that is, the book on the management of a household, which Xenophon, a disciple of Socrates and a man of great eloquence, put out; and this Tully also translated the book of Plato entitled with the name of Protagoras, his disciple. For Plato entitled his books with the names of his disciples, for whose sake he put them out. This Protagoras, however, was a disciple of Plato, and not that famous Pythagoras, as one reads in the common Bibles. This Tully likewise translated the book of Demosthenes which he composed in defence of Ctesiphon.

paras.t: Aut aliter de eisdem libris per LXX interpretes, aliter per Apostolos Spiritus Sanctus testimonia texuit, ut quod illi, scilicet LXX, tacuerunt, hi scriptum esse mentiti sint. Ista est alia argumentatio Hieronymi, quasi dicat: Si LXX spiritu prophetico transtulerunt, ergo Spiritus Sanctus aliter locutus est per LXX, aliter per Apostolos, qui ea quæ LXX omiserunt, scripta allegant. Ista argumenta (secundum Henricum de Hassia) non sunt magni vigoris, et qualiter a sequentibus Augustinum solverentur, tactum est ante. Cetera in prologo isto contenta, facilia sunt et clara.
paras.en: Or else the Holy Ghost wove his testimonies out of the same books in one way through the Seventy interpreters, and in another through the Apostles, so that what they, namely the Seventy, kept silent, these falsely claimed to be written. This is another argument of Jerome's, as if he said: If the Seventy translated by the prophetic spirit, then the Holy Ghost spoke in one way through the Seventy and in another through the Apostles, who cite as written what the Seventy left out. These arguments (according to Henry of Hesse) are not of great force, and how they would be answered by the followers of Augustine has been touched on before. The rest of what this prologue contains is easy and clear.

1.title: De multiplici distinctione, atque divisione totius divinæ Scripturæ.
1.title_en: On the manifold distinction and division of the whole of divine Scripture.

paras.t: Sicut in prologo super libros Regum sanctus ait Hieronymus, viginti duo sunt libri veteris Testamenti. Hebræi enim dividunt Scripturam veteris Testamenti in tria, hoc est in legem, in Prophetas, et in hagiographa. Itaque quinque libros Moysis vocant legem, alios octo libros, videlicet Josue, et librum Judicum, sub quo comprehendunt et librum Ruth, et libros Regum quos dividunt in duo volumina, Isaiam quoque, Jeremiam, Ezechielem ac librum duodecim Prophetarum, appellant prophetales. Ad hagiographa vero asserunt pertinere alios novem libros, utpote librum Job, Psalterium, tria volumina Salomonis, Paralipomenon, Esdram et Esther. Hagiographon autem dicitur ab ἅγιος, quod est sacrum, et γραφή, scriptura, quasi scriptura sacra. Hos libros vocant canonicos, alios vero apocryphos.
paras.en: As St. Jerome says in the prologue to the books of Kings, there are twenty-two books of the Old Testament. For the Hebrews divide the Scripture of the Old Testament into three, that is, into the Law, the Prophets and the Hagiographa. Thus they call the five books of Moses the Law; the other eight books, namely Josue, the book of Judges (under which they also include the book of Ruth), the books of Kings, which they divide into two volumes, and also Isaias, Jeremias, Ezechiel and the book of the Twelve Prophets, they call prophetical. To the Hagiographa they assign nine other books, such as the book of Job, the Psalter, the three volumes of Solomon, Paralipomenon, Esdras and Esther [Denis names only eight; the ninth in Jerome's list is Daniel]. Now *hagiographon* comes from ἅγιος, which means sacred, and γραφή, writing, as though to say sacred writing. These books they call canonical, and the others apocryphal.

paras.t: Insuper, Scriptura sacra dividi potest in duas partes principales, hoc est, in Scripturam veteris Testamenti, atque in evangelicam legem, seu in Scripturam novi Testamenti. Et quamvis utraque Scriptura principaliter sit de Deo, tamen Scriptura veteris Testamenti specialius est de Deo ut creatore ac provisore seu gubernatore; Scriptura autem novi Testamenti præcipue est de Deo ut salvatore et remuneratore. Rursus, utriusque Testamenti Scriptura partitur in libros legales et historiales, ac sapientiales et prophetales. Nam quatuor Evangelia, quæ sunt libri legales novi Testamenti, correspondent quinque libris Moysis, qui sunt libri legales veteris Testamenti. Liber Actuum Apostolorum, correspondet libris historialibus Testamenti antiqui. Epistolæ Pauli et aliæ septem canonicæ, correspondent libris sapientialibus veteris Testamenti. Apocalypsis vero, prophetalibus libris Testamenti prioris.
paras.en: Moreover, sacred Scripture can be divided into two principal parts, that is, into the Scripture of the Old Testament and the law of the Gospel, or the Scripture of the New Testament. And although both Scriptures are principally about God, yet the Scripture of the Old Testament is more especially about God as creator and provider, or governor, while the Scripture of the New Testament is chiefly about God as saviour and rewarder. Again, the Scripture of each Testament is divided into books of law and of history, and books of wisdom and of prophecy. For the four Gospels, which are the books of law of the New Testament, correspond to the five books of Moses, which are the books of law of the Old Testament. The book of the Acts of the Apostles corresponds to the historical books of the old Testament; the Epistles of Paul and the seven other canonical Epistles correspond to the books of wisdom of the Old Testament; and the Apocalypse to the prophetical books of the former Testament.

paras.t: Postremo, quoniam lex directe communitatem, non singularem personam concernit, ut dicit Isidorus, idcirco in primo Moysis libro enarratur congregatio seu adunatio Israeliticæ plebis, sub fide et cultu unius Dei; deinde describitur ipsa legislatio huic populo facta, quod fit in tribus libris sequentibus, scilicet Exodo, Levitico, et libro Numerorum, in quibus tamen alia multa miscentur. Tertio, fit repetitio ac elucidatio legis ejusdem, quod fit in Deuteronomio.
paras.en: Lastly, since the law concerns the community directly, not the single person, as Isidore says, therefore the first book of Moses relates the gathering or uniting of the Israelite people under the faith and worship of the one God; next the giving of the law itself to this people is described, which is done in the three following books, namely Exodus[[Ex 20:1||]], Leviticus[[Lev 14:1||]] and the book of Numbers[[Num 16:1||]], in which, however, many other things are mixed in. Thirdly, there is the repetition and elucidation of the same law, which is done in Deuteronomy.

1.title: De expositione exordii Genesis, scilicet, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, secundum Augustinum.
1.title_en: On the exposition of the opening of Genesis, namely, In the beginning God created heaven and earth, according to Augustine.

paras.t: Beatissimus Moyses legifer Judæorum, volens plebem Israeliticam sibi commissam, ad unius veri Dei notitiam, cultum, honorificentiamque reducere, ita exorsus est librorum suorum scripturam: In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Quasi dicat: Solus Deus increatus est atque æternus: cetera omnia profluxerunt, et condita sunt ab eo Deo ipse solus adorandus est et colendus. Et valde convenienter ita incepit, quoniam tempore suo idololatria undique viguit, ita ut veri Dei cognitio et cultus in perpaucis remanserit hominibus. Nam et ipsi filii Israel in Ægypto pro maxima parte ad idololatriam erant dilapsi. Diversi quoque tunc eruperunt errores de mundo, quem aliqui æstimabant increatum, quidam vero creatum sive productum, et tamen Creatori coæternum: quorum omnium Moyses exclusit errorem, In principio, inquiens, creavit Deus cœlum et terram.
paras.en: The most blessed Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, wishing to bring the Israelite people committed to him back to the knowledge, worship and honouring of the one true God, began the writing of his books thus: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. As if to say: God alone is uncreated and eternal; all other things flowed forth from him, God, and were established by him; he alone is to be adored and worshipped. And very fittingly did he begin thus, since in his time idolatry flourished everywhere, so that the knowledge and worship of the true God remained in very few men. For even the children of Israel themselves had for the most part fallen away into idolatry in Egypt. Diverse errors about the world also broke out then: some thought it uncreated, others created or produced, and yet coeternal with the Creator. Moses shut out the error of all of these, saying: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], [[1:1|God created heaven, and earth|creavit Deus cœlum et terram]].

paras.t: Præterea, sicut Thomas ait in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 46, exordium istud tripliciter explanatur, ad removendum tripartitum errorem circa mundum et ejus initium. Quidam enim dixerunt mundum non habuisse temporalem inceptionem. Ad quod reprobandum exponitur primo sic: In principio, scilicet temporis, creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Alii posuerunt duo principia rerum, videlicet summum et per se bonum, a quo dixerunt spiritualia, invisibilia, et incorruptibilia emanasse, videlicet Manichæi: et summum ac per se malum, a quo dixerunt corruptibilia et corporalia omnia, quantum ad suam substantiam esse creata. Ad quorum confutandam insaniam, rudissimumque errorem, exponitur sic secundo: In principio, hoc est in Filio, creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Filius namque est Patris imago, et omnis rei creatæ exemplar. De quo ait Apostolus: Per ipsum et in ipso condita sunt omnia. Hinc Filio convenit ratio principii exemplaris. Propter quod scriptum est: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Sicque exponit Origenes, dicendo: Quod est principium, nisi Dominus noster et salvator omnium Jesus Christus, primogenitus omnis creaturæ? In hoc ergo principio, hoc est in Verbo suo, fecit Deus cœlum terramque.
paras.en: Moreover, as Thomas says in the First Part of his Summa, question 46, this opening is explained in three ways, to remove a threefold error about the world and its beginning. For some said that the world had no beginning in time. To refute this it is expounded first thus: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, of time, [[1:1|God created heaven, and earth|creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. Others, namely the Manichæans, posited two principles of things: a supreme good, good of itself, from which they said that spiritual, invisible and incorruptible things emanated; and a supreme evil, evil of itself, by which they said that all corruptible and bodily things were created as to their substance. To confute their madness and most uncouth error, it is expounded secondly thus: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, in the Son, [[1:1|God created heaven, and earth|creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. For the Son is the image of the Father[[2 Cor 4:4||]] and the exemplar of every created thing. Of him the Apostle says: [[Col 1:16|All things were created by him and in him|Per ipsum et in ipso condita sunt omnia]]. Hence the character of exemplar principle [*principium*, the word rendered "beginning" in the verse; an exemplar is the pattern after which a thing is made] belongs to the Son. For which reason it is written: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil]]. And so Origen expounds it, saying: What is the beginning[[Col 1:18||]], but our Lord and the Saviour of all, Jesus Christ, [[Col 1:15|the firstborn of every creature|primogenitus omnis creaturæ]]? In this beginning, then, that is, in his Word, God made heaven and earth.

paras.t: Quidam dixerunt corporalia non esse immediate creata a Deo, sed per angelos aut intelligentias quasdam. Ad quod destruendum, exponitur tertio: In principio, id est ante cetera omnia, juxta illud in Psalmo: Initio tu, Domine, terram fundasti, et opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli. Itaque juxta primam et hanc tertiam expositiones, per Deum intelligitur tota Trinitas unus Deus, quum dicitur, In principio creavit Deus, etc. In secunda vero expositione, per Deum intelligitur Pater, qui dicitur universa creasse in Filio sive per Filium. Non quod ipse Pater non sit immediata causa ac fontale rerum principium, sed quoniam Filio appropriatur causalitas exemplaris: imo tota superincomprehensibilis Trinitas est una omnium causa, et unus creator, ac unum principium universorum, quum sit unus Deus, et trium supervenerabilium Personarum sit una natura et una potestas.
paras.en: Some said that bodily things were not created immediately by God, but through angels or certain intelligences. To destroy this it is expounded thirdly: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, before all other things, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 101:26|In the beginning, O Lord, thou foundedst the earth: and the heavens are the works of thy hands|Initio tu, Domine, terram fundasti, et opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli]]. Thus according to the first and this third exposition, by God is understood the whole Trinity, one God, when it is said: [[1:1|In the beginning God created|In principio creavit Deus]], etc. But in the second exposition, by God is understood the Father, who is said to have created all things in the Son or through the Son. Not that the Father himself is not the immediate cause and the fountain-principle of things, but because exemplar causality is appropriated to the Son [appropriation: ascribing to one Person what is common to all three, because of its likeness to what is proper to him]; indeed the whole super-incomprehensible Trinity is the one cause of all things, and one creator, and one principle of all things, since it is one God, and the three supremely venerable Persons have one nature and one power.

paras.t: Denique hæc triplex expositio hujus propositionis, In principio erat Verbum, specialiter respicit hoc, quod dicitur hic: In principio. Id quoque quod subditur, Cœlum et terra, multipliciter a sanctis Patribus doctoribusque catholicis invenitur expositum.
paras.en: Lastly, this threefold exposition of the statement [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]] bears specially on what is said here: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]]. What is added, too, [[1:1|heaven, and earth|Cœlum et terra]], is found expounded in many ways by the holy Fathers and the catholic doctors.

paras.t: Quocirca pensanda sunt multa: et primo, quod in multis locis tangit S. Hieronymus, dicens: Principium Genesis et Canticum canticorum, prima quoque ac ultima visio Ezechielis, tot sunt difficultatibus involuta, ut ab Hebræis ante tricesimum ætatis eorum annum non legantur. Quod quam verum sit, ostendit diversitas expositionum textuum horum. Nam et principium Genesis a doctoribus Hebræorum et Græcorum ac Latinorum tam diversimode explanatur, ut Magister Sententiarum secundo libro testetur: Quidam sanctorum Patrum, qui verba Dei atque arcana Scripturæ excellenter scrutati sunt, circa hunc passum quasi diversa scripsisse videntur.
paras.en: Wherefore many things must be weighed. And first, what St. Jerome touches on in many places, saying: The beginning of Genesis and the Canticle of Canticles, and also the first and the last vision of Ezechiel, are wrapped in so many difficulties that they are not read by the Hebrews before the thirtieth year of their age. How true this is, the diversity of the expositions of these texts shows. For the beginning of Genesis too is explained in such different ways by the doctors of the Hebrews, the Greeks and the Latins, that the Master of the Sentences [Peter Lombard, as the margin notes] testifies in his second book: Some of the holy Fathers, who searched out the words of God and the secrets of Scripture excellently, seem to have written as it were different things about this passage.

paras.t: Secundo pensandum, quod undecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Divini sermonis, id est sacræ Scripturæ, obscuritas ad hoc utilis est, quod plures veritatis sententias parit, atque in notitiæ lucem producit, dum alius intelligit eum sic, alius sic: ita tamen, ut quod in obscuro loco intelligitur, attestatione rerum manifestarum aut aliis locis Scripturæ non dubiis comprobetur. Et iterum Augustinus effatur: In expositionibus et quæstionibus istis circa litteram Genesis, duo sunt observanda: Primum est, ut inviolabiliter teneamus Scripturam sacram esse veracem. Secundum, ne quis nimis uni expositioni adhæreat, quando Scriptura multipliciter potest exponi. De hoc diffuse et humiliter, imo et sapientissime scribit duodecimo ac tertiodecimo libro Confessionum, quemadmodum ad indagandum sensum scripturæ Geneseos debeamus accedere sine temeraria assertione hujus aut illius expositionis.
paras.en: Secondly, it must be weighed that Augustine says in the eleventh book of the City of God: The obscurity of the divine discourse, that is, of sacred Scripture, is useful for this, that it brings forth many opinions of the truth and draws them into the light of knowledge, while one understands it thus and another thus; yet so that what is understood in an obscure place is confirmed by the witness of manifest things or by other passages of Scripture that are not in doubt. And again Augustine declares: In these expositions and questions about the letter of Genesis two things are to be observed. The first is that we hold inviolably that sacred Scripture is truthful. The second, that no one cling too closely to one exposition when Scripture can be expounded in many ways. Of this he writes at length and humbly, nay most wisely, in the twelfth and thirteenth books of the Confessions: how we ought to approach the search for the sense of the scripture of Genesis without rash assertion of this or that exposition.

paras.t: Tertio est pensandum, quod super secundum Sententiarum, distinctione 12, scribit Thomas: Eorum quæ spectant ad fidem, quædam sunt per se de substantia fidei, ut Deum esse unum ac trinum, et in talibus omnes sancti Patres atque catholici expositores concordant, nec licet in talibus diversimode opinari. Alia vero non sunt per se de substantia fidei, sed per accidens se habent ad eam, in quantum videlicet in Scriptura traduntur, quam fides præsupponit esse a Spiritu Sancto, et in talibus Sancti quandoque diversimode sentiunt. Sic quoque circa principium mundi aliquid ad substantiam fidei pertinet, ut quod mundus per creationem a Deo incepit, et hoc omnes Catholici unanimiter tenent.
paras.en: Thirdly, it must be weighed that Thomas writes on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 12: Of the things that concern the faith, some belong of themselves to the substance of the faith, as that God is one and three; and in such things all the holy Fathers and catholic expositors agree, nor is it lawful to hold different opinions in them. Others do not belong of themselves to the substance of the faith, but relate to it accidentally, namely in so far as they are handed down in Scripture, which faith presupposes to be from the Holy Ghost; and in such things the Saints sometimes think differently. So too about the beginning of the world something belongs to the substance of the faith, namely that the world began by creation from God; and this all Catholics hold with one accord.

paras.t: Porro, quo modo ac ordine factus sit mundus, non pertinet ad fidem, nisi per accidens, utpote in quantum hoc traditur in Scriptura, quæ diversimode potest exponi, et veritas ejus per diversas expositiones salvatur. Sicque circa creationem mundi doctores diversimode sentiunt, variis modis exponendo Scripturas, non tamen recedentes a fidei veritate, nec sibi invicem præjudicantes aut derogantes incauta assertione. Hinc ait Albertus libro de IV Coæquævis: Spiritus Sanctus duobus modis inspirat expositores Scripturæ. Primo, quantum ad consentaneum rationi, et non contrarium fidei, hoc est, ut sequantur id quod ratio magis dictat, nec tamen est contra fidem. Secundo inspirat eos, quantum ad consentaneum auctoritati. Primo itaque modo motus est ac processit Augustinus, exponendo exordium Genesis, prout rationi magis consentaneum esse videtur, non tamen negando quod auctoritas exigit. Alii vero expositores magis secuti sunt quod auctoritas Scripturæ videtur prætendere, non tamen negantes quod secundum rationem est consequens.
paras.en: But how and in what order the world was made does not belong to the faith except accidentally, namely in so far as this is handed down in Scripture, which can be expounded in different ways, and whose truth is kept safe through different expositions. And so the doctors think differently about the creation of the world, expounding the Scriptures in various ways, yet not departing from the truth of the faith, nor prejudging or disparaging one another by incautious assertion. Hence Albert says in the book On the Four Coequals [Albert the Great's treatise on the four things created together at the beginning: matter, time, the empyrean heaven and the angels]: The Holy Ghost inspires the expositors of Scripture in two ways. First, as to what accords with reason and is not contrary to the faith, that is, so that they follow what reason rather dictates, and yet is not against the faith. Secondly, he inspires them as to what accords with authority. In the first way, then, Augustine was moved and proceeded, expounding the opening of Genesis as seems more in accord with reason, yet not denying what authority demands. But other expositors followed rather what the authority of Scripture seems to put forward, yet not denying what follows according to reason.

paras.t: His præmissis, tangendæ sunt expositiones celebriores hujus, quod dicitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, quantum ad ultimam istam particulam, scilicet cœlum et terram; et etiam quantum ad textum sequentem, cujus intelligentia ex intellectu et expositione particulæ hujus pro magna parte dependet. Deinde propositio ista, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, per se sumpta, non videtur ad intelligendum difficilis; sed verba textus statim sequentia, difficultatem ejus inducunt. Mox enim subjungitur: Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas.
