In quibus verbis insinuatur, quod cœlo et terra creatis, abyssus et aqua pariter exstiterunt, de quorum creatione non videbatur aliquid tangi in verbis his, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Rursus paulo post legitur, firmamentum quod vocatum est cœlum, esse factum secunda die: idcirco obscurum fit de quo cœlo dicatur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram.
paras.en: These things premised, we must touch on the more celebrated expositions of what is said, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], as to this last little part, namely [[1:1|heaven, and earth|cœlum et terram]], and also as to the text that follows, the understanding of which depends in great part on the understanding and exposition of this part. Now this statement, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], taken by itself, does not seem hard to understand; but the words of the text that follow straight after bring in its difficulty. For straightway is added: [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God moved over the waters|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]]. In these words it is implied that when heaven and earth had been created, the deep and the water existed as well, of whose creation nothing seemed to be touched on in these words, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. Again, a little after we read that the firmament, which was called heaven, was made on the second day; and so it becomes obscure of which heaven it is said: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]].

paras.t: Sanctus igitur Augustinus, considerans quod littera Genesis, quantum ad superficiem suam, patet irrisioni calumniisque infidelium, et eos a conversione ad fidem avertere potest, eo quod videatur instar poetarum et quorumdam philosophorum ab Aristotele satis reprobatorum, ponere quoddam chaos confusum in exordio mundi, excogitavit quamdam expositionem subtilem, per quam defendit Scripturam ab irrisione hujusmodi, et tamen salvavit Scripturæ ac fidei veritatem. Itaque dixit, quod sicut Deus omnipotens omnia in seipso unico actu intelligendi perfecte et distincte concipit et cognoscit, ac intra se exprimit, sic in eodem instanti omnia opera sex dierum simul et distincte produxit, eadem practice intelligendo atque ut essent jubendo. Cui expositioni videtur consonare illud in Psalmo: Ipse dixit, et facta sunt: ipse mandavit, et creata sunt. Et quod in Ecclesiastico legitur: Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul. Quod item Moyses ait: Dei perfecta sunt opera. Et quod in hoc ipso Genesis libro paulo post subditur: Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ, in die qua creavit Dominus cœlum et terram, et omne virgultum agri, omnemque herbam regionis, quum tamen virgulta et herbæ infra legantur tertia die producta.
paras.en: Holy Augustine, then, considering that the letter of Genesis, as to its surface, lies open to the mockery and calumnies of unbelievers and can turn them away from conversion to the faith, because, like the poets and certain philosophers well enough refuted by Aristotle, it seems to posit a kind of confused chaos at the beginning of the world, devised a subtle exposition by which he defended Scripture from mockery of this kind and yet kept safe the truth of Scripture and of the faith. And so he said that just as almighty God conceives and knows all things perfectly and distinctly in himself by a single act of understanding, and expresses them within himself, so in the same instant he produced all the works of the six days together and distinctly, understanding them practically [that is, with the knowledge that makes, not merely the knowledge that beholds] and commanding that they be. With this exposition that in the Psalm seems to agree: [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made: he commanded and they were created|Ipse dixit, et facta sunt: ipse mandavit, et creata sunt]]. And what is read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:1|He that liveth for ever created all things together|Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul]]. And what Moses likewise says: [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Dei perfecta sunt opera]]. And what is added a little after in this very book of Genesis: [[Gen 2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ]], [[Gen 2:4|in the day that the Lord God made the heaven and the earth|in die qua creavit Dominus cœlum et terram]], [[Gen 2:5|and every plant of the field|et omne virgultum agri]], [[Gen 2:5|and every herb of the ground|omnemque herbam regionis]] [the margin gives Gen. ii, 5 only; the quotation begins in 2:4], whereas the plants and herbs are read further on to have been brought forth on the third day.

paras.t: Hæc ergo intuens Augustinus, dicit opera sex dierum simul facta distincte. Unde ait Albertus libro de Coæquævis: Augustinus revera ponit omnia simul creata in materia et forma, quæ scilicet natura non potest per se producere motu superiorum, videlicet cœlestium corporum et commixtione elementorum. Et ideo cœlum a principio factum est cum suis stellis, et terra cum animalibus suis, aqua quoque cum natatilibus atque volucribus: et breviter, omnia in speciebus suis simul educta sunt, quæ per simplicem virtutem motus cœli, et per virtutem stellarum, educi non poterant sine alio motore, id est particulari agente univoco, utpote speciei ejusdem, sicut sunt homo, leo, equus, et consimilia, quæ præter virtutem cœli et elementorum, requirunt specialem motorem ad sui generationem. Sunt tamen quædam non habentia magnam diversitatem in partibus corporis, ut plantæ et animalia aliqua, præsertim quædam reptilia et aliqui pisces, quæ non oportuit primo fieri in propriis speciebus, sed tantum in rationibus suis causalibus, id est seminalibus suis virtutibus, quia ad horum productionem sufficit motus cœli atque stellarum ex materia diversimode commiscibili. Propter quod dicit Avicenna in libro de Diluviis, quod mures quandoque generantur ex terra, et serpentes ex capillis. Hæc Albertus.
paras.en: Looking, then, at these things, Augustine says that the works of the six days were made together, and distinctly. Whence Albert says in the book On the Coequals: Augustine in truth holds that all those things were created together in matter and form which nature cannot produce of itself by the motion of the higher bodies, namely the heavenly bodies, and by the mingling of the elements. And therefore heaven was made from the beginning with its stars, and the earth with its animals, the water too with the swimming things and the birds; and in short, all those things were brought forth together in their species which could not be brought forth by the simple power of the motion of heaven and by the power of the stars without another mover, that is, a particular univocal agent [one of the same species as what it brings forth], such as man, lion, horse and the like, which besides the power of heaven and of the elements require a special mover for their generation. Yet there are some things that have no great diversity in the parts of the body, such as plants and some animals, especially certain reptiles and some fishes, which did not need to be made first in their own species, but only in their causal reasons, that is, in their seminal powers [Augustine's *rationes causales* or *seminales*: powers set in creation from the start, from which things later come forth], because for their production the motion of heaven and of the stars suffices, out of matter that can be mixed in different ways. For which reason Avicenna says in the book On Floods that mice are sometimes generated from earth, and serpents from hairs. Thus far Albert.

paras.t: Denique, ut Thomas super secundum Sententiarum fatetur, Augustinus vult quasdam creaturas in ipso creationis principio, id est primo instanti, fuisse in propria natura distinctas per species suas, ut elementa et corpora cœlestia ac angelos. Alia vero in rationibus seminalibus tantum, ut animalia, plantas et hujusmodi, quæ omnia in naturis propriis sunt producta illo opere, quo Deus post sex dies illos naturam prius conditam administrat. De quo ait Salvator: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Nec in distinctione rerum attendendum esse ordinem temporis, sed naturæ atque doctrinæ: naturæ, sicut sonus præcedit cantum, sicque quæ naturaliter sunt priora, prius facta scribuntur, quemadmodum terra priusquam animalia, et aqua priusquam pisces; ordine vero doctrinæ, sicut patet in docentibus geometriam. Quamvis enim partes figuræ sine ordine temporis figuram constituant, nihilo minus geometria docet constitutionem figuræ, lineam post lineam protrahendo. Et istud fuit exemplum Platonis, ut dicitur primo Cœli. Sic quoque secundum Augustinum, Moyses rudem instruens populum de mundi creatione, divisit per partes quæ facta sunt simul. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: Lastly, as Thomas states on the second book of the Sentences, Augustine holds that some creatures were distinct in their own nature by their species in the very beginning of creation, that is, in the first instant, such as the elements, the heavenly bodies and the angels; but others only in their seminal reasons, such as animals, plants and the like, all of which were produced in their own natures by that work by which God, after those six days, administers the nature he formed before. Of this the Saviour says: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Nor, he holds, is the order of time to be looked to in the distinction of things, but the order of nature and of teaching: of nature, as sound precedes song, and so the things that are naturally prior are written to have been made first, as the earth before the animals and the water before the fishes; and the order of teaching, as is plain in those who teach geometry. For although the parts of a figure make up the figure without order of time, geometry nevertheless teaches the construction of the figure by drawing line after line. And this was Plato's example, as is said in the first book On the Heavens [Aristotle's *De caelo*]. So too, according to Augustine, Moses, instructing an unlettered people about the creation of the world, divided into parts the things that were made together. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Sed circa hæc oritur quæstio, quoniam verba horum doctorum videntur ab invicem discordare, ita quod opinionem Augustini contrarie recitant, ut apparet. Albertus etenim ait, quod secundum Augustinum terra facta est cum animalibus, et aqua cum piscibus, etc. Porro Thomas refert, quod secundum Augustinum, elementa et cœlestia corpora sanctique angeli simul producta sunt, animalia vero et plantæ postea. Et respondendum, quod Albertus loquitur de animalibus, piscibus ac avibus, primo et immediate a Deo productis: et illa simul esse producta cum terra et aqua, secundum Augustinum, ostenditur ex præhabitis Thomæ verbis. Nam ait terram præcedere animalia, et aquam pisces ordine naturæ, non temporis, quemadmodum sonus cantum. Rursus circa hoc quæritur, quot animalia et pisces ac volucres, secundum istam opinionem, fuerint simul cum terra et aqua tunc facta. Ad quod pro nunc breviter dici potest, quod in qualibet specie duo individua, loquendo de his quæ ex commixtione maris ac feminæ naturaliter producuntur.
paras.en: But a question arises about these things, since the words of these doctors seem to disagree with one another, so that they report Augustine's opinion in contrary ways, as appears. For Albert says that according to Augustine the earth was made with the animals and the water with the fishes, etc. But Thomas relates that according to Augustine the elements, the heavenly bodies and the holy angels were produced together, but the animals and plants afterwards. The answer is that Albert speaks of the animals, fishes and birds produced first and immediately by God; and that these were produced together with the earth and the water, according to Augustine, is shown from the words of Thomas given above. For he says that the earth precedes the animals, and the water the fishes, in the order of nature, not of time, as sound precedes song. Again, it is asked about this how many animals and fishes and birds, according to this opinion, were then made together with the earth and the water. To which for now it can briefly be said: two individuals in each species, speaking of those that are naturally produced from the union of male and female.

paras.t: Præterea, quia nunc dictum est, quod secundum Augustinum omnia opera sex dierum sunt simul producta: quærendum, quid Augustinus ad litteram intelligat per cœlum et terram, quum dicitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Ad quod concorditer dicunt expositores, et super secundum Sententiarum doctores, quod per cœlum intelligit naturam angelicam seu angelos; per terram vero, materiam prorsus informem omnium corporalium rerum, tam elementorum quam cœlestium corporum ac mixtorum, utpote materiam primam, ab omni forma per intellectum abstractam, quam dicit corporalia præcessisse ordine naturæ, non temporis, quia materia non potest realiter stare nuda, id est, ab omni forma substantiali abstracta. Per cœlum vero, intelligit naturam angelicam ut informem, seu in se consideratam. Cujus tamen informitas non præcessit tempore formationem ejus per dona gratuita, secundum Augustini doctrinam, qui dicit quod Deus fuit in angelis, simul condens naturam, et largiens gratiam. Quod autem ista sint de mente Augustini, patet aperte ex verbis ipsius super Genesim ad litteram, et in libris Confessionum, atque in libro de Civitate Dei, et infra tangetur.
paras.en: Moreover, since it has now been said that according to Augustine all the works of the six days were produced together, we must ask what Augustine understands literally by [[1:1|heaven, and earth|cœlum et terram]] when it is said: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. To this the expositors, and the doctors on the second book of the Sentences, say with one accord that by *heaven* he understands the angelic nature, or the angels; but by *earth*, the wholly formless matter of all bodily things, of the elements as well as of the heavenly bodies and of mixed bodies: namely prime matter, abstracted by the intellect from every form, which he says preceded bodily things in the order of nature, not of time, because matter cannot really stand bare, that is, stripped of every substantial form [that is, prime matter never exists without some form; it comes first only in the order of nature]. By *heaven*, again, he understands the angelic nature as unformed, or considered in itself. Yet its formlessness did not precede in time its formation by the gifts of grace, according to the teaching of Augustine, who says that God was in the angels at once establishing their nature and bestowing grace. That these things are Augustine's mind is plain from his own words on Genesis to the letter, and in the books of the Confessions, and in the book of the City of God, and it will be touched on below.

1.title: De expositione ejusdem verbi, secundum alios sanctos
1.title_en: On the exposition of the same words according to the other Saints

paras.t: QUEMADMODUM Bonaventura ait in scripto suo super secundum Sententiarum, circa intellectum litteræ hujus, diversæ fuerunt opiniones Sanctorum. Quidam enim Sancti in hac re magis secuti sunt theologicam viam, trahentes rationem ad ea quæ fidei sunt. Quidam vero, inter quos præcipuus exstitit Augustinus, magis secuti sunt viam philosophicam, ea ponentem quæ magis sunt consona rationi. Unde Augustinus intellectum hujus scripturæ ad rationis attestationem atque dictamen flectit ac trahit, dicendo omnia simul esse producta. Et expositio ejus fuit multum rationabilis et valde subtilis. Verumtamen, quia ex ea videtur intellectus Scripturæ distrahi, et securius est magisque meritorium, proprium intellectum et rationem Scripturæ omnino subjicere, quam Scripturam aliquo modo distrahere, idcirco communiter alii doctores, tam qui Augustinum præcesserunt, quam qui eum secuti sunt, intellexerunt et exposuerunt scripturam hanc sicut sonare videtur, dicentes opera sex dierum non simul esse producta nisi in materia, sed per intervalla dierum ea esse producta, quantum ad formam et speciem.
paras.en: As Bonaventure says in his writing on the second book of the Sentences, there were different opinions of the Saints about the understanding of this text. For some of the Saints in this matter followed rather the theological way, drawing reason to the things that are of faith; others, chief among whom was Augustine, followed rather the philosophical way, which lays down the things more consonant with reason. Hence Augustine bends and draws the understanding of this scripture to the witness and dictate of reason, saying that all things were produced at once. And his exposition was very reasonable and most subtle. Nevertheless, since by it the understanding of Scripture seems to be wrenched aside, and since it is safer and more meritorious to subject one's own understanding and reason wholly to Scripture than in any way to wrench Scripture, the other doctors in general, both those who went before Augustine and those who followed him, understood and expounded this scripture as it seems to sound, saying that the works of the six days were not produced at once except in their matter, but were produced at intervals of days as to their form and species.

paras.t: Rursus eadem distinctione loquitur Bonaventura : Quamvis multæ sint expositiones hujus verbi, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, quatuor tamen sunt principales. Prima est, quod cœlum et terra eamdem nominant informem materiam omnium corporalium rerum, prout de ipsa fieri debebant duplicia corpora, puta cœlestia et elementaria, ut sit sensus: In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, id est materiam ex qua debebat fieri cœlum et omnia elementa. Hæc autem expositio confirmatur per litteram mox sequentem, quæ describit qualiter factum sit cœlum. Secunda expositio, per cœlum intelligit naturam angelicam, per terram vero materiam primam. Tertia expositio, et quasi media inter has, est Hugonis, qui per terram intelligit elementum terrenum, atque per cœlum tria alia elementa, quæ secundum eum, erant super terram per modum nebulæ circumquaque oppansa, in una confusione permixta, seu potius in una permixtione confusa, et circumquaque suspensa, quæ extendebantur tam alte, sicut pertingit nunc summitas corporalis naturæ. Hinc libro de Sacramentis ait venerabilis Hugo: Nomine terræ significatum puto terrenum hoc elementum. Eratque elementum hoc subsidens seu situm in imo ac medio loco, ceteris in confusione permixtis.
paras.en: Again, Bonaventure says in the same distinction: Although there are many expositions of these words, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], there are nevertheless four principal ones. The first is that heaven and earth name the same formless matter of all bodily things, inasmuch as from it twofold bodies were to be made, namely the heavenly and the elemental; so that the sense is: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], that is, the matter from which heaven and all the elements were to be made. And this exposition is confirmed by the text that follows soon after, which describes how heaven was made. The second exposition understands by heaven the angelic nature, and by earth prime matter. The third exposition, a kind of middle between these, is Hugh's, who understands by earth the element of earth, and by heaven the three other elements, which, according to him, were spread all round above the earth in the manner of a mist, mingled in one confusion, or rather confused in one mingling, and hanging all round, and reaching as high as the summit of bodily nature now reaches. Hence the venerable Hugh says in the book On the Sacraments: By the name of earth I think this earthly element is signified. And this element was settling, or lying, in the lowest and middle place, while the others were mingled in confusion.

paras.t: Quarta expositio per cœlum hoc loco intelligit cœlum empyreum, quod statim in sua creatione angelis est repletum. Per terram vero, materiam omnium corporalium, sive cœlestium, sive terrestrium, sub cœlo empyreo contentorum. Et ista positio est Bedæ et Strabi, imo et S. Basilii in suo Hexaemeron, saltem quantum ad id, quod dictum est de cœlo empyreo. De quo ait Basilius: Sicut damnati in tenebras ultimas abiguntur, ita pro dignis operibus remuneratio restauratur Beatis in ea luce, quæ est extra hunc mundum, ubi quietis domicilium sortiuntur. Strabus quoque: In principio, inquit, creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Cœlum, non hoc visibile firmamentum, sed empyreum, hoc est igneum, non ab ardore, sed a splendore, quod statim repletum est angelis. De quo cœlo loquitur Beda: Hoc superius cœlum, quod a volubilitate mundi secretum est, mox ut creatum est, sanctis angelis est repletum, quos Dominus protestatur in principio conditos cum cœlo et terra, dicens: Ubi eras quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei? Ubi per astra matutina, intelliguntur angeli ac filii Dei.
paras.en: The fourth exposition understands by heaven in this place the empyrean heaven [that is, the highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed, above the visible sky], which at its very creation was filled with angels; and by earth the matter of all bodily things, whether heavenly or earthly, contained beneath the empyrean heaven. And this position is that of Bede and Strabo, and indeed of St Basil in his Hexaemeron, at least as to what is said of the empyrean heaven. Of it Basil says: As the damned are driven away into the uttermost darkness, so for worthy works a reward is restored to the Blessed in that light which is outside this world, where they are allotted a dwelling of rest. Strabo too: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], he says, [[1:1|God created heaven, and earth|creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. Heaven: not this visible firmament, but the empyrean, that is, the fiery heaven, so called not from its heat but from its splendour; which was at once filled with angels. Of this heaven Bede says: This upper heaven, which is set apart from the turning of the world, as soon as it was created was filled with the holy angels, whom the Lord declares to have been made in the beginning with heaven and earth, saying: [[Job 38:4|Where wast thou|Ubi eras]] when [[Job 38:7|the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei?]] Where by the morning stars are understood the angels and sons of God.

paras.t: Præterea, Nicolaus de Lyra scribit hoc loco: Circa principium Genesis sunt tres expositiones solennes, ad quas aliæ videntur reduci. Prima est Augustini, de qua præcedenti articulo dictum est, quæ expositio videtur Lyræ valde longinqua a littera: propter quod, inquit, dimittatur. Aliæ duæ expositiones videntur sibi textui consonare.
paras.en: Further, Nicholas of Lyra writes on this place: About the beginning of Genesis there are three received [*solennes*] expositions, to which the others seem to be reduced. The first is Augustine's, of which we spoke in the preceding article; and this exposition seems to Lyra very far from the letter, for which reason, he says, let it be set aside. The other two expositions seem to him to agree with the text [the margin gives the reading *ipsi textui*, "with the text itself"].

paras.t: Ad quarum declarationem præmittit tres opiniones philosophorum de materia. Prima est opinio Commentatoris, qui in libro de Substantia orbis, dicit in corporibus cœlestibus non esse materiam proprie dictam, quæ scilicet pars sit essentialis compositi, et subjectum formæ substantialis; sed quod ibi dicitur esse materia, dicit esse intelligendum de materia improprie dicta, utpote eam sumendo pro subjecto motus localis, et prout ipse orbis est in potentia ad Ubi. Secunda opinio est, quod in corporibus cœlestibus est materia proprie dicta, tamen alterius rationis a materia mixtorum et elementorum. Hanc opinionem sequuntur Albertus, Thomas, et alii multi. Tertia opinio est, quod omnium corporalium sit una seu ejusdem rationis materia prima. Hæc est opinio Avicennæ, quam sequitur Bonaventura.
paras.en: To explain them he first sets out three opinions of the philosophers about matter. The first is the opinion of the Commentator [Averroes], who in the book On the Substance of the Sphere says that in the heavenly bodies there is no matter properly so called, that is, matter which is an essential part of the composite and the subject of a substantial form; but what is there called matter he says must be understood of matter improperly so called, taking it for the subject of local motion, inasmuch as the sphere itself is in potency to place [*ad Ubi*: to the category of "where"]. The second opinion is that in the heavenly bodies there is matter properly so called, yet of another kind than the matter of mixed bodies and of the elements. This opinion Albert, Thomas and many others follow. The third opinion is that the prime matter of all bodily things is one, or of the same kind. This is the opinion of Avicenna, which Bonaventure follows.

paras.t: His prolixe ab eo præmissis, ponit duas expositiones prætactas, quarum prima est, quod partes hujus sensibilis mundi principales, videlicet omnia cœlestia corpora et quatuor elementa, fuerunt a principio per creationem simul producta distincte in suis substantialibus formis: quod item totum opus distinctionis, et etiam opus ornatus cœlestium corporum, quod factum est quarto die, quæ infra describuntur, intelligenda sint quantum ad qualitates, proprietates, et virtutes accidentales, superadjunctas prælatis operibus creationis. Secunda expositio est, quod materia omnium corporalium, primo creata sit solum sub una forma substantiali communi, videlicet sub forma corporeitatis, et diebus sequentibus sit distincta secundum diversas sui partes per formas substantiales specificas, tam cœlestes quam elementares.
paras.en: Having set these out at length, he gives the two expositions touched on above. The first of them is that the principal parts of this sensible world, namely all the heavenly bodies and the four elements, were produced together from the beginning by creation, distinct in their substantial forms; and that the whole work of distinction [the dividing of light from darkness, waters from waters, and sea from dry land], and also the work of adornment of the heavenly bodies, which was done on the fourth day, both of which are described below, are to be understood as to the accidental qualities, properties and powers added on to the aforesaid works of creation. The second exposition is that the matter of all bodily things was first created under one common substantial form only, namely the form of corporeity, and on the following days was distinguished according to its various parts by specific substantial forms, heavenly as well as elemental.

paras.t: Insuper dicit, quod illi qui sequuntur Commentatorem, et qui dicunt materiam cœlestium corporum specie distinctam a materia inferiorum, non possunt tenere expositionem istam secundam, sed primam. Porro qui dicunt omnium corporalium esse unam materiam, sequi possunt expositionem istam secundam.
paras.en: Besides, he says that those who follow the Commentator, and who say that the matter of the heavenly bodies differs in species from the matter of the lower bodies, cannot hold that second exposition, but only the first; whereas those who say that there is one matter of all bodily things can follow the second exposition.

paras.t: Denique Nicolaus de Lyra, ista scribendo, affirmat quod intellectus operum sex dierum, dependet ex cognitione prætactæ simplicis opinionis de materia prima. Sed contra hoc scribit Rabbi Paulus, ex Judaismo conversus, qui fuit Burgensis episcopus, atque in multis redarguit Lyram. Itaque contra prætactum verbum testatur, quod inconvenienter sit positum, quoniam philosophi diversimode opinando de materia, non habuerunt rationes demonstrativas, sed persuasivas, unde non debet sensus Scripturæ propter hoc variari. Et ideo sancti doctores modicum curaverunt de diversitate talium opinionum in præsenti materia, sicut nec refert ad articulum creationis credendum, an cœli sint immateriales, vel habeant materiam ejusdem rationis cum inferioribus istis, an non.
paras.en: Lastly, Nicholas of Lyra, in writing this, affirms that the understanding of the works of the six days depends on knowledge of the aforesaid simple [*simplicis*; perhaps a slip for *triplicis*, threefold] opinion about prime matter. But against this writes Rabbi Paul, a convert from Judaism, who was bishop of Burgos, and who refutes Lyra in many things. And so against the aforesaid statement he testifies that it is unfittingly put, since the philosophers, holding diverse opinions about matter, had not demonstrative but persuasive reasons; hence the sense of Scripture ought not to vary on that account. And therefore the holy doctors cared little about the diversity of such opinions in the present matter, just as it makes no difference to the article of creation, which must be believed, whether the heavens are immaterial or have matter of the same kind as these lower things or not.

paras.t: Ad istud dicendum, quod præhabitum verbum Nicolai rationabiliter potest salvari. Quemadmodum enim omnis creatura servit Creatori, ita naturalis scientia deservit theologicæ veritati. Unde asserit Augustinus, quod cognitio proprietatum naturalium rerum, pandit abdita Scripturarum. Quamvis ergo veritas Scripturarum non dependet a notitia opinionum et scientiarum philosophicarum, attamen intellectus ejuscemodi veritatis in tantum dependet ex cognitione talium opinionum et scientiarum, in quantum cognitio talium confert ad intelligendum limpidius ipsas Scripturas. Nec Lyra dicit, quod propter diversas opiniones philosophorum varietur sensus Scripturæ.
paras.en: To this it must be said that the aforesaid statement of Nicholas can reasonably be upheld. For just as every creature serves the Creator[[Ps 118:91||]], so natural science serves theological truth. Hence Augustine asserts that knowledge of the properties of natural things lays open the hidden things of the Scriptures. Although, then, the truth of the Scriptures does not depend on knowledge of philosophical opinions and sciences, yet the understanding of that truth depends on knowledge of such opinions and sciences in so far as knowing them helps to understand the Scriptures themselves more clearly. Nor does Lyra say that the sense of Scripture varies because of the diverse opinions of the philosophers.

paras.t: Præterea, quod Rabbi Paulus ait, sanctos doctores parum curasse de talium varietate opinionum, non videtur satis considerate prolatum, quia non solum S. Thomas, Bonaventura, Albertus, et similes super secundum Sententiarum, sed Ambrosius quoque, Basilius, aliique antiqui expositores, ubertim ac diligenter recitant philosophorum opiniones, in quantum hoc confert ad intelligendum Scripturas. Verumtamen in præfata positione, Lyra dicit aliud quiddam quod patet calumniæ. Siquidem ait : Illi qui dicunt quod in corporibus cœlestibus non est materia, consequenter dicere habent, quod omnia corpora cœlestia a principio sint producta in suis substantialibus formis distincte. Nempe qui dicunt in corporibus cœlestibus non esse materiam, dicunt et dicere compelluntur, quod corpora cœlestia non habent formas substantiales, quum forma substantialis non dicatur, nisi respectu materiæ cui dat esse. Nec aliquid dicitur proprie forma substantialis, nisi sit pars compositi. Cœlum autem, secundum istam opinionem, non est compositum ex forma et materia. Commentator quoque in libro de Substantia orbis, dicit quod ipse orbis seu corpus cœleste sit actu ens, etiam per intellectum excluso suo motore, seu qualibet forma substantiali.
paras.en: Again, what Rabbi Paul says, that the holy doctors cared little about the variety of such opinions, seems not to have been said with enough consideration; for not only St Thomas, Bonaventure, Albert and the like on the second book of the Sentences, but also Ambrose, Basil and other ancient expositors recount the opinions of the philosophers abundantly and carefully, in so far as this helps to understand the Scriptures. Nevertheless, in the aforesaid position Lyra says something else which lies open to attack. For he says: Those who say that there is no matter in the heavenly bodies must say in consequence that all the heavenly bodies were produced from the beginning distinct in their substantial forms. But in fact those who say that there is no matter in the heavenly bodies say, and are compelled to say, that the heavenly bodies have no substantial forms, since a form is not called substantial except with respect to the matter to which it gives being; nor is anything properly called a substantial form unless it is part of a composite. But heaven, according to that opinion, is not composed of form and matter. The Commentator too, in the book On the Substance of the Sphere, says that the sphere itself, or heavenly body, is a being in act even when its mover, or any substantial form, is set aside in thought.

paras.t: Amplius, ad intelligendum perfectius præhabitam duplicem expositionem de informitate materiæ, seu qualiter fuit creata sub forma corporeitatis, aut sub propriis substantialibus formis elementorum atque cœlestium corporum, advertendum quod super secundum, distinctione 12, recitat Thomas : Quidam antiqui philosophi posuerunt materiam totam sub una forma substantiali, ponentes unum elementorum esse primam materiam omnium, et ex illo omnia generari. Alii posuerunt eam sub pluribus formis substantialibus, non tamen ad invicem ordinatis, sed quadam confusione permixtis, et postea operatione primi Opificis ad distinctionem ordinemque reductis. Moderni etiam in duas vias has dividuntur. Quidam enim ponunt, materiam illam primo creatam totam sub una forma substantiali fuisse : sed ne videantur in antiquum labi errorem, dicunt formam illam non fuisse aliquid formarum elementarium, sed aliquid quod se habet in via ad eas, ut imperfectum ad perfectum, quemadmodum forma embryonis se habet ad formam animalis completi in specie sua. Alii dicunt, materiam illam primo creatam sub diversis substantialibus formis, sicut narratum est.
paras.en: Further, to understand more perfectly the twofold exposition given above about the formlessness of matter, that is, whether it was created under the form of corporeity or under the proper substantial forms of the elements and of the heavenly bodies, it should be noted that on the second book, distinction 12, Thomas recounts: Some ancient philosophers held that all matter was under one substantial form, holding that one of the elements was the prime matter of all things and that all things were generated from it. Others held it to be under several substantial forms, not, however, ordered to one another, but mingled in a kind of confusion, and afterwards brought to distinction and order by the working of the first Maker. The moderns too are divided into these two ways. For some hold that the matter first created was wholly under one substantial form; but lest they seem to slip into the ancient error, they say that this form was not any of the elemental forms, but something that stands on the way to them, as the imperfect to the perfect, just as the form of the embryo stands to the form of the animal complete in its species. Others say that the matter first created was under diverse substantial forms, as has been told.

paras.t: Has item opiniones narrat Bonaventura super secundum : Quidam, inquiens, voluerunt dicere, quod materia illa diceretur chaos, propter formarum multitudinem, et contrarietatem existentem in partibus materiæ, ita quod partes illæ non distinguebantur ad invicem secundum loca determinata, nec ita proportionabiliter invicem jungebantur, ut ex eis resultaret aliquod mixtum completum : ideo erat ibi quædam mixtio non proportionis, sed confusionis : unde nec agebant contra se invicem. Alius modus dicendi est, quod materia illa producta est sub aliqua forma, sed illa non erat forma completa, nec dans materiæ esse completum. Unde nec satiavit appetitum materiæ, nec sic eam informavit, quin adhuc mansit informis, sed erat dispositio ad formas ulteriores. Et quamvis forma illa non habebat in se diversas naturas, tamen quia ad multas formas habuit inclinationem, habuit in partibus suis quamdam imperfectam diversitatem, propter quod permixta dicitur et confusa : sicut exemplum ponitur in embryone, quod licet actu habet unam formam atque figuram massæ carnis, illa tamen dispositio est ad diversas membrorum figurationes, quamvis istud non sit per omnia simile, quoniam forma illa non erat tantæ actualitatis sicut est forma embryonis, neque in tanta propinquitate ad eductionem formarum sequentium, sicut forma embryonis ad eductionem membrorum. Forma etenim seu figura embryonis, est visibilis, et vi naturæ ad perfectionem perducibilis. Illa vero materia sub tali forma erat invisibilis, atque ad formas subsequentes sola divina virtute et operatione ducibilis : ideo propter indeterminatum appetitum formarum multarum, confusa dicitur et permixta.
paras.en: Bonaventure likewise relates these opinions on the second book: Some, he says, wished to say that that matter was called chaos because of the multitude of forms and the contrariety existing in the parts of the matter, so that those parts were not distinguished from one another in fixed places, nor joined to one another in such proportion that some complete mixed body resulted from them; and so there was there a mixing not of proportion but of confusion; hence neither did they act against one another. The other way of speaking is that that matter was produced under some form, but that this was not a complete form, nor one giving the matter complete being. Hence it neither satisfied the appetite of the matter, nor so informed it that it did not still remain formless; but it was a disposition to further forms. And although that form did not have diverse natures in itself, yet because it had an inclination to many forms, it had in its parts a certain imperfect diversity, for which reason it is called mingled and confused; as the example is given of the embryo, which, although it actually has one form and shape, that of a mass of flesh, yet that is a disposition to the diverse shapings of the members. This, however, is not alike in every respect, since that form was not of such actuality as the form of the embryo, nor so near to the drawing forth of the following forms as the form of the embryo is to the drawing forth of the members. For the form or shape of the embryo is visible, and can be brought to perfection by the power of nature; but that matter under such a form was invisible, and could be brought to the subsequent forms only by divine power and working. Therefore, because of its undetermined appetite for many forms, it is called confused and mingled.

paras.t: Postremo, verbum hoc, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, ita exponit Chrysostomus, quod Moyses hoc sermone summarie explicavit et præmisit, quidquid Deus postea per sex dies effecit ; et postea per partes explicat, quod ante in summa præmisit : sicque per duo ista extrema, cœlum et terram, intellexit cetera corporalia omnia in eis contenta ; quemadmodum si dicatur, artifex fecit hanc domum : et postea subdatur, primo posuit fundamentum, secundo statuit parietes, tertio tectum erexit. Et ita quod ait, In principio, exponitur et refertur ad totum tempus productionis operum sex dierum. Sicque idem est cœlum, quod legitur in principio factum : et firmamentum, quod legitur secunda die productum. Hanc expositionem præ ceteris sequitur Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: Finally, these words, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], Chrysostom expounds thus: that Moses in this sentence set forth in summary, and put first, whatever God afterwards made through the six days; and afterwards he unfolds part by part what he had first put in summary. And so by these two extremes, heaven and earth, he meant all the other bodily things contained in them; just as if one should say: The builder made this house; and then add: First he laid the foundation, secondly he set up the walls, thirdly he raised the roof. And so what he says, [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], is expounded and referred to the whole time of the production of the works of the six days. And thus the heaven which is read to have been made in the beginning is the same as the firmament which is read to have been produced on the second day. This exposition Rabbi Paul follows above the others.

1.title: Cui expositionum præinductarum videatur magis esse consentiendum
1.title_en: Which of the foregoing expositions seems the more to be agreed with

paras.t: QUAMVIS juxta præhabita, expositio S. Augustini videatur subtilior, atque humanæ consonantior rationi, ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod verior sit, quemadmodum Deum non esse trinum in personis, magis consonat rationi humanæ, quam quod in unitate essentiæ trinus consistat, non tamen est verum. Nam ea quæ fidei sunt, quamvis non sint contra rationem, sunt tamen supra omnem rationem humanam. Ratio quoque humana plene comprehendere nequit opera Dei, et multo minus comprehendere potest rationes eorum, hoc est, cur Dei sapientia sic agendum dictavit, cujus judicia et secreta sapientiæ ejus penetrare non possumus.
paras.en: Although, according to what has been said, the exposition of St Augustine seems subtler and more consonant with human reason, it does not follow from this that it is truer; just as it is more consonant with human reason that God is not three in persons than that He subsists as three in the unity of essence, and yet it is not true. For the things that are of faith, though they are not against reason, are yet above all human reason. Human reason, too, cannot fully comprehend the works of God, and much less can it comprehend their reasons, that is, why the wisdom of God dictated that it should be done so: God, whose judgments and the secrets of whose wisdom we cannot penetrate[[Rom 11:33||]].

paras.t: Verumtamen Albertus libro de Coæquævis, et Thomas super secundum, magis consentiunt expositioni Augustini præfatæ. Verumtamen Thomas in prima parte Summæ suæ, minus declinat se ad aliquam partem. Porro (ut tactum est) Bonaventura magis sequitur eos, qui per intervalla temporum dicunt omnia esse producta. Attamen sapienter hortatur, ut in hac materia, in qua certitudo haberi non valet, nihil incaute aut præcipitanter quis asserat.
paras.en: Albert, however, in the book On the Coequaevals [that is, on the four things created together at the beginning: matter, time, the empyrean heaven and the angelic nature], and Thomas on the second book of the Sentences, rather agree with the aforesaid exposition of Augustine. Yet Thomas in the first part of his Summa inclines less to either side. Bonaventure, on the other hand, as has been touched on, rather follows those who say that all things were produced at intervals of time. Yet he wisely exhorts that in this matter, in which certainty cannot be had, no one should assert anything incautiously or rashly.

paras.t: Insuper, quamvis Thomas super secundum, sequatur (ut dictum est) Augustinum, attamen recitando alias duas opiniones, quibus materia prima in principio dicitur creata informis, seu aliquo modo formata, magis approbat expositionem eorum, qui dicunt materiam primo creatam sub substantialibus formis distinctis, ita quod corpora cœlestia et elementa in principio condita sint sub formis suis specificis, ut plenius dictum est. Aliam autem positionem, quæ dicit materiam primo creatam sub communi forma corporeitatis, potius reprobat, eo quod juxta philosophos, inter materiam primam et formas elementares, non sit intermedia forma substantialis. Quod si quis cum Avicebron in libro Fontis vitæ, formam corporeitatis a materia inseparabilem esse affirmet, non videtur hoc posse salvari, eo quod forma substantialis det esse simpliciter, et quod advenit enti in actu, est accidens. Sic quoque viderentur duæ formæ substantiales in eodem esse composito.
paras.en: Moreover, although Thomas on the second book follows Augustine, as has been said, yet in reciting the two other opinions, by which prime matter is said to have been created in the beginning formless, or in some way formed, he rather approves the exposition of those who say that the matter first created was under distinct substantial forms, so that the heavenly bodies and the elements were made in the beginning under their specific forms, as was said more fully above. The other position, however, which says that the matter first created was under the common form of corporeity, he rather rejects, because according to the philosophers there is no intermediate substantial form between prime matter and the elemental forms. And if anyone, with Avicebron in the book Fount of Life, affirms that the form of corporeity is inseparable from matter, this does not seem tenable, because a substantial form gives being simply, and what comes to a being already in act is an accident. So too there would seem to be two substantial forms in the same composite.

paras.t: Porro Bonaventura magis approbat opinionem dicentium materiam primo productam sub communi forma corporeitatis. Sed, quoniam brevitati nunc studeo, et ista materia super secundum Sententiarum a doctoribus plenissime ventilatur, disputatur, ac pertractatur, ideo horum doctorum rationes et solutiones ac replicationes dimitto.
paras.en: Bonaventure, on the other hand, rather approves the opinion of those who say that matter was first produced under the common form of corporeity. But since I am now studying brevity, and this matter is very fully aired, disputed and treated by the doctors on the second book of the Sentences, I leave aside the arguments, solutions and replies of these doctors.

paras.t: Et quantum capere valeo, opinio ista quam approbat Thomas magis quam aliam, inter omnes opiniones et expositiones verior mihi apparet. Primo, quoniam textui consonantior esse censetur. Nam in exordio Genesis statim ante opus secundæ diei, cœlum, terra, et aqua, propriis exprimuntur nominibus : similiter de abysso fit mentio nomine speciali. Ergo apparet quod propriis formis fuerint tunc distincta, quantum ad esse specificum. Ista quoque positio minus recedit ab Augustini opinione. Rursus, qui dicunt materiam sub forma corporeitatis productam, dicunt terram tertio die formatam seu factam : quod textui consonum non videtur, quum infra in descriptione operis tertiæ diei dicatur : Congregentur aquæ in unum locum, et appareat arida : ergo terra seu arida tunc fuit ostensa, non facta. In Psalmo quoque habetur : Initio tu Domine terram fundasti ; ergo fundata et facta est in principio creationis.
paras.en: And as far as I can grasp, the opinion which Thomas approves more than the other seems to me the truer among all the opinions and expositions. First, because it is judged more consonant with the text. For at the opening of Genesis, immediately before the work of the second day, heaven, earth and water are expressed by their proper names; likewise the abyss [in the Douay-Rheims "the deep", v. 2] is mentioned by a special name. It appears, therefore, that they were then distinct by their proper forms, as to their specific being. This position also departs less from Augustine's opinion. Again, those who say that matter was produced under the form of corporeity say that the earth was formed or made on the third day: which does not seem consonant with the text, since below, in the description of the work of the third day, it is said: [[1:9|Let the waters|Congregentur aquæ]] [[1:9|be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|in unum locum, et appareat arida]]: therefore the earth, or dry land, was then shown, not made. In the Psalm too we have: [[Ps 101:26|In the beginning, O Lord, thou foundedst the earth|Initio tu Domine terram fundasti]]; therefore it was founded and made in the beginning of creation.

paras.t: Insuper Rabbi Moyses dicit, quod Moyses in exordio Genesis expressit duo elementa aperte, videlicet terram et aquam : alia duo obscure, ita quod aerem designavit per spiritum, dicens, Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas : ignem vero per tenebras, quoniam ignis in propria sphæra non lucet ad extra, ob suæ raritatem seu subtilitatem materiæ. Amplius, secundum quod recitant Lyra et Rabbi Paulus, multi alii Hebræorum doctores sunt hujus opinionis. Sed et Hugo in libris de Sacramentis, magis assentit huic positioni. Ad idem quoque allegat Thomas Magistrum Sententiarum, et verum est, quod Magister in aliquibus passibus hoc sentire videtur : nihilo minus ponit et aliqua verba pro alia opinione.
paras.en: Moreover, Rabbi Moses [Maimonides] says that Moses at the opening of Genesis expressed two elements openly, namely earth and water, and the other two obscurely: so that he signified air by the spirit [*spiritus*, which also means breath or wind], saying, [[1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas]], and fire by the darkness, since fire in its own sphere does not shine outwards, because of the rarity or subtlety of its matter. Further, according to what Lyra and Rabbi Paul relate, many other doctors of the Hebrews are of this opinion. Hugh too, in the books On the Sacraments, rather assents to this position. To the same effect Thomas also cites the Master of the Sentences; and it is true that the Master seems to hold this in some passages; nevertheless he also puts down some words for the other opinion.

paras.t: Postremo, ad consentiendum expositioni eorum, qui dicunt opera creationis condita sex diebus, potissime movet me auctoritas divini et sacratissimi Dionysii, studiosissimi et illuminatissimi viri, qui fuit apostoli Pauli discipulus, aliisque Apostolis notus et carus, qui in rebus difficillimis et locis obscurissimis Prophetarum, informationem petivit ab ipsis Apostolis, præsertim a beatissimo Paulo, atque ab aliis apostolicis viris, prout ipse in suis crebro voluminibus tangit : a quibus si intellexisset omnia simul distincte producta, verisimile reor quod in suis libris hoc tetigisset : quum ergo non tangat hoc, sed ejus oppositum, utpote quod per intervalla dierum sint facta, patet propositum. Quod autem Dionysius insinuet res factas per temporum intervalla, probatur ex his, quæ scribit in libro de Divinis nominibus capitulo 4. Unde et Thomas super secundum, et in prima parte, quæstione 67, allegat Dionysium ibidem dicentem, quod lumen solis est lux illa, quam Moyses in primis tribus diebus nostri temporis narrat, quamvis tunc esset informe, prout infra dicetur. Unde elicitur, quod juxta Dionysii mentem, etiam substantia solis facta sit prima die, quia lux solis non fuit ante substantiam ejus. Parique ratione alia corpora cœlestia in suis formis substantialibus facta sunt prima die. Ex quibus probatur, quod ista positio de productione materiæ sub formis distinctis, quantum ad essentiales mundi partes, fuit de mente maximi theologi Dionysii : quod potissime me induxit ad consentiendum positioni præfatæ.
paras.en: Lastly, what most moves me to agree with the exposition of those who say that the works of creation were made in six days is the authority of the divine and most sacred Dionysius, a most studious and most enlightened man, who was a disciple of the apostle Paul, and known and dear to the other Apostles; who in the most difficult matters and the most obscure places of the Prophets sought instruction from the Apostles themselves, especially from the most blessed Paul, and from other apostolic men, as he himself often touches on in his volumes. If he had understood from them that all things were produced distinct at once, I think it likely that he would have touched on this in his books; since, then, he does not touch on this, but on its opposite, namely that they were made at intervals of days, the point is clear. And that Dionysius implies that things were made at intervals of time is proved from what he writes in the book On the Divine Names, chapter 4. Hence Thomas too, on the second book and in the first part, question 67, cites Dionysius saying there that the light of the sun is that light which Moses tells of in the first three days of our time, though it was then formless, as will be said below. From this it is gathered that, in Dionysius's mind, the substance of the sun too was made on the first day, since the light of the sun was not before its substance; and by like reasoning the other heavenly bodies were made on the first day in their substantial forms. From which it is proved that this position on the production of matter under distinct forms, as to the essential parts of the world, was the mind of that greatest of theologians, Dionysius: and this most of all led me to agree with the aforesaid position.

1.title: Expositio verborum sequentium: Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, et spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas
1.title_en: Exposition of the words that follow: “And the earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moved over the waters”

paras.t: Licet præcedenti articulo magis approbaverim atque secutus sim eos, qui dicunt, opera sex dierum per temporum intervalla esse producta, et materiam in exordio creatam sub substantialibus formis distinctis, quantum ad essentiales principalesque partes mundi sensibilis, quæ sunt corpora cœlestia et quatuor elementa: nihilo minus intendo textum exponere, etiam juxta aliorum intentionem. Itaque sequendo expositionem illam amplius approbatam, eo quod textui et antiquioribus Patribus ac doctoribus sanctis consonantior videatur, sic exponenda sunt verba sequentia:
paras.en: Although in the preceding article I have rather approved and followed those who say that the works of the six days were produced over intervals of time, and that matter was created in the beginning under distinct substantial forms as regards the essential and principal parts of the sensible world, which are the heavenly bodies and the four elements, I nevertheless mean to expound the text according to the mind of the others as well. And so, following the exposition that is more approved, because it seems more in keeping with the text and with the more ancient Fathers and holy doctors, the following words are to be expounded thus:

paras.t: Terra autem erat inanis et vacua. Pro eo quod hic dicitur, Terra erat inanis et vacua, alia translatio qua utitur Origenes, sic continet: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita. Idcirco quidam exponunt hanc litteram sic: Terra erat inanis, id est invisibilis corporali adspectu, quoniam erat aquis undique cooperta, quæ etiam aquæ fuerunt in inferiori parte densiores seu grossiores. Et vacua, hoc est, plantis et herbis ac ceteris fructibus ex ea tunc nascituris, nondum impleta aut decorata: quod alia littera vocat, incomposita. Unde Josephus refert: Sed dum terra ad adspectum non veniret, et profunditate aquarum ac tenebris celaretur, Deus lumen fieri jussit.
paras.en: [[1:2|And the earth was void and empty|Terra autem erat inanis et vacua]]. In place of what is said here, [[1:2|the earth was void and empty|Terra erat inanis et vacua]], another translation, which Origen uses, reads thus: But the earth was invisible and unformed [*incomposita*: not yet put together or set in order]. Therefore some expound this text thus: [[1:2|the earth was void|Terra erat inanis]], that is, invisible to bodily sight, because it was covered on every side by waters, which waters were also denser or thicker in the lower part. [[1:2|and empty|Et vacua]], that is, not yet filled or adorned with the plants and herbs and other fruits that were then to spring from it: which the other reading calls *unformed*. Hence Josephus relates [Jewish Antiquities I, 1, as the margin notes]: But while the earth did not come into sight, and was hidden by the depth of the waters and by darkness, God commanded light to be made.

paras.t: Hinc alii sic exponunt: Terra erat inanis et vacua, id est, elementum terræ erat adhuc infructuosum, sive inutile ac sine ornatu. Nondum etenim apta fuit habitationi ac usui hominum, propter quos fuit creata. Hinc ait Strabus: Terra erat inanis et vacua, id est inutilis, infructuosa, et incomposita. Omnia namque elementa commixta fuerant et confusa, et totum hoc aeris spatium exstitit aquis plenum, non quales nunc sunt, sed instar nebulæ tenues erant.
paras.en: Hence others expound thus: [[1:2|the earth was void and empty|Terra erat inanis et vacua]], that is, the element of earth was as yet unfruitful, or useless and without adornment; for it was not yet fit for the dwelling and use of men, for whose sake it was created. Hence Strabo says: [[1:2|the earth was void and empty|Terra erat inanis et vacua]], that is, useless, unfruitful and unformed. For all the elements had been mingled and confused, and the whole of this space of the air was full of waters, not such as they are now: they were thin, like a mist.

paras.t: Quod si ista sunt verba Strabi, ut allegatur in Glossa, quomodo verum est quod quidam asserit, secundum Strabum et Bedam, materiam primo fuisse creatam sub communi forma corporeitatis, non sub distinctis formis substantialibus elementorum, præsertim quum in eadem Glossa inducantur verba Bedæ, dicentis, Deus aquas cum cœlo prius creavit? Denique Damascenus libro secundo aperte insinuat, terram et aquam in principio sub propriis formis substantialibus esse creatas, dicendo: Terra est unum elementorum siccum, frigidum, grave, immobile, ex non ente ad esse prima die a Deo deductum. In principio enim creavit Deus cœlum et terram. De aqua quoque sic ait: Aqua est unum quatuor elementorum, humidum, frigidum. Hæc in principio super omnem terram redundavit. His concordat Basilius, dicens: Moyses primo non exprimit, nisi cœlum et terram, quatenus per hæc duo extrema, intelligantur et media. Ex quibus ostenditur, quod quum dicitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram: nomine terræ intelligitur elementum terræ explicite, et alia tria elementa implicite, et per cœlum, omnia cœlestia corpora, quantum ad suæ substantiæ productionem.
paras.en: But if these are the words of Strabo, as they are cited in the Gloss, how is it true, as a certain writer asserts, that according to Strabo and Bede matter was first created under the common form of corporeity [that is, the bare form of being a body, without the distinct forms of the elements], and not under the distinct substantial forms of the elements; especially since in the same Gloss are brought in the words of Bede, who says: God first created the waters together with the heaven? Then too Damascene, in his second book [On the Orthodox Faith], plainly indicates that earth and water were created in the beginning under their own substantial forms, when he says: Earth is one of the elements, dry, cold, heavy, immovable, brought by God from non-being into being on the first day. For [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. Of water too he says thus: Water is one of the four elements, moist and cold. In the beginning it overflowed over all the earth. With these Basil agrees, saying: Moses at first expresses only heaven and earth, so that by these two extremes the middle ones too may be understood. From which it is shown that when it is said, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], by the name of earth the element of earth is understood explicitly and the other three elements implicitly, and by heaven all the heavenly bodies, as regards the production of their substance.

paras.t: Et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi. Per abyssum, quidam intelligunt congeriem seu universitatem quatuor elementorum; alii, alia tria elementa simul permixta, videlicet aquam, aerem et ignem; alii aquam. Ait equidem Damascenus: Abyssus aliud nihil est, nisi aqua multa, cujus finis incomprehensibilis est hominibus. Et Rabbi Paulus: Abyssus, inquit, secundum grammaticos, impenetrabilem aquarum multitudinem signat, quæ impenetrabilitas intelligi potest non solum ex magna aquæ profunditate, sed item ex hoc quod ex sua circumfusione, qua ambit terram, visu penetrari non potest. Per quod intelligitur aqua elementaris, quæ ante suam congregationem confuse permixta fuit igni et aeri: quod totum dicitur nunc abyssus. Qualitercumque autem sumatur abyssus, constat quod tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi. Nondum enim creata fuit lux corporalis, idcirco tenebræ, quæ sunt carentia hujuscemodi lucis, operiebant omnia elementa, imo et cœlestia corpora, dempto cœlo empyreo.
paras.en: [[1:2|and darkness was upon the face of the deep|Et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]]. By the deep [*abyssus*] some understand the mass or totality of the four elements; others, the other three elements mingled together, namely water, air and fire; others, water. Damascene indeed says: The deep is nothing else than a great water, whose end is beyond the comprehension of men. And Rabbi Paul [of Burgos]: The deep, he says, according to the grammarians, signifies an impenetrable multitude of waters; and this impenetrability can be understood not only from the great depth of the water, but also from this, that because it is spread round about and encircles the earth, it cannot be penetrated by sight. By this is understood elemental water, which before its gathering together was confusedly mingled with fire and air: the whole of which is here called the deep. But however the deep be taken, it is certain that [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]]. For bodily light had not yet been created; therefore darkness, which is the lack of such light, covered all the elements, and even the heavenly bodies, except the empyrean heaven.

paras.t: Et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas. Per Spiritum Domini, intelligi potest voluntas Dei seu Spiritus Sanctus, quæ et qui ferebatur non motu locali, sed dispositione mentali super aquas, sicut voluntas artificis fertur super materiam quam habet præ oculis, dum eam formare ac decorare proponit. Et potest per aquas, elementum aquæ intelligi, quia ex aqua generantur plurima animalium genera, et semina rerum sunt humida: nec terra sine aqua est fructuosa, sed sterilis. Propter quod asserit Damascenus: Aqua est creatura Dei optima. Alii per aquas intelligunt congeriem elementorum, quia non aquam tantum, sed et alia elementa voluit Deus formare ornare, et diversa mixta ex eis producere. Hunc secundum Hieronymum in Hebræo habetur, […], quod tantum valet sicut, Fovebat aut Incubabat: ad insinuandum quod Spiritus Sanctus instar avis ova suo calore foventis, super aquas incubabat et eas fovebat, dando eis virtutem causalem tam specialem.
paras.en: [[1:2|and the spirit of God moved over the waters|Et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]] [Denis reads *Spiritus Domini*, “the Spirit of the Lord”, where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have “spirit of God”; his argument below turns on the word]. By the Spirit of the Lord can be understood the will of God, or the Holy Ghost, which moved over the waters not by local motion but by the disposition of the mind, as the will of a craftsman moves over the material he has before his eyes when he purposes to form and adorn it. And by the waters the element of water can be understood, because from water very many kinds of animals are generated, and the seeds of things are moist; nor is the earth fruitful without water, but barren. For which reason Damascene asserts: Water is a most excellent creature of God. Others understand by the waters the mass of the elements, because God willed to form and adorn not water only but the other elements too, and to produce various mixed bodies from them. Here, according to Jerome, the Hebrew has […] [the word is illegible in the scan; the Hebrew of this verse has *merachepheth*], which is as much as to say, *was cherishing* or *was brooding*: to signify that the Holy Ghost, like a bird cherishing its eggs with its warmth, brooded over the waters and cherished them, giving them a causal power so special.

paras.t: Insuper, ut recitat Augustinus libro de Civitate Dei, Plato per Spiritum Domini qui ferebatur super aquas, intellexit aerem, qui sæpe spiritus appellatur, et in hoc Rabbi Moyses Platonem secutus est, sed convenientius exponitur de Spiritu Sancto. Aer enim nondum divisus fuit ab aqua, nec superior ea; imo aqua totum occupaverat spatium usque ad cœlestium corporum regionem. Nec videtur cur Moyses potius dixisset de aere, spiritus Domini, quam de terra aut aqua, terra Domini, aut aqua Domini. Præterea, Rabbi Paulus scribit hoc loco: Antiqui expositores Hebræorum, compendiose ac notabilissime exposuerunt hoc verbum in libro qui dicitur, Bresith Rabba, ubi interrogative sic dicitur: Quid est quod dicitur, Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas? Et respondetur, Nihil aliud est quam qui dicitur Spiritus Messiæ, de quo scriptum est: Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini. Unde constat quod per Spiritum Domini, intelligatur nunc Spiritus Sanctus.
paras.en: Moreover, as Augustine relates in the book of the City of God, Plato understood by the Spirit of the Lord that moved over the waters the air, which is often called *spirit* [*spiritus*: “breath”, “wind”], and in this Rabbi Moses followed Plato; but it is more fittingly expounded of the Holy Ghost. For the air had not yet been divided from the water, nor was it above it; rather, the water had filled the whole space up to the region of the heavenly bodies. Nor is it plain why Moses should have said *spirit of the Lord* of the air rather than *earth of the Lord* or *water of the Lord* of the earth or the water. Further, Rabbi Paul writes on this place: The ancient expositors of the Hebrews expounded this word briefly and most notably in the book called Bresith Rabba, where it is asked thus: What is it that is said, [[1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]]? And the answer is: It is nothing else than what is called the Spirit of the Messias, of whom it is written: [[Is 11:2|the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him|Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini]]. Whence it is plain that by the Spirit of the Lord is here understood the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Quantum ad aliorum opinionem, exponendo hunc passum, sciendum quod quamvis Augustinus dicat opera sex dierum simul distincte producta, in hoc tamen convenit cum his, qui dicunt materiam primo creatam sub sola forma corporeitatis, quod materiam primam informem dicit in principio Genesis designari nomine terræ, et etiam nomine aquæ atque abyssi: per quæ omnia, etiam illi dicunt designari non ipsa elementa, sed eamdem informem materiam, de qua dicunt elementa esse formata.
paras.en: As for the opinion of the others, in expounding this passage it is to be known that although Augustine says the works of the six days were produced distinctly all at once, he nevertheless agrees with those who say that matter was first created under the form of corporeity alone in this: that he says unformed prime matter is designated at the beginning of Genesis by the name of earth, and also by the name of water and of the deep; by all of which those others too say is designated, not the elements themselves, but that same unformed matter from which, they say, the elements were formed.

paras.t: Itaque secundum Augustinum, tenebræ erant super terram, id est informem illam materiam, non temporali duratione, cum dicat omnia simul facta, distincta, formata, sed ordine naturæ: quia materia illa secundum se accepta et considerata, fuit in se tenebrosa, carens omni perfectione et claritate formali. Fuit quoque materia illa secundum se inanis et vacua, utpote destituta formis et omni ornatu. Hinc super secundum Thomas testatur: Si per terram intelligatur informis materia, tunc per verba hæc designatur receptibilitas materiæ, quæ quodammodo similis est receptibilitati loci. Propter quod Plato materiam vocavit locum. Ideo quæ sunt loci, similitudinarie dicuntur de ea, ut materia dicatur vacua, in quantum forma replet capacitatem materiæ; inanis vero, in quantum forma est finis appetitus ipsius. Sed Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas, hoc est super hanc ipsam materiam, in quantum intendebat ex ea producere multa, sicut mens seu consideratio artificis fertur super artificiata.
paras.en: And so, according to Augustine, darkness was upon the earth, that is, upon that unformed matter, not in temporal duration, since he says that all things were made, distinguished and formed at once, but in the order of nature: because that matter, taken and considered in itself, was dark in itself, lacking all perfection and formal brightness. That matter too was, in itself, [[1:2|void and empty|inanis et vacua]], being destitute of forms and of all adornment. Hence Thomas, on the second book [of the Sentences], testifies: If by the earth unformed matter is understood, then by these words is designated the receptivity of matter, which is in a way like the receptivity of place. For which reason Plato called matter place. Therefore what belongs to place is said of it by likeness, so that matter is called *empty* inasmuch as form fills the capacity of matter, and *void* inasmuch as form is the end of its appetite. But [[1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]], that is, over this same matter, inasmuch as he intended to produce many things from it, as the mind or thought of a craftsman moves over the things he makes.

paras.t: Porro secundum alios, super materiam illam forma corporeitatis informatam, sed respectu specificarum formarum informem, erant tenebræ quousque producta est lux corporalis; eratque terra, id est materia illa, inanis et vacua, quoniam distinctis et propriis formis carebat, nec fuit polita nec fructifera. Ferebatur itidem super eam Spiritus Domini, juxta sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: According to the others, again, there was darkness over that matter, formed by the form of corporeity but unformed as regards the specific forms, until bodily light was produced; and [[1:2|the earth was|eratque terra]], that is, that matter, [[1:2|void and empty|inanis et vacua]], since it lacked distinct and proper forms, and was neither finished nor fruitful. The Spirit of the Lord likewise moved over it, in the sense given above.

paras.t: Postremo Rabbi Paulus hoc loco per faciem abyssi intelligit cœlum crystallinum, in quo dicit fuisse tenebras, quoniam capax fuit lucis tanquam diaphanum. Multitudinem vero aquarum dicit fuisse abyssum, vel aquam tam turbidam et opacam, quod non fuerat lucis capax sicut nec terra. Idcirco non dicuntur proprie fuisse tenebræ in abysso, sicut nec cæcitas in ligno. Istud non videtur solide dictum. Primo, quia Scriptura non dicit, Tenebræ erant super superficiem abyssi, sed super faciem abyssi. Secundo, quoniam nec cœlum crystallinum, nec aliquod cœlum dicitur proprie superficies aquæ, sive loquamur de superficie extrinseca, sive de superficie intrinseca. Locus quippe est extrinseca superficies corporis locati, atque intrinseca superficies corporis continentis. Locus autem est in genere quantitatis, cælum autem in prædicamento substantiæ. Quod si cælum ratione sui ultimi seu suæ superficiei, dicatur superficies aquæ illius, hoc oportet intelligi de superficie aquæ extrinseca. Per faciem autem aquæ, intelligenda esset potius superficies ejus intrinseca, utpote ei inhærens, quam superficies ejus extrinseca. Sic enim in Scripturis communiter accipitur facies corporalium inanimatarumque rerum. Tertio, quia ex verbis Sanctorum et expositorum jam patuit, quod aqua illa erat instar nebulæ tenuis et subtilis, præsertim in superioribus partibus, ubi lux magis fulgebat atque vicinior fuit statim ut facta est: ergo aqua illa erat valde capax lucis illius, nec fuit opaca. Quarto, nam dato quod fuisset turbida et opaca, tamen potuisset illuminari, quemadmodum modo terra et densissimæ nubes recipiunt influentiam lucis. Quinto, nam ubi nostra translatio habet, Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi: alia translatio, quam et Origenes exponit, sic continet, Tenebræ erant super abyssum. Sexto, nam dato quod lux non potuisset eam attingere, nihilo minus tenebræ, proprie loquendo, fuissent in ea: quia ex sua natura ipsi competit esse lucis capacem, quemadmodum cæcus a nativitate, dicitur proprie cæcus. Septimo, quoniam secundum omnes expositores præfatos, per faciem abyssi, intelligitur ipsa abyssus. Unde et undecimo de Civitate Dei, cap. 9, loquitur Augustinus: Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, id est super quamdam terræ et aquæ indistinctam confusionem. Hinc ait Magister libro secundo: Nec mirum lucem posse in aquis lucere, quæ multo rariores fuerunt in principio, quam sint modo.
paras.en: Lastly, Rabbi Paul on this place understands by [[1:2|the face of the deep|faciem abyssi]] the crystalline heaven, in which he says there was darkness, since, being transparent, it was capable of light. But the multitude of the waters, he says, was the deep, or water so turbid and opaque that it was no more capable of light than the earth; and therefore there is not properly said to have been darkness in the deep, any more than blindness in a piece of wood. This does not seem soundly said. First, because Scripture does not say, Darkness was upon the surface of the deep, but [[1:2|upon the face of the deep|super faciem abyssi]]. Secondly, because neither the crystalline heaven nor any heaven is properly called the surface of the water, whether we speak of the outer surface or of the inner. For place is the outer surface of the body placed, and the inner surface of the body containing it; and place is in the genus of quantity, but heaven in the category of substance. And if heaven, by reason of its outermost part or its surface, were called the surface of that water, this would have to be understood of the outer surface of the water; but by the face of the water would rather be understood its inner surface, as inhering in it, than its outer surface: for so is the face of bodily and lifeless things commonly taken in the Scriptures. Thirdly, because it has already been made plain from the words of the Saints and the expositors that that water was like a thin and fine mist, especially in the upper parts, where the light shone more brightly and was nearer as soon as it was made: therefore that water was very capable of that light, and was not opaque. Fourthly, because, granted that it had been turbid and opaque, it could still have been lit up, as now the earth and the densest clouds receive the influence of light. Fifthly, because where our translation has, [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]], another translation, which Origen also expounds, reads thus: Darkness was upon the deep. Sixthly, because, granted that the light could not have reached it, there would nonetheless, properly speaking, have been darkness in it: for it belongs to it by its nature to be capable of light, just as one blind from birth is properly called blind. Seventhly, because according to all the expositors mentioned, by the face of the deep the deep itself is understood. Whence Augustine too says in the eleventh book of the City of God, chapter 9: [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]], that is, upon a certain undistinguished confusion of earth and water. Hence the Master [of the Sentences] says in the second book: Nor is it strange that light could shine in the waters, which were much rarer in the beginning than they are now.

paras.t: Iterum ait hic Rabbi Paulus, quod per id quod dictum est, Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas: intelligitur motus primi mobilis, per quem Deus aquam vivificavit; quia ut dicitur octavo Physicorum, Motus cœli est quasi vita omnium inferiorum, qui motus adscribendus est Deo, tanquam causæ primæ ac principali. Istud stare non potest: Scriptura enim hic loquitur de virtute causali, aquæ collata immediate a Deo a suæ creationis exordio, quam non habet per motum cœli aut mobilis primi. Et istud plenius scribit Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 74, ubi ad hoc allegat Basilium.
paras.en: Again, Rabbi Paul says here that by what is said, [[1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]], is understood the motion of the first movable [that is, the outermost moving sphere, whose motion carries the heavens beneath it], by which God gave life to the water; because, as is said in the eighth book of the Physics, the motion of the heaven is as it were the life of all lower things; and this motion is to be ascribed to God as to the first and principal cause. This cannot stand: for Scripture here speaks of a causal power bestowed on the water immediately by God from the very beginning of its creation, which it does not have through the motion of the heaven or of the first movable. And Thomas writes of this more fully in the First Part [of the Summa], question 74, where he cites Basil for it.

paras.t: At vero circa hæc verba, Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas, in Scholastica fertur historia: Hunc locum male intellexit Plato, putans hoc dictum de anima mundi. Miror unde auctor Historiæ illius acceperit hoc, præsertim quia jam dictum est, quod (ut recitat Augustinus) Plato per Spiritum Domini aerem intellexit. Quid autem Plato senserit de anima mundi, dictum est in expositione prologi hujus libri.
paras.en: But concerning these words, [[1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]], it is said in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]: Plato misunderstood this place, thinking it was said of the soul of the world. I wonder where the author of that History got this, especially since it has already been said that (as Augustine relates) Plato understood the air by the Spirit of the Lord. What Plato thought about the soul of the world was said in the exposition of the prologue of this book.

paras.t: Sed circa hæc quæri posset: Quid Plato scivit de ista scriptura, aut qualiter intromisit se de expositione ipsius? Respondendum, quia (ut octavo de Civitate Dei Augustinus tangit et sentire videtur) Plato in Ægypto per interpretem didicit libros Moysis. Nam et id quod Dominus dixit ad Moysen, Ego sum qui sum, Qui est, etc. Plato tenuit vehementer, et diligentissime commendavit memoriæ.
paras.en: But concerning this it might be asked: What did Plato know of this scripture, or how did he come to take a hand in expounding it? The answer is that (as Augustine touches on in the eighth book of the City of God, and seems to hold) Plato learned the books of Moses in Egypt through an interpreter. For that too which the Lord said to Moses, [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]], [[Ex 3:14|HE WHO IS|Qui est]], etc., Plato held to strongly and committed most diligently to memory.

1.title: Elucidatio ejus quod dicitur, Fiat lux, usque ad id, Dixit quoque Deus, Fiat firmamentum, etc.
1.title_en: Explanation of what is said from “Be light made” as far as “And God said: Let there be a firmament made”, etc.
