paras.t: Postquam Moyses dixit, Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, mox subdidit: Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat lux. Non enim decuit opus Dei tenebrosum manere. Denique, juxta expositores, hoc loco incipit Moyses opus distinctionis describere, declarando qualiter a principio una creatura divisa sit ac distincta ab aliis. Primo, ostendit qualiter divisa sit dies a nocte; secundo, tangit distinctionem cœlestium corporum; tertio, elementorum. Et quia eorum positio magis jam placuit, qui dicunt elementa atque cœlestia corpora ab initio simul producta, quantum ad eorum substantiam, ita quod distinctio et ornatus eorum attenduntur penes virtutes activas et passivas, et penes qualitates et proprietates accidentales: ita quod distinctio attenditur penes virtutes activas atque passivas communes, moventes ad omnem formam seu speciem corporalium ac generabilium rerum, sicut sunt calidum, frigidum, lux et humor; ornatus vero penes virtutes activas et passivas speciales, quæ movent ad formas et species determinatas, ut est virtus seminum, equi, leonis, et consimilium, secundum quod Thomas super secundum, distinctione 13, plenius docet: hinc per lucem, de qua nunc sermo, intelligitur lumen solis adhuc informe seu imperfectum, ut capitulo 4 de Divinis nominibus divinus Dionysius contestatur. Nam ante quartum diem, lux ista non est sortita determinatam ac plenam virtutem ad producendum particulares effectus.
paras.en: After Moses had said, [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]], he straightway added: [[1:3|And God said: Be light made|Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat lux]]. For it was not fitting that the work of God should remain in darkness. Further, according to the expositors, Moses begins at this place to describe the work of distinction [that is, the setting of creatures apart from one another, which follows the work of creation and goes before the work of adornment], declaring how from the beginning one creature was divided and distinguished from the others. First he shows how the day was divided from the night; secondly he touches on the distinction of the heavenly bodies; thirdly, on that of the elements. And since the position of those has now been preferred who say that the elements and the heavenly bodies were produced together from the beginning as regards their substance, so that their distinction and adornment are reckoned by active and passive powers and by accidental qualities and properties (distinction being reckoned by the common active and passive powers, which move toward every form or species of bodily and generable things, such as hot, cold, light and moisture; and adornment by the special active and passive powers, which move toward determinate forms and species, such as the power of seeds, of the horse, of the lion and the like, as Thomas teaches more fully on the second book [of the Sentences], distinction 13): therefore by the light of which there is now question is understood the light of the sun, still unformed or imperfect, as the divine Dionysius testifies in chapter 4 of On the Divine Names. For before the fourth day this light had not received a determinate and full power for producing particular effects.

paras.t: Dixit itaque Deus: Fiat lux. Quemadmodum autem Deus artifex summus est, simplicissimus spiritus, et sapientissimus actor: sic dicere ejus est spirituale ac intellectuale, non vocale aut transitorie sonans. Nec dixit istud per creaturam subjectam, sed sicut immediate produxit, ita per se dixit. Et hoc dicere Dei, est practicum intelligere ejus, quo vult seu præcipit aliquid esse. Sic igitur Deus trinitas, unus universorum creator, dixit, id est, intra se concepit, cogitavit ac jussit, Fiat lux, id est, substantia solis lucem aliqualem recipiat. Sol enim, quantum ad substantiam suam, factus est in principio, sed non splenduit clare. Et facta est lux: hoc est, Deo creante, sol lucem tantam accepit, sicut tunc decuit, et statui illi expediens fuit. Etenim idem est, rem fieri Deo jubente, et Deo agente; et dicere Dei, fecisse est; et ubi præcipit omnipotens virtus, mox servit effectus.
paras.en: So then [[1:3|God said: Be light made|Dixit itaque Deus: Fiat lux]]. Now as God is the supreme craftsman, the most simple spirit and the most wise maker, so his saying is spiritual and intellectual, not spoken aloud or sounding and passing away. Nor did he say this through some creature subject to him; but as he produced immediately, so he spoke by himself. And this saying of God is his practical understanding [that is, knowledge directed to making and doing], by which he wills or commands something to be. Thus God the Trinity, the one creator of all things, said, that is, conceived within himself, thought and commanded, [[1:3|Be light made|Fiat lux]], that is: let the substance of the sun receive some light. For the sun, as regards its substance, was made in the beginning, but it did not shine clearly. [[1:3|And light was made|Et facta est lux]]: that is, God creating, the sun received as much light as was then fitting and was expedient for that state. For it is the same for a thing to be made at God's command and by God's acting; and for God to say is to have made; and where the almighty power commands, the effect at once obeys.

paras.t: Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona: hoc est, intra se, atque in sapientia sua, æternaliter invariabiliterque cognovit, et tunc per effectum se cognoscere demonstravit, quod lux illa conveniens esset ac utilis, et placuit ei ut esset ac permaneret. Et divisit lucem a tenebris, id est, distinxit ac discrevit ab alio, ita quod ab invicem distinguuntur natura ac loco, tempore ac subjecto. Lux enim fuit in sole, tenebræ autem in loco, ad quem non pervenit diffusio seu emicatio lucis. Lux quoque est habitus, tenebræ autem privatio. Et quando lux fuit seu dies in uno hemisphærio, fuit caligo seu nox in hemisphærio alio; imo et in eodem hemisphærio erat jam lux, jam tenebræ, secundum motum ipsius solis, sicut et modo.
paras.en: [[1:4|And God saw the light that it was good|Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona]]: that is, within himself and in his wisdom he knew eternally and unchangeably, and then showed by the effect that he knew, that that light was fitting and useful; and it pleased him that it should be and remain. [[1:4|and he divided the light from the darkness|Et divisit lucem a tenebris]], that is, he distinguished and set the one apart from the other, so that they are distinguished from each other in nature and place, in time and subject. For the light was in the sun, but the darkness in the place to which the spreading or shining forth of the light did not reach. Light too is a habit [that is, a positive quality possessed], darkness a privation. And when there was light, or day, in one hemisphere, there was gloom, or night, in the other; and even in the same hemisphere there was now light, now darkness, according to the motion of the sun itself, just as there is now.

paras.t: Appellavitque lucem diem: hoc est, lucis illius emicationem super nostrum horizontem, seu spatium aut durationem illuminationis illius, cognovit atque instituit debere diem vocari in omni idiomate hominum per diversa vocabula. Simili sensu appellavit tenebras, id est absentiam lucis solaris, noctem. Denique, sicut Magister Sententiarum ait libro secundo, dies diversis modis accipitur: Primo, pro luce illa quæ in primo triduo mundi fulsit. Secundo, pro aeris illuminatione. Tertio, pro spatio viginti quatuor horarum, quod vocatur dies naturalis. Quarto, pro tempore motionis solis super nostrum horizontem, quod dicitur dies artificialis, et continet duodecim horas tempore æquinoctiali. Nox quoque diversis modis accipitur: Primo, pro lucis privatione; secundo, pro parte naturalis diei. Imo, utrumque horum accipitur in Scripturis aliis pluribus modis. Nunc autem quod dictum est, Appellavitque lucem diem, intelligendum est de die artificiali.
paras.en: [[1:5|And he called the light Day|Appellavitque lucem diem]]: that is, the shining forth of that light above our horizon, or the space or duration of that illumination, he knew and appointed was to be called day in every tongue of men, by their different words. In a like sense he called [[1:5|the darkness|tenebras]], that is, the absence of the sun's light, [[1:5|Night|noctem]]. Further, as the Master of the Sentences says in the second book, day is taken in various ways: first, for that light which shone in the first three days of the world; secondly, for the lighting of the air; thirdly, for the space of twenty-four hours, which is called the natural day; fourthly, for the time of the sun's movement above our horizon, which is called the artificial day, and contains twelve hours at the time of the equinox. Night too is taken in various ways: first, for the privation of light; secondly, for a part of the natural day. Indeed, each of these is taken in the Scriptures in many other ways besides. But what has been said here, [[1:5|And he called the light Day|Appellavitque lucem diem]], is to be understood of the artificial day.

paras.t: Porro quod subditur, Factumque est vespere et mane dies unus: intelligendum est de die naturali, qui noctem includit, ut sit sensus: Factum est vespere, id est, spatium diei seu illuminationis illius, pervenit usque ad vesperam seu noctis initium, sole recedente ab hemisphærio nostro, et postea factum est mane, nocte ipsa completa, soleque redeunte ad hemisphærium nostrum. Et mane illud fuit exordium diei sequentis, quia tunc dies incepit a luce. Sicque Moyses exprimendo imprimis finem diei artificialis, videlicet vesperam, deinde finem noctis ejusdem diei, insinuat consummationem naturalis diei unius seu primi. Ista expositio juxta prætactam positionem procedit.
paras.en: Again, what is added, [[1:5|and there was evening and morning one day|Factumque est vespere et mane dies unus]], is to be understood of the natural day, which includes the night, so that the sense is: [[1:5|there was evening|Factum est vespere]], that is, the space of the day, or of that illumination, reached to the evening or beginning of the night, as the sun withdrew from our hemisphere; and afterwards there was [[1:5|morning|mane]], the night itself being completed and the sun returning to our hemisphere. And that morning was the beginning of the following day, since the day then began from the light. And so Moses, by expressing first the end of the artificial day, namely the evening, and then the end of the night of the same day, indicates the completion of one natural day, the first. This exposition proceeds according to the position touched on above.

paras.t: Præterea, qui dicunt materiam primo creatam sub sola forma corporeitatis, intelligunt per hanc lucem, quamdam splendidam nubem factam in ea parte ubi sol currit, quam dicunt factam ex informi illa materia, et motam motu circulari, sicut movetur nunc sol: ac motu suo causasse diem ac noctem, non tamen fuisse tam claram et efficacem, sicut nunc sol est. Et aliqui dicunt eam factam in oriente, ubi sol factus est. Quidam vero in altiori spatio seu medio, utpote in meridie, unde descendit: quia secundum Bedam, dies illa a plena luce incepit. Cetera verba litteræ hujus, secundum istam opinionem proportionabiliter intelliguntur, sicut præhabitum est.
paras.en: Moreover, those who say that matter was first created under the form of corporeity alone understand by this light a certain bright cloud, made in that part where the sun runs its course, which they say was made from that unformed matter and moved with a circular motion, as the sun now moves, and by its motion caused day and night, yet was not so bright and effective as the sun now is. And some say it was made in the east, where the sun was made; others in a higher or middle space, namely at midday, whence it descended, because according to Bede that day began from full light. The other words of this text are understood correspondingly according to this opinion, as was set out above.

paras.t: De hac luce ac nube ait Magister: Lux illa corpus lucidum fuit, velut lucida nubes, et vicem ac locum solis tenebat. Fuit quoque nox in triduo illo penitus tenebrosa, quia nec luna nec stellæ tunc erant. Insuper, quemadmodum Augustinus per cœlum in exordio factum, intelligit naturam angelicam, ut informem, seu ut nondum ad Creatorem per amorem conversam; ita per lucem, de qua Scriptura nunc agit, intelligit eamdem naturam seu angelos sanctos, ut formatos, atque ad incommutabile lumen conversos, in quibus tunc divisa est lux a tenebris, id est formatio eorum ab informitate prætacta. Nam angeli in se considerati, quantum ad naturalia sua, quasi tenebræ sunt respectu perfectionis et lucis, quam habent per dona gratuita, et ex conversione sua ad Creatorem. Verumtamen de expositione Augustini, et qualiter secundum eam salvetur et accipiatur sex seu septem dierum distinctio, infra in speciali articulo plenius ostendetur.
paras.en: Of this light and cloud the Master says: That light was a luminous body, like a bright cloud, and held the office and place of the sun. And the night in those three days was wholly dark, since there was then neither moon nor stars. Moreover, just as Augustine understands by the heaven made in the beginning the angelic nature as unformed, that is, as not yet turned to the Creator by love, so by the light of which Scripture now treats he understands the same nature, or the holy angels, as formed and turned to the unchangeable light; in whom the light was then divided from the darkness, that is, their formation from the unformedness just mentioned. For the angels considered in themselves, as to their natural endowments, are as it were darkness in respect of the perfection and light which they have through the gifts of grace and from their turning to the Creator. But of Augustine's exposition, and of how according to it the distinction of six or seven days is kept and understood, more will be shown below in an article of its own.

paras.t: Præterea, circa hanc litteram dubitationes occurrunt: Prima est, an inter creationem et distinctionem fuerit aliqua temporis mora. Secunda est, an ante primam diem et noctem fuerit aliquod tempus. Tertia, quare distinctio creaturarum incepit a luce. Quarta, de varia inceptione diei ac noctis. Quinta, an Deus incepit opus suum a tenebris. Sexta, quid factum sit de luce illa secundum eos, qui dicunt eam fuisse candidam nubem. Septima, quæ positio videatur rationabilior de modo, quo lux illa causavit diem noctemque.
paras.en: Further, concerning this text questions arise [seven questions, as the margin notes]. The first is whether there was any lapse of time between creation and distinction. The second, whether before the first day and night there was any time. The third, why the distinction of creatures began from light. The fourth, of the different reckonings of the beginning of day and night. The fifth, whether God began his work from darkness. The sixth, what became of that light, according to those who say that it was a white cloud. The seventh, which position seems more reasonable about the way in which that light caused day and night.

paras.t: Ad primam quæstionum istarum respondet Bonaventura super secundum, distinctione 12 ac 13, dicens: Creatio cœli ac terræ, secundum omnes doctores, fuit ante omnem diem prioritate naturæ; quantum vero ad ordinem temporis sive durationis, diversimode senserunt diversi. Quidam namque dixerunt, quod non fuerit aliqua mora inter creationem et distinctionis inceptionem; sed statim quando producta est informis illa materia, lux quoque quæ diem faciebat, producta sit. Aliis videtur, quod intervenerit aliqua mora, quod videtur magis consonum sententiæ expositorum. Quid autem horum sit verius, non est certum. Hæc Bonaventura. Thomas quoque super secundum ait: Quidam dicunt, quod opus distinctionis statim cum opere creationis incepit, et quod ideo lux statim creata sit cum primo creatis, sicque Deus non incepisset opus suum a tenebris. Et hoc oportet dicere secundum expositionem Augustini, qui etiam vult quod creatio informis materiæ intelligatur ante omnem diem, non tempore, sed natura. Alii dicunt, quod prius tempore fuit opus creationis, et postea per aliquod temporis intervallum formata sit lux. Sicque affirmant opus creationis ante omnem diem fuisse. Et hoc magis consonat textui Genesis secundum planitiem suam. Nam creatione cœli et terræ descripta, mox subdit, tenebras super faciem fuisse abyssi, deinde agit de lucis productione. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: To the first of these questions Bonaventure answers, on the second book [of the Sentences], distinctions 12 and 13, saying: The creation of heaven and earth, according to all the doctors, was before every day by priority of nature; but as to the order of time or duration, different men have thought differently. For some have said that there was no lapse between creation and the beginning of distinction, but that as soon as that unformed matter was produced, the light too which made the day was produced. To others it seems that some lapse came between, which seems more in keeping with the mind of the expositors. Which of these is truer is not certain. Thus far Bonaventure. Thomas too says on the second book: Some say that the work of distinction began at once with the work of creation, and that therefore light was created at once with the things first created, and so God would not have begun his work from darkness. And this must be said according to the exposition of Augustine, who also holds that the creation of unformed matter is to be understood as before every day, not in time but in nature. Others say that the work of creation was first in time, and that afterwards, after some interval of time, light was formed; and so they affirm that the work of creation was before every day. And this agrees better with the text of Genesis taken in its plain sense. For when the creation of heaven and earth has been described, it straightway adds that darkness was upon the face of the deep, and then treats of the production of light. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Porro Hugo de S. Victore, videtur primæ consentire opinioni, quoniam in libro de Sacramentis fatetur, quod mora interjecta non fuit inter creationem et distinctionis inchoationem, quæ distinctio incepit in lucis formatione. Præterea, qui dicunt lucem illam fuisse nubem, atque in meridie factam, dicere compelluntur, quod inter creationem et distinctionem fuerat mora: sic enim a principio primæ diei usque ad mane diei sequentis, non fuissent viginti quatuor horæ, sed decem et octo tantum. Ideo dicunt, præcessisse sex horas diei illius successione temporis, ex mutatione informis materiæ; et quum esset tunc tempus æquinoctiale, fuerunt deinde sex horæ usque ad occasum seu vesperam.
paras.en: Hugh of St Victor, again, seems to agree with the first opinion, since in the book On the Sacraments he declares that no lapse was set between creation and the beginning of distinction, which distinction began with the forming of light. Moreover, those who say that that light was a cloud, and was made at midday, are compelled to say that there was a lapse between creation and distinction: for otherwise, from the beginning of the first day to the morning of the following day, there would have been not twenty-four hours but only eighteen. Therefore they say that six hours of that day went before in the succession of time, through the change of the unformed matter; and since it was then the time of the equinox, there followed six hours until sunset, or evening.

paras.t: Ad secundam quæstionem respondet Magister in secundo, quod ante lucis productionem non fuit dies, nec nox, sed tempus: quod verum est, si creatio duratione præcessit distinctionis inceptionem, non autem, secundum aliam opinionem.
paras.en: To the second question the Master answers in the second book that before the production of light there was neither day nor night, but there was time: which is true if creation went before the beginning of distinction in duration, but not according to the other opinion.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæri potest, an creatio fuit in tempore: hoc est, an cœlum et terra sint creata in tempore. Ad quod respondet Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei: Mundus non incepit in tempore, sed simul cum tempore. Unde et Hugo in libro de Sacramentis: Primo momento temporis, in quo creata est omnium visibilium invisibiliumque natura, neque nox fuit, nec dies.
paras.en: On this it can be asked whether creation was in time: that is, whether heaven and earth were created in time. To which Augustine answers in the book of the City of God: The world did not begin in time, but together with time. Whence Hugh too, in the book On the Sacraments: In the first moment of time, in which the nature of all things visible and invisible was created, there was neither night nor day.

paras.t: Ad tertiam quæstionem dicendum, quod lux est qualitas corporibus cœlestibus inferioribusque communis; nam igni et aliquibus mixtis inest. Quum ergo distinctio attendatur secundum qualitates et proprietates accidentales, secundum positionem magis acceptam, recte inchoata fuit a luce, quæ est qualitas quædam communis, quemadmodum etiam in naturali generatione a communioribus formis incipitur. Propter quod, juxta Philosophum, embryo primo vivit vita plantæ, secundo, vita animalis, tertio, vita equi aut hominis. Secundo, quia per lucem omnia manifestantur, secundum Basilium. Tertio, propter expulsionem tenebrarum quæ operiebant abyssum. Quarto, quoniam sine luce nec dies prima, nec aliqua potuit esse. Quinto, propter eminentiam lucis. Unde secundo libro loquitur Damascenus: In principio, scilicet prima die, fecit Deus lucem, quæ est pulchritudo et ornatus omnis visibilis creaturæ. Aufer enim lumen, et omnia in tenebris ignota manebunt, quum non possint proprium demonstrare decorem. Sed contra hoc objici posset, quia ex verbis his Damasceni sequi videtur, quod lux pertinet ad ornatum. Dicendum, quod lux secundum virtutem suam communem pertinet ad distinctionem; sed in quantum quarta die perfecta est, et virtutem sortita ad determinatos variosque effectus, pertinet potius ad ornatum. Opus autem ornatus non dicitur ideo solum, quoniam ornat, sed ob aliam causam, ut dictum est.
paras.en: To the third question it must be said that light is a quality common to the heavenly bodies and to the lower ones; for it is found in fire and in some mixed bodies. Since, then, distinction is reckoned according to accidental qualities and properties, according to the more accepted position, it was rightly begun from light, which is a certain common quality; just as in natural generation, too, the beginning is made from the more common forms. For which reason, according to the Philosopher [Aristotle, as the margin notes], the embryo lives first the life of a plant, secondly the life of an animal, thirdly the life of a horse or of a man. Secondly, because by light all things are made manifest, according to Basil. Thirdly, to drive away the darkness that covered the deep. Fourthly, because without light neither the first day nor any day could be. Fifthly, because of the excellence of light. Whence Damascene says in the second book: In the beginning, that is, on the first day, God made light, which is the beauty and adornment of every visible creature. For take away light, and all things will remain unknown in darkness, since they cannot show their own beauty. But against this it might be objected that from these words of Damascene it seems to follow that light belongs to the adornment. It must be said that light, according to its common power, belongs to distinction; but inasmuch as it was perfected on the fourth day and received power for determinate and various effects, it belongs rather to adornment. The work of adornment, however, is not so called only because it adorns, but for the other reason, as has been said.

paras.t: Ad quartam respondet dominus Bonaventura super secundum: Quatuor, inquiens, modis consueverunt dies distingui secundum diversorum computationes. Græci enim incipiunt seu computant diem a mane in mane, quia de mane sol prius apparet. Hebræi vero a vespera in vesperam, quia in vespera incipiunt solennitatem. Astronomi autem a meridie in meridiem, quia tunc sol est in majori virtute. Porro, sancta Ecclesia a media nocte in mediam noctem, quia tunc natus est Christus.
paras.en: To the fourth the lord Bonaventure answers on the second book: In four ways, he says, days are commonly marked off, according to the reckonings of different peoples. For the Greeks begin or count the day from morning to morning, because in the morning the sun first appears; the Hebrews from evening to evening, because they begin their solemnities in the evening; the astronomers from noon to noon, because the sun is then in its greater strength; and holy Church from midnight to midnight, because Christ was then born.

paras.t: Ad quintam dicendum, quod si in eodem instanti fuit creatio et lucis formatio seu distinctionis inceptio, certum est quod opus creationis non cœpit a tenebris. Si autem dicatur fuisse intervallum, non sequitur quod incepit a tenebris, quasi tenebræ sint res aliqua a Deo primum creata, quum non sint nisi privatio lucis. Non est autem incongruum, si incepit a creatura non luminosa. Imo tenebræ quæ fuerunt ante lucis productionem, non fuerunt proprie in genere privationis, quia privatio esse non potuit, antequam natura habitus sui oppositi, scilicet lucis, indita esset corporibus, quemadmodum catulus leonis non dicitur cæcus ante diem nonum. Hinc per tenebras illas designatur imperfectio corporalis naturæ, quam non habet a Deo.
paras.en: To the fifth it must be said that if creation and the forming of light, or the beginning of distinction, were in the same instant, it is certain that the work of creation did not begin from darkness. But if it is said that there was an interval, it does not follow that it began from darkness, as if darkness were some thing first created by God, since it is nothing but the privation of light. Nor is it unfitting if it began from a creature that was not luminous. Indeed, the darkness that was before the production of light was not properly in the genus of privation, because privation could not be before the nature of its opposite habit, namely light, had been given to bodies; just as a lion's whelp is not called blind before the ninth day. Hence by that darkness is designated the imperfection of bodily nature, which it does not have from God.

paras.t: Ad sextam dicendum, quod illorum aliqui dicunt solem esse factum ex luce seu nube illa. Alii dicunt non solem tantum, sed et alia sidera facta ex ea. Quod alii reprobant, eo quod sol et sidera non sint de elementari natura. Alii dicunt eam redactam in præjacentem materiam. Quod rursum reprobatur ab aliis, quia sic Deus destruxisset seu perire permisisset principalia opera sex dierum. Hinc ceteri opinati sunt, lucem vel nubem illam soli esse conjunctam, nec posse videri propter prædominantiam lucis solaris. Quod item ab aliis reprobatur, quia sic frustra mansisset. Probabilius ergo est, ut cum S. Dionysio teneatur, illam fuisse lucem solis juxta sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: To the sixth it must be said that some of them say that the sun was made from that light, or cloud. Others say that not the sun only but the other stars too were made from it; which others reject, because the sun and the stars are not of elemental nature. Others say that it was turned back into the matter that lay beneath it; which again is rejected by others, because so God would have destroyed, or let perish, the principal works of the six days. Hence the rest have thought that that light, or cloud, was joined to the sun and cannot be seen because the sun's light prevails over it; which again is rejected by others, because so it would have remained to no purpose. It is more probable, then, to hold with St Dionysius that it was the light of the sun, in the sense given above.

paras.t: Ad septimam responsio data est, quia rationabilius esse persuasum est, quod dies et nox in triduo illo sint factæ, ex revolutione solis cum luce illa informi. Post illam vero positionem rationabilior esset positio Bedæ et imitantium eum, dicentium quod nubes illa suo circuitu causavit diem ac noctem. Hoc enim possibilius fuisset secundum naturam, ut ait Bonaventura.
paras.en: To the seventh the answer has been given, since it has been shown to be more reasonable that day and night in those three days were made by the revolution of the sun with that unformed light. After that position, the more reasonable would be the position of Bede and those who follow him, who say that that cloud caused day and night by its circling: for this would have been more possible according to nature, as Bonaventure says.

paras.t: Porro positio Basilii ac Damasceni, qui dicunt diem et noctem tunc esse causatum ex emissione seu effusione lucis et retractione ejusdem secundum Dei imperium, minorem habet probabilitatem. Talis enim efficientia diei et noctis, fuisset supernaturalis et miraculosa. In operibus autem sex dierum quæritur, non quid Deus potuerit, sed quid naturæ et ordini rerum convenerit. Denique, si lux illa immediate processit per creationem a Deo, non ab aliquo corpore lucido, ergo periisset quando retrahebatur, et die sequente effusa fuisset lux alia, nisi forte dicatur quod Deus per omnipotentiam suam conservasset eam in esse. Rursus, ubi permansit quando retrahebatur, et an fuit in aliquo subjecto? Et apparet quod non, quia tunc dies fuisset aut claritas in illo subjecto. Si autem dicatur quod Deus conservavit eam sine subjecto, sicut fit in Sacramento altaris de accidentalibus formis, hoc totum fuisset super naturam, nec rerum ordini convenisset. Hinc Rabbi Paulus, dicens quod in hac re opinio S. Basilii magis concordet rationi ac litteræ, probatur errare, et argumenta ejus vigorem non habent: quod, brevitati studens, declarare omitto, quia a quolibet mediocriter erudito potest faciliter considerari.
paras.en: But the position of Basil and Damascene, who say that day and night were then caused by the sending forth or pouring out of light and its drawing back again at God's command, has less probability. For such a making of day and night would have been supernatural and miraculous; and in the works of the six days the question is not what God could have done, but what befitted nature and the order of things. Further, if that light proceeded immediately from God by creation, and not from some luminous body, then it would have perished when it was drawn back, and on the following day another light would have been poured out; unless perhaps it be said that God by his omnipotence kept it in being. Again, where did it remain when it was drawn back, and was it in any subject? It appears not, for then there would have been day, or brightness, in that subject. And if it be said that God kept it without a subject, as happens in the Sacrament of the altar with the accidental forms [that is, the appearances of bread and wine, which remain without their substance], all this would have been above nature, and would not have befitted the order of things. Hence Rabbi Paul, when he says that in this matter the opinion of St Basil agrees better with reason and with the letter, is shown to err, and his arguments have no force: which, for the sake of brevity, I omit to show, because anyone moderately learned can easily see it.

paras.t: Insuper ex præinductis patescit, cur secundum Magistrum et Bedam ac alios, prima dies dicatur non habuisse mane, quoniam mane est finis præcedentis noctis, et principium diei sequentis; jam autem ostensum est, quod ante creationem lucis non fuit nox.
paras.en: Moreover, from what has been brought forward it is plain why, according to the Master and Bede and others, the first day is said to have had no morning: since morning is the end of the preceding night and the beginning of the following day; and it has already been shown that before the creation of light there was no night.

paras.t: Consimiliter soliditate veritatis carere ostenditur, quod quidam ait, nubem illam fuisse alterius speciei a nubibus aliis; quoniam nubes illa fuit naturæ cœlestis, aliæ autem nubes sunt naturæ elementaris. Illa etenim nubes, secundum ponentes eam, facta fuit de materia præjacenti, utique non cœlesti, sed de materia prima informi, quæ informata fuit (secundum eos) sola forma corporeitatis; de qua materia constat quod non fuit de natura cœlesti magis quam elementari. Denique S. Thomas probat, solem non esse factum de nube illa per hoc, quod sol non est factus de natura elementari. Quo patet, quod juxta Thomam, nubes illa fuit elementaris naturæ, secundum eos qui ponunt eam. Quamvis quis neget Thomam in hoc, tamen (ut tactum est) nubes illa non potius exstitisset naturæ cœlestis, quam elementaris: imo quum unum corpus cœleste non sit transmutabile in aliud corpus cœleste, si nubes illa fuisset naturæ cœlestis, dici non posset quod sol factus esset de ea: quod tamen Bonaventura et alii plures dicunt.
paras.en: In like manner it is shown to lack solid truth when a certain writer says that that cloud was of another species from the other clouds, because that cloud was of heavenly nature, while the other clouds are of elemental nature. For that cloud, according to those who posit it, was made of matter lying beneath it, and that not heavenly matter but unformed prime matter, which (according to them) was informed by the form of corporeity alone; and of that matter it is certain that it was no more of heavenly than of elemental nature. Further, St Thomas proves that the sun was not made of that cloud by this, that the sun was not made of elemental nature; from which it is plain that according to Thomas that cloud was of elemental nature, according to those who posit it. And even if someone should deny Thomas in this, still (as was touched on) that cloud would not have been of heavenly rather than of elemental nature. Indeed, since one heavenly body cannot be changed into another heavenly body, if that cloud had been of heavenly nature it could not be said that the sun was made of it: which nevertheless Bonaventure and many others say.

paras.t: Postremo adjiciendum, quod in Scholastica historia compendiose ac notabiliter dicitur. Dixit autem Deus: Fiat lux, et Facta est lux, id est, æternum Verbum genuit, in quo erat ut fieret lux: hoc est, tam facile fecit lucem, ut quis potest dicere verbo. Per Fiat, intelligitur essentia lucis in Deo, id est, in præscientia Dei antequam fieret; per Facta est, essentia lucis in actu. Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona: hoc est, quæ placuit in præscientia et præordinatione Dei, ut fieret; placuit in essentia jam producta, ut maneret. Vel tropice vidit, id est, videri fecit ab angelis. Et divisit lucem a tenebris. Intelligitur hic angelorum facta divisio: stantes enim, lux: cadentes vero, tenebræ dicti sunt.
paras.en: Lastly, there must be added what is said briefly and notably in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]. [[1:3|And God said: Be light made|Dixit autem Deus: Fiat lux]], and [[1:3|light was made|Facta est lux]]: that is, he begot the eternal Word, in whom it lay that light should be made; that is, he made light as easily as one can say a word. By [[1:3|Be light made|Fiat]] is understood the essence of light in God, that is, in God's foreknowledge, before it was made; by [[1:3|light was made|Facta est]], the essence of light in act. [[1:4|And God saw the light that it was good|Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona]]: that is, it pleased him in the foreknowledge and foreordaining of God, that it should be made; it pleased him in its essence once produced, that it should remain. Or *saw* is said figuratively, that is, he made it to be seen by the angels. [[1:4|and he divided the light from the darkness|Et divisit lucem a tenebris]]: here is understood the division made among the angels; for those who stood were called light, but those who fell, darkness.

paras.t: Dicitur quoque in Historia ista: Primo cum cœlo et terra est lux creata, quod favet opinioni eorum, qui dicunt inter creationem et distinctionis initium, non fuisse aliquod temporis intervallum. Præinducta quoque verba sententiosa, ex Augustino super Genesim sumpta sunt. Consentit etiam auctor hujus Historiæ expositioni Bedæ, dicendo: Lucem Scriptura vocat quamdam nubem lucidam, illuminantem superiores mundi partes tenui claritate, quæ instar solis circumagitata, id est circumvoluta, per suam præsentiam superius atque inferius hemisphærium vicissim illuminabat.
paras.en: It is said too in that History: Light was first created together with heaven and earth; which favours the opinion of those who say that there was no interval of time between creation and the beginning of distinction. The pithy words brought forward above, moreover, are taken from Augustine on Genesis. The author of this History also agrees with Bede's exposition, saying: Scripture calls light a certain bright cloud, lighting the upper parts of the world with a faint brightness, which, being carried round like the sun, that is, revolving, lit by its presence the upper and the lower hemisphere in turn.

1.title: Expositio litteræ, in qua describitur opus secundæ diei.
1.title_en: Exposition of the text in which the work of the second day is described.

paras.t: DESCRIPTA distinctione lucis a tenebris, modo describitur distinctio cœlestium corporum ab invicem. Dixit quoque Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis. Qualiter intelligenda sint verba hæc, Dixit Deus, Fiat, expositum est præcedenti articulo. Quid vero intelligendum sit nomine firmamenti, constat ex eo quod paulo post stellæ dicuntur positæ in firmamento. Itaque Deo dicente seu præcipiente, factum est firmamentum, id est cœlum stellatum, quod est sphæra octava, quia sub ea sunt septem sphæræ seu orbes ac cœli planetarum. Et factum est firmamentum hoc in medio aquarum ad dividendum aquas ab aquis. Et sumitur nunc firmamentum, prout includit septem sphæras præfatas.
paras.en: Having described the distinction of light from darkness, he now describes the distinction of the heavenly bodies from one another. [[1:6|And God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters|Dixit quoque Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis]]. How these words, [[1:6|God said|Dixit Deus]], [[1:6|Let there be|Fiat]], are to be understood was explained in the preceding article. What is to be understood by the name of firmament is clear from the fact that a little later the stars are said to be set in the firmament. And so, God saying or commanding it, the firmament was made, that is, the starry heaven, which is the eighth sphere, since beneath it are the seven spheres, or orbs and heavens, of the planets. And this firmament was made in the midst of the waters, to divide the waters from the waters. And firmament is taken here as including the seven spheres aforesaid.

paras.t: Et fecit Deus firmamentum. Jam ante ostensum est, expositionem illorum esse rationabiliorem, et textui atque antiquis ac sanctis doctoribus consonantiorem, qui dicunt in principio corpora cœlestia ac elementa simul producta sub distinctis et propriis substantialibus formis. Ideo, firmamentum et orbes planetarum in principio sunt creata, quantum ad totam suam substantiam : verumtamen non in tanta perfectione, quantum ad accidentales proprietates, virtutes et qualitates, ut postea. Unde, quod firmamentum dicitur factum die secundo, intelligendum est non de productione suæ substantiæ, sed de quadam sui completione, qua factum est magis completum et vigorosum in qualitate et proprietate suæ substantiæ, et in virtute causali, ad influendum elementis ac mixtis ad quosdam generales effectus, ut præinducto dixi articulo. Quemadmodum enim in Scripturis novi ac veteris Testamenti cœli dicuntur perituri et corrumpendi, non utique quantum ad suam substantiam, substantialeque esse, sed quantum ad accidentales quasdam dispositiones, qualitates et actiones, ita firmamentum et stellæ ac luminaria facta dicuntur post primum diem. Denique in Scripturis consuetus est iste loquendi modus, ut dicatur res fieri, quando accidentale aliquid agitur circa ipsam sive in ea : sicut quum filii Israel leguntur sibi fecisse præputia, in quantum non præsciderunt sua præputia juxta legem. In ultima quoque Ezechielis visione multoties dicitur : Facietis vitulos sive agnos, hoc est, illa aut illa die offeretis tot agnos ac vitulos. Sic et Jacobus apostolus in sua ait Canonica : Ecce dicitis, faciemus ibi annum, etc. id est, per annum unum manebimus illo in loco, qui ignoratis quid erit in crastinum. Fecit itaque Deus firmamentum, perficiendo illud in soliditate et causalitate, qua influit ad inferiorum conservationem ac regimen ; quia (ut ait Philosophus) oportet hunc mundum inferiorem, esse contiguum lationibus seu motibus et influxionibus superiorum, videlicet cœlestium corporum, ut tota ejus virtus inde gubernetur.
paras.en: [[1:7|And God made a firmament|Et fecit Deus firmamentum]]. It has already been shown that the exposition of those is the more reasonable, and the more in keeping with the text and with the ancient and holy doctors, who say that in the beginning the heavenly bodies and the elements were produced together under distinct and proper substantial forms. Therefore the firmament and the orbs of the planets were created in the beginning as to their whole substance, yet not in such perfection, as to their accidental properties, powers and qualities, as afterwards. Hence, that the firmament is said to have been made on the second day is to be understood not of the production of its substance, but of a certain completion of it, by which it was made more complete and vigorous in the quality and property of its substance, and in causal power, so as to exert influence on the elements and on mixed bodies for certain general effects, as I said in the preceding article. For just as in the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament the heavens are said to be destined to perish and be corrupted[[Agg 2:7||]][[Agg 2:22||]][[Matt 24:29||]][[Matt 24:35||]], not indeed as to their substance and substantial being, but as to certain accidental dispositions, qualities and actions, so the firmament and the stars and lights are said to have been made after the first day. Moreover, this manner of speaking is customary in the Scriptures, that a thing is said to be made when something accidental is done about it or in it: as when the children of Israel are read to have [[1 Mach 1:16|made themselves prepuces|sibi fecisse præputia]], inasmuch as they did not cut off their foreskins according to the law. In the last vision of Ezechiel too it is said many times: You shall make calves or lambs[[Ezech 46:15||]], that is, on this or that day you shall offer so many lambs and calves [the Latin *facere*, "to make", stands here for "to offer"; the margin gives Ezech. xlvi, 15, where the Vulgate has *Faciet agnum*, "he shall offer (make) the lamb"]. So also the apostle James says in his Canonical Epistle: Behold, you say: [[Jas 4:13|there we will spend a year|faciemus ibi annum]] [literally "we will make a year there"], etc., that is, we will stay in that place for one year; you who [[Jas 4:14|know not what shall be on the morrow|ignoratis quid erit in crastinum]]. God, then, made the firmament by perfecting it in solidity and in causality, by which it exerts its influence for the preservation and governance of lower things; for (as the Philosopher says) this lower world must be contiguous to the courses, that is, the motions and influences, of the higher, namely of the heavenly bodies, so that all its power may be governed from there [Aristotle, *Meteorology* I, 2].

paras.t: Divisitque aquas quæ erant super firmamentum, ab his quæ erant sub firmamento. Quæ et quales sint aquæ super cœlum existentes, magna atque difficilis quæstio est, de qua infra plenius tangam. Nunc breviter dico, quod quidam per aquas illas intelligunt nonam sphæram, quæ cœlum crystallinum ac aqueum appellatur : non quod vere et univoce sit de natura aquæ elementaris, sed quia cum ea in diaphaneitate communicet : sicut et cœlum empyreum dicitur igneum, non quod in calore, sed quia in splendore cum visibili convenit igni. Alii dicunt firmamentum esse veraciter naturæ elementaris, et similiter aquas quæ super firmamentum esse scribuntur, de quibus opinionibus paulo post diffusius referetur. Porro, quod aquæ dicuntur fuisse sub firmamento, non est intelligendum quod erant immediate sub cœlo stellato, sed manebant sub orbe lunari, secundum positionem superius amplius approbatam. Aqua autem et aer et ignis erant confuse permixta usque ad infimam sphæram cœlestem, secundum sic sentientes. Et factum est ita actualiter et in re, sicut dixit, id est, intelligendo ac volendo præcepit Deus.
paras.en: And he [[1:7|divided the waters|Divisitque aquas]] [[1:7|that were above the firmament|quæ erant super firmamentum]], [[1:7|from those that were|ab his]] [[1:7|under the firmament|quæ erant sub firmamento]]. What the waters existing above the heaven are, and of what kind, is a great and difficult question, which I will touch on more fully below. For now I say briefly that some understand by those waters the ninth sphere, which is called the crystalline and watery heaven: not that it is truly and univocally of the nature of elemental water, but because it shares with water in transparency; just as the empyrean heaven too is called fiery, not because it agrees with visible fire in heat, but because it agrees with it in splendour. Others say that the firmament is truly of an elemental nature, and likewise the waters which are written to be above the firmament; of these opinions more will be related at length a little later. Further, that the waters are said to have been under the firmament is not to be understood as if they were immediately under the starry heaven; rather, they remained under the orb of the moon, according to the position approved more fully above. Water, air and fire were mixed together confusedly up to the lowest heavenly sphere, according to those who hold this view. [[1:7|And it was so|Et factum est ita]] in act and in reality, as he said, that is, as God, by understanding and willing, commanded.

paras.t: Vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum. Sphæra octava dicitur firmamentum, quia firmissimum medium est inter aquas præfatas. In sua quoque natura est firmum ac solidum, juxta illud Job : Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt. Est item impertransibilis terminus prædictarum aquarum inter quas dividit. Vocatur etiam cœlum, quoniam celat et tegit sensibilia ista, atque a nostro abscondit adspectu exsistentia per ipsum. Et factum est vespere et mane dies secundus. Hoc exponendum est, sicut præcedenti articulo est expositum.
paras.en: And [[1:8|God called the firmament, Heaven|Vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum]]. The eighth sphere is called the firmament because it is a most firm medium between the aforesaid waters. In its own nature too it is firm and solid, according to that of Job: [[Job 37:18|Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him, which are most strong, as if they were of molten brass|Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt]]. It is likewise the impassable boundary of the aforesaid waters, between which it divides. It is called heaven too, because it hides and covers these things of sense, and conceals from our sight what lies beyond it [Denis derives *cœlum*, "heaven", from *celat*, "it hides"]. [[1:8|and the evening and morning were the second day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies secundus]]. This is to be explained as it was explained in the preceding article.

paras.t: Præterea juxta eos qui dicunt, materiam primo creatam sub sola corporeitatis forma, et de materia illa esse producta elementa atque cœlestia corpora, sic exponenda est littera ista : Dixit Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, id est, cœlum sidereum producatur de materia illa informi et communi, et subsistat in medio illius materiæ, quæ interdum designatur nomine aquæ, quandoque nomine terræ, aliquando appellatione abyssi, ut dictum est plenius. Sicque dividat aquas ab aquis, id est unam illius materiæ partem ab alia. Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas quæ erant super firmamentum : hoc est, præfatam partem illius materiæ, existentem in loco eminentiori firmamento, divisit ab his quæ erant sub firmamento. Nunc enim per firmamentum designantur etiam orbes septem planetarum, qui facti sunt cum firmamento die secundo : quo etiam die (secundum istam opinionem) factum est cœlum crystallinum de suprema parte ejusdem materiæ, quæ in superioribus partibus suis subtilior fuit. De parte vero materiæ quæ mansit sub orbe lunæ, facta sunt elementa secundum istos non hoc die, sed postea. Sicque hæc dicta sunt fieri, quoniam proprias formas substantiales specificas acceperunt a Deo hoc die aut postmodum.
paras.en: Moreover, according to those who say that matter was first created under the form of corporeity alone, and that the elements and the heavenly bodies were produced from that matter, this text is to be explained thus: [[1:6|God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters|Dixit Deus : Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum]], that is, let the starry heaven be produced from that formless and common matter, and let it stand in the midst of that matter which is sometimes designated by the name of water, sometimes by the name of earth, sometimes by the name of the deep, as was said more fully above. [[1:6|And let it divide the waters from the waters|Sicque dividat aquas ab aquis]], that is, one part of that matter from another. [[1:7|And God made a firmament, and divided the waters|Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas]] [[1:7|that were above the firmament|quæ erant super firmamentum]]: that is, the aforesaid part of that matter, which was in a place higher than the firmament, he divided [[1:7|from those that were|ab his quæ erant]] [[1:7|under the firmament|sub firmamento]]. For here the firmament designates also the orbs of the seven planets, which were made with the firmament on the second day; and on that day too (according to this opinion) the crystalline heaven was made out of the highest part of the same matter, which was subtler in its higher parts. But out of the part of the matter which remained under the orb of the moon the elements were made, according to these, not on this day but afterwards. And so these things are said to be made, because they received their proper specific substantial forms from God on this day or afterwards.

paras.t: Præterea, quod primo dicitur, Fiat firmamentum ; deinde, Fecit Deus firmamentum ; et tertio, Factum est firmamentum : nequaquam superflue positum est. Insuper patet, quod dies ista secunda habuit non vesperam tantum, sed etiam mane, quoniam nox diei alterius eam præcessit ; et idem dicendum est de diebus sequentibus.
paras.en: Further, that it is said first, [[1:6|Let there be a firmament made|Fiat firmamentum]]; then, [[1:7|God made a firmament|Fecit Deus firmamentum]]; and third, [[1:7|it was so|Factum est firmamentum]] [Denis gives this as *Factum est firmamentum*, "the firmament was made"], is by no means set down superfluously. It is plain moreover that this second day had not only an evening but also a morning, since the night of the other day went before it; and the same must be said of the days that follow.

paras.t: Circa hanc litteram quæritur primo, an corpora cœlestia sint naturæ elementaris. Et videtur quod imo, ex textu præsenti, quum firmamentum sit factum in medio aquarum. Unde videtur sola divisione ab eis differre, et iterum quoniam supra ipsum sunt aquæ. Hanc quæstionem doctores super secundum Sententiarum satis discutiunt, et communiter Aristotelem assequuntur, dicentes quod sint alterius naturæ quam elementa.
paras.en: On this text it is asked first whether the heavenly bodies are of an elemental nature. And it seems that they are, from the present text, since the firmament was made [[1:6|amidst the waters|in medio aquarum]]; so that it seems to differ from them only by being divided from them; and again, because there are waters above it. The doctors on the second book of the Sentences discuss this question well enough, and commonly follow Aristotle, saying that the heavenly bodies are of another nature than the elements.

paras.t: Denique specialis est quæstio, an saltem cœlum crystallinum seu aqueum, designatum per aquas quæ supra firmamentum consistunt, sit vere de natura et specie aquæ. Et videtur quod imo, quia scriptura ista apertissime dicit quod supra firmamentum sint aquæ, et sub eodem contextu utitur nomine aquæ, ita quod videtur de aqua univoce loqui. Hoc quoque videntur prætendere manifeste alia loca Scripturæ veteris Testamenti, ut quum fertur in Psalmo : Qui extendis cœlum sicut pellem, et tegis aquis superiora ejus. Itemque : Laudate eum cœli cœlorum, et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt, laudent nomen Domini. Et rursus in trium cantico Puerorum : Benedicite aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino. Quum igitur magis debeamus sequi auctoritatem Scripturæ divinæ, quam dictamen rationis humanæ : videtur absolute dicendum, quod super cœlos sunt vere ac proprie aquæ, et quod cœlum crystallinum sit de natura aquæ : firmamentum quoque sit elementaris naturæ, videlicet igneæ, ut aliqui dicunt : vel partim igneæ, quantum ad stellas ; partimque aqueæ, utpote quantum ad reliquas ejus partes. Denique antiqui et sancti doctores, Augustinus, Basilius, Gregorius, Ambrosius, ita senserunt : quos Beda, Strabus, Damascenus, Magister Sententiarum, auctor Scholasticæ historiæ, Glossa, et alii multi secuti sunt.
paras.en: There is, further, a particular question: whether at least the crystalline or watery heaven, designated by the waters which stand above the firmament, is truly of the nature and species of water. And it seems that it is, because this scripture says most plainly that there are waters above the firmament, and in the same context uses the name of water, so that it seems to speak of water univocally. Other places of the Scripture of the Old Testament also seem plainly to point to this, as when it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:2|Who stretchest out the heaven like a pavilion|Qui extendis cœlum sicut pellem]]: [[Ps 103:3|Who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water|et tegis aquis superiora ejus]]. And again: [[Ps 148:4|Praise him, ye heavens of heavens: and let all the waters that are above the heavens|Laudate eum cœli cœlorum, et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt]] [[Ps 148:5|Praise the name of the Lord|laudent nomen Domini]]. And again in the canticle of the three Children: [[Dan 3:60|O all ye waters that are above the heavens, bless the Lord|Benedicite aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino]]. Since, then, we ought rather to follow the authority of divine Scripture than the dictate of human reason, it seems that we must say absolutely that above the heavens there are truly and properly waters, and that the crystalline heaven is of the nature of water; and that the firmament too is of an elemental nature, namely fiery, as some say; or partly fiery, as to the stars, and partly watery, as to its other parts. Indeed the ancient and holy doctors, Augustine, Basil, Gregory and Ambrose, held this; and Bede, Strabo, Damascene, the Master of the Sentences, the author of the Scholastic History, the Gloss and many others have followed them.

paras.t: Circa hujus quæstionis decisionem scribit Bonaventura super secundum : In hac quæstione, propter diversitatem positionum et debilitatem rationum, vix certum aliquid dici potest. Deinde post multa verba declinat ad hoc, quod per aquas quæ super cœlos sunt, intelligatur nona sphæra, quæ dicitur cœlum crystallinum, non propter veritatem naturæ aquæ, sed propter similitudinem in diaphaneitate, qua aqua non solum est luminis receptiva, sed etiam aliqualiter retentiva, ut patet in quibusdam lapidibus, qui non videntur de nocte nisi ponantur in aqua. Deinde, quasi concordando theologos atque philosophos, dicit quod Augustinus et alii Sancti dixerunt firmamentum esse de natura ignis, non quod habeat formam substantialem et speciem specialissimam ignis, sed quia participat lucis naturam secundum analogiam. Et quamvis istud sit bene dictum, quantum ad hoc quod videtur verba sanctorum theologorum pie salvare, et quantum ad homines concordare ; verumtamen si quis plenius curiosiusque voluerit informari, inveniet quod secundum intentionem et mentem Patrum jam præfatorum, cœlum crystallinum sit vere de natura aquæ atque formaliter frigidum, præsertim quum ponant aquas super firmamentum, ad temperandum solis et aliorum cœlestium corporum calorem. Unde Saturnum affirmant ceteris planetis frigidiorem, quamvis eis velocius moveatur, utpote altius situs propter propinquitatem suam ad aquas illas.
paras.en: On the settling of this question Bonaventure writes on the second book: In this question, because of the diversity of positions and the weakness of the arguments, hardly anything certain can be said. Then, after many words, he inclines to this: that by the waters which are above the heavens is understood the ninth sphere, which is called the crystalline heaven, not because it truly has the nature of water, but because of a likeness in transparency, by which water is not only receptive of light but also in some way retentive of it, as appears in certain stones which are not seen at night unless they are put in water. Then, as though reconciling the theologians and the philosophers, he says that Augustine and the other Saints said that the firmament is of the nature of fire, not that it has the substantial form and the most specific species of fire [that is, the lowest species, which makes a thing exactly what it is], but because it shares in the nature of light by analogy. And although this is well said, so far as it seems piously to save the words of the holy theologians and to bring men into agreement; yet if anyone wishes to be more fully and more carefully informed, he will find that according to the intention and mind of the Fathers already named, the crystalline heaven is truly of the nature of water and formally cold, especially since they place waters above the firmament to temper the heat of the sun and of the other heavenly bodies. Hence they affirm that Saturn is colder than the other planets, although it moves faster than they, being placed higher, because of its nearness to those waters.

paras.t: Hinc Thomas scribit super secundum : Circa hanc quæstionem fuit philosophorum diversa positio. Omnes enim ante Aristotelem dixerunt cœlum esse de natura elementorum : quod Aristoteles primitus improbavit, ponens cœlum esse sine gravitate et levitate aliisque contrariis, ut patet primo Cœli et mundi. Et propter efficaciam rationum ejus, posteriores philosophi, scilicet Peripatetici, consenserunt ei : unde nunc omnes opinionem ejus sequuntur. Similiter expositores Scripturæ in hac diversitate fuerunt, secundum quod diversorum philosophorum doctrinis erant instructi. Basilius enim, Augustinus, ac plures Sanctorum, sequuntur in his quæ philosophiam concernunt, nec spectant ad fidem, opiniones Platonis : ideo ponunt cœlum esse naturæ elementaris. Dionysius autem fere ubique in talibus Aristotelem sequitur, ut patet diligenter inspicienti libros ipsius. In talibus ergo dicta Sanctorum non sunt majoris auctoritatis, quam philosophi quos sequuntur, nisi quod sunt ab omni infidelitatis suspicione immunia. Hæc Thomas. Dicta autem Alberti libro de Coæquævis, concordant dicta Bonaventuræ.
paras.en: Hence Thomas writes on the second book: On this question the philosophers held different positions. For all before Aristotle said that the heaven is of the nature of the elements; which Aristotle was the first to disprove, holding that the heaven is without heaviness and lightness and the other contraries, as appears in the first book On the Heavens and the World. And because of the force of his arguments the later philosophers, namely the Peripatetics, agreed with him, so that now all follow his opinion. The expositors of Scripture likewise differed on this, according as they had been instructed in the doctrines of different philosophers. For Basil, Augustine and many of the Saints follow the opinions of Plato in matters which concern philosophy and do not pertain to faith; and therefore they hold that the heaven is of an elemental nature. But Dionysius almost everywhere follows Aristotle in such matters, as is plain to anyone who looks carefully into his books. In such matters, then, the sayings of the Saints are of no greater authority than the philosophers whom they follow, except that they are free from all suspicion of unbelief. Thus far Thomas. And the sayings of Albert in the book On the Coevals agree with the sayings of Bonaventure [Albert's treatise *De quatuor coæquævis*, on the four things created together at the beginning].

paras.t: Denique Beda ait : Cœlum sidereum constat esse in medio aquarum, quod de aquis factum credi potest. Nam lapis crystallinus, qui est magnæ firmitatis et perspicuitatis, de aquis est factus. Et secundum eumdem Bedam, aquæ sunt super cœlum instar glaciei firmæ ac solidæ. Hæc et plura similia habentur in Glossa, et allegantur a Magistro in secundo Sententiarum. In Scholastica item historia dicitur : Fecit Deus in aquarum medio firmamentum, id est quandam exteriorem mundi superficiem, solidam ex aquis congelatis instar crystalli et lucidam, super quam sunt aquæ ad modum crystalli congelatæ, ne igne solvantur. Quibus consonare videtur quod Josephus ait : Secunda die Deus cœlum super omnia collocavit, illudque ab aliis distinguens, in se ipso constitutum esse præcepit, et ei crystallum circumfigens humidum et pluviale, ad utilitatem quæ fit ex imbribus terræ, congrue fabricatus est. Ecce quomodo eruditissimi ac ingeniosissimi viri, propter auctoritatem Scripturæ, postposita philosophorum peripateticorum doctrina, sentiunt cœlos, id est sidera, esse elementaris naturæ.
paras.en: Again, Bede says: It is agreed that the starry heaven is in the midst of the waters, and it may be believed that it was made of waters; for the crystal stone, which is of great firmness and transparency, is made of waters. And according to the same Bede, the waters are above the heaven like firm and solid ice. These things and many like them are found in the Gloss, and are cited by the Master in the second book of the Sentences. Likewise in the Scholastic History it is said: God made the firmament in the midst of the waters, that is, a certain outer surface of the world, solid, of waters congealed like crystal, and shining; above which are waters congealed in the manner of crystal, lest they be melted by fire. With these what Josephus says seems to agree: On the second day God placed the heaven above all things, and distinguishing it from the rest, commanded it to be established by itself; and he fittingly fashioned it, fixing round it a crystal moist and rainy, for the benefit that comes to the earth from showers. See how most learned and ingenious men, on account of the authority of Scripture, setting aside the doctrine of the Peripatetic philosophers, hold that the heavens, that is, the stars, are of an elemental nature.

paras.t: Porro, quam acriter scribat Ambrosius in suo Hexaemeron contra aliter opinantes, patet in libro illo. Arbitror ergo in hac materia sobrie esse loquendum. Rationes quoque Aristotelis, quibus probat cœlum esse alterius naturæ, non sunt demonstrativæ, sed solum probabiles. Nempe, quod arguit de specialitate motus cœlestium corporum, quod non moventur ad medium, nec a medio, sed circa medium, quid demonstrat, quum et ignis in propria sphæra circa medium seu circulariter moveatur ? Et si dicatur hoc esse per accidens, utpote virtute sphæræ superioris ipsum continentis, non tamen motus ille est igni violentus aut penitus innaturalis. Denique in generationibus mixtorum, elementa levia, scilicet ignis et aer, naturaliter moventur deorsum : qui motus est eis naturalis per respectum ad naturam universalem. Sic dici posset de motu cœlestium corporum, quæ etsi essent elementaris naturæ, non tamen sequeretur ea corruptibilia esse : quum nec ipsa elementa sint corruptibilia secundum se tota, et aliæ rationes incorruptibilitatis possent assignari in eis.
paras.en: Further, how sharply Ambrose writes in his Hexaemeron against those who think otherwise is plain in that book. I judge, therefore, that one must speak soberly in this matter. The arguments of Aristotle too, by which he proves that the heaven is of another nature, are not demonstrative but only probable. For what does his argument from the special character of the motion of the heavenly bodies demonstrate, namely that they are moved neither towards the centre nor away from the centre, but about the centre, since fire too is moved in its own sphere about the centre, that is, in a circle? And if it be said that this is accidental, namely by the power of the higher sphere which contains it, still that motion is not violent to fire [in the old physics, a violent motion is one forced on a body against its nature] nor wholly unnatural. Moreover, in the generation of mixed bodies the light elements, namely fire and air, are naturally moved downwards; and this motion is natural to them in respect of universal nature. So it could be said of the motion of the heavenly bodies; and even if they were of an elemental nature, it would not follow that they are corruptible, since not even the elements themselves are corruptible in their entirety, and other reasons for their incorruptibility could be assigned.

paras.t: Hinc Thomas super secundum, positionem Aristotelis vocat opinionem, atque in prima parte, quæstione 68, multum sobrie loquitur de ista materia, dicens : Si dicamus firmamentum esse cœlum sidereum, tunc aquæ quæ sunt supra firmamentum, possunt dici illius naturæ cujus est hoc cœlum. Unde qui dicunt cœlum esse de natura elementorum, dicere possunt aquas illas esse elementares. Qui autem asserunt cœlum esse specialis naturæ, dicunt has aquas non elementaris, sed cœlestis naturæ esse ; et qui ponunt aquas elementares supra cœlum, dicere possunt quod non sint graves, sed subtiles ; nec fluidæ, sed tanquam glacies firmæ ac duræ. Unde a quibusdam cœlum crystallinum vocantur. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: Hence Thomas, on the second book, calls Aristotle's position an opinion; and in the First Part, question 68, he speaks very soberly of this matter, saying: If we say that the firmament is the starry heaven, then the waters which are above the firmament can be said to be of the same nature as this heaven. Hence those who say that the heaven is of the nature of the elements can say that those waters are elemental. But those who assert that the heaven is of a special nature say that these waters are not of an elemental but of a heavenly nature; and those who place elemental waters above the heaven can say that they are not heavy but subtle, nor fluid but firm and hard like ice. Hence by some they are called the crystalline heaven. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Amplius, sicut Bonaventura tangit super secundum. Hi dicunt quod Deus in ordine universi magis attendit commune bonum et finis utilitatem, quam formæ qualitatem aut bonum specialis naturæ. Ideo sicut in minori mundo Deus posuit cerebrum sursum ad temperandum cordis calorem, sic supra cœlum sidereum posuit aqueum cœlum ad ardorem ætheris refrigerandum. Atque per istud solvunt argumenta quæ contra hæc fieri solent. Ego in ista materia assertive nil dico. Neque intentio mea est, in hoc loco horum discussioni plene insistere. Sed propter sanctorum Patrum reverentiam tetigi ista. Hinc in discussione hujus materiæ ait Bonaventura : Hoc præcipue attendendum est, ne in incerta materia aliquid certitudinaliter asseratur. Melius enim est pie dubitare, quam temerarie aliquid definire.
paras.en: Further, as Bonaventure touches on in the second book, these say that God in the order of the universe looks more to the common good and the usefulness of the end than to the quality of the form or the good of a particular nature. Therefore, just as in the lesser world [that is, in man, the microcosm] God placed the brain above to temper the heat of the heart, so above the starry heaven he placed the watery heaven to cool the burning of the ether. And by this they answer the arguments commonly brought against these views. For my part I assert nothing in this matter. Nor is it my intention in this place to dwell fully on the discussion of these things; but I have touched on them out of reverence for the holy Fathers. Hence, in his discussion of this matter, Bonaventure says: This above all must be heeded, that nothing be asserted as certain in an uncertain matter. For it is better to doubt piously than to define anything rashly.

paras.t: Insuper quæritur, cur in descriptione operis secundæ diei non dicitur, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, quemadmodum in descriptionibus operum aliorum dierum. Ad quod eleganter respondetur in Glossa his verbis : Notandum quod opera secundæ diei, secundum Hebræos, non dicuntur bona, quum bona sint sicut et cetera : quod fit propter binarium principem alteritatis, qui primus ab unitate discedit, et in figura bigamiæ ac multorum reprehensibilium ponitur. Unde animalia quæ bina introierunt in arcam, immunda fuerunt. Impar autem numerus mundus est. Hinc Magister in secundo testatur : Non est hic dictum, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, eo quod binarius esset principium alteritatis et signum divisionis.
paras.en: It is asked further why in the description of the work of the second day it is not said, [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], as in the descriptions of the works of the other days. To this an elegant answer is given in the Gloss in these words: It is to be noted that the works of the second day, according to the Hebrews, are not called good, though they are good like the rest. This is because of the number two, the beginning of otherness, which is the first to depart from unity, and is set down as a figure of bigamy and of many things worthy of blame. Hence the animals which went into the ark two by two were unclean[[Gen 7:2||]]; but the odd number is clean. Hence the Master testifies in the second book: It is not said here, [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], because the number two is the beginning of otherness and the sign of division.

paras.t: Verumtamen quidam dicit, quod responsio ista videtur trufatica esse, quia in Evangelio binarius laudabilis ac mysticus designatur. Unde Christus misit discipulos suos binos ad prædicandum. Ad quod breviter respondendum, quod tam indecens reprobatio potius posset dici talis, qualem ipse reputat præfatam responsionem, quæ etiam ex verbis Augustini sumpta videtur, quam et doctores super secundum concorditer approbant, utpote Thomas, Albertus, ac alii. Unde et Bonaventura scribit ibidem : Quamvis binarius minus ab unitate recedit, primo tamen habet rationem recessus in se. Idcirco per ipsum intelligitur divisio et recessus ab unitate virtutis et perfectionis, magis quam per alios numeros. Argumentum quoque illius non valet. Quamvis enim binarius quandoque accipiatur in bono, quia in omni creato invenitur aliquid perfectionis, nihilo minus secundum considerationem prætactam in malo accipitur : quemadmodum per leonem quandoque intelligitur Christus, quandoque diabolus.
paras.en: Yet a certain writer says that this answer seems to be a trifling one [Latin *trufatica*; the editors gloss it *falsa*, "false", referring to Du Cange's Glossary under *trufa*], because in the Gospel the number two is presented as praiseworthy and mystical: so Christ sent his disciples two by two to preach[[Luke 10:1||]]. To this we must answer briefly that so unseemly a rejection could more fairly be called what he reckons the aforesaid answer to be; for that answer also seems to be taken from the words of Augustine, and the doctors on the second book approve it with one accord, namely Thomas, Albert and others. Hence Bonaventure too writes in the same place: Although the number two departs less from unity, yet it is the first to have in itself the character of departure. Therefore by it is understood division and departure from the unity of virtue and perfection, more than by the other numbers. His argument, too, is not valid. For although the number two is sometimes taken in a good sense, since in every created thing something of perfection is found, nevertheless, according to the consideration touched on above, it is taken in a bad sense: just as by the lion sometimes Christ is understood[[Apoc 5:5||]], sometimes the devil[[1 Pet 5:8||]].

paras.t: Nihilo minus est etiam alia ratio, cur in descriptione operis secundæ diei omittatur illud, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum : quia videlicet distinctio aquarum ab aquis secundo die incepta, tertio die completa est, quantum ad aquas elementares, quando in unum congregatæ sunt locum. Nec ad introducendum hanc rationem magis litteralem, oportuit allegare infidelem in Judæum Judæorum doctorem Rabbi Salomonem, quasi ille melius dixerit quam tot doctores catholici : quia et ipsi doctores catholici jam prælati, eamdem rationem assignant, quam et Magister in historiis tangit.
paras.en: There is, nevertheless, another reason why in the description of the work of the second day the words [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]] are left out: namely, that the distinction of waters from waters, begun on the second day, was completed on the third day as regards the elemental waters, when they were [[1:9|gathered together into one place|in unum congregatæ sunt locum]]. Nor, to bring in this more literal reason, was there any need to cite the unbelieving Jew, the doctor of the Jews, Rabbi Salomon [that is, Rashi], as though he had spoken better than so many Catholic doctors; for the Catholic doctors already named themselves give the same reason, which the Master also touches on in the Histories [Peter Comestor, the "Master of the Histories", in the *Scholastic History*].

1.title: Expositio textus, describentis opus tertii diei
1.title_en: Exposition of the text that describes the work of the third day

paras.t: Tertio die distincta atque ab invicem divisa sunt elementa, quæ tamen in principio fuerunt in propriis formis substantialibus distincte producta, ac specifica ratione divisa, sed localiter erant confuse permixta, et hoc tertio die ab invicem divisa sunt loco, et quasdam accidentales proprietates, qualitates, et virtutes activas acceperunt communes ad generales quosdam effectus, ut supra ex doctoribus est ostensum.
paras.en: On the third day the elements were distinguished and divided from one another. In the beginning, indeed, they had been produced distinct in their own substantial forms and divided by their specific nature, but in place they were confusedly mingled together; and on this third day they were divided from one another in place, and received certain accidental properties, qualities and active powers, common to certain general effects, as was shown above from the doctors.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Dixit vero Deus. Frequenter in isto capitulo legitur Deus dixisse, et quasi per intervalla dierum locutus et operatus esse describitur, quum tamen in ipso invariabili ac simplicissimo Deo nulla sit diversitas, nulla mutatio, nullaque novitas: sed quidquid produxit in tempore, et per temporum vices, hoc ab æterno tunc et taliter facere incommutabiliter ordinavit. Ipse enim omnium rerum ideas continet in se. Porro in idea duo notantur, videlicet cognitio rei, et determinatio quando ac qualiter fiet.
paras.en: So he says: [[1:9|God also said|Dixit vero Deus]]. Often in this chapter we read that God said, and he is described as speaking and working, as it were, at intervals of days; whereas in God himself, unchangeable and most simple, there is no diversity, no change, and nothing new: but whatever he produced in time and through the succession of times, this he ordained unchangeably from eternity to do then and in such a way. For he contains in himself the ideas of all things. Now in an idea two things are noted, namely the knowledge of the thing, and the determination of when and how it shall be made.

paras.t: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cælo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Notanter ait, Aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, ad differentiam aquarum exsistentium super cœlos, hoc est, Ego creator omnipotens definio, volo ac jubeo, ut aquæ elementares, quæ sua raritate et extensione ac abundantia occupant spatium aeris, descendant et confluant in unum locum communem, qui est locus Oceani, et ambit terram. Et appareat arida, id est terra, quæ ex sua natura est sicca. Et factum est ita. Deo namque jubente, mox cœpit aqua celerrimo motu descendere, congregari, atque ad locum sibi connaturalem concurrere.
paras.en: [[1:9|Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cælo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. He says pointedly, [[1:9|the waters that are under the heaven|Aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt]], to distinguish them from the waters that are above the heavens; that is: I, the almighty Creator, determine, will and command that the elemental waters, which by their thinness, their extension and their abundance fill the space of the air, come down and flow together into one common place, which is the place of the Ocean, and which surrounds the earth. [[1:9|and let the dry land appear|Et appareat arida]], that is, the earth, which of its own nature is dry. [[1:9|And it was so done|Et factum est ita]]. For at God's command the water at once began with the swiftest motion to come down, to be gathered together, and to run together to the place natural to it.

paras.t: Et vocavit Deus aridam terram, id est, in sua præscientia instituit aridam sic debere vocari, et proprietatem indidit ei, a qua merito terra vocatur. Ideo enim voluit terram discooperiri ab aquis, et apparere, ut fieret apta habitationi hominum ac brutorum, sicque eorum pedibus tereretur. Unde dicitur terra, quasi pedibus trita.
paras.en: [[1:10|And God called the dry land, Earth|Et vocavit Deus aridam terram]], that is, in his foreknowledge he appointed that the dry land should be so called, and put into it a property from which it is rightly called earth. For he willed the earth to be uncovered from the waters and to appear for this reason: that it might become fit for the dwelling of men and beasts, and so be trodden by their feet. Hence it is called *terra*, earth, as being *trita*, trodden, by feet [a play on *terra* and *terere*, "to tread"].

paras.t: Congregationesque aquarum appellavit maria. Si aqua congregata est in uno loco, cur non ait singulariter, Congregationem aquarum appellavit mare? Respondetur, quod quamvis aqua pro maxima sui parte in loco Oceani sit collecta, attamen in diversis terræ partibus manserunt partes aquæ, quæ fuerunt particulares congregationes aquarum, et continuationem aliquam habuerunt ad Oceanum seu ipsum aquæ elementum. Talia quoque loca aquarum, vocantur lacus et sinus ac receptacula. Et partim fuerunt et sunt sub terra, partim quoque supra terram secundum necessitatem, utilitatem, et exigentiam vitæ hominum ac brutorum, prout infinita atque omnipotens sapientia Creatoris, hoc præcognovit ac ordinavit: nihilominus aquæ dicuntur veraciter congregatæ ad locum unum, quoniam pro ma[…] per partes ad unum collecta sunt locum, et omnes naturaliter inclinantur ad locum unum.
