Et sicut egrediuntur ab illo propter commune bonum prælatum, sic naturaliter regrediuntur ad ipsum, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant. Et iterum Salomon ait: Omnia flumina in mare intrant, et ipsum non redundat. Has itaque aquarum congregationes Deus maria appellavit, juxta proprietatem linguæ Hebrææ, qua omnis congregatio magna aquarum, mare vocatur, sicut in Evangelio legitur mare Tiberiadis, et mare Galilææ.
paras.en: [[1:10|and the gathering together of the waters, he called Seas|Congregationesque aquarum appellavit maria]] [the Latin is plural, *congregationes*, "the gatherings"]. If the water was gathered in one place, why does he not say in the singular, *He called the gathering of the waters the sea*? The answer is that, although the water for the greatest part of it was collected in the place of the Ocean, yet in various parts of the earth there remained parts of water, which were particular gatherings of waters and had some continuity with the Ocean, that is, with the element of water itself. Such places of waters are also called lakes, gulfs and basins. And they were and are partly under the earth, and partly above the earth, according to the need, the usefulness and the requirements of the life of men and beasts, as the infinite and almighty wisdom of the Creator foreknew and ordained. Nevertheless the waters are truly said to be gathered together into one place, since for the most […] by parts they were collected into one place, and all of them naturally tend towards one place. And as they go out from it for the sake of the common good preferred to it, so they naturally go back to it, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Eccles 1:7|unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again|Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant]] [the margin note here is illegible; Denis names Ecclesiasticus, but the words are from Ecclesiastes 1:7]. And again Solomon says: [[Eccles 1:7|All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea doth not overflow|Omnia flumina in mare intrant, et ipsum non redundat]]. These gatherings of waters, then, God called seas, according to the usage of the Hebrew tongue, in which every great gathering of waters is called a sea; as in the Gospel we read of the sea of Tiberias and the sea of Galilee[[John 6:1||]] [the margin note here is illegible; John 6:1 names both].

paras.t: Præterea, unum est mare principale, totale, et maximum, quod est quasi cingulum terræ, quod vocatur oceanum et abyssus. Sunt quoque multa minora et particularia maria, quæ sunt Oceani brachia. Magnum vero et totale mare, est ipsum aquæ elementum. Hinc loquitur Beda: Quum multa sint maria, attamen dicit aquas congregatas in unum locum, quoniam magno mari omnia illa junguntur. Et si aliqui lacus in se ipsis stricti videntur, occultis tamen meatibus revolvuntur in mare. Fossores quoque puteorum hoc probant, quoniam tota tellus per invisibiles venas aquis repleta est, quibus omnibus ex mari origo est. Sed posset quis dicere: Quum aqua sit multo major quam terra, imo (ut aliqui dicunt) sicut est decies rarior ac subtilior terra, ita est decies major et diffusior ea, quomodo ergo potuit congregari et collocari in uno terræ loco? Rursus, quum aqua sit multo levior terra, quomodo fuit ei naturale, a superficie terræ quam operuerat, discedere, atque in concavitatibus recipi terræ?
paras.en: Moreover, there is one principal sea, entire and greatest, which is as it were a girdle of the earth, and which is called the ocean and the deep. There are also many lesser and particular seas, which are arms of the Ocean. But the great and entire sea is the element of water itself. Hence Bede says: Though there are many seas, yet he says that the waters were gathered into one place, because all of them are joined to the great sea. And if some lakes seem to be enclosed in themselves, yet by hidden passages they flow back into the sea. The diggers of wells also prove this, since the whole earth is filled with waters through unseen veins, all of which have their origin from the sea. But someone might say: Since water is much greater than earth, indeed (as some say) just as it is ten times thinner and finer than earth, so it is ten times greater and more widely spread than it, how then could it be gathered together and placed in one place of the earth? Again, since water is much lighter than earth, how was it natural for it to leave the surface of the earth which it had covered, and to be received into the hollows of the earth?

paras.t: Ad intelligendum horum solutionem, commemoranda sunt verba Bedæ, quæ Magister secundo libro allegat, et habentur in Glossa. Itaque Beda super Genesim loquitur: Congregatæ sunt aquæ cœlo inferiores in unam matricem, ut lux quæ præterito biduo illustraverat aquas in aere puro, clarior fulgeat, et appareat terra quæ cooperta aquis latebat, et quæ aquis limosa erat, fieret arida atque graminibus apta. Si autem quæratur, ubi congregatæ sunt aquæ, quæ totum texerant spatium usque ad cœlum, hoc est usque ad orbem lunæ, potuit fieri ut terra subsidens, concavas partes præberet, in quibus fluctuantes aquas reciperet. Potest etiam credi, primas illas aquas rariores fuisse, quæ sicut nebula tegerent terras, sed congregatas et spissatas, et ideo facile in unum potuisse redigi locum. His concordat quod in Scholastica dicitur historia. Hinc alii dicunt, divina virtute concavitates factas esse in terra, in quibus aqua reciperetur. Et quia tunc debitam densitatem accepit, locum occupavit minorem. Unde et Damascenus ait libro secundo: Deo jubente, aquarum receptacula facta sunt, et tunc montes exstiterunt. Alii quoque dicunt, aquas in Oceano ac aliis locis, hinc inde in magnam altitudinem elevari ac crescere: quod verum esse probatur in sphæra mundi, quoniam aqua tendit ex sua natura ad sphæricam rotunditatem, sicut in gutta aquæ potest perpendi. Unde Basilius ait: Experimento compertum est aquas maris Rubri esse altiores quam terram. Et Thomas in prima parte: Potuit, inquit, aqua in altiorem elevationem uniri. Denique aquis sic congregatis, ignis et aer in suis locis steterunt, et ab aliis sunt divisi.
paras.en: To understand the solution of these difficulties, we must recall the words of Bede which the Master [Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences] cites in his second book, and which are found in the Gloss. Bede, then, says on Genesis: The waters below the heaven were gathered together into one bed, so that the light which for the past two days had lit up the waters in the pure air might shine more brightly, and the earth, which lay hidden covered by the waters, might appear, and, having been muddy from the waters, might become dry and fit for grasses. But if it is asked where the waters were gathered which had covered the whole space up to the heaven, that is, up to the sphere of the moon, it may have been that the earth, settling down, offered hollow parts in which to receive the surging waters. It can also be believed that those first waters were thinner, covering the lands like a mist, but being gathered and thickened could therefore easily be brought together into one place. With this agrees what is said in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]. Hence others say that by divine power hollows were made in the earth in which the water was received; and because it then took on its due density, it occupied a smaller place. Hence Damascene also says in his second book: At God's command, receptacles of the waters were made, and then the mountains came to be. Others again say that the waters in the Ocean and in other places are raised up and swell here and there to a great height: which is shown to be true in the sphere of the world, since water by its nature tends to a spherical roundness, as can be seen in a drop of water. Hence Basil says: It has been found by experience that the waters of the Red Sea are higher than the land. And Thomas, in the First Part: The water, he says, could have been gathered together to a higher elevation. Finally, the waters being thus gathered together, fire and air stood in their own places and were divided from the others.

paras.t: Verumtamen præinductis contradicit Rabbi Paulus, et quia in multis sermonibus invenitur stultitia, ipse circa hæc multa scribendo, videtur crebrius insipienter locutus. Primo itaque dicit, quod quum aqua sit multo rarior et major terra, non potuit terra habere capacitatem recipiendi in concavitatibus suis totam quantitatem aquæ, quanta erat super terram habitabilem, quæ est fere quarta pars orbis totius terræ secundum astronomos. Istud argumentum videtur ad oppositum militare. Quum enim aqua illa fuerit valde rara, potuit multum inspissari, et in minori loco uniri.
paras.en: Rabbi Paul, however, contradicts what has been brought forward [Paul of Burgos, in his Additions to Lyra]; and since folly is found in many words, he, writing much on these matters, seems rather often to have spoken unwisely. First, then, he says that since water is much thinner and greater than earth, the earth could not have had the capacity to receive in its hollows the whole quantity of water that lay over the habitable earth, which is almost a fourth part of the whole globe of the earth according to the astronomers. This argument seems to tell for the opposite: for since that water was very thin, it could be greatly thickened and brought together in a smaller place.

paras.t: Insuper arguit contra hanc aquæ condensationem, quia videmus quod aquæ in concavitatibus receptæ, non sunt densiores quam aliæ. Ad quod dicendum, quod imo aquæ marinæ et puteales sunt grossiores aquis vaporabiliter elevatis in aere. Et quamvis non sint multum spissiores aliis aquis nunc existentibus, sunt tamen multum densiores aquis illis primariis. Præterea contra elevationem aquæ in mari dicit, quod cum tota aqua sit fluida, non potest habere partes aliquas aliis altiores et montuosas, sicut in terra propter suam soliditatem hoc accidit. Ad quod dico, quod quamvis in aquis una et eadem pars non maneat fixe sic altior, sed nunc defluat, nunc ascendat, semper tamen aliquæ partes sic intumescunt in maribus: quod plenius probavi super illud in Psalmo, Super montes stabunt aquæ. Sed et Paulus iste postea istud concedit, quod scilicet in aliquibus locis aquæ maris sint altiores altissimis montibus terræ, et ita verba sua non videntur ad invicem concordare. Alia multa scribit quæ astronomiam concernunt, nec certitudinem habent, nec paucis queunt sermonibus expediri; idcirco dimitto.
paras.en: Further, he argues against this condensing of the water, because we see that the waters received in hollows are not denser than others. To which it must be said that, on the contrary, the waters of the sea and of wells are coarser than the waters raised as vapour into the air. And although they are not much thicker than the other waters that now exist, they are yet much denser than those first waters. Moreover, against the raising of the water in the sea he says that, since all water is fluid, it cannot have some parts higher than others and like mountains, as happens in the earth because of its solidity. To which I say that, although in the waters one and the same part does not stay fixed as higher, but now flows down and now rises, yet some parts always swell up in this way in the seas: as I have shown more fully on that verse in the Psalm, [[Ps 103:6|above the mountains shall the waters stand|Super montes stabunt aquæ]]. And this Paul himself afterwards grants it, namely that in some places the waters of the sea are higher than the highest mountains of the earth; and so his words do not seem to agree with one another. He writes many other things which concern astronomy, which neither have certainty nor can be dealt with in a few words; therefore I leave them aside.

paras.t: Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum, id est, distinctio et ordinatio ista elementorum placuit sibi, quia perutilis exstitit et decora, imo et necessaria vitæ hominum ac brutorum: sicque quod ante placuit Deo in sua præscientia, nunc placuit in effectu. Circa hoc verbum allegat Thomas super secundum Rabbi Moysen, dicentem: In secundo die medium elementum, scilicet aqua, a supremo distinguebatur, et ita non erat perfecta distinctio medii elementi, nisi etiam ab infimo distingueretur: quod factum est tertio die. Sicque opus secundæ diei tertio die completum est, propter quod benedictio tertiæ diei, videlicet istud, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, ad utrumque refertur. Et hoc est melius dictum, quam quod quidam hic scribit, dicens quod hoc dicitur pro opere secundæ diei, imo dicitur pro opere isto utriusque diei.
paras.en: [[1:10|And God saw that it was good|Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], that is, this distinction and ordering of the elements pleased him, because it was most useful and comely, indeed necessary for the life of men and beasts: and so what had before pleased God in his foreknowledge now pleased him in effect. On this word Thomas, on the second book [of the Sentences], cites Rabbi Moses, who says: On the second day the middle element, namely water, was distinguished from the highest; and so the distinction of the middle element was not complete unless it was also distinguished from the lowest, which was done on the third day. And so the work of the second day was completed on the third day; for which reason the blessing of the third day, namely this, [[1:10|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], refers to both. And this is better said than what a certain writer writes here, saying that this is said for the work of the second day: rather it is said for this work of both days.

paras.t: Et ait: Germinet, id est producat, terra herbam virentem. Ponitur hic singulare pro plurali, ut sit tenor: producat terra herbas recentes et omnes hujusmodi fructus instar herbarum ex terra nascentes. Et facientem semen, hoc est, habentem in se rationem seminalem seu vim causalem ad producendum simile sibi in specie. Et lignum pomiferum faciens fructum juxta genus suum, id est universas arbores fructuosas cum fructibus suis, qui fructus sunt juxta genus arborum, ex quibus nascuntur, id est, secundum quod convenit naturæ ac speciei arborum singularum. Itaque per lignum pomiferum, designatur omne lignum faciens fructum, quia per pomum intelligi solet in Scripturis quicumque arborum fructus. Unde in Evangelio, quo legitur quod Jesus quæsivit fructum in ficu, habetur quod non erat tempus pomi illius.
paras.en: [[1:11|And he said|Et ait]]: [[1:11|let the earth bring forth|Germinet]] [*germinet*, literally "let it sprout"], that is, let it produce, [[1:11|green herb|herbam virentem]]. The singular is put here for the plural, so that the sense is: let the earth produce fresh herbs and all such produce springing from the earth after the manner of herbs. [[1:11|and such as may seed|Et facientem semen]], that is, having in itself a seminal reason, or causal power, to produce what is like itself in species. [[1:11|and the fruit tree yielding fruit after its kind|Et lignum pomiferum faciens fructum juxta genus suum]], that is, all fruitful trees with their fruits, which fruits are after the kind of the trees from which they grow, that is, according as befits the nature and species of each tree. So by *the fruit tree* [*lignum pomiferum*, literally "the apple-bearing tree"] is meant every tree that yields fruit, since in the Scriptures *pomum* is commonly taken for any fruit of trees. Hence in the Gospel, where we read that Jesus sought fruit on the fig tree, we have that [[Mark 11:13|it was not the time for figs|non erat tempus pomi illius]] [Denis reads *pomi illius*, "of that fruit", where the Vulgate has *ficorum*, "of figs": hence his point].

paras.t: Cujus semen in semetipso sit super terram. Quid intelligatur per semen, jam dictum est. In pomis enim et aliis fructibus sunt grana ut semina, estque in eis virtus propagandi consimilia sibi in specie, sicut videmus ad oculum, qualiter ex modico grano aut simili quodam grandis nascitur arbor. Nec solum tunc productæ sunt herbæ evidenter utiles ac arbores fructuosæ, sed etiam spinæ ac tribuli, infructuosaque ligna, secundum quod pertinent ad ordinem universi. Non tamen producebantur homini ad pœnam ante ipsius transgressionem.
paras.en: [[1:11|which may have seed in itself upon the earth|Cujus semen in semetipso sit super terram]]. What is meant by seed has been said already. For in apples and other fruits there are grains as seeds, and in them is the power of propagating things like themselves in species; as we see with our eyes how from a small grain or some such thing a great tree grows. And not only were herbs plainly useful and fruitful trees produced then, but also thorns and thistles and unfruitful trees, inasmuch as they belong to the order of the universe. They were not, however, produced as a punishment to man before his transgression.

paras.t: Denique sicut præhabitum est, duplex informitas fuit primo in terra: Una, quoniam fuit aquis operta, et hæc ei ablata est per congregationem aquarum in unum locum. Alia, quia fuit infructuosa, et hæc ei ablata est per germinationem præfatam. Si autem objiciatur quod germinatio ista magis pertineat ad terræ ornatum, quam ad ejus distinctionem: dicendum quod ornatus elementorum attenditur penes quædam extrinseca, non penes ea quæ radicitus inseparabiliterque adhærent, sicut in homine vestimenta, monilia, gemmæ, et consimilia, proprie pertinent ad ejus ornatum; sicque animalia spectant ad terræ ornatum, non proprie herbæ ac arbores.
paras.en: Finally, as was said before, there was at first a twofold formlessness in the earth: one, because it was covered with waters, and this was taken from it by the gathering of the waters into one place; the other, because it was unfruitful, and this was taken from it by the germination spoken of. But if it is objected that this germination belongs rather to the adornment of the earth than to its distinction, it must be said that the adornment of the elements is reckoned by certain things outward to them, not by things that cleave to them at the root and inseparably; as in a man clothes, necklaces, gems and the like properly belong to his adornment; and so the animals belong to the adornment of the earth, not, properly speaking, herbs and trees.

paras.t: Et […] ut ita. Et protulit terra herbam virentem, et afferentem semen juxta genus suum, id est juxta speciem suam, lignumque faciens fructum, et habens unumquodque […] secundum speciem suam, ita quod quodlibet lignum seu quælibet arbor habuit in se semen secundum naturam suam specificam. Sensus verborum istorum elucescit ex introductis.
paras.en: [[1:11|And|Et]] […] [[1:11|so done|ita]]. [[1:12|And the earth brought forth the green herb, and such as yieldeth seed according to its kind|Et protulit terra herbam virentem, et afferentem semen juxta genus suum]], that is, according to its species, [[1:12|and the tree that beareth fruit, having|lignumque faciens fructum, et habens]] [[1:12|each one|unumquodque]] […] [[1:12|according to its kind|secundum speciem suam]], so that each tree, or every tree whatever, had in itself seed according to its specific nature. The sense of these words is clear from what has been brought in.

paras.t: Præterea, quod dictum est, Germinet terra herbam virentem, etc., quidam ita exponunt, quod tunc data est terræ virtus productiva ad germinandum ex se herbas ac arbores. Alii vero intelligunt, quod Deus præcepit tunc eas nasci ex terra. Sed dicendum, quod intelligendum sit utroque modo, ut patet ex textu. Nempe quum dictum est, Germinet terra herbam virentem, paulò post subditur, Et factum est ita; deinde apertius additur, Et protulit terra herbam virentem. Propter quod ait S. Ambrosius, quod herba est antiquior sole. Utroque etiam modo plantarum productio ad distinctionis pertinet opus, quoniam ad plantarum pullulationem seu productionem sufficit virtus influentialis cœlestium corporum loco patris, et virtus terræ loco matris, ut ait Philosophus. Sicque principia activa communia ad opus distinctionis spectantia, sufficiunt ad generationem plantarum, non autem ad productionem animalium perfectorum, ad quæ requiritur virtus formativa exsistens in semine particularis agentis. Idcirco ipsorum productio pertinet ad ornatum, et facta sunt sexta die, ut infra habetur.
paras.en: Moreover, what was said, [[1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Germinet terra herbam virentem]], etc., some expound thus: that the earth was then given a productive power to sprout herbs and trees out of itself. Others understand that God then commanded them to spring from the earth. But it must be said that it is to be understood in both ways, as is clear from the text. For when it has been said, [[1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Germinet terra herbam virentem]], a little after is added, [[1:11|And it was so done|Et factum est ita]]; and then more plainly is added, [[1:12|And the earth brought forth the green herb|Et protulit terra herbam virentem]]. For which reason St. Ambrose says that the herb is older than the sun. In either way, too, the production of plants belongs to the work of distinction, since for the sprouting or production of plants the influence of the heavenly bodies in the place of a father, and the power of the earth in the place of a mother, suffice, as the Philosopher says. And so the common active principles that belong to the work of distinction suffice for the generation of plants, but not for the production of the perfect animals, for which is required a formative power existing in the seed of a particular agent. Therefore their production belongs to the adornment, and they were made on the sixth day, as is found below.

paras.t: Amplius, quia in textu habetur, Producat terra herbam virentem, Ambrosius, Glossa, ac alii multi dixerunt mundum factum in vere, quia tunc apparent herbæ virentes. Et idem dicit Damascenus libro secundo. Sed quia subjungitur, Et faciens fructum, alii dicunt mundum conditum in autumno, quando maturi sunt fructus. Hinc refert Lyra, quod quidam Hebræorum doctores dicunt mundum factum in Martio, quia tunc terra incipit herbas producere. Unde in Exodo Martius primus mensium appellatur. Alii Hebræorum doctores affirmant mundum in Septembri creatum, quia tunc fructus maturi sunt, habentque semina in se ipsis. Et hæc opinio a Judæis (ut ait) tenetur communius, tanquam rationabilior, quoniam Dei perfecta sunt opera. Quemadmodum enim homo factus est in statu perfecto quo potuit generare, sic videtur quod terræ nascentia matura producta sunt, utpote habentia semina in se ipsis.
paras.en: Further, because the text has, [[1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Producat terra herbam virentem]], Ambrose, the Gloss and many others have said that the world was made in spring, because then green herbs appear. And Damascene says the same in his second book. But because there follows, [[1:11|yielding fruit|faciens fructum]], others say that the world was founded in autumn, when fruits are ripe. Hence Lyra relates that some doctors of the Hebrews say the world was made in March, because then the earth begins to bring forth herbs; and so in Exodus March is called the first of the months[[Ex 12:2||]]. Other doctors of the Hebrews affirm that the world was created in September, because then fruits are ripe and have seeds in themselves. And this opinion (he says) is held more commonly by the Jews, as the more reasonable, since [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Dei perfecta sunt opera]]. For as man was made in a perfect state, in which he could beget, so it seems that the growths of the earth were produced ripe, as having seeds in themselves.

paras.t: Constat quoque ex dictis, quod dictum eorum qui dicunt, unumquodque opus sex dierum factum in momento aut instanti, salvari non valeat: quia aquarum congregatio exstitit successiva, herbæ autem et arbores de terra productæ sunt absque concursu influentiæ cœlestium corporum, imo et absque præviis specierum suarum seminibus. Hinc fertur in Glossa: Omnia creata sunt perfecta, et homo perfectus ætate; arbores quoque cum fructu et foliis, et ligna pomis onusta. Nec primæ herbæ ac arbores prodierunt de semine, sed de terra, quæ ad unam Conditoris jussionem apparuit herbis compta, nemoribusque vestita, quæ deinde produxerunt ex se fructus et semina specierum suarum.
paras.en: It is clear also from what has been said that the saying of those who say that each work of the six days was done in a moment or instant cannot be upheld: for the gathering of the waters was successive; while the herbs and trees were produced from the earth without the concurrence of the influence of the heavenly bodies, and indeed without previous seeds of their species. Hence it is said in the Gloss: All things were created perfect, and man perfect in age; the trees too with fruit and leaves, and the trees laden with apples. Nor did the first herbs and trees come forth from seed, but from the earth, which at one command of the Maker appeared adorned with herbs and clothed with woods, which then brought forth from themselves the fruits and seeds of their species.

paras.t: Quæri posset, an inter terræ discoopertionem et germinationem præfatam intervenerit aliqua mora, an etiam herbæ ac arbores cum fructibus suis maturis in instanti productæ sint. Deinde tangenda est breviter expositio litteræ hujus, secundum opinionem dicentium materiam primo creatam sub forma corporeitatis dumtaxat, quorum opinioni non videtur hæc littera consonare, quemadmodum jam patebit.
paras.en: It might be asked whether any delay came between the uncovering of the earth and the germination spoken of, and whether the herbs and trees with their ripe fruits were produced in an instant. Next, the exposition of this text must be touched on briefly according to the opinion of those who say that matter was first created under the form of corporeity only [that is, with no more than the bare form of being a body]; with whose opinion this text does not seem to accord, as will now be clear.

paras.t: Dixit vero Deus: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Ex tenore verborum istorum patet quod littera hæc loquitur de aqua et terra, tanquam de rebus jam exsistentibus. Et ita expositores præfati et Glossa exponunt hunc passum, ut patuit. Hi autem dicunt, quod hoc tertio die elementa in substantialibus suis formis producta sunt, ex ea parte illius primæ materiæ, quæ adhuc mansit informis, atque sub forma communi, cœlestibus orbibus ex ea formatis die secundo, juxta opinionem eorum, ut præcedenti articulo dictum est. Sicque per hoc quod dicit, Congregentur aquæ in locum unum, et appareat arida, designetur elementorum istorum productio substantialis, et cum hoc naturalis inclinatio eis impressa ad propria loca: quod non videtur sonare, nec textui concordare. Congregari namque et apparere non competunt nisi enti in actu. Rursum, congregari et apparere, præsupponunt esse, quemadmodum actus secundus actum primum. Et quamvis Deus vocet ea quæ non sunt, tanquam ea quæ sunt, sic tamen non præcipit aliquid agere aut pati, nisi his quæ sunt. Reliqua verba litteræ hujus propter hanc opinionem, non exigunt aliam expositionem.
paras.en: [[1:9|God also said; Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Dixit vero Deus: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. From the tenor of these words it is clear that this text speaks of water and earth as of things already existing; and so the expositors mentioned and the Gloss expound this passage, as has appeared. But these men say that on this third day the elements were produced in their substantial forms, out of that part of the first matter which still remained formless and under the common form, the heavenly spheres having been formed from it on the second day, according to their opinion, as was said in the preceding article. And so by his saying, [[1:9|Let the waters|Congregentur aquæ]] [[1:9|be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|in locum unum, et appareat arida]], there would be signified the substantial production of these elements, and with it the natural inclination impressed on them towards their proper places: which does not seem to be the sound of it, nor to agree with the text. For to be gathered and to appear belong only to a being in act. Again, to be gathered and to appear presuppose being, as second act presupposes first act. And although God [[Rom 4:17|calleth those things that are not, as those that are|vocet ea quæ non sunt, tanquam ea quæ sunt]], yet he does not in this way command anything to act or to be acted upon except those things that are. The other words of this text call for no further exposition on account of this opinion.

paras.t: Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum, hoc est, quod præscripta germinatio utilis esset ad multa, et pertinens ad universi decentiam.
paras.en: [[1:12|And God saw that it was good|Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], that is, that the germination described was useful for many things and belonged to the seemliness of the universe.

paras.t: Et factum est vespere et mane dies tertius: quorum verborum expositio habita est articulo nono ac decimo. Et ait quidam hoc loco, quod verba ista nunc repetuntur pro approbatione operis hujus tertiæ diei. Sed quia hæc verba semel relata sunt ad congregationem aquæ hoc tertio die factam, ideo verius nunc referuntur ad residuum opus diei istius, videlicet ad germinationem præfatam.
paras.en: [[1:13|And the evening and the morning were the third day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies tertius]]: the exposition of these words was given in the ninth and tenth articles. And a certain writer says in this place that these words [that is, *God saw that it was good*] are now repeated in approval of the work of this third day. But since these words were already once referred to the gathering of the water done on this third day, they are now more truly referred to the remaining work of this day, namely the germination spoken of.

paras.t: Postremo, quantum capere queo, de congregatione aquarum in unum locum, non est tanta difficultas, ut quidam prætendunt. Locus quippe in quo congregatæ sunt aquæ, est concavitas terræ, ambiens totam habitabilem terram: in qua concavitate aqua dicitur congregata, non quod utramque extremitatem aquæ circumcludat in se illa concavitas, imo aqua immensurabiliter eam excedit, et ultra eam latissime prorsus diffunditur, non tamen in infinitum, sed in extremitate sua se diffusa, est contigua aeri elementari, qui cingit et ambit aquam, quemadmodum aqua terram, imo et plus. Terminatur autem fluxus aquæ in extremitate illa contigua aeri naturaliter in se ipso, quoniam quælibet pars aquæ naturaliter inclinatur ad centrum ipsius, quemadmodum dici solet de terra. Hinc Salomon: Certa, inquit, lege et gyro vallabat abyssos. Et quoniam elementum aquæ in utraque sua extremitate servat terminum sibi præfixum, et manet in loco sortito, quasi ab utraque parte esset concavitate terræ circumclusa atque arctata, ideo in Psalmo asseritur: Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos. Unde ad sanctum Job Deus loquitur: Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens? Posui vectes et ostia, et dixi: Hucusque venies, et non procedes amplius, et hic confringes tumentes fluctus tuos. Per Jeremiam quoque loquitur Deus: Posui arenam terminum mari, præceptum sempiternum, quod non præteribit. Intumescent fluctus ejus, et non transibunt illud. Ad salvandum ergo, quod aqua elementaris tam grandis in unum collecta est locum, non oportet inquirere, an terra sit satis magna ad hoc. Quod si rursus quæratur, quid terminat extrema fluidæ aquæ, jam responsio data est, quia ex propria natura sibi divinitus indita habet terminum sibi præfixum. Unde et Aristoteles subtilissime dixit: Omnium natura constantium, certa est mensura et finis et ratio magnitudinis.
paras.en: Lastly, as far as I can grasp it, there is not so great a difficulty about the gathering of the waters into one place as some make out. For the place in which the waters were gathered is the hollow of the earth that surrounds the whole habitable earth: in which hollow the water is said to be gathered, not because that hollow encloses both extremities of the water within itself (rather, the water exceeds it beyond measure and spreads out beyond it very widely indeed), yet not to infinity; but, spread out, at its outer limit it is in contact with the elemental air, which girds and surrounds the water as the water does the earth, and even more. And the flow of the water at that limit where it touches the air is naturally bounded in itself, since every part of the water naturally tends towards its centre, as is commonly said of the earth. Hence Solomon: [[Prov 8:27|with a certain|Certa]], he says, [[Prov 8:27|law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]] [the margin gives Prov. xiii, 27; the words are Prov 8:27]. And since the element of water at each of its limits keeps the bound set for it and stays in the place allotted to it, as though it were enclosed and confined on either side by a hollow of the earth, therefore it is asserted in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:7|Gathering together the waters of the sea, as in a vessel; laying up the depths in storehouses.|Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos]] Hence God speaks to holy Job: [[Job 38:8|Who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke forth as issuing out of the womb:|Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens?]] I [[Job 38:10|made it bars and doors|Posui vectes et ostia]], [[Job 38:11|And I said: Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further, and here thou shalt break thy swelling waves.|et dixi: Hucusque venies, et non procedes amplius, et hic confringes tumentes fluctus tuos]] Through Jeremias too God speaks: [[Jer 5:22|I have set the sand a bound for the sea, an everlasting ordinance, which it shall not pass over|Posui arenam terminum mari, præceptum sempiternum, quod non præteribit]]; [[Jer 5:22|they shall swell, and shall not pass over it|Intumescent fluctus ejus, et non transibunt illud]]. To uphold, then, that so great an elemental water was gathered into one place, there is no need to inquire whether the earth is large enough for it. And if it is asked again what bounds the outer limits of the fluid water, the answer has already been given: that from its own nature, put into it by God, it has a bound set for it. Hence Aristotle too said most subtly: Of all things that exist by nature there is a fixed measure and limit and proportion of size.

1.title: Elucidatio litteræ, in qua recitatur opus quarti diei
1.title_en: Explanation of the letter, in which the work of the fourth day is recounted

paras.t: Sex diebus facta sunt omnia, in quibus describitur triplex opus, puta creatio, distinctio, et ornatus. Prima autem die creata sunt cœlum et elementa. Eodemque die cœpit distinctio per lucis productionem, qua cœlum distinctionem accepit. Secundo die aquæ ab invicem sunt distinctæ, per firmamenti formationem. Tertio die terra distinctionem sumpsit, dum aquæ ab ea subtractæ, atque in unum collectæ sunt. Juxta hunc ordinem atque processum, tribus sequentibus diebus prædicta ornata sunt, utpote primo cœlum quarto die; deinde aqua et aer quinto die, per avium pisciumque productionem; ultimo terra, videlicet sexto die, per animalium et hominis formationem. Idcirco nunc dicitur: Dixit autem Deus: Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli.
paras.en: All things were made in six days, in which a threefold work is described: namely creation, distinction and adornment. On the first day the heaven and the elements were created; and on the same day distinction began, through the production of light, by which the heaven received its distinction. On the second day the waters were distinguished from one another, through the forming of the firmament. On the third day the earth took its distinction, when the waters were withdrawn from it and gathered together into one place. Following this order and procedure, the things just named were adorned on the three following days: first the heaven, on the fourth day; then the water and the air on the fifth day, by the production of birds and fishes; last the earth, namely on the sixth day, by the forming of the animals and of man. Therefore it is now said: [[1:14|And God said: Let there be lights made in the firmament of heaven|Dixit autem Deus: Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli]].

paras.t: Quemadmodum super Genesim docet Augustinus, sic exponenda est littera ista Geneseos, ut infidelibus non præludatur via conversionis ad fidem. Si enim viderint nos male irrationabiliterque sentire de rebus præteritis et mundi exordio, naturalibus quoque effectibus, non credent nos bene sentire de rebus futuris, et fine mundi, atque operibus gratiæ et gloriæ consummatæ. Quum ergo textus nunc exponendus, secundum superficiem suam videretur eruditis in naturali philosophia, non solum rudis et falsus, sed etiam irridendus, idcirco exponendus est sapienter et caute. Si enim, juxta Philosophum, stella est densior pars sui orbis, quomodo stellæ dicuntur factæ quarto die, cum orbis eorum sit antea factus? Rursus, quum cœlum sit indivisibile et incorruptibile, integrum, nec porosum, quomodo stellæ dicuntur positæ tunc in cœlo? Iterum, quum unusquisque planeta proprium habeat orbem, quomodo sol et luna dicuntur posita in firmamento cœli? Hæc et multa similia objici possent Scripturæ.
paras.en: As Augustine teaches on Genesis, this text of Genesis is to be expounded in such a way that the road of conversion to the faith is not closed to unbelievers [the print has *præludatur*; the sense requires *præcludatur*, "be closed"]. For if they see that we think wrongly and irrationally about past things and the beginning of the world, and about natural effects too, they will not believe that we think rightly about things to come and the end of the world, and about the works of grace and of consummated glory. Since, then, the text now to be expounded would seem on its surface, to men learned in natural philosophy, not only crude and false but even laughable, it must be expounded wisely and with caution. For if, according to the Philosopher, a star is the denser part of its orb, how are the stars said to have been made on the fourth day, when their orb had been made before? Again, since the heaven is indivisible and incorruptible, whole and without pores, how are the stars said to have been placed in the heaven at that time? And again, since each planet has its own orb, how are the sun and moon said to have been placed in the firmament of heaven? These and many like objections could be raised against Scripture.

paras.t: Itaque, juxta positionem supra amplius approbatam, iste est sensus: Fiant luminaria, videlicet sol et luna et ceteri planetæ ac stellæ; in firmamento cœli, id est in cœlo stellato et sphæris seu orbibus sub ipso contentis, reddendo singula singulis. Firmamentum quippe nunc sumitur pro octava sphæra, et aliis septem sphæris planetarum. Et quod ait, In firmamento cœli, intransitive sumendum est, ac si dicatur: virtus Dei, seu corpus carnis. Dicuntur autem luminaria facta, non quod tunc creata sint, aut ex materia præjacenti producta, sed quia tunc acceperunt plenariam lucem sibi congruentem, et virtutem activam perfectam ad determinatos variosque producendos effectus in inferioribus istis, ut dictum est plenius. Juxta quem modum aliquid dicitur fieri, quando recipit notabilem in accidentalibus mutationem, quemadmodum David libro secundo Regum a magna persecutione ereptus, dixit: An ignoro me hodie factum regem super Israel?
paras.en: Therefore, according to the position more fully approved above, this is the sense: [[1:14|Let there be lights made|Fiant luminaria]], namely the sun and moon and the other planets and the stars; [[1:14|in the firmament of heaven|in firmamento cœli]], that is, in the starry heaven and in the spheres or orbs contained beneath it, assigning each to its own. For the firmament is here taken for the eighth sphere and for the other seven spheres of the planets. And where it says, [[1:14|in the firmament of heaven|In firmamento cœli]], this is to be taken intransitively [that is, "of heaven" does not name a second thing beyond the firmament: the firmament is itself the heaven], as if one said "the power of God" or "the body of the flesh". Now the lights are said to have been made, not because they were then created or produced from pre-existing matter, but because they then received the full light befitting them, and the perfect active power to produce determinate and various effects in these lower things, as was said more fully above. In this way a thing is said to be made when it receives a notable change in its accidents; as David, in the second book of Kings, when delivered from a great persecution, said: [[2 Kings 19:22|do not I know that this day I am made king over Israel?|An ignoro me hodie factum regem super Israel?]]

paras.t: Hinc asserit Thomas super secundum, distinctione 15: Præter principia communia activa in tota natura, exiguntur determinatæ virtutes moventes ad determinatas formas ac species; hujusmodique virtutes rebus sunt inditæ per opus ornatus. Sicut autem actio virtutum inferiorum communiter agentium, reducitur in virtutem cœlestem universaliter activam; sic virtutes in inferioribus moventes ad determinatos effectus seu species, reducuntur in quasdam virtutes cœlestes determinatas: et tales virtutes præcipue sunt in stellis atque planetis, quæ secundum diversos adspectus et conjunctiones imprimunt ad species determinatas, prout undecimo Metaphysicæ asserit Commentator. Hinc inferiores virtutes causales sunt tanquam instrumenta superiorum virtutum, secundum eumdem Commentatorem octavo Physicorum. Itaque propter tam notabilem in accidentalibus proprietatibus, dispositionibus, virtutibus et influentiis immutationem ac meliorationem, recte dicuntur luminaria facta die quarta, qua complementum suum sortita sunt.
paras.en: Hence Thomas asserts on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 15: Besides the common active principles in the whole of nature, there are required determinate powers that move toward determinate forms and species; and such powers were put into things through the work of adornment. And as the action of the lower powers that act in a common way is traced back to the universally active heavenly power, so the powers in lower things that move toward determinate effects or species are traced back to certain determinate heavenly powers: and such powers are chiefly in the stars and planets, which, according to their different aspects and conjunctions, work toward determinate species, as the Commentator [that is, Averroes] asserts on the eleventh book of the Metaphysics. Hence the lower causal powers are as it were instruments of the higher powers, according to the same Commentator on the eighth book of the Physics. Therefore, because of so notable a change and improvement in their accidental properties, dispositions, powers and influences, the lights are rightly said to have been made on the fourth day, on which they obtained their completion.

paras.t: Et dividant diem ac noctem, id est, successive producant, ab invicem quoque discernant, et ordinate perficiant diem noctemque. Sol enim suo accessu ac præsentia causat diem, et sua absentia noctem. Dies quoque et nox dividuntur ab invicem successione et luce ac tenebrositate, sed et aliis proprietatibus multis, quas medici diligenter assignant. Luna vero et stellæ aliquid claritatis et proprietatis ac virtutis influunt nocti. Hæc autem vicissitudo diei ac noctis, est hominibus multipliciter utilis, imo et necessaria. Nam tempus diurnum est aptius ad laborandum, ad conveniendum, atque ad diversa exercitia exsequenda. Propter quod scriptum est: Ortus est sol, et exibit homo ad opus suum, et ad operationem suam usque ad vesperam. Tempus vero nocturnum est aptius ad quiescendum. Unde in libro de Compunctione ait Chrysostomus, quod sicut mater volens infantulum suum facere dormientem, operit oculos ejus; sic Deus pater volens homines in nocte dormire, obducit visui eorum caliginem, quasi oculorum operculum.
paras.en: [[1:14|to divide the day and the night|Et dividant diem ac noctem]], that is, let them bring about day and night in succession, distinguish them from one another, and complete them in due order. For the sun by its approach and presence causes the day, and by its absence the night. Day and night are also divided from one another by succession, by light and darkness, and by many other properties too, which physicians carefully set down. The moon and the stars, for their part, pour some brightness, property and power into the night. This alternation of day and night is useful to men in many ways, indeed necessary. For the daytime is better suited to labouring, to coming together, and to carrying out various tasks. Wherefore it is written: [[Ps 103:22|The sun ariseth|Ortus est sol]], and [[Ps 103:23|Man shall go forth to his work, and to his labour until the evening|exibit homo ad opus suum, et ad operationem suam usque ad vesperam]]. The night-time, on the other hand, is better suited to rest. Hence Chrysostom says in the book On Compunction that as a mother who wishes to put her little child to sleep covers his eyes, so God the Father, wishing men to sleep at night, draws a darkness over their sight, as it were a lid over the eyes.

paras.t: Et sint in signa et tempora et dies et annos. Hunc locum exponit Bonaventura sic super secundum: Duplex est usus seu actio signi, videlicet significare et distinguere. Si ergo accipiatur signum ab actu significandi, sensus est, quod luminaria facta sunt in signa, id est in significationem futurorum, et in variationem temporum et annorum atque dierum: ita ut temporum variatio attendatur penes aeris immutationem, quantum ad calorem et frigus: variatio autem dierum, penes lucem et tenebras: variatio vero annorum, juxta renovationem horum duorum: sicque luminaria sunt in signum non quorumlibet futurorum, sed eorum quorum ipsa sunt quodammodo causa, videlicet imbrium ac ventorum, serenitatis ac tempestatis, seu etiam eorum, quæ divina providentia per ea præsignare decrevit, puta illorum quæ circa judicium sunt futura, juxta quod scriptum est: Erunt signa in sole et luna. Porro eorum quæ dependent ex libero arbitrio, non sunt signa ex institutione divina; sed potius traxit ea ad talia designanda, fictio curiositasque humana.
paras.en: [[1:14|and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years|Et sint in signa et tempora et dies et annos]]. Bonaventure expounds this passage thus, on the second book of the Sentences: The use or act of a sign is twofold, namely to signify and to distinguish. If, then, *sign* is taken from the act of signifying, the sense is that the lights were made for signs, that is, to signify things to come, and for the variation of seasons and years and days: so that the variation of seasons is reckoned by the change of the air as to heat and cold; the variation of days by light and darkness; and the variation of years by the renewal of these two. And so the lights are a sign not of any future things whatever, but of those of which they are in some way the cause, namely of rains and winds, of fair weather and storm; or else of those which divine providence has decreed to foreshow by them, such as the things that are to come about at the judgment, according to what is written: [[Luke 21:25|there shall be signs in the sun and in the moon|Erunt signa in sole et luna]]. But of the things that depend on free will they are not signs by divine institution; rather, human invention and curiosity has drawn them to signify such things.

paras.t: Si autem signum sumatur ab actu distinguendi, sensus est: Sint in signa, etc., id est in distinctiones temporum, et dierum, ac annorum. Luminaria autem ex motu diurno, quem habent a nona sphæra, causant ac dividunt diem et noctem, potissime sol. Ex motu vero proprio, quem habent in propriis sphæris sub zodiaco, causant distinctionem temporum et dierum ac annorum: quod tamen sol potissime agit, qui per motum istum causat ver, æstatem, autumnum, et hiemem, distinctionem quoque dierum et noctium in longitudine ac brevitate, secundum quod magis ac minus accedit ad nos, aut recedit a nobis, in ascendendo et descendendo in circulo illo obliquo, puta zodiaco. Sunt item in distinctionem annorum, secundum consummationem motus solis in circulo obliquo. Similiter luna suo modo est in signationem temporum et dierum atque annorum apud Judæos, præsertim quantum ad solennitates, sicut apud Christianos est sol. Unde in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: A luna signum diei festi. Verumtamen Ecclesia, sicut et Synagoga, celebrat solennitatem Paschalem et per consequens Pentecosten secundum motum lunæ, quia Paschalis solennitas celebratur non solum in rememorationem dominicæ resurrectionis præteritæ, sed item in præsignationem resurrectionis futuræ. Sicque facit hoc Ecclesia non judaizando, sed futuram illam solemnitatem præfigurando: in quo etiam conformis est quodammodo Synagogæ. Hæc Bonaventura.
paras.en: But if *sign* is taken from the act of distinguishing, the sense is: [[1:14|let them be for signs|Sint in signa]], etc., that is, for the distinctions of seasons, of days and of years. Now by their daily motion, which they have from the ninth sphere, the lights cause and divide day and night, above all the sun. By their proper motion, which they have in their own spheres beneath the zodiac, they cause the distinction of seasons and of days and years. This, however, the sun does above all, which by this motion causes spring, summer, autumn and winter, and also the distinction of days and nights in length and shortness, according as it comes nearer to us or goes further from us, rising and descending in that oblique circle, namely the zodiac. They are likewise for the distinction of years, according to the completion of the sun's motion in the oblique circle. Similarly the moon in its own way serves to mark the seasons and days and years among the Jews, especially as regards the solemn feasts, as the sun does among Christians. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:7|From the moon is the sign of the festival day|A luna signum diei festi]]. Yet the Church, like the Synagogue, celebrates the Paschal solemnity, and consequently Pentecost, according to the motion of the moon, because the Paschal solemnity is celebrated not only in remembrance of the Lord's resurrection that is past, but also in foreshadowing of the resurrection to come. And so the Church does this not by judaizing, but by prefiguring that future solemnity; and in this she is also in some way conformed to the Synagogue. Thus far Bonaventure.

paras.t: Præterea luminaria, taliter distinguendo et efficiendo dies, annos et tempora, conferunt commoda multa hominibus, utpote relevamen fastidii, juxta illud in Hymno: Temporum das tempora, ut alleves fastidium. Item ad seminandum, arandum, metendum, et consimilia opera, quæ exigunt tempora distincta et opportuna, ideo subditur: ut luceant in firmamento cœli, et illuminent terram, id est habitantes in terra, potissime homines, quibus non solum ad videndum, sed etiam ad alia innumerabilia, necessaria est illuminatio solis in die, et etiam suo modo illuminatio lunæ in nocte. Et factum est ita.
paras.en: Moreover the lights, by distinguishing and bringing about days, years and seasons in this way, confer many benefits on men: such as relief from weariness, according to that line in the hymn: Thou givest times their seasons, to relieve our weariness [*Temporum das tempora, ut alleves fastidium*, from St Ambrose's hymn *Æterne rerum conditor*]. Likewise for sowing, ploughing, reaping and similar works, which require distinct and fitting seasons. Therefore it is added: [[1:15|To shine in the firmament of heaven|ut luceant in firmamento cœli]], [[1:15|and to give light upon the earth|et illuminent terram]], that is, those who dwell on the earth, above all men, for whom the light of the sun by day, and also in its own way the light of the moon by night, is necessary not only for seeing but for countless other things. [[1:15|and it was so done|Et factum est ita]].

paras.t: Fecitque Deus duo luminaria magna, videlicet solem et lunam, quorum unumquodque tam magnum est, ut in quacumque parte terræ stet homo, appareant sibi æqualiter magna, hoc est unumquodque æque magnum. Et si objiciatur, quia (ut probant astrologi) multæ stellæ sunt luna majores, respondet Thomas in scripto secundi, quod sol dicitur magnum luminare, propter quantitatem et propter suam virtutem et causalitatem. Luna vero dicitur magnum luminare, non tam propter quantitatem veram, quam apparentem, et propter excessum claritatis suæ respectu aliarum stellarum ex propinquitate ejus ad nos, et propter evidentiam sui effectus in inferioribus, præsertim in humidis rebus, et quia præ ceteris astris illuminat noctem. Verumtamen in Scholastica fertur historia: Sol et luna dicuntur magna luminaria, in duobus et ex duobus: utpote non solum propter magnitudinem luminis, sed etiam corporis; nec tantum comparatione stellarum, sed etiam secundum se, quia sol dicitur octies major terra. Luna quoque dicitur terra major. Alii nihilo minus dicunt, quod luna sit tanta sicut tertia pars terræ. Sed de his non habetur certitudo. Nam et Alfraganus dicit in sua Astrologia, si bene recordor, quod sol sit centies sexagesies sexies major quam terra. Alii, quod sit septies major terra.
paras.en: [[1:16|And God made two great lights|Fecitque Deus duo luminaria magna]], namely the sun and the moon, each of which is so great that in whatever part of the earth a man stands, they appear to him equally great, that is, each of them alike great. And if it is objected that (as the astronomers prove) many stars are greater than the moon, Thomas answers in his writing on the second book of the Sentences that the sun is called a great light because of its size and because of its power and causality. The moon, however, is called a great light not so much because of its true size as because of its apparent size, and because of the excess of its brightness over the other stars, owing to its nearness to us, and because of the evidence of its effect in lower things, especially in moist things, and because more than the other heavenly bodies it lights up the night. Yet in the Scholastic History it is said: The sun and moon are called great lights in two respects and on two grounds: that is, not only because of the greatness of their light but also of their body; and not only in comparison with the stars but also in themselves, for the sun is said to be eight times greater than the earth. The moon too is said to be greater than the earth. Others, however, say that the moon is as great as a third part of the earth. But about these things there is no certainty. For Alfraganus too says in his Astronomy, if I remember rightly, that the sun is one hundred and sixty-six times greater than the earth. Others, that it is seven times greater than the earth.

paras.t: Refert hic Lyra, quod Judæi dicunt, solem et lunam fuisse a principio æquales in claritate, sed lumen lunæ esse diminutum a Deo, eo quod suggesserit ei ut minueret lumen solis. Mahometus quoque in libello disputationis suæ cum Abdia Judæo, etiam asserit, quod sol et luna fuerunt primo æqualiter splendidi, causam vero minorationis luminis lunæ assignat, quod angelus volans per aerem, ala sua tetigit lunam, et inde obscurationem contraxit. Hæc autem tam fatua sunt, ut sint relatione indigna. Deus enim primo fecit luminaria ista secundum quod congruebat ordini universi. Et rursus, si primo fuissent pares in luce, falsum esset quod ait Scriptura, lunam esse factam ut præsit nocti. Sol quoque et luna creduntur non esse animata. Et quamvis hoc ipsum Augustinus relinquat sub dubio, asserit tamen quod si animata sunt, societatem cum angelis habent: idcirco luna non fuisset tam vana ac invida, quod suggessisset Deo diminuere solis lucem.
paras.en: Lyra relates here that the Jews say that the sun and moon were equal in brightness at the beginning, but that the moon's light was diminished by God, because she had suggested to Him that He should diminish the light of the sun. Mahomet too, in the little book of his disputation with Abdias the Jew, likewise asserts that the sun and moon were at first equally bright; but as the cause of the lessening of the moon's light he gives this, that an angel flying through the air touched the moon with his wing, and from this she contracted her darkening. These things, however, are so foolish that they are not worth reporting. For God made these lights from the first as befitted the order of the universe. And again, if they had at first been equal in light, what Scripture says would be false, that the moon was made [[1:16|to rule the night|ut præsit nocti]]. The sun and moon, moreover, are believed not to be animate [that is, not living bodies moved by a soul of their own]. And although Augustine leaves this very point in doubt, he nonetheless asserts that if they are animate, they have fellowship with the angels: therefore the moon would not have been so vain and envious as to suggest to God that He diminish the sun's light.

paras.t: Creditur item luna facta plena, quemadmodum herbæ et arbores, et etiam homo, in suo genere perfecta sunt facta. Unde alia translatio habet: Luminare minus in inchoatione noctis; nempe, in exordio noctis non oritur luna, nisi rotunda et plena. Et quamvis ante luminarium productionem fuerit tempus ac triduum, dicuntur tamen facta in tempora, quia per ea fit distinctio temporum: et dies deinde sequentes, clariores fuerunt, quam tres dies priores. Ideo dicit Glossa: Si quæratur, quale potuit esse lumen diurnum ante luminarium productionem: respondemus, quale videmus solis ortu proximante, nondum apparente.
paras.en: The moon, likewise, is believed to have been made full, just as the plants and trees, and man too, were made perfect in their kind. Hence another translation has: The lesser light at the beginning of the night [the Old Latin, made from the Greek Septuagint, where the Vulgate has "to rule the night"]; for at the beginning of the night the moon does not rise unless round and full. And although before the production of the lights there was time, three days of it, yet they are said to have been made [[1:14|for seasons|in tempora]], because through them the distinction of seasons comes about; and the days that followed were brighter than the first three days. Therefore the Gloss says: If it is asked what kind of daylight there could have been before the production of the lights, we answer: such as we see when the sunrise is near, while the sun is not yet appearing.

paras.t: Fecit itaque duo luminaria magna: luminare majus, videlicet solem, ut præesset diei: ut sua virtute et claritate diem causaret, ornaret, ac vigoraret; et luminare minus, ut præesset nocti, hoc est, noctem aliqualiter venustaret suo splendore pro mundi decore, et item pro relevamine atque solatio itinerantium, laborantium, navigantiumque in nocte. Luna tamen non causat noctem sicut sol diem.
paras.en: He made, then, two great lights: [[1:16|a greater light|luminare majus]], namely the sun, [[1:16|to rule the day|ut præesset diei]]: so that by its power and brightness it might cause, adorn and quicken the day; [[1:16|and a lesser light to rule the night|et luminare minus, ut præesset nocti]], that is, to beautify the night somewhat with its splendour, for the comeliness of the world, and also for the relief and comfort of those who travel, labour and sail by night. The moon, however, does not cause the night as the sun causes the day.

paras.t: Fecit quoque et stellas, et posuit eas in firmamento cœli. Hic sumitur firmamentum pro cœlo stellato seu sphæra octava, nisi forte per stellas intelligantur non solum stellæ quæ dicuntur fixæ in firmamento, sed et alii quinque planetæ. Denique stellæ quæ sunt in sphæra octava, secundum Aristotelem et eum sequentes, sunt fixæ in ipsa, nec habent proprium motum, sed motu sui orbis moventur. Suntque de natura ejusdem orbis, et unaquæque earum est densior pars ipsius. Unde dispositæ sunt ad suscipiendum lumen præclarius, quam ceteræ orbis partes. Planetæ vero dicuntur stellæ erraticæ, puta non fixæ in propriis sphæris, sed proprium motum habentes. Verumtamen Plato in Timæo dicit, stellas non esse fixas in firmamento, sed meare et choream ducere in eodem: et in hoc Ptolemæus Platonem secutus est. Unde dicunt non cœlum, sed stellas cœli moveri et circumferri.
paras.en: He made also [[1:16|the stars|et stellas]], and [[1:17|he set them in the firmament of heaven|posuit eas in firmamento cœli]]. Here the firmament is taken for the starry heaven or eighth sphere, unless perhaps by the stars are understood not only the stars that are called fixed in the firmament, but also the other five planets. Now the stars in the eighth sphere, according to Aristotle and those who follow him, are fixed in it and have no proper motion, but are moved by the motion of their orb. And they are of the nature of that same orb, and each of them is a denser part of it; hence they are disposed to receive light more brightly than the other parts of the orb. The planets, on the other hand, are called wandering stars, that is, not fixed in their own spheres, but having a motion of their own. Plato, however, says in the Timæus that the stars are not fixed in the firmament, but travel and lead a dance within it; and in this Ptolemy followed Plato. Hence they say that it is not the heaven but the stars of the heaven that move and are carried round.

paras.t: Ut lucerent super terram de nocte, sicut de luna jam dictum est, et propter easdem causas; itemque ut homines ex adspectu stellarum incitarentur ad laudem ac honorificentiam Creatoris earum, et scrutarentur quæ astrologiam concernunt; et rursus, ne nox sua caligine nimis esset horrenda.
paras.en: [[1:17|to shine upon the earth|Ut lucerent super terram]] by night, as was said already of the moon, and for the same reasons; and also that men, from the sight of the stars, might be roused to the praise and honour of their Creator, and might search out the things that concern astronomy; and again, that the night might not be too dreadful in its darkness.

paras.t: Et præessent diei ac nocti. Hoc quidam referunt ad solem et lunam ac stellas, ita ut illa particula, præessent diei, intelligatur de sole; et quod subditur, et nocti, ad lunam ac stellas. Sed quia de sole hoc semel prolatum est ut præsit diei, atque de luna quod præsit nocti, potest istud totum referri ad stellas: quarum etsi claritas non percipiatur in die, eo quod obfuscetur a prædominante solis splendore, nihilo minus semper unius seu alicujus hemisphærii stellæ lumen suum diffundunt ad habitabilem terram, et quosdam effectus causant in ea: quod nec soli competit, nec lunæ.
paras.en: [[1:18|And to rule the day and the night|Et præessent diei ac nocti]]. Some refer this to the sun and moon and stars, so that the phrase [[1:18|to rule the day|præessent diei]] is understood of the sun, and what follows, [[1:18|and the night|et nocti]], of the moon and stars. But since it has already been said once of the sun that it was made [[1:16|to rule the day|ut præsit diei]], and of the moon that it was made [[1:16|to rule the night|præsit nocti]], the whole of this can be referred to the stars: for although their brightness is not perceived by day, because it is dimmed by the prevailing splendour of the sun, nevertheless the stars of one hemisphere or another always pour their light upon the habitable earth and cause certain effects in it: which belongs neither to the sun nor to the moon.

paras.t: Et divisit lucem a tenebris, id est, eam claritatem quam causant in terra, dum aer serenus est, a caligine noctium tali luce carentium, propter aeris obnubilationem. Dividunt quoque lucem a tenebris, quoniam lucem quam sua præsentia exerunt et diffundunt, sua absentia ac recessu tollunt ac subtrahunt. Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum. Opus enim hujus diei exstitit multipliciter atque sublimiter bonum. Et factum est vespere et mane dies quartus, juxta sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: [[1:18|and to divide the light and the darkness|Et divisit lucem a tenebris]], that is, the brightness which they cause on the earth while the air is clear, from the darkness of nights that lack such light because the air is clouded over. They also divide the light from the darkness, since the light which they put forth and spread by their presence, they take away and withdraw by their absence and departure. [[1:18|And God saw that it was good|Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum]]. For the work of this day was good in many ways and in a lofty manner. [[1:19|And the evening and morning were the fourth day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies quartus]], in the sense given before.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum aliam opinionem, ponentem materiam primo sub sola forma corporeitatis creatam, luminaria et stellæ factæ sunt quarto die, quantum ad formas suas substantiales specificas, ita quod de nube candida, quam dicunt primo die formatam, factus sit sol: de qua nube aliqui eorum dicunt esse factas lunam et stellas, ut dictum est. Alii vero dicunt eas esse factas ex aliqua suorum orbium parte; contra quæ omnia, præsertim contra hoc ultimum, quod scilicet factæ essent ex aliqua orbium parte, possent argumenta multa ac fortia introduci. Si enim cœlestes orbes incorruptibiles sunt, qualiter aliquæ partes eorum ad aliam substantialem formam poterant transmutari? Et si stellæ sunt cœli stellati partes integrales ac densiores, non habent formas substantiales a forma illius cœli distinctas. Sed ista quæ in secundo Sententiarum libro habent tractari, dimitto.
paras.en: Moreover, according to another opinion, which holds that matter was first created under the form of corporeity alone [that is, as body only, without yet the specific form of any kind of body], the lights and stars were made on the fourth day as to their specific substantial forms, in such a way that the sun was made from the bright cloud which they say was formed on the first day; and some of them say that the moon and stars were made from that cloud, as has been said. Others, again, say that they were made from some part of their orbs. Against all of these, and especially against this last, namely that they were made from some part of the orbs, many strong arguments could be brought. For if the heavenly orbs are incorruptible, how could any parts of them be changed into another substantial form? And if the stars are integral and denser parts of the starry heaven, they do not have substantial forms distinct from the form of that heaven. But I leave these matters aside, since they belong to be treated in the second book of the Sentences.

paras.t: Præterea quidam hoc loco redarguit Thomam, in prima parte Summæ suæ dicentem, Dici non posse, quod ex nube illa factus sit sol: quia si sic, sequeretur quod in prima rerum productione sit aliquid factum satis cito corrumpendum. Quocirca sciendum, quod reprehensor ille sancti Doctoris, in hac parte non mediocriter deviat. Quamvis enim S. Doctor dicat, quod dici non posset ex nube illa solem esse productum, non tamen assignat ad hoc probandum rationem prætactam: sed hanc rationem inducit ad probandum, quod dici non valeat, nubem illam esse resolutam in præjacentem materiam. Insuper dicit Thomam incidere id, quod reprobare intendit, quoniam quinto die facti sunt pisces et aves ex elementis: quod esse non potuit sine elementarium corruptione formarum. Ista reprobatio S. Thomæ, prorsus nil valet. Quamvis enim ex elementis sint facta animalia, non tamen ob id elementa prima die producta, secundum se tota corrupta sunt aut esse desierunt.
paras.en: Moreover, a certain writer in this place reproves Thomas, who says in the First Part of his Summa that it cannot be said that the sun was made from that cloud, because if it were so, it would follow that in the first production of things something was made that was to be corrupted quite soon. On this it should be known that this critic of the holy Doctor goes not a little astray here. For although the holy Doctor says that it could not be said that the sun was produced from that cloud, he does not give the reason just mentioned to prove it; rather, he brings this reason to prove that it cannot be said that that cloud was resolved into pre-existing matter. Furthermore, he says that Thomas falls into what he means to disprove, since on the fifth day fishes and birds were made from the elements, which could not be without the corruption of the forms of the elements. This refutation of St Thomas is worth nothing at all. For although the animals were made from the elements, it does not follow that the elements produced on the first day were wholly corrupted in themselves, or ceased to be.

paras.t: Amplius circa hanc litteram possent multæ quæstiones moveri, quas doctores super secundum movent, magistraliterque determinant, utpote de natura et numero orbium seu cœlorum, et an moveantur ab anima, hoc est, an corpora cœlestia sint animata, an habeant causalitatem et influentiam super inferiora, et præcipue an super mentem rationalem, liberumque arbitrium, an necessitatem imponant inferioribus, an stellæ moveantur in cœlo sicut aves in aere, et pisces in aqua. Horum discussionem, brevitati studens, dimitto, quoniam alibi locum habent. Hoc breviter dico, quod orbes et stellæ, sol, luna, ceterique planetæ, multiplicem habent causalitatem et efficientiam in elementis et mixtis, in tantum ut S. Dionysius capitulo 4 de Divinis nominibus protestetur, quod radius solis generationi cooperetur et moveat ad vitam, quam et auget, et nutrit, ac perficit. Similiter Augustinus quinto de Civitate Dei fatetur: Non absurde credi potest, afflatus quosdam sidereos ad corporum differentias pervenire. Tertio quoque de Trinitate disseruit: Quemadmodum corpora crassiora et inferiora per subtiliora et potentiora ordine quodam reguntur, ita omnia corpora per spiritum vitæ rationalem; et spiritus vitæ rationalis, desertor atque peccator, videlicet dæmon, per spiritum vitæ rationalem, pium ac justum, et ille per Deum.
paras.en: Further, many questions could be raised about this text, which the doctors raise on the second book of the Sentences and settle in masterly fashion: such as the nature and number of the orbs or heavens; whether they are moved by a soul, that is, whether the heavenly bodies are animate; whether they have causality and influence over lower things, and especially whether over the rational mind and free will; whether they impose necessity on lower things; whether the stars move in the heaven as birds in the air and fishes in the water. Studying brevity, I leave the discussion of these aside, since they have their place elsewhere. This much I say briefly: that the orbs and stars, the sun, the moon and the other planets, have a manifold causality and efficacy in the elements and in mixed bodies, so much so that St Dionysius, in chapter 4 of On the Divine Names, declares that the ray of the sun cooperates in generation and moves to life, which it also increases, nourishes and perfects. Likewise Augustine in the fifth book of the City of God grants: It may be believed, not absurdly, that certain influences of the stars reach to the differences of bodies. And in the third book On the Trinity he set forth: As the grosser and lower bodies are ruled in a certain order by the subtler and more powerful, so all bodies are ruled by the rational spirit of life; and the rational spirit of life that is a deserter and a sinner, namely the devil, by the rational spirit of life that is devout and just; and that one by God.

paras.t: Porro super mentem rationalem et arbitrii libertatem, non habent directe causalitatem aut aliquam impressionem, sed dispositive duntaxat, in quantum ex diversa corporis complexione, dispositione et immutatione, mens liberumque arbitrium ad diversa inclinantur, afficiuntur et aptantur: quorum inclinationem quamplures sequuntur, sed non necessitantur ex eis. Ad quod Damascenus libro secundo multas rationes adducit, in quo de ista materia tractat diffuse. Ex quibus ostenditur pessimus error quorumdam astronomorum et philosophorum, præsertim Alkindi in libro suo de Radiis, ubi asserit omnia in hoc mundo de necessitate accidere: quod etiam opinatus est Avicenna, si totus ordo causarum et influentiarum cœlestium simul accipiatur. Quorum insanias non solum christianæ fidei, sed Aristoteli quoque contrarias, doctores sancti atque catholici plenissime improbarunt.
paras.en: Over the rational mind and freedom of choice, however, they have no causality or impression of any kind directly, but only dispositively, inasmuch as, through the varied complexion [that is, the bodily temperament, the mixture of the humours], disposition and alteration of the body, the mind and free will are inclined, affected and fitted to different things: and very many follow this inclination, yet they are not necessitated by them. On this Damascene brings many reasons in his second book, in which he treats this matter at length. From these is shown the very bad error of certain astronomers and philosophers, especially of Alkindi in his book On Rays, where he asserts that everything in this world happens of necessity: which Avicenna also held, if the whole order of causes and heavenly influences be taken together. Their follies, contrary not only to the Christian faith but to Aristotle as well, the holy and catholic doctors have most fully refuted.

1.title: Explanatio textus de opere quintæ diei.
1.title_en: Explanation of the text on the work of the fifth day.

paras.t: Dixit etiam Deus : Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis, et volatile super terram sub firmamento cœli. Quemadmodum sæpius tactum est, nunc ordine condecenti describitur ornatus duorum mediorum elementorum, videlicet aquæ et aeris, per hoc quod jam describitur productio animalium, quorum quædam moventur in aqua, quædam in aere. Nempe per hoc quod Moyses ait, Super terram sub firmamento, aerem designavit. Sed quum aqua sit res inanimata, quomodo potuit producere animalia ista ? Est itaque sensus : Producant aquæ, id est, divina jussione producantur ex aqua, tamquam ex materiali et passivo principio, reptile animæ viventis, hoc est pisces habentes in se animas non solum vegetative, sed etiam sensitive viventes. Et volatile super terram sub firmamento, id est, aves quibus conveniat volare in aere. Horum corpora Deus immediate perhibetur formasse ex aqua, et in qualibet specie fecit duo prima individua, ex quibus generata sunt alia juxta positionem prætactam. Itaque singularia ista, reptile atque volatile, nunc sumuntur pluraliter.
paras.en: [[1:20|God also said: let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having life|Dixit etiam Deus : Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis]], [[1:20|and the fowl that may fly over the earth under the firmament of heaven|et volatile super terram sub firmamento cœli]]. As has often been touched on, there is now described, in fitting order, the adornment of the two middle elements, namely water and air, in that the production of the animals is now described, of which some move in the water and some in the air. For by Moses' saying [[1:20|over the earth under the firmament|Super terram sub firmamento]], he designated the air. But since water is an inanimate thing, how could it bring forth these animals? The sense, then, is this: [[1:20|let the waters bring forth|Producant aquæ]], that is, by the divine command let there be brought forth out of water, as out of a material and passive principle, [[1:20|the creeping creature having life|reptile animæ viventis]], that is, fishes having in them souls that live not only vegetatively but also sensitively [that is, with the life of sense, not only with the life of growth and nourishment that plants have]. [[1:20|and the fowl that may fly over the earth under the firmament|Et volatile super terram sub firmamento]], that is, birds, whose part it is to fly in the air. God is said to have formed their bodies immediately out of water, and in each species he made the first two individuals, from which the others were begotten, according to the position touched on before. So these singulars, *creeping creature* and *fowl*, are here taken in the plural.

paras.t: Circa hæc plurima possent inquiri : Primo, cur animalia ista dicuntur facta ex aqua, quum corpora animalium mixta sint ex quatuor elementis. Secundo, si pisces et aves ex aquis producti sunt, cur non utrumque hoc genus mansit in aqua, et cur unum magis quam aliud, accommodatum est aeri. Tertio, an animæ animalium horum creatæ sint. Ad hæc breviter respondendum. Et primo ad primum, quod utique pisces et aves ex quatuor elementis formati sunt, et in eorum corporibus prædominatur elementum terræ, quantum ad corporis quantitatem ; ignis vero secundum quantitatem virtutis, eo quod calor instrumentum sit animæ, nec aliquid sit sensitivum sine calore, ut habetur secundo de Anima. Aqua autem continuat partes terræ in mixto. Verumtamen illa animalia dicuntur constare ex aqua, quæ plus habent de aqua in se, quam animalia cetera, complexione eorum propria pensata per comparationem ad complexionem animalium aliorum, seu debitam communi generi animalis. Et ita ex aqua dicuntur esse pisces, quantum ad id quod in aqua est grossius ; aves autem, quantum ad id quod in aqua est subtilius, et in vaporem resolvitur, et est quasi medium inter aquam et aerem. Hinc aves in aera elevantur, et pisces gurgiti remittuntur. Istud super secundum Thomas clarius docet. Unde et alii dicunt, quod pisces et aves specialiter ex aqua facti dicuntur propter convenientiam quamdam. Habet etenim aqua humorem atque vaporem. Per humorem convenit cum piscibus, per vaporem cum avibus. Istud tamen non est satis resolute prolatum, quoniam aqua per humorem cum universis animalibus competit. In Scholastica quoque historia dicitur : Pisces et aves ex aquis sunt orti, quoniam facilis est transitus aquæ in aera per attenuationem, et aeris in aquam per spissationem. Ex quibus patet ad duo prima quæsita responsio. Ad tertium respondet Bonaventura super secundum, quod animæ primorum illorum irrationabilium animalium non fuerunt creatæ, sed seminaliter ex materiis suis productæ, tamen sine concursu causalitatis cœlestium corporum. Rationales enim, seminales seu occultæ virtutes causales a principio sunt impressæ elementis, quemadmodum loquitur Augustinus : In corporeis, inquiens, hujus mundi elementis semina quædam occulta latent.
paras.en: Many things might be asked about this. First, why these animals are said to be made out of water, when the bodies of animals are mixed of the four elements. Second, if fishes and birds were brought forth out of the waters, why both kinds did not remain in the water, and why the one rather than the other was fitted to the air. Third, whether the souls of these animals were created. These must be answered briefly. And first, to the first: fishes and birds were indeed formed out of the four elements, and in their bodies the element of earth predominates as to the quantity of the body, but fire as to the quantity of power, because heat is the instrument of the soul and nothing is sensitive without heat, as is said in the second book *On the Soul*. Water, for its part, holds together the parts of earth in the mixture.
