Nevertheless those animals are said to consist of water which have more of water in them than the other animals, when their own complexion [that is, the proportion in which the elements and their qualities are mingled in a body] is weighed in comparison with the complexion of other animals, or with that which is due to the common genus of animal. And so fishes are said to be of water as to what is grosser in water, and birds as to what is subtler in water, and is resolved into vapour, and is as it were midway between water and air. Hence birds are raised up into the air, and fishes are sent back to the deep. Thomas teaches this more clearly on the second book [of the *Sentences*]. And so others too say that fishes and birds are said to be made out of water in particular because of a certain agreement. For water has moisture and vapour: by its moisture it agrees with fishes, by its vapour with birds. This, however, is not stated decisively enough, since by its moisture water is common to all animals. In the *Scholastic History* too it is said: Fishes and birds arose out of the waters, because the passage of water into air by thinning, and of air into water by thickening, is easy. From all this the answer to the first two questions is plain. To the third, Bonaventure answers on the second book that the souls of those first irrational animals were not created, but brought forth seminally from their matter, though without the concurrence of the causality of the heavenly bodies. For seminal reasons [Latin *rationes seminales*: Augustine's term for the causal powers God placed in the elements at creation, from which things later unfold], that is, hidden causal powers, were impressed on the elements from the beginning, as Augustine says: In the bodily elements of this world, he says, certain hidden seeds lie concealed.

paras.t: Præterea, ad intelligendum qualiter corpora animalium ex quatuor elementis constant et mixta sunt, advertenda sunt verba doctorum. Itaque in scripto secundi, distinctione 15, scribit Bonaventura : Corpora animalium habent in se quatuor elementa, ut idonea sint ad sensum, ad motum, ad multiplicem actionem, atque ut habeant in se dignitatem complexionis. Perfecta autem mixtio non est, quousque concurrant quatuor elementa. Aqua namque (quum sit subtilior decies terra) penetrat partes terræ, sed non perfecte, quoniam habet grossitudinem quamdam. Aer autem qui est centies subtilior terra, intimius se profundat in terram. Ignis vero, qui millies rarior subtiliorque consistit quam terra, sua subtilitate penetrat usque ad intima : et ita fit alteratio plena, mixtioque perfecta. Hinc ait et Thomas : Oportet ut elementa inferiora grossiora, excedant elementa subtiliora in mixto secundum quantitatem seu molem ; subtiliora vero, videlicet aer et ignis, secundum virtutem, hoc est secundum calidum et humidum, in quibus vita consistit. Quum enim corpora animalium debeant esse temperatiora aliis mixtorum corporibus, utpote magis remota a contrarietate per complexionis æqualitatem, et ita assimilentur naturæ et æqualitati cœlestium corporum : oportet inferiora elementa, quæ sunt minus activa, quia plus habent de materia, scilicet terram et aquam, secundum quantitatem in mixto excedere, ut virtutis defectum suppleat quantitatis excessus. His concordat quod asserit Augustinus, et habetur in Glossa : Ignis omnia penetrat, ut in eis faciat motum. Inchoat enim anima motum suum in omnibus sensibus ab ignis subtilitate.
paras.en: Further, to understand how the bodies of animals consist of the four elements and are mixed of them, the words of the doctors must be noted. Thus in his writing on the second book, distinction 15, Bonaventure writes: The bodies of animals have the four elements in them, so that they may be fit for sense, for motion, for manifold action, and may have in them the dignity of a complexion. But there is no perfect mixture until the four elements come together. For water (being ten times subtler than earth) penetrates the parts of earth, but not perfectly, since it has a certain grossness. Air, which is a hundred times subtler than earth, sinks more inwardly into the earth. But fire, which is a thousand times rarer and subtler than earth, penetrates by its subtlety to the inmost parts; and so there comes about a full alteration and a perfect mixture. Hence Thomas too says: The lower and grosser elements must exceed the subtler elements in the mixture in quantity or bulk; but the subtler, namely air and fire, must exceed in power, that is, in heat and moisture, in which life consists. For since the bodies of animals ought to be more temperate than the other mixed bodies, as being further removed from contrariety through the evenness of their complexion, and so being likened to the nature and evenness of the heavenly bodies, the lower elements, which are less active because they have more of matter, namely earth and water, must exceed in quantity in the mixture, so that the excess of quantity may make up the lack of power. With this agrees what Augustine asserts, and is found in the Gloss: Fire penetrates all things, so as to cause motion in them. For the soul begins its motion in all the senses from the subtlety of fire.

paras.t: Sed quæri potest : Quum ignis sit nobilissimum elementum, cur non describitur aliquis ejus ornatus. Ad hoc Thomas respondet, quod quamvis aliqua mixta possint ad tempus in igne absque læsione durare, nulla tamen res est, quæ non consumatur tandem ab igne, si diu in eo permaneat, ut asserit Galenus in Simplici medicina. Idcirco (ut Philosophus in libro de Proprietatibus elementorum testatur) nullum animal vivere potest in igne, nisi forte ad modicum tempus, ut fertur de salamandra.
paras.en: But it may be asked: since fire is the noblest element, why is no adornment of it described? To this Thomas answers that, although some mixed bodies can last for a time in fire without harm, there is nevertheless nothing that is not consumed by fire at last if it stays in it long, as Galen asserts in his *Simple Medicine*. Therefore (as the Philosopher testifies in the book *On the Properties of the Elements*) no animal can live in fire, unless perhaps for a short time, as is told of the salamander.

paras.t: Item quæritur, cur reptilia dicuntur ad aquæ pertinere ornatum, quum sint multa terrestria reptilia. Et infra habetur, quod reptilia spectant ad ornatum sextæ diei. Respondetur, quod multiplex est genus reptilium : Unum, quod trahit ac rapit se vi oris, ut aliqui vermes. Secundum, quod trahit se vi costarum, sicut serpentes. Tertium, quod se rapit et trahit vi pinnarum, ut pisces. Quartum, quod rapit se vi annulorum quorumdam, quemadmodum animalia annulosa. Quinto, extense loquendo, omne animal dicitur reptile, quod movendo se, magnam partem corporis sui applicat terræ, quamvis habeat pedes, ut stellio et lacerta. Itaque patet, quod reptilia aquatica spectant ad aquæ ornatum, cetera ad ornatum terræ. Verumtamen, secundum eundem Philosophum libro de Animalibus, sunt quædam animalia media inter aquatica atque terrestria, ut crocodili, qui moventur et gradiuntur in terra, interdum autem morantur et natant in aqua : sed hæc computantur cum illo extremo, cum quo magis communicant.
paras.en: It is also asked why creeping things are said to belong to the adornment of the water, since there are many creeping things of the land; and further on it is said that creeping things belong to the adornment of the sixth day. The answer is that the kind of creeping things is manifold. One kind drags and hauls itself along by the force of its mouth, as some worms do. A second drags itself by the force of its ribs, as serpents do. A third hauls and drags itself by the force of its fins, as fishes do. A fourth hauls itself by the force of certain rings, as ringed animals do. Fifthly, speaking broadly, every animal is called a creeping thing which in moving brings a great part of its body against the ground, though it has feet, as the newt [Latin *stellio*, a spotted lizard] and the lizard. So it is plain that the creeping things of the water belong to the adornment of the water, the others to the adornment of the earth. Nevertheless, according to the same Philosopher in the book *On Animals*, there are certain animals midway between those of the water and those of the land, such as crocodiles, which move and walk on land but at times stay and swim in the water; but these are counted with that extreme with which they have more in common.

paras.t: Creavitque Deus cete grandia, qui sunt maximi pisces in mari. Unde in Evangelio legitur : Fuit Jonas in ventre ceti. Et omnem animam viventem atque motabilem. Hic ponitur pars pro toto, ut sit sensus : Creavit omnem rem animatam motabilem. Quam produxerant aquæ in species suas, id est, quæ secundum corpus suum formatæ erant ex aqua secundum exigentiam suæ naturæ specificæ, non quod prius productæ sint ex aqua, et postea creatæ a Deo, sed eædem numero, a Deo effective principaliterque plasmatæ sunt, atque ex aqua materialiter aut etiam seminaliter. Et omne volatile formavit, secundum genus suum, hoc est, secundum quod competebat naturæ et speciei uniuscujusque volatilis. Qualiter autem intelligenda sit distributio ista, patet ex præinductis. Intelligenda est namque de omnibus illis primis individuis in qualibet specie binis, quibus competit per commixtionem seminum generare, quæ fecit in tali dispositione ac robore, quod generare mox poterant. Sed quum ista ex aquis producta sint, quomodo creata dicuntur ? Et respondendum, quod creare sumitur nunc extense pro facere seu plasmare.
paras.en: [[1:21|And God created the great whales|Creavitque Deus cete grandia]], which are the greatest fishes in the sea. Hence we read in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:40|Jonas was in the whale's belly|Fuit Jonas in ventre ceti]]. [[1:21|And every living and moving creature|Et omnem animam viventem atque motabilem]] [literally "every living and movable soul"]. Here the part is put for the whole, so that the sense is: he created every animate thing that moves. [[1:21|which the waters brought forth, according to their kinds|Quam produxerant aquæ in species suas]], that is, which as to their bodies had been formed out of water according to what their specific nature required: not that they were first brought forth out of the water and afterwards created by God, but the very same in number were fashioned by God, effectively and principally, and out of water materially, or also seminally. [[1:21|and every winged fowl|Et omne volatile]] he formed, [[1:21|according to its kind|secundum genus suum]], that is, according as befitted the nature and species of each fowl. How this distribution [that is, the word *every*] is to be understood is plain from what was brought forward before: it is to be understood of all those first individuals, two in each species, to whom it belongs to beget by the mingling of seeds, and whom he made in such a disposition and strength that they could beget straightway. But since these were brought forth out of the waters, how are they said to be created? The answer is that *to create* is here taken broadly for to make or to fashion.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum recitat Lyra, quod Hebræi dicunt cete esse pisces incredibilis magnitudinis. Quumque Deus in exordio fecisset marem et feminam speciei istius, occidit feminam ne multiplicarentur individua : quia si multiplicata fuissent, sæculum esset destructum, eo quod mare innavigabile esset, et alii pisces non possent durare in mari ; carnes vero feminæ interfectæ salivit, reservans eas justis in sæculo futuro. Ex quo Lyra concludit, quod Judæi inciderunt errores Sarracenorum, ponendo beatitudinem vitæ futuræ in delectationibus ciborum ac venereorum.
paras.en: On this place Lyra relates that the Hebrews say the whales are fishes of incredible size; and that when God in the beginning had made a male and a female of this species, he killed the female, so that the individuals might not multiply: for if they had multiplied, the world would have been destroyed, since the sea would have been unnavigable and the other fishes could not have lasted in the sea; but he salted the flesh of the slain female, keeping it for the just in the world to come. From this Lyra concludes that the Jews fell into the errors of the Saracens, placing the happiness of the life to come in the pleasures of food and of venery.

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit Rabbi Paulus: Quemadmodum inter Christianos fuerunt quidam hæretici, quorum errores non sunt veris Christianis adscribendi, sic inter Judæos fuerunt nonnulli habentes opiniones erroneas, quæ non approbantur a Judæis communiter. Quamvis ergo in quibusdam opusculis eorum appareat, quod in alia vita sint corporales delectationes, communitas tamen eorum respuit hoc omnino. Est enim contra id Isaiæ: Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti expectantibus te. Ex quibus verbis manifeste habetur, quod remuneratio justis parata, superat omnem sensum. Unde determinatio communis est apud eos, quod in alia vita non est cibus nec potus, nec actus venereorum, sed justi delectantur ex splendore divinæ gloriæ. Quapropter attribuere ipsum errorem Judæis in communi, non est utile ad reductionem eorum: credunt enim quod fingamus mendacia contra eos: quod præstat impedimentum non modicum ad hoc ut reddamur credibiles eis. Hæc Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted Jew, whose *Additions* to Lyra's postill Denis often cites] writes: Just as among Christians there have been certain heretics whose errors are not to be ascribed to true Christians, so among the Jews there have been some holding erroneous opinions which are not approved by the Jews in common. So although in some of their little works it appears that there are bodily pleasures in the other life, their community nevertheless utterly rejects this. For it is against that saying of Isaias: [[Is 64:4|the eye hath not seen, O God, besides thee, what things thou hast prepared for them that wait for thee|Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti expectantibus te]][[1 Cor 2:9||]]. From these words it is plainly had that the reward prepared for the just surpasses all sense. Hence the common determination among them is that in the other life there is no food nor drink nor venereal act, but the just delight in the splendour of the divine glory. Therefore to attribute this error to the Jews in common is not useful for bringing them back; for they believe that we invent lies against them, which puts no small hindrance in the way of our being believed by them. Thus far Rabbi Paul.

paras.t: Sed Paulus iste non reprehendendo primam partem dicti Lyræ, quo ait, Judæos asserere, quod Deus in principio feminam ceti occiderit: videtur innuere, quod Lyra recte id recitat. Nec Lyra hoc loco adducit specialem rationem hoc reprobantem, idcirco aliquid breviter tangi potest ad reprobandum tam fatuum verbum. Si enim Deus occidit feminam ceti, jam species illa perisset, nisi dicatur cetus ille primus usque nunc vivere: quod naturale non esset, nisi forte dicatur quod occiderit feminam illam postquam genuerat, quo dato, idem sequeretur periculum, si genuisset femellam, idemque inconveniens, si masculum genuisset. Denique, quum Deus sit sapientiæ ac providentiæ infinitæ, ipse ante mundi productionem universa prævidit: cur ergo fecisset quod propter periculum imminens mox necasset?
paras.en: But this Paul, by not finding fault with the first part of Lyra's statement, where he says the Jews assert that God in the beginning killed the female whale, seems to imply that Lyra relates it rightly. Nor does Lyra in this place bring any particular reason refuting it; so something may briefly be touched on to refute so foolish a saying. For if God killed the female whale, that species would long since have perished, unless it be said that that first whale is living until now, which would not be natural; unless perhaps it be said that he killed that female after she had brought forth; and granting that, the same danger would follow if she had brought forth a female, and the same unfitness if she had brought forth a male. Lastly, since God is of infinite wisdom and providence, he foresaw all things before the bringing forth of the world: why then would he have made what he would soon have killed because of an impending danger?

paras.t: Insuper super illud, Producat terra herbam virentem, et super istud, Producant aquæ reptile, scribit Lyra, quod terra et aqua non produxerunt ista, nisi solum passive. Contra quod scribit hic Paulus, quod elementa non solum passive, sed etiam active produxerunt ea quæ Deus præcepit produci ex eis, quoniam actio causæ primæ non semper excludit actionem secundarum causarum. Augustinus quoque exponit sic, Producat, id est, virtutem producendi accipiat. Ista reprobatio videtur satis idonea, dempto hoc, quod Augustinum pro se allegat, quia expositio Augustini procedit secundum hoc, quod omnia opera sex dierum sint simul producta. Si enim elementa solum habuerunt se passive ad productionem eorum quæ Deo præcipiente produxerunt, videretur sequi quod formæ rerum productarum ex eis, essent omnino ab extra, et per consequens creatæ, sicut de anima rationali tenetur.
paras.en: Moreover, on the words [[1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Producat terra herbam virentem]] [Denis's wording; the Vulgate of v. 11 has *Germinet terra*, "let the earth bud forth"], and on these, [[1:20|let the waters bring forth the creeping creature|Producant aquæ reptile]], Lyra writes that the earth and the water brought these things forth only passively. Against which Paul writes here that the elements brought forth not only passively but also actively the things God commanded to be brought forth from them, since the action of the first cause does not always exclude the action of secondary causes. Augustine too expounds it thus: *Let it bring forth*, that is, let it receive the power of bringing forth. This refutation seems fitting enough, except that he cites Augustine on his side; for Augustine's exposition proceeds on the view that all the works of the six days were brought forth together. For if the elements stood only passively toward the production of the things they brought forth at God's command, it would seem to follow that the forms of the things brought forth from them were wholly from without, and consequently created, as is held of the rational soul.

paras.t: Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum, id est, opus hujus quintæ diei sibi complacuit: benedixitque, id est, virtutem generativam seu productivam similium sibi in specie aut saltem in genere contulit eis, dicens: Crescite et multiplicamini, id est, similia generate, et replete aquas maris, multiplicando individua specierum vestrarum. Avesque multiplicentur super terram. Quare non ait, Aves multiplicentur in aere? Nisi forte dicendo super terram, insinuet aerem. Melius tamen dicendum, quod aves quamvis naturaliter volent in aere, nihilo minus naturaliter quiescunt et generant super terram. In quantum enim sunt mixta et gravia, in quibus prædominatur terra secundum quantitatem, non sine labore volant sive moventur, naturaliterque quiescunt in terra. Pisces autem et aves generant ova, ex quibus individua suæ speciei tandem nascantur. Dicitur quoque in Glossa, quod multæ sunt aves quæ non de terra, sed de mari vivunt, et libentius utuntur mari seu aqua, quam terra. Aliæ vero aves vivunt ex his quæ in terra inveniunt. Et factum est vespere et mane dies quintus, secundum sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: [[1:21|And God saw that it was good|Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], that is, the work of this fifth day was pleasing to him. [[1:22|And he blessed|benedixitque]], that is, he conferred the power of begetting or producing things like themselves in species, or at least in genus, [[1:22|them, saying|eis, dicens]]: [[1:22|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]], that is, beget your like, [[1:22|and fill the waters of the sea|et replete aquas maris]], by multiplying the individuals of your species. [[1:22|and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth|Avesque multiplicentur super terram]]. Why does he not say, Let the birds be multiplied in the air? Unless perhaps by saying *upon the earth* he hints at the air. But it is better to say that birds, though by nature they fly in the air, nonetheless by nature rest and beget upon the earth. For inasmuch as they are mixed and heavy bodies, in which earth predominates in quantity, they do not fly or move without labour, and by nature they rest on the earth. Fishes and birds, moreover, beget eggs, from which the individuals of their species are in time born. It is also said in the Gloss that there are many birds which live not from the land but from the sea, and make use of the sea or water more gladly than the land; while other birds live on what they find on the land. [[1:23|And the evening and morning were the fifth day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies quintus]], in the sense given before.

paras.t: Denique circa illud, Producant aquæ volatile super terram, legitur in Scholastica historia : Ex hoc quod dictum est, volatile super terram, erravit Plato, qui descendens in Ægyptum, libros Moysis legit, putavitque Moysen sensisse, volatilia esse ornatum aëris circa terram dumtaxat : ornatum autem aëris superioris, esse calodæmones et cacodæmones. Sed non est ita, quoniam calodæmones, id est angeli boni, sunt in cœlo empyreo, et cacodæmones, id est angeli mali, detrusi sunt in aërem caliginosum, non ad ejus ornatum, sed ad ipsorum supplicium. De hoc plus habetur in Glossa ex verbis Augustini.
paras.en: Lastly, on the words [[1:20|let the waters bring forth|Producant aquæ]] [[1:20|the fowl that may fly over the earth|volatile super terram]], we read in the *Scholastic History*: From its being said [[1:20|fowl that may fly over the earth|volatile super terram]], Plato erred, who, going down into Egypt, read the books of Moses, and thought that Moses meant that the fowls are the adornment only of the air about the earth, while the adornment of the higher air is the *calodæmones* and *cacodæmones* [Greek, "good spirits" and "evil spirits"]. But it is not so, since the *calodæmones*, that is, the good angels, are in the empyrean heaven, and the *cacodæmones*, that is, the evil angels, have been thrust down into the dark air, not for its adornment but for their own punishment. More on this is found in the Gloss, from the words of Augustine.

paras.t: Rursus, animæ piscium et avium dictæ sunt viventes atque motabiles, ad differentiam animæ rationalis, quæ immortalis est. Illæ autem mutari possunt de esse et vivere, ad non esse ac mori. Tamen secundum Albertum, dicuntur motabiles propter motum processivum, quem habent seu causant in suis corporibus.
paras.en: Again, the souls of fishes and birds are called [[1:21|living and moving|viventes atque motabiles]] [*motabilis* can mean both "moving" and "changeable"] to distinguish them from the rational soul, which is immortal; whereas these can be changed from being and living to not being and dying. Yet according to Albert, they are called *motabiles* because of the progressive motion [that is, the motion from place to place] which they have, or cause, in their bodies.

paras.t: Postremo, circa hæc ait Albertus in libro de Coæquævis : Aer et aqua simul ornati sunt, quum sint elementa media et communicantia in natura diaphani, et passiva qualitate humidi. Pisces autem magis sunt ex humido constante per frigidum, secundum generis sui naturam. Ideo secundum genus suum sunt frigidi, sicut et aqua in qua sunt. Aves vero magis sunt ex humido vaporabili conjuncto cum calido, secundum naturam generis sui. Idcirco calidæ sunt naturæ. Porro animalia media et utrique elemento communia, comprehenduntur sub ornatu utriusque elementi ; magis tamen sunt ornatus illius, in quo frequentius morantur atque moventur, prout septimo de Animalibus ait Philosophus de delphinis, quod habitant in mari, et pariunt juxta littus in terra. Hæc Albertus. Tales quoque sunt vituli marini, qui pedes habent et super terram aliquando gradiuntur. Natura enim non transit a distanti in distans, nisi per medium, ut divinus Dionysius protestatur.
paras.en: Lastly, on these things Albert says in the book *On the Coævals* [*De coæquævis*, on the things created together at the beginning]: Air and water were adorned together, since they are middle elements, sharing in the nature of the transparent and in the passive quality of moisture. Fishes are made more of moisture held firm by cold, according to the nature of their kind; therefore by their kind they are cold, as is the water they are in. Birds are made more of vaporous moisture joined with heat, according to the nature of their kind; therefore they are of a warm nature. Further, animals midway and common to both elements are included under the adornment of both elements, but belong more to the adornment of that in which they more often stay and move, as the Philosopher says of dolphins in the seventh book *On Animals*, that they live in the sea and give birth near the shore on land. Thus far Albert. Such too are the seals [Latin *vituli marini*, "sea calves"], which have feet and sometimes walk upon the land. For nature does not pass from one extreme to a distant one except through a mean, as the divine Dionysius declares.

1.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli, ab illo loco, Dixit quoque Deus: Producat terra animam viventem
1.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this chapter, from the place: “And God said: Let the earth bring forth the living creature”

paras.t: Dixit quoque Deus : Producat terra animam viventem in genere suo. Hic describitur ornatus sextæ diei, quo terra ornata est : et correspondet operi tertiæ diei, quo terra fuit discooperta ab aquis. Denique quum dicitur, Producat terra animam viventem, sumitur pars pro toto, et singulare pro plurali, ut sit sensus : Producat terra animam viventem, id est, ex terra jam producantur animalia viva in genere suo, hoc est, quibus ex communi ratione generis sui competit vita sensitiva, quæ tamen specifice distinguantur. Propterea subditur, jumenta et reptilia et bestias terræ secundum species suas, id est, specie differentes, et prout convenit eis secundum naturas suas specificas. Hic tangitur triplex species subalterna animalium, ad ornatum terræ spectantium, quarum quælibet continet sub se varias species specialissimas. Jumenta enim dicuntur animalia domestica, quæ deserviunt homini in necessariis actibus, ut sunt equi, boves, oves, et consimilia. Unde dicuntur jumenta, quasi juvamenta. Reptilia appellantur, quæ rependo procedunt, de quibus præcedenti articulo dictum est. Jamque fit mentio de reptilibus terrestribus, non de aquaticis. Bestiæ vero vocantur animalia sæva indomita, quæ dentibus et unguibus lædunt.
paras.en: [[1:24|And God said: Let the earth bring forth the living creature in its kind|Dixit quoque Deus : Producat terra animam viventem in genere suo]]. Here is described the adornment of the sixth day, by which the earth was adorned; and it corresponds to the work of the third day, by which the earth was uncovered from the waters. Further, when it is said, [[1:24|Let the earth bring forth the living creature|Producat terra animam viventem]], the part is taken for the whole and the singular for the plural, so that the sense is: [[1:24|Let the earth bring forth the living creature|Producat terra animam viventem]], that is, let living animals now be brought forth from the earth [[1:24|in its kind|in genere suo]], that is, animals to which sensitive life belongs by the common nature of their genus, but which are nevertheless distinguished by species. Therefore it is added, [[1:24|cattle and creeping things, and beasts of the earth, according to their kinds|jumenta et reptilia et bestias terræ secundum species suas]], that is, differing in species, and as befits them according to their specific natures. Here are touched on three subordinate species [that is, intermediate classes, each a species of *animal* and itself a genus of further species] of the animals that belong to the adornment of the earth, each of which contains under it various lowest species. For those are called cattle [*jumenta*] which are domestic animals serving man in necessary tasks, such as horses, oxen, sheep and the like; hence they are called *jumenta*, as if *juvamenta* [that is, "helps", from *juvare*, to help]. Those are called creeping things which go forward by creeping, of which there was talk in the preceding article; and here mention is made of creeping things of the land, not of the water. But those are called beasts which are fierce, untamed animals that wound with teeth and claws.

paras.t: Factumque est ita. Et fecit Deus bestias terræ juxta species suas, et jumenta, et omne reptile, id est reptilia terræ in genere suo, hoc est in multiplici diversitate, juxta sensum prætactum. Intelligentia quippe horum verborum, ex præcedentibus clara est. Multa quoque circa præexposita opera præcedentium dierum quæsita, possent circa hæc verba inquiri : quorum solutio ex illis est evidens, utpote an Deus per se immediate formavit et organizavit corpora animalium horum. Et utrum fecit hoc in instanti, quia infinitæ virtuti competit agere in instanti, nisi aliunde sit impedimentum seu ratio aliter faciendi. An etiam animæ irrationabilium animalium illorum fuerunt creatæ. Et utrum corpora illa ex sola terra formata sint. Et quot individua ex qualibet specie specialissima tunc facta sint simul. Et an terra solum passive habuerit se in productione animalium talium.
paras.en: [[1:24|And it was so done|Factumque est ita]]. [[1:25|And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle|Et fecit Deus bestias terræ juxta species suas, et jumenta]], [[1:25|and every thing that creepeth|et omne reptile]], that is, the creeping things, [[1:25|on the earth after its kind|terræ in genere suo]], that is, in manifold diversity, in the sense touched on above. For the meaning of these words is clear from what has gone before. Many of the questions raised about the works of the preceding days, expounded above, could also be asked about these words, and their solution is evident from what was said there: for instance, whether God by himself immediately formed and organized the bodies of these animals; and whether he did this in an instant, since it belongs to infinite power to act in an instant unless there is some hindrance from elsewhere or some reason for doing otherwise; whether the souls of those irrational animals were also created; whether those bodies were formed from earth alone; how many individuals of each lowest species were then made together; and whether the earth stood merely passive in the production of such animals.

paras.t: Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum, et ait, etc. Potest specialiter hic inquiri, cur Deus non legitur benedixisse animalibus istis terræ, sicut paulo ante legitur benedixisse piscibus et avibus ex aqua plasmatis, dicendo : Crescite et multiplicamini. Ad hoc respondetur in Glossa : Forte, quod de animalibus illis ex aqua formatis Moyses dixit, de istis subintelligendum reliquit, maxime quia de operibus hujus diei adhuc multa erat dicturus, et quia in plantis et herbis non est multiplicatio individuorum per commixtionem maris et feminæ, idcirco non est eis data benedictio talis. Insuper S. Basilius ait, quod animalia terrena sint piscibus digniora, quoniam pisces carent memoria. Verumtamen B. Augustinus hoc ultimum, scilicet quod pisces non habent memoriam, improbat, affirmans quod in Bullensi regione sit fons piscibus plenus, qui gregatim natando, cum supergredientibus eunt ac redeunt, atque cum stantibus stant, exspectantes ut aliquid eis projiciant ad edendum, quia sic consueverunt.
paras.en: [[1:25|And God saw that it was good|Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], [[1:26|And he said|et ait]], etc. Here it may be asked in particular why God is not read to have blessed these animals of the earth, as a little before he is read to have blessed the fishes and birds formed from the water, saying: [[1:22|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]]. To this the Gloss answers: Perhaps what Moses said of those animals formed from the water he left to be understood of these, especially since he was still to say much about the works of this day; and since in plants and herbs there is no multiplying of individuals by the union of male and female, therefore such a blessing was not given to them. Moreover St. Basil says that the land animals are nobler than the fishes, because fishes lack memory. But Bl. Augustine rejects this last point, namely that fishes have no memory, affirming that in the region of Bulla [*Bullensi regione*: Bulla Regia in Africa] there is a spring full of fish which, swimming in shoals, go and come back with those who walk along it, and stand still with those who stand, waiting for them to throw them something to eat, since they are used to this.

paras.t: Præterea circa hunc locum quæri solet, an animalia immunda quæ ex cadaveribus aut humoribus nasci solent, tunc producta fuerunt. Ad hoc in Scholastica historia respondetur : Talium animalium sex sunt genera. Nam quædam ex exhalationibus generantur, ut bibiones ex vino, et papiliones ex aqua. Quædam ex corruptione humorum aquaticorum, ut vermes in cisternis. Quædam ex cadaveribus, sicut apes ex juvencis ; scabrones, videlicet muscæ grandes, quæ sonant volando, et scarabei ex equis. Quædam ex corruptione lignorum, ut teredines. Quædam ex corruptione herbarum, ut tineæ ex oleribus. Quædam ex corruptione fructuum, ut gurguliones ex fabis. Itaque dicitur, quod illa quæ ex corruptionibus producuntur, orta sunt post primi parentis peccatum ex rebus corruptis. Quæ vero sine corruptione nascuntur, ut quæ ex exhalationibus fiunt, facta sunt sexto die. His concordat quod habetur in Glossa ex Augustino.
paras.en: Further, it is commonly asked about this place whether the unclean animals that are usually born from carcasses or from moistures were produced then. To this the Scholastic History answers: There are six kinds of such animals [a note in the margin here cannot be read]. For some are generated from vapours, as wine-flies from wine and butterflies from water; some from the corruption of watery moistures, as the worms in cisterns; some from carcasses, as bees from young bullocks, and hornets (that is, large flies that hum as they fly) and beetles from horses; some from the corruption of wood, as woodworms; some from the corruption of herbs, as moths from garden plants; some from the corruption of fruits, as weevils from beans. And so it is said that those which are produced from corruption arose after the sin of the first parent, from things corrupted; but those which are born without corruption, as those that come from vapours, were made on the sixth day. With this agrees what is found in the Gloss from Augustine.

paras.t: Denique Thomas ait in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 72 : Animalia venenosa ante peccatum homini noxia non fuisse, nec naturaliter neque totaliter mala sunt, quamvis sint naturali particulari bono nociva : siquidem ad decorem pertinent universi, et multas habent commoditates Deo notas, quamvis hominibus sæpe incognitas. Hinc loquitur Damascenus libro secundo : Eduxit terra, Creatore jubente, diversa genera animalium, reptilium et ferarum ac jumentorum. Omnia ad opportunum hominis usum, et quædam ad escam, puta cervos, oves, dorcades, et consimilia : alia vero ad ministerium, puta camelos, boves, equos, asinos, et quæ talia : alia autem ad jucunditatem, ut simias, psittacos, et picas. Plantarum quoque et herbarum quædam fructiferæ et comestibiles, quædam odoriferæ et floridæ ad jucunditatem nobis tributæ, ut rosæ : aliæ ad ægritudinum sanationes. Non est ens, neque animal, neque planta, in qua Conditor non posuerit optationem quamdam utilitati hominum conferentem : nec modo inutilis est ferarum usus, perterrens, et […] nos ad cognitionem invocationemque Dei, qui fecit nos. Hæc Damascenus.
paras.en: Further, Thomas says in the first part of his Summa, question 72, that poisonous animals were not harmful to man before sin; nor are they evil by nature or wholly, although they are hurtful to some particular natural good: for they belong to the beauty of the universe, and have many advantages known to God, though often unknown to men. Hence Damascene says in the second book: The earth, at the Creator's command, brought forth the different kinds of animals, of creeping things, of wild beasts and of cattle; all for the fitting use of man: some for food, such as deer, sheep, gazelles and the like; others for service, such as camels, oxen, horses, asses and suchlike; others again for delight, such as apes, parrots and magpies. Of plants and herbs too, some bear fruit and are good to eat; some are fragrant and flowering, given us for delight, as roses; others for the healing of sicknesses. There is no being, neither animal nor plant, in which the Maker has not put some provision [*optationem*, literally "a wish"; the sense is some power or property] contributing to the benefit of men: nor is the use of wild beasts useless now, terrifying us and […] us to the knowledge and invocation of God, who made us. Thus far Damascene.

paras.t: Hinc alii dicunt : Animalia nociva facta sunt homini nociva post peccatum ex triplici causa. Primo, propter hominis punitionem. Punitur enim, quum læditur aut lædi veretur ab eis, quoniam timor maxima pœna est. Secundo, propter hominis admonitionem. Admonetur quippe ex eis, ut sciat hæc sibi accidere pro peccato. Tertio, propter hominis informationem, quia ex consideratione illorum informatur in multis, utpote quanta sit crudelitas invisibilium adversariorum nostrorum, quam horrenda sint supplicia inferorum, quanta sit humana fragilitas, quæ a minimis ac vilibus illis tam cito ac graviter læditur.
paras.en: Hence others say: Harmful animals were made harmful to man after sin for a threefold reason. First, for the punishment of man: for he is punished when he is hurt by them or fears to be hurt, since fear is a very great punishment. Secondly, for the admonition of man: for he is admonished by them, so that he may know that these things befall him for sin. Thirdly, for the instruction of man, since by considering them he is instructed in many things: for instance, how great is the cruelty of our invisible adversaries, how dreadful are the torments of hell, how great is human frailty, which is so quickly and so grievously hurt by those least and vilest creatures.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur animalia ad terræ ornatum pertinentia, non continentur sub una differentia animalis, quemadmodum animalia ad ornatum aquæ spectantia, quæ omnia reptilia appellantur ; animalia quoque quæ aerem ornant, quæ omnia volatilia nuncupantur. Respondet Bonaventura, quoniam terra inter cetera elementa est minus decora, ideo magis indiguit decorari, videlicet pluribus differentiis animalium : et item, quia præ ceteris elementis præstat animalibus nutrimentum. Sufficientia vero irrationabilium animalium, quæ versantur in terra, sic sumitur ex parte finis : Facta sunt enim propter hominem. Aut ergo ordinata sunt ad hominis juvamentum, et sic sunt jumenta ; aut ad hominis exercitium, et hoc dupliciter : aut enim exercent manifeste nocendo, et ita sunt bestiæ ; aut occulte, et sic sunt reptilia. Et quamvis non haberent hos actus et fines realiter, si homo non peccasset, haberent tamen in aptitudine ; atque ex aptitudine illa melius erudiretur homo in statu innocentiæ, quam erudiatur nunc ex actu in statu culpæ.
paras.en: It is asked why the animals belonging to the adornment of the earth are not contained under one difference of animal, as the animals belonging to the adornment of the water, which are all called creeping things, and likewise the animals that adorn the air, which are all named fowls. Bonaventure answers: since the earth is less comely than the other elements, it had more need of being adorned, namely with more differences of animals; and again, because more than the other elements it provides nourishment for animals. But the sufficiency [that is, why there are just these three kinds and no more] of the irrational animals that live on the earth is taken from their end, thus: they were made for man. Either, then, they are ordered to man's help, and so they are cattle [*jumenta*, "helps"]; or to man's exercise, and this in two ways: either they exercise him openly by doing harm, and so they are beasts; or secretly, and so they are creeping things. And although they would not have had these acts and ends in reality had man not sinned, yet they would have had them in aptitude; and from that aptitude man would have been better taught in the state of innocence than he is now taught by the act in the state of guilt.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur productio hominis, propter quem cetera omnia corporalia sunt creata. Quemadmodum enim rex terrenus facit filio suo palatium, deinde ponit in eo filium suum : sic Rex omnipotens primo fecit hunc mundum sensibilem, cumque distinxit ac decoravit, deinde hominem quem elegit in filium adoptivum, constituit in eodem.
paras.en: Next is described the production of man, for whose sake all the other bodily things were created. For as an earthly king makes a palace for his son and then places his son in it, so the almighty King first made this sensible world, and when he had distinguished and adorned it, then placed in it man, whom he chose as his adopted son[[Rom 8:15||]].

paras.t: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Hoc non est verbum Dei ad angelos, quoniam angeli non sunt Deo cooperati in hominis productione, præsertim quantum ad animam, in qua imago et similitudo Dei consistit ; sed est verbum Dei Patris ad Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum, aut totius superdignissimæ Trinitatis ad se ipsam, et ita per verba hæc insinuatur distinctio Personarum in Deo. Primo, quum dicitur, Faciamus ; secundo, quum additur, Ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Et item, quod supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis operatio ad extra sit indivisa. Denique, quemadmodum Origenes in prima homilia super Genesim loquitur, in his verbis designatur dignitas hominis : nam neque de cœlo, neque de luminaribus cœli locutus est Deus, sicut de homine ; imo creationem cœli et terræ Moyses, a Deo edoctus, uno atque communi verbo expressit, dicendo : In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, deinde productionem firmamenti et luminarium ac stellarum per consimilia verba describit, dicens : Dixit Deus, Fiat firmamentum, Fiant luminaria. At ubi ad hominis productionem deventum est, usus est Conditor universitatis speciali sermone, et quasi præcipuum producturus effectum, per modum deliberantis et excitantis se ipsum, locutus est. Hinc Beda testatur : Apparet quare dictum sit, ut cetera fierent juxta genus suum et species suas. Erat namque homo creandus, qui non solum generi suo ac speciei congrueret, sed ad imaginem fieret Creatoris : cujus dignitatis magnitudo ostenditur, dum quasi consilio creatur ; nec simpliciter dicitur, sicut de ceteris, Fiat homo, sed, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram.
paras.en: [[1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]]. This is not a word of God to the angels, since the angels did not work together with God in the production of man, above all as regards the soul, in which the image and likeness of God consists; but it is the word of God the Father to the Son and the Holy Ghost, or of the whole most exalted Trinity to itself; and so by these words the distinction of the Persons in God is indicated: first, when it is said, [[1:26|Let us make|Faciamus]]; secondly, when it is added, [[1:26|to our image and likeness|Ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]]. And also that the working of the most glorious Trinity outside itself is undivided. Further, as Origen says in the first homily on Genesis, the dignity of man is pointed out in these words: for God did not speak of the heaven, nor of the lights of heaven, as he did of man. Indeed, Moses, taught by God, expressed the creation of heaven and earth in a single, common word, saying: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]; then he describes the production of the firmament and of the lights and stars in like words, saying: God said, [[1:6|Let there be a firmament|Fiat firmamentum]]; [[1:14|Let there be lights|Fiant luminaria]]. But when it came to the production of man, the Maker of the universe used a special form of speech, and, as one about to produce his chief work, he spoke in the manner of one deliberating and rousing himself. Hence Bede testifies: It appears why it was said that the other things should be made according to their genus and their species: for man was to be created, who should not only agree with his genus and species but should be made to the image of the Creator. The greatness of his dignity is shown in that he is created as it were by counsel; and it is not said simply, as of the rest, Let man be made, but, [[1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]].

paras.t: Præterea, ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei creatus est homo, non quantum ad corporalia lineamenta ac corporis figurationem, quasi Deus in divinitatis natura habeat corporalem figuram, ad cujus imitationem atque effigiem factus sit homo, ut quidam hæretici et etiam quidam rudes atque indocti ex detestabili simplicitate dixerunt, quum Deus altissimus et æternus sit supersimplicissima mens, actualissima vita, superpurissimum esse, incircumscriptibilis veritas, indivisibilis unitas, ipsaque sapientia immaterialissima. Et sicut Aristoteles subtiliter demonstravit, Deus est purus actus. Est itaque homo ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei creatus, quantum ad animam rationalem, quæ in parte sua potestativa superiori habet memoriam, intellectum et voluntatem, per quas Deo creatori suo assimilatur, ipsum contemplando ac diligendo. Et quia per actum magis assimilatur Deo, quam per nudas potentias, aut per habitus solos : idcirco imago et similitudo Dei in anima præsertim attenditur, secundum quod intellectus et voluntas animæ decorantur non solum habitibus, sed etiam actibus suis.
paras.en: Moreover, man was created to the image and likeness of God, not as regards bodily features and the shape of the body, as though God in the nature of his godhead had a bodily shape, in imitation and likeness of which man was made, as certain heretics, and also certain rude and unlearned men, have said out of a detestable simplicity: since God most high and eternal is a mind simple beyond all simplicity, a life supremely in act, a being pure beyond all purity, a truth that cannot be circumscribed, an indivisible unity, and wisdom itself, wholly immaterial. And as Aristotle has subtly demonstrated, God is pure act [that is, wholly actual, with no unrealized potency]. Man, then, was created to the image and likeness of God as regards the rational soul, which in its higher part of powers has memory, understanding and will, by which it is made like to God its creator, contemplating him and loving him. And because it is made like to God more by act than by bare powers or by habits alone, the image and likeness of God in the soul is reckoned chiefly according as the understanding and will of the soul are adorned not only with their habits but also with their acts.

paras.t: Denique anima potest dici imago Dei, quantum ad trinitatem Personarum ; et similitudo ejusdem, quantum ad unitatem ac simplicitatem divinæ essentiæ. Quemadmodum enim in divinis sunt tres Personæ, quarum una ac prima a nulla est, secunda, videlicet Filius, est a solo Patre, tertia ab utroque ; ita in anima intellectus actuatur a fecunda memoria, et voluntas ab utrisque. Rursus, in superiori parte animæ, est verbum internum ab intellectu procedens, et amor ex voluntate et verbo emanans. Dicitur quoque anima similitudo Dei, in quantum est simplex, spiritualis, intellectualis ac immortalis quædam essentia quemadmodum Deus. Attenditur autem imago Dei in anima, per comparationem ad increatum objectum. De ista materia, quum sit communis, pertranseo : hoc tamen adjiciendum, quod homo seu anima dicitur Dei imago, non quod essentialiter Dei imago existat, sed quia imaginem Dei sibi habet impressam, sicut denarius dicitur imago Imperatoris. Rursus, unigenitus Dei Filius est imago naturalis atque perfecta æterni Patris. Homo autem seu anima est imago Dei imitativa ac imperfecta. Iterum, imago Dei in homine, non solum consistit in actu contemplandi ac diligendi, sive in actu proferendi verbum mentale et actu producendi amorem, sed item in aptitudine ad hos actus. Idcirco in omni homine quantumvis iniquo et otioso, permanet Dei imago, sed deformata et plurimum imperfecta.
paras.en: Further, the soul can be called the image of God as regards the trinity of Persons, and his likeness as regards the unity and simplicity of the divine essence. For as in God there are three Persons, of whom one, the first, is from none, the second, namely the Son, is from the Father alone, the third from both, so in the soul the understanding is brought into act by the fruitful memory, and the will by both. Again, in the higher part of the soul there is the inner word proceeding from the understanding, and love flowing from the will and the word. The soul is also called the likeness of God inasmuch as it is a simple, spiritual, intellectual and immortal essence, as God is. And the image of God in the soul is reckoned by its relation to the uncreated object [that is, to God himself as known and loved]. I pass over this matter, since it is commonly treated; but this must be added, that man or the soul is called the image of God, not because it is essentially the image of God, but because it has the image of God impressed upon it, as a penny is called the image of the Emperor. Again, the only-begotten Son of God is the natural and perfect image of the eternal Father; but man or the soul is an imitative and imperfect image of God. Again, the image of God in man consists not only in the act of contemplating and loving, or in the act of uttering the mental word and the act of producing love, but also in the aptitude for these acts. Therefore in every man, however wicked and idle, the image of God remains, but deformed and very imperfect.

paras.t: Et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cæli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ, omnique reptili quod movetur super terram, id est, omnibus istis sit dignior, et eis præcipiat, eis quoque utatur ad libitum, secundum quod congruit sibi a Deo. Istud enim competebat homini eo ipso, quo fuit ad Dei imaginem similitudinemque creatus, præsertim quamdiu mansit Deo obediens ac subjectus, imo et post peccatum mansit illis sublimior ; sed in punitionem suæ transgressionis, amisit dominium super illa, potissimum super ferocia ac super minima quædam ac vilia, sicut sunt pulices, ut inobedientiam suam miseriamque advertat ac defleat. Aliqua tamen manserunt ei subjecta, propter necessitatem vitæ humanæ, et ut penset quid amisit in aliis. Porro quod dictum est, Universæ creaturæ, de creaturis corporalibus est sumendum ; nam et cœlestia corpora in obsequium cunctis gentibus sunt plasmata.
paras.en: [[1:26|and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and the beasts, and the whole earth, and every creeping creature that moveth upon the earth|Et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cæli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ, omnique reptili quod movetur super terram]] [Denis reads *et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ*, "and the beasts of the earth, and all creation", where the Vulgate has *et bestiis, universæque terræ*, "and the beasts, and the whole earth"]: that is, let him be of higher dignity than all these, and command them, and also use them at his pleasure, as befits him by God's gift. For this belonged to man by the very fact that he was created to the image and likeness of God, above all as long as he remained obedient and subject to God; and even after sin he remained higher than they. But in punishment of his transgression he lost dominion over them, above all over the fierce ones and over certain very small and vile ones, such as fleas, so that he may take note of his disobedience and misery and bewail it. Some, however, remained subject to him because of the needs of human life, and so that he may weigh what he has lost in the others. Again, what was said, *all creation*, is to be taken of bodily creatures; for the heavenly bodies too were formed for the service of all nations.

paras.t: Et creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam. Per hoc insinuatur summæ Trinitatis unitas substantialis. Dicitur autem Deus creasse hominem, quantum ad animam, proprie loquendo de creatione, quoniam illam fecit ex nihilo ; sed quantum ad corpus, dicitur eum creasse, sumendo creare extense pro plasmare seu facere : nam infra habetur, quod formavit hominem de limo terræ. Et ad imaginem Dei creavit illum. Quare hoc addit, quod jam satis videbatur expressum, nisi ad commendandam dignationem et beneficentiam Dei in hominis institutione, atque ad inculcandum hoc ipsum memoriæ nostræ, ut caritatem et pietatem ac munificentiam Dei circa nos perpendamus, et grati simus eidem, propriamque dignitatem pensantes, irrationalem vitam abhorreamus. Denique modus iste loquendi, est frequens in Veteri Testamento, ita quod aliquid narratur de Deo quasi de alio, quum totum de eodem dicatur, quemadmodum infra habetur, quod Deus pluit ignem et sulfur a Domino. Verumtamen posset in his verbis personalis distinctio designari in Deo. Quamvis enim, secundum expositores, Deus Pater dicat ad Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum, seu Trinitas tota ad se ipsam, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram, ita quod Pater dicitur creasse hominem non ad imaginem Filii, nihilo minus dici potest, quod homo creatus est ad imaginem et similitudinem cujuslibet divinæ Personæ, eo modo quo illi qui trinitatem Personarum in Deo non credunt, fatentur hominem ad Dei imaginem similitudinemque creatum. Atque ad hoc insinuandum, posset quis dicere nunc esse adjectum, Ad imaginem Dei creavit illum. Unicuique quippe divinæ et increatæ Personæ assimilatur homo, per memoriam, intellectum et voluntatem.
paras.en: [[1:27|And God created man to his own image|Et creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam]] [Denis reads *ad imaginem et similitudinem suam*, "to his own image and likeness"; the Vulgate has *ad imaginem suam*]. By this the substantial unity of the most high Trinity is indicated. Now God is said to have created man as regards the soul, speaking properly of creation, since he made it from nothing; but as regards the body he is said to have created him by taking *create* in a wider sense, for *form* or *make*: for below it is said that he [[Gen 2:7|formed man of the slime of the earth|formavit hominem de limo terræ]]. And [[1:27|to the image of God he created him|ad imaginem Dei creavit illum]]. Why does he add this, which already seemed expressed clearly enough, unless to commend the condescension and kindness of God in the making of man, and to impress this very thing on our memory, so that we may weigh the charity, goodness and bounty of God towards us, and be grateful to him, and, considering our own dignity, shrink from an irrational life? Further, this manner of speaking is frequent in the Old Testament, so that something is told of God as though of another, while the whole is said of the same, as it is said below that God rained fire and brimstone from the Lord[[Gen 19:24||]]. Yet a personal distinction in God might be signified in these words. For although, according to the expositors, God the Father says to the Son and the Holy Ghost, or the whole Trinity to itself, [[1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]], so that the Father is said to have created man not to the image of the Son, nevertheless it can be said that man was created to the image and likeness of each divine Person, in the way in which those who do not believe in the trinity of Persons in God confess that man was created to the image and likeness of God. And to indicate this, someone might say that there is now added, [[1:27|to the image of God he created him|Ad imaginem Dei creavit illum]]. For man is made like to each divine and uncreated Person by memory, understanding and will.

paras.t: Quæritur, quare in ceterorum animalium productione facta sunt plura individua simul, puta duo ad minus in qualibet specie animalis perfecti, cui per utriusque sexus commixtionem competit generare ; in creatione autem speciei humanæ, primo factum est unum suppositum tantum. Ad hoc Glossa ex Augustino respondet, ut humanum genus firmiori caritatis copula constringatur, dum se totum ex uno genitum recordatur. Hinc duodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Animalia bruta, tam ea quæ solitudinem diligunt, quam illa quæ in gregibus vivere malunt, Deus non ex singulis propagavit, sed plura simul jussit exsistere ; hominem vero, quem inter angelos bestiasque constituit, ex uno voluit multiplicari, ut commendaretur eidem unitas societatis, vinculum quoque concordiæ et cognationis affectus.
paras.en: It is asked why in the production of the other animals several individuals were made together, at least two, say, in each species of perfect animal [that is, of the higher animals, as distinct from those thought to arise from corruption], to which it belongs to generate by the union of both sexes, whereas in the creation of the human species at first only one individual [*suppositum*, that is, one subsisting person] was made. To this the Gloss answers from Augustine: so that the human race might be bound by a firmer bond of charity, remembering that it was wholly begotten from one. Hence Augustine says in the twelfth book of The City of God: The brute animals, both those that love solitude and those that prefer to live in herds, God did not propagate from single ones, but commanded many to exist together; but man, whom he set between the angels and the beasts, he willed to be multiplied from one, so that the unity of fellowship, the bond of concord and the affection of kinship might be commended to him.

paras.t: Insuper, pro pleniori dictorum intellectu habendo quærendum est, quum Deus dicitur creasse hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam, an accipiendum sit hoc de imagine et similitudine creata, an increata. Ad hoc Bonaventura respondet in scripto secundi, distinctione 16 : Duplex est modus exponendi istam auctoritatem, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Unus, intelligendo de imagine increata ; alter vero, intelligendo de imagine creata. Primus modus triplicatur : Unus modus est, ut imago et similitudo referantur ad idem, videlicet ad essentiam in tribus Personis unam. Secundus est, ut imago et similitudo referantur ad personam Filii tantum. Tertius modus exponendi est, ut imago referatur ad Filium, similitudo ad Spiritum Sanctum. Porro alius modus exponendi est, ut intelligatur de imagine creata. Et ille modus similiter triplex est. Unus sic exponit, ut imago præcedat similitudinem. Et dicit quod imago attenditur in naturalibus, similitudo in gratuitis. Secundus sic exponit, ut similitudo concomitetur imaginem. Et dicit quod imago sit in potentia cognoscendi, similitudo in potentia diligendi. Tertius modus est, ut imago sequatur similitudinem, quia similitudo est in plus seu communius quam imago. Et dicit quod similitudo attenditur in natura, hoc est quantum ad ea quæ sunt essentiæ in communi ; imago in forma, id est quantum ad propria. Omnes hi modi possunt secundum Bonaventuram sustineri.
paras.en: Moreover, for a fuller understanding of what has been said, it must be asked, when God is said to have created man to his image and likeness, whether this is to be taken of a created or an uncreated image and likeness. To this Bonaventure answers in his writing on the second book [of the Sentences], distinction 16: There is a twofold way of expounding this authority, [[1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]]: one, understanding it of the uncreated image; the other, understanding it of the created image. The first way is threefold. One way is that *image* and *likeness* be referred to the same thing, namely to the essence that is one in three Persons. The second is that *image* and *likeness* be referred to the person of the Son alone. The third way of expounding is that *image* be referred to the Son, *likeness* to the Holy Ghost. The other way of expounding is that it be understood of the created image; and this way likewise is threefold. One expounds it so that the image goes before the likeness, and says that the image is reckoned in natural gifts, the likeness in gifts of grace. The second expounds it so that the likeness accompanies the image, and says that the image is in the power of knowing, the likeness in the power of loving. The third way is that the image follows the likeness, since likeness extends further, or is more common, than image; and it says that the likeness is reckoned in the nature, that is, as regards what belongs to the essence in common; the image in the form, that is, as regards what is proper. All these ways, according to Bonaventure, can be upheld.

paras.t: Verum ut hoc clarius intelligatur, introducenda sunt verba Magistri in libro secundo quo ait : Imago et similitudo in hoc loco vel increata intelligitur, id est Trinitatis essentia, ad quam factus est homo; vel creata, in qua factus est homo, quæ hominis est concreta, hoc est concreata vel a principio suæ creationis impressa. Increatam enim imaginem quæ Deus est, intellexisse videtur Beda, cum ait: Non esse unam imaginem Dei et angelorum, sed trium Personarum. Idcirco Personis divinis, videlicet Filio et Spiritui Sancto, non angelis, dicitur: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Improprie tamen divina essentia imago vocatur, quia imago proprie dicitur relative ad id, cujus similitudinem gerit, atque ad quod repræsentandum peracta est. Attamen imago improprie dicitur id, ad quod fit aliud: sicut exemplum proprie appellatur, quod ex aliquo sumitur et formatur; exemplar autem id, ad quod seu ex quo fit aut sumitur aliquid. Nihilo minus unum pro alio abusive interdum accipitur, ita et minus proprie essentia Trinitatis vocatur imago. Porro Filius proprie dicitur Patris imago: ideo quidam hoc loco per imaginem, Filium intellexerunt: hominem vero non imaginem, sed ad imaginem factum, dixerunt, quibus obviat quod ait Apostolus: Vir quidem est imago et gloria Dei. Alii ergo perspicacius per imaginem, intellexerunt Filium: per similitudinem, Spiritum Sanctum, qui est similitudo Patris et Filii. Et quod additur, Nostram, retulerunt ad similitudinem tantum. Ad imaginem autem, putaverunt subintelligendum esse, meam. De hac materia scribit ibidem et plura alia. Homo itaque dicitur imago Dei, et ad imaginem ejus factus; sed Filius Dei dicitur imago Patris, non autem ad imaginem genitus, quum sit perfecta et naturalis imago, per omnia Patri æqualis.
paras.en: But that this may be understood more clearly, the words of the Master in the second book must be brought in, where he says: The image and likeness in this place is understood either as uncreated, that is, the essence of the Trinity, to which man was made; or as created, in which man was made, which is *concreta* to man, that is, created together with him [*concreata*], or impressed on him from the beginning of his creation. For Bede seems to have understood the uncreated image, which is God, when he says that it is not one image of God and of the angels, but of the three Persons; and therefore it is said to the divine Persons, namely to the Son and the Holy Ghost, not to the angels: [[1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram]]. Yet the divine essence is called an image improperly, since *image* is properly said relatively to that whose likeness it bears and to represent which it was made. Still, that to which another thing is made is improperly called an image: just as *exemplum* [copy] is properly the name of what is taken and formed from something, and *exemplar* [pattern] of that to which, or from which, something is made or taken. Nevertheless the one is sometimes loosely taken for the other, and so too the essence of the Trinity is less properly called an image. Again, the Son is properly called the image of the Father[[2 Cor 4:4||]] [the margin sets this reference a few lines higher, beside the words on the divine essence called an image]: and so some have understood the Son by *image* in this place, and have said that man is not the image, but made to the image; against whom stands what the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:7|The man indeed|Vir quidem]] [[1 Cor 11:7|is the image and glory of God|imago et gloria Dei]]. Others, then, more keenly, have understood by *image* the Son, by *likeness* the Holy Ghost, who is the likeness of the Father and the Son; and what is added, [[1:26|our|Nostram]], they referred to *likeness* only, while with *to the image* they thought that *my* is to be understood. On this matter he writes many other things in the same place. Man, then, is called the image of God and made to his image; but the Son of God is called the image of the Father, yet not begotten to the image, since he is the perfect and natural image, equal to the Father in all things.

paras.t: Masculum et feminam creavit eos. Hoc per anticipationem est dictum; non enim creavit Deus tunc nisi virum. Quando autem et qualiter fecerit feminam, sequenti narratur capitulo; sed ita anticipative nunc dicitur virum feminamque formasse, quia volebat statum subjungere, motum multiplicationis generis humani, qui fit per commixtionem maris et feminæ. Ideo ait Glossa: Bene hoc loco creati dicuntur, ut benedictio Dei congrue inducatur. Nam subditur: Benedixitque illis Deus, et ait: Crescite et multiplicamini. Circa hoc quæritur, qualiter Deus dicatur illis benedixisse atque dixisse, Crescite et multiplicamini, quum femina nondum fuerit facta. Ad quod poterit responderi, quod dicitur eis benedixisse, quoniam benedictio data viro, pertinebat ad feminam, et quoniam femina mox erat plasmanda, atque in præscientia Dei jam fuit. Consuetudo quoque Scripturæ est, ut frequenter numerus singularis pro plurali, et pluralis pro singulari ponatur; et item, ut id adscribatur pluribus, quod uni eorum est competens. Itaque benedixit eis, hoc est, virtutem, auctoritatem, et gratiam generandi matrimonialiter ac virtuose contulit ipsis. Nam matrimonium inter eos instituit, per quod reprobantur hæretici qui nuptias damnant, nec matrimonialem concubitum credunt posse fieri sine peccato.
paras.en: [[1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum et feminam creavit eos]]. This is said by anticipation, for God then created only the man; but when and how he made the woman is told in the following chapter. It is said thus by anticipation now that he formed the man and the woman because he wished to add straightway the movement [*motum*] of the multiplying of the human race, which comes about by the union of male and female. Hence the Gloss says: They are rightly said in this place to have been created, so that the blessing of God may fittingly be brought in. For it is added: [[1:28|And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply|Benedixitque illis Deus, et ait: Crescite et multiplicamini]]. About this it is asked how God is said to have blessed them and to have said, [[1:28|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]], when the woman had not yet been made. To which it can be answered that he is said to have blessed them because the blessing given to the man belonged to the woman, and because the woman was soon to be formed and was already in God's foreknowledge. It is also the custom of Scripture that the singular number is often put for the plural and the plural for the singular, and likewise that what befits one of several is ascribed to several. So [[1:28|God blessed them|benedixit eis]], that is, he conferred on them the power, the authority and the grace to beget in marriage and virtuously. For he instituted marriage between them; by which are condemned the heretics who condemn marriage and do not believe that the marriage act can take place without sin.

paras.t: Et replete terram semine vestro, videlicet filiis et filiabus, utpote paradisum terrestrem, si non peccaveritis; sin autem, expulsi inde, replebitis ceteras terras. Non quod primi parentes per se immediate repleverint terram, sed per se et posteros suos. Et subjicite eam, id est, ad commoda vestra utimini terra; et dominamini piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et universis animantibus quæ moventur super terram. Omnia enim hæc, sicut jam patuit, fuerunt homini in statu innocentiæ obedientia et subjecta; et eo modo dominabatur eis, quo et præfuit eis, juxta sensum expositum.
paras.en: [[1:28|and fill the earth|Et replete terram]] with your seed, namely with sons and daughters: that is, the earthly paradise, if you do not sin; but if you do, then, cast out of it, you will fill the other lands. Not that the first parents filled the earth immediately by themselves, but by themselves and their descendants. [[1:28|and subdue it|Et subjicite eam]], that is, use the earth for your benefit; [[1:28|and rule over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth|et dominamini piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et universis animantibus quæ moventur super terram]]. For all these, as has already appeared, were obedient and subject to man in the state of innocence; and he ruled over them in the same way in which he had dominion over them, in the sense expounded above.

paras.t: Dixitque Deus: Ecce dedi vobis. Quare non ait, Ecce do vobis, quum ante hæc verba non legatur eis ista dedisse? Sed ideo ait, Dedi, quia quod nunc actualiter ac præsentialiter dat, in præscientia sua dare eis decrevit. Itaque dedi vobis, id est ad usum et commodum vestrum, omnem herbam afferentem semen, id est, habentem in se virtutem causalem, seu semen ad producendum simile sibi, ut plenius expositum est in opere tertiæ diei ; et universa ligna, hoc est arbores, quæ habent in semetipsis sementem generis sui, id est rationem seminalem vimque causalem, seu semen aut granum, ad producendum consimilia sibi in specie sua, sicut expositum est. Et sint vobis in escam, in quantum vestræ naturæ congruum fuerit atque placuerit. Non tamen universa ac singula illa conveniebant esui hominis, quod patet ex consequentibus, nam sequitur : Et cunctis animantibus terræ, omnique volucri cæli, et universis quæ moventur in terra, et in quibus est anima vivens, hoc est animalibus terrestribus, ut habeant ad vescendum. Non enim per omnia eadem erant alimenta hominis et brutorum ; idcirco in verbis his reddenda sunt singula singulis, ut sit sensus, quod unicuique animali dedit Deus ista aut aliquid horum ad esum, secundum congruentiam et indigentiam ipsius.
paras.en: [[1:29|And God said: Behold I have given you|Dixitque Deus: Ecce dedi vobis]]. Why does he not say, Behold I give you, since before these words he is not read to have given them these things? He says, [[1:29|I have given|Dedi]], because what he now gives actually and presently he had decreed in his foreknowledge to give them. So [[1:29|I have given you|dedi vobis]], that is, for your use and benefit, [[1:29|every herb bearing seed|omnem herbam afferentem semen]], that is, having in itself a causal power, or seed, for producing its like, as was more fully expounded in the work of the third day; [[1:29|and all trees|et universa ligna]], that is, trees [Denis glosses *ligna*, literally "woods", by *arbores*], [[1:29|that have in themselves seed of their own kind|quæ habent in semetipsis sementem generis sui]], that is, a seminal reason [that is, the power planted in a thing to bring forth its kind] and causal force, or seed or grain, for producing things like themselves in their species, as has been expounded; [[1:29|to be your meat|Et sint vobis in escam]], in so far as it befits and pleases your nature. Yet not each and every one of them was suited to man's eating, as is clear from what follows; for there follows: [[1:30|And to all beasts of the earth, and to every fowl of the air|Et cunctis animantibus terræ, omnique volucri cæli]], [[1:30|and to all that move upon the earth, and wherein there is life|et universis quæ moventur in terra, et in quibus est anima vivens]], that is, to the land animals, [[1:30|that they may have to feed upon|ut habeant ad vescendum]]. For the food of man and of the brutes was not the same in all respects; therefore in these words each thing is to be assigned to each, so that the sense is that God gave to every animal these things, or some of them, for food, according to what suits it and what it needs.

paras.t: Circa quod quidam scribit, quod fructus arborum dedit ad vescendum hominibus, quia infra habetur, Ex omni ligno paradisi comede ; herbas autem et semina earum, irrationabilibus animalibus. Sed melius dicitur, quod sicut quædam irrationabilia ex sua natura vescuntur ac vescebantur tunc etiam quarumdam fructibus arborum, sic homini in statu innocentiæ naturale fuisset vesci aliquibus herbis ac fructibus terræ, sicut et nunc est. Nec obstat quod allegatum est, Ex omni ligno paradisi comede. Hoc quippe non est dictum per exclusionem universarum herbarum, sed magis ad innuendum quod fructus arborum erant speciales cibi ipsius.
paras.en: On this someone writes that he gave the fruits of the trees to men for food, since it is said below, [[Gen 2:16|Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Ex omni ligno paradisi comede]], but the herbs and their seeds to the irrational animals. But it is better said that, as certain irrational animals by their nature feed, and fed then too, on the fruits of certain trees, so it would have been natural for man in the state of innocence to feed on some herbs and fruits of the earth, as it is now too. Nor does what was alleged stand in the way, [[Gen 2:16|Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Ex omni ligno paradisi comede]]; for this was not said to exclude all herbs, but rather to hint that the fruits of the trees were his special food.

paras.t: Ex his trahunt doctores, quod in statu innocentiæ non fuisset esus carnium aut piscium, sed tantum fructuum arborum ac herbarum ; imo usus carnium et piscium, primo concessus est homini post diluvium. Nam Beda hic ait : Omnis herba et ligna data sunt hominibus et volatilibus et animantibus terræ in escam. Ex quo patet, quod tunc animalia esu animalium, hoc est, unum animal ex carnibus alterius, non vivebant, sed concorditer herbis et fructibus vescebantur. Iterum ait Beda hoc loco : Ante peccatum hominis terra nil noxium protulit, non herbam venenatam, nec arborem sterilem. Verumtamen Albertus quærit, an plantæ nocivæ ex figura, ut spinæ, vel ex humore, ut venenosæ, fuerint tertio die productæ. Ad quod respondet : Plantæ quæ modo nocivæ sunt, non essent nocivæ, si homo non peccasset ; nihilo minus essent in suis figuris atque humoribus, in quibus nunc sunt. Sicut nec ignis ureret, nec aqua suffocaret, si non fuisset peccatum : nihilo minus ignis esset calidus, et aqua humida. Simili modo respondet ad quæstionem qua quæritur, an animalia, perniciosa et venenosa facta sint ante peccatum originale, vel postea tantum. Thomas quoque in prima parte : Spinæ, inquit, et tribuli oriebantur in terra, antequam dictum est homini, Maledicta terra in opere tuo ; sed non in hominis pœnam. Attamen verbis Bedæ consonare videtur, quod in Scholastica historia legitur : Ante peccatum nil noxium aut sterile terra produxit, sed ista intelligi possunt, quod non erant venenata aut noxia ante peccatum, quantum ad actum seu usum.
paras.en: From this the doctors gather that in the state of innocence there would have been no eating of flesh or of fish, but only of the fruits of trees and of herbs; indeed, the use of flesh and fish was first granted to man after the flood. For Bede says here: Every herb and the trees were given for food to men and to the fowls and to the living creatures of the earth. From which it is clear that the animals did not then live by eating animals, that is, one animal on the flesh of another, but fed peaceably on herbs and fruits. Again Bede says at this place: Before man's sin the earth brought forth nothing harmful, no poisonous herb, no barren tree. Albert, however, asks whether the plants harmful by their shape, as thorns, or by their juice, as poisonous ones, were produced on the third day. To which he answers: The plants that are now harmful would not be harmful had man not sinned; nevertheless they would have the shapes and juices they have now. Just as fire would not burn nor water drown had there been no sin; nevertheless fire would be hot and water moist. In like manner he answers the question whether destructive and poisonous animals were made before original sin, or only afterwards. Thomas too, in the first part: Thorns and thistles, he says, sprang up on the earth before it was said to man, [[Gen 3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|Maledicta terra in opere tuo]]; but not for man's punishment. Yet what is read in the Scholastic History seems to agree with Bede's words: Before sin the earth produced nothing harmful or barren; but these words can be understood to mean that they were not poisonous or harmful before sin as regards act or use.

paras.t: Insuper quæritur : Cur Deus dedit homini quem immortalem condiderat, ista corporea elementa ? Respondetur, quod immortalitas illa non fuit perfecta, nec talis qualis post resurrectionem communem speratur, videlicet necessitas non moriendi, seu impossibilitas moriendi ; sed erat talis, quod poterat non mori, et nisi peccasset, mortem non incurrisset. Talis autem immortalitas erat cibis sustentanda, quousque ad meliorem statum ac vitam perduceretur.
paras.en: Moreover it is asked: Why did God give these bodily foods [*elementa*] to man, whom he had made immortal? It is answered that that immortality was not perfect, nor such as is hoped for after the general resurrection, namely a necessity of not dying, or an impossibility of dying; but it was such that he was able not to die, and had he not sinned he would not have incurred death. And such an immortality had to be sustained by food until he should be brought to a better state and life.

paras.t: Quærit præterea Beda : Qua utilitate accepit homo dominium super animalia cetera, et ad quos usus, sive ad quæ solatia sunt homini hæc producta ? Respondet, quod quia Deus prævidit hominem peccaturum, fecit illa ad usum ejus futurum, ut essent ei in alimentum, indumentum, et laboris auxilium.
paras.en: Bede asks further: For what use did man receive dominion over the other animals, and for what uses, or for what comforts, were these things produced for man? He answers that since God foresaw that man would sin, he made them for his future use, that they might serve him for food, clothing and help in his labour.

paras.t: Augustinus etiam quærit : Quum homo ad Dei imaginem sit creatus, cur de eo dictum non est, Vidit Deus quod esset bonum, quod tamen de bestiis dictum est ? Respondet : Forsitan ideo, quia præscivit eum statim casurum, nec in imaginis perfectione mansurum. Potest et alia ratio dari, quia videlicet non sufficiebat esse virum solum.
