Propter quod infra habetur : Non est bonum esse hominem solum, faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi.
paras.en: Augustine too asks: Since man was created to the image of God, why was it not said of him, [[1:25|God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]], as was said of the beasts? He answers: Perhaps because he foreknew that he would soon fall and would not remain in the perfection of the image. Another reason can also be given, namely that it was not enough for the man to be alone; for which reason it is said below: [[Gen 2:18|It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself|Non est bonum esse hominem solum, faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi]].

paras.t: Amplius, circa illud, Masculum et feminam creavit eos, recitat Lyra, quod propter verba illa quidam Hebræi dicunt, primum virum ac mulierem, in specie humana esse simul formatos, eorumque corpora sic in lateribus fuisse conjuncta, quod reddebant unum continuum : postea vero divina virtute esse ab invicem separata. Sed tam fatuum dictum satis improbat Lyra : Primo, quoniam manifeste est contra textum sequentis capituli, quo habetur, quod formatis cunctis atque ad Adam productis, non inveniebatur adjutor similis ei ; et quod Deus tunc dixit, Non est bonum hominem esse solum, faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi ; quod item ex costa Adæ ædificavit mulierem, de qua Adam tunc fatebatur : Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea. Secundo, quoniam talis productio viri et feminæ, fuisset opus monstruosum, quemadmodum legitur, quod in confinio Normanniæ et Britanniæ, natæ fuerunt duæ mulieres in corpore uno, ita quod omnia membra superiora usque ad umbilicum erant duplicia, inferiora vero simplicia. Porro quod vere fuerint duæ mulieres, hinc patuit, quod interdum una tristante, alia lætabatur ; et aliquando una dormiente, alia vigilavit ; una quoque mortua fuit ante aliam, amplius quam per annum : unde illa tandem defuncta est ex pondere et fœtore cadaveris prioris defunctæ. In Scholastica vero historia legitur, quod ideo Scriptura pluraliter ait, Masculum et feminam creavit eos, ne putaremus eos factos hermaphroditos.
paras.en: Further, concerning the words [[1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum et feminam creavit eos]], Lyra relates that because of those words certain Hebrews say that the first man and woman were formed together in the human species, and that their bodies were so joined at the sides that they made one continuous whole, but were afterwards separated from each other by divine power. But Lyra rejects so foolish a saying well enough: first, because it is plainly against the text of the following chapter, where it is said that when all things had been formed and brought to Adam, [[Gen 2:20|there was not found a helper like himself|non inveniebatur adjutor similis ei]]; and that God then said, [[Gen 2:18|It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself|Non est bonum hominem esse solum, faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi]]; and again that he built the woman from Adam's rib[[Gen 2:22||]], of whom Adam then confessed: [[Gen 2:23|This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh|Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea]]. Secondly, because such a production of man and woman would have been a monstrous work, as it is read that on the borders of Normandy and Brittany two women were born in one body, so that all the upper members down to the navel were double, but the lower ones single. And that they were truly two women was clear from this, that sometimes when one was sad the other was glad, and sometimes when one slept the other was awake; and one died before the other by more than a year, whence the other at length died from the weight and stench of the corpse of the one that had died first. But in the Scholastic History it is read that Scripture says in the plural, [[1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum et feminam creavit eos]], lest we should think that they were made hermaphrodites.

paras.t: Denique, in testimonium primæ conditionis et subjectionis brutorum sub homine, sæpius contigit, quod aves et bestiæ, serpentes et pisces cesserunt, servierunt et obedierunt hominibus, ac beatissimis martyribus reverentiam, non læsionem, exhibuerunt : quod potissime in novo Testamento sæpissime accidit.
paras.en: Further, in witness of the first condition and of the subjection of the brutes to man, it has often happened that birds and beasts, serpents and fishes, have given way to men, served and obeyed them, and have shown reverence, not injury, to the most blessed martyrs: which happened most often of all in the New Testament.

paras.t: Et factum est ita. Quomodo verum est hoc, quum jam paulo ante legatur Deus dixisse, Crescite et multiplicamini, quod nondum fuerat factum ? Itaque Augustinus refert istud, Et factum est ita, ad id quod immediate prædictum est, Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam, etc., ut sit sensus : Factum est ita, id est, homo cognovit hæc sibi ac aliis esse concessa in cibum. Potest quoque absolute referri ad illos actus, de quibus jam dictum est : Benedixitque eis, et dixit Deus : Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam.
paras.en: [[1:30|And it was so done|Et factum est ita]]. How is this true, when it has been read a little before that God said, [[1:28|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]], which had not yet been done? So Augustine refers this, [[1:30|And it was so done|Et factum est ita]], to what was said immediately before, [[1:29|Behold I have given you every herb|Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam]], etc., so that the sense is: [[1:30|it was so done|Factum est ita]], that is, man knew that these things had been granted to him and to the others for food. It can also be referred simply to those acts of which it has already been said: [[1:28|And God blessed them|Benedixitque eis]], and [[1:29|God said: Behold I have given you every herb|dixit Deus : Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam]].

paras.t: Viditque Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona. Omnia namque simul accepta, erant præcipue bona, ita quod unum auxit bonitatem et utilitatem alterius, et mutuo se ornabant ; universaque simul accepta, optima apparebant, utpote sapientissime coordinata, et invicem deservientia, quemadmodum in exercitu unus confortatur ac adjuvatur ab alio, et universi se invicem ornant, protegunt, et constipant. Ordo quippe (ut divinus Dionysius testatur) est optimum quid in rebus. Unde ex coordinatione specierum, causarum et entium universi ad primum principium, major et admirabilis pulchritudo consurgit, quemadmodum in corpore naturali partes et membra invicem se perornant, bonificant, atque perficiunt. Vidit itaque Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona, hoc est, valde complacuerunt ei. Unde undecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Plato dixit Deum gaudio elatum, mundi universitate perfecta : per quod ostendit opus jam factum et conditum, placuisse suo Artifici. Hunc quoque Psalmista : Lætabitur Deus in operibus suis. Et factum est vespere et mane dies sextus, juxta expositionem præhabitam.
paras.en: [[1:31|And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good|Viditque Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona]]. For all things taken together were especially good, so that one increased the goodness and usefulness of another, and they adorned one another; and all of them taken together appeared best, being most wisely ordered together and serving one another, as in an army one is strengthened and helped by another, and all adorn, protect and close ranks about one another. For order (as the divine Dionysius testifies) is the best thing in things. Hence from the ordering of the species, causes and beings of the universe together toward the first principle there arises a greater and wonderful beauty, as in a natural body the parts and members adorn, better and perfect one another. So [[1:31|God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good|Vidit itaque Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona]], that is, they greatly pleased him. Hence Augustine says in the eleventh book of The City of God: Plato said that God was transported with joy when the whole of the world was completed; by which he shows that the work, now made and established, pleased its Maker. So too the Psalmist: [[Ps 103:31|the Lord shall rejoice in his works|Lætabitur Deus in operibus suis]] [the numerals of the margin's reference cannot be read; the verse is Ps 103:31, where the Vulgate has *Dominus*, "the Lord", for Denis's *Deus*]. [[1:31|And the evening and morning were the sixth day|Et factum est vespere et mane dies sextus]], according to the exposition given earlier.

1.title: De expositione hujus capituli secundum Augustinum
1.title_en: On the exposition of this chapter according to Augustine

paras.t: Sicut aliquoties prætactum est, beatus Augustinus specialem habuit considerationem circa primam rerum productionem, et expositionem sex vel septem dierum, de quibus in exordio hujus capituli agitur : accipit enim dies illos non pro consuetis cursibus, seu spatiis temporis, nec prout temporalem important successionem, sed prout dicunt cognitionem mentis angelicæ, relatam seu comparatam ad sex genera rerum, in exordio mundi factarum.
paras.en: As has been touched on several times already, blessed Augustine had a view of his own concerning the first production of things and the exposition of the six or seven days spoken of at the beginning of this chapter. For he takes those days not as the usual courses or spaces of time, nor as implying a succession in time, but as meaning the knowledge of the angelic mind, referred or compared to the six kinds of things made at the beginning of the world.

paras.t: Porro cognitio illa angelorum est duplex. Una, qua cognoscunt res in proprio genere : et hæc appellatur cognitio vespertina, quoniam omnis creatura per comparationem ad Deum, qui substantialiter lux est, est quasi caligo. Cognitio quoque rerum in se ipsis seu proprio genere, est quasi tenebra, respectu cognitionis qua cognoscuntur in Verbo æterno, seu immediate in Deo. Unde cognitio qua cognoscunt angeli res creatas in Verbo, dicitur matutina. Sicque exponit quod dicitur. Factum est vespere et mane dies unus, seu secundus aut tertius, in quantum idem opus alicujus diei cognoverunt in proprio genere, quod est in vespere, atque in Verbo matutina cognitione, quæ dicitur mane.
paras.en: Now this knowledge of the angels is twofold. One is that by which they know things in their own kind; and this is called evening knowledge, since every creature, compared with God, who is light by His very substance, is as it were a mist. The knowledge of things in themselves, or in their own kind, is also as it were darkness, compared with the knowledge by which they are known in the eternal Word, that is, immediately in God. Hence the knowledge by which the angels know created things in the Word is called morning knowledge. And so he expounds what is said: [[1:5|and there was evening and morning one day|Factum est vespere et mane dies unus]], or [[1:8|the second day|secundus]], or [[1:13|the third day|tertius]]: inasmuch as they knew the same work of any day in its own kind, which is in the evening, and in the Word by morning knowledge, which is called morning.

paras.t: Denique, ut istud plenius intelligatur, advertendum quod Thomas scribit super secundum, distinctione 12, dicens : Secundum Augustinum, illi sex dies sunt unus dies, simul præsentatus seu applicatus sex distinctionibus rerum secundum quas numeratur, quemadmodum unum Verbum est in Deo, per quod facta sunt omnia, scilicet Filius Patris, quamvis frequenter legatur, dixit Deus. Et sicut opera illa salvantur, et quodammodo manent in cunctis operibus sequentibus, quæ propagantur ex eis operatione naturæ, ita sex dies illi manent in tota temporis successione.
paras.en: Further, that this may be more fully understood, note what Thomas writes on the second book [of Peter Lombard's Sentences], distinction 12, saying: According to Augustine those six days are one day, presented, or applied, at once to the six distinctions of things according to which it is numbered; just as there is one Word in God, by whom all things were made[[John 1:3||]], namely the Son of the Father, although we often read, [[1:3|God said|dixit Deus]]. And just as those works are preserved, and in a manner remain, in all the works that follow, which are propagated from them by the operation of nature, so those six days remain in the whole succession of time.

paras.t: Quomodo autem hoc sit, videndum est. Natura angelica, intellectualis est et lux est ; et si proprie lux est, illustratio ejus dicitur proprie dies. Angelica autem natura in principio conditionis rerum, cognitionem earum accepit : et ita lux mentis angelicæ, præsentabatur seu applicabatur quodammodo rebus creatis, in quantum cognoscebantur ab ea. Hinc ipsa cognitio rerum in mente angelica, dicitur dies : atque secundum diversa genera ac ordinem entium cognitorum, distinguuntur et ordinantur dies : ut primus dies accipiatur penes formationem spiritualis creaturæ in Verbo, secundus dies penes formationem corporalis creaturæ, quantum ad superiorem partem quæ firmamentum vocatur ; sicque de reliquis diebus, juxta comparationem ad opera cæterorum dierum. Sed quia creatura ex eo quod ex nihilo est, tenebras possibilitatis et imperfectionis habet admixtas ; ideo cognitio qua creatura cognoscitur a mente creata, tenebris est permixta. Potest autem ab angelo cognosci dupliciter : puta in Verbo secundum quod exit ab arte divina. Et hæc ejus cognitio dicitur matutina. Nam sicut mane finis est tenebrarum, et principium lucis, ita creatura sumit a Verbo principium sui esse ac luminis, post suum non esse, seu postquam prius non fuerat. Cognoscitur etiam prout est in propria natura subsistens : et talis cognitio dicitur vespertina, propter hoc, quod sicut vespera est terminus lucis, et tendit ad noctem, sic creatura in se subsistens, est terminus operationis Verbi, utpote facta per Verbum, et de se in defectibilitatis tenebras tendens, nisi conservetur a Verbo. Nihilo minus ista cognitio dicitur dies, in comparatione ad ignorantiam, quæ omnino est tenebra, quemadmodum præsens vita justorum, caliginosa est respectu gloriæ Beatorum, quæ tamen lux est respectu vitæ pravorum.
paras.en: But how this is so must be seen. The angelic nature is intellectual and is light; and if it is light in the proper sense, its illumination is properly called day. Now the angelic nature, at the beginning of the founding of things, received the knowledge of them; and so the light of the angelic mind was in a manner presented or applied to created things, inasmuch as they were known by it. Hence the very knowledge of things in the angelic mind is called day; and the days are distinguished and ordered according to the different kinds and the order of the beings known: so that the first day is taken with respect to the formation of the spiritual creature in the Word, the second day with respect to the formation of the bodily creature as to its upper part, which is called the firmament; and so with the remaining days, according to their relation to the works of the other days. But because the creature, from the very fact that it is from nothing, has the darkness of potentiality [*possibilitas*: the creature's capacity to be or not to be, as against God, who is pure act] and of imperfection mixed in it, therefore the knowledge by which the creature is known by a created mind is mingled with darkness. Now it can be known by an angel in two ways: namely in the Word, as it goes forth from the divine art; and this knowledge of it is called morning knowledge. For as the morning is the end of darkness and the beginning of light, so the creature takes from the Word the beginning of its being and of its light after its not-being, that is, after it had not been before. It is known also as it subsists in its own nature; and such knowledge is called evening knowledge, because, as the evening is the end of light and tends toward night, so the creature subsisting in itself is the end of the Word's working, as being made through the Word, and of itself tending into the darkness of failing [that is, of falling back into nothing], unless it be preserved by the Word. Nonetheless this knowledge is called day in comparison with ignorance, which is utter darkness; just as the present life of the just is dim in respect of the glory of the Blessed, and yet is light in respect of the life of the wicked.

paras.t: Insuper sustinentes cum Augustino, quod omnia sint simul creata, dicere possunt, quod dies præfati sumuntur penes illustrationem lucis corporalis, ita tamen, quod ordo dierum attendatur penes distinctionem ordinemque eorum, in quæ lux illa corporalis refulsit. Sicut enim angeli acceperunt cognitionem omnium naturalium rerum, ita lux corporalis super omnia corporalia se diffundit : ideo sicut Augustinus distinguit sex dies penes præsentationem lucis spiritualis primo die factæ, videlicet mentis angelicæ, relatam ad sex genera rerum : ita secundum præsentationem lucis corporalis ad sex genera rerum, sive ad opera sex dierum, possunt eodem modo sex dies distingui absque temporis distinctione et successione. Hæc Thomas in scripto secundi, et concordat secum Albertus in libro de Coæquævis, ac alibi.
paras.en: Moreover, those who hold with Augustine that all things were created at once can say that the said days are taken with respect to the shining of bodily light, yet so that the order of the days is reckoned by the distinction and order of the things upon which that bodily light shone. For as the angels received the knowledge of all natural things, so bodily light spreads itself over all bodily things. Therefore, as Augustine distinguishes the six days by the presenting of the spiritual light made on the first day, namely the angelic mind, referred to six kinds of things, so in the same way six days can be distinguished by the presenting of bodily light to six kinds of things, that is, to the works of the six days, without any distinction or succession of time. So far Thomas, in his writing on the second book; and Albert agrees with him in the book On the Coaevals [*De coaequaevis*: on the things created together at the beginning, such as matter, time, the empyrean heaven and the angels], and elsewhere.

paras.t: Præterea in prima parte, quæstione 74. […] ait : Augustinus hos septem dies, de quibus in Genesi fertur, dicit esse unam diem, rebus septempliciter præsentatam, quia per diem intelligitur angelicæ mentis cognitio, ut prima dies sit cognitio primi operis divini, seu operis primæ diei, secunda dies cognitio secundi operis, sicque deinceps. Et dicitur unumquodque opus factum in aliquo die, quia nil fit in rerum natura, quod non innotescat menti angelicæ per impressionem illuminationis divinæ. Ex his videtur Thomas innuere, quod secundum Augustinum opera sex dierum, sint distincte atque realiter simul facta, præsertim quum dicat in scripto secundi : In distinctione rerum Augustinus vult attendendum esse ordinem naturæ et doctrinæ, non temporis : naturæ, sicut sonus præcedit cantum ; et ita quæ naturaliter sunt priora, prius facta dicuntur, ut terra prius quam animalia, et aqua prius quam pisces. Et iterum dicit, declarando, quomodo dies illi possint esse una dies, et partes diei secundum lucem spiritualem, non secundum diversa cognita, sed secundum diversos modos cognitionis ejusdem rei. Et sicut dies tales non sunt successivi, quoniam angelus diversa rerum genera simul intuetur in Verbo; ita nec partes diei unius, quoniam simul videt.
paras.en: Again, in the First Part [of the Summa], question 74, […] he says: Augustine says that these seven days of which Genesis tells are one day, presented to things in seven ways; for by day is understood the knowledge of the angelic mind, so that the first day is the knowledge of the first divine work, that is, of the work of the first day, the second day the knowledge of the second work, and so on. And each work is said to be made on some day because nothing is made in the nature of things that does not become known to the angelic mind through the impression of the divine illumination. From these words Thomas seems to hint that according to Augustine the works of the six days were made distinctly and really at once; especially since he says in his writing on the second book: In the distinction of things Augustine would have us look to the order of nature and of teaching, not of time: of nature, as sound comes before song; and so the things that are naturally prior are said to have been made first, as the earth before the animals and the water before the fishes. And again he says, explaining how those days can be one day, and how there can be parts of the day [that is, its evening and morning], according to the spiritual light: not according to different things known, but according to different modes of knowing the same thing. And as such days are not successive, since the angel beholds the different kinds of things at once in the Word, so neither are the parts of one day, since he sees them at once.

paras.t: Insuper Albertus libro de Coæquævis apertissime scribit, quod secundum Augustinum omnia opera sex dierum, sint realiter ac distincte, seu actualiter et complete simul producta in uno instanti atque eodem momento. Primo quippe allegat sanctum Augustinum, dicentem : Omnia simul in uno momento sunt facta in materia, et distincta in forma et loco atque ornatu propriis speciebus. Deinde responsionem adjungit : Dicendum, quod Augustinus revera ponit omnia simul creata in materia et forma, quæ natura per se non potest producere motu superiorum et commixtione elementorum ; ideo a principio factum est cœlum cum stellis, terra cum animalibus, aqua cum natatilibus atque volucribus. Breviterque dicendo, omnia in speciebus suis simul educta sunt, quæ per virtutem simplicem motus cœli, et per virtutem stellarum ex commixtione elementorum, sine alio motore educi non poterant, ut homo, leo, et consimilia, quæ præter virtutem cœli et elementorum, requirunt specialem motorem ad suam generationem.
paras.en: Moreover Albert, in the book On the Coaevals, writes most plainly that according to Augustine all the works of the six days were produced really and distinctly, that is, actually and completely, at once, in one instant and in the same moment. For first he cites Saint Augustine, saying: All things were made at once in one moment in their matter, and distinguished in form and place and adornment by their proper species. Then he adds the answer: It must be said that Augustine does indeed hold that all those things were created at once in matter and form which nature cannot produce of itself by the motion of the higher bodies and the mixing of the elements; so from the beginning the heaven was made with the stars, the earth with the animals, the water with the swimming things and the birds. And to put it briefly, all those things were brought forth at once in their species which could not be brought forth, without another mover, by the simple power of the motion of the heaven and by the power of the stars from the mixing of the elements: such as man, the lion and the like, which beyond the power of the heaven and the elements require a special mover for their generation.

paras.t: Hinc undecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Quales sint dies illi primi, valde difficile aut etiam impossibile nobis est cogitare : quanto magis dicere ? Videmus quippe istos dies qui nunc sunt, non habere vesperam, nisi ex solis occasu ; nec mane, nisi ex solis ortu. Illorum autem dierum tres primi, sine sole peracti sunt, quum sol quinto die factus legatur.
paras.en: Hence Augustine speaks thus in the eleventh book of The City of God: What those first days were like is very hard, or even impossible, for us to think: how much more to say! For we see that these days which are now have no evening but from the setting of the sun, nor morning but from its rising. But the first three of those days were passed without the sun, since the sun is read to have been made on the fifth day [so printed; Augustine has *quarto*, the fourth day, as in vv. 14–19].

paras.t: Denique Apostolus ait : Omnes vos filii lucis estis et filii diei ; non sumus noctis neque tenebrarum. Si tamen aliquatenus valeamus intelligere congruenter mane et vesperam hujus diei, quoniam scientia creaturæ, comparatione scientiæ Creatoris, vesperascit ; lucescit autem et mane fit, quum et ipsa refertur ad laudem dilectionemque Creatoris ; nec in noctem mergitur, ubi Creator non relinquitur creaturæ amore. Quumque dies illos Scriptura dinumeraret ex ordine, nunquam interposuit nomen noctis. Cognitio namque creaturæ in se ipsa, est decoloratior, quam quum sub Dei sapientia cognoscitur, velut in arte qua facta est : ideo congruentius dici potest vespera, quam nox : quæ tamen dum refertur ad laudandum amandumque Creatorem, recurrit in mane ; et quum hoc facit in cognitione sui ipsius, dies unus est : dum in cognitione firmamenti, dies secundus ; dum in cognitione terræ et maris et omnium quæ radicibus continuata sunt terræ, dies tertius ; dum in cognitione luminarium et stellarum, dies quartus ; dum in cognitione omnium animalium natantium et volantium, quæ sunt ex aquis, dies quintus ; dum in cognitione omnium animalium terrenorum ac hominis, dies sextus. Porro quum die septimo requiescit Deus ab omnibus operibus suis, requies Dei significat requiem eorum, qui requiescunt in eo, et quos ipse requiescere facit. Hoc namque significatum est in populo veteris Testamenti sabbati vacatione et legis præcepto.
paras.en: Lastly the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:5|all you are the children of light and children of the day: we are not of the night nor of darkness|Omnes vos filii lucis estis et filii diei ; non sumus noctis neque tenebrarum]] [the margin reference here is unreadable; the words are 1 Thess 5:5]. If, however, we can in some measure fittingly understand the morning and evening of this day: since the knowledge of the creature, compared with the knowledge of the Creator, grows toward evening; but it dawns and becomes morning when it too is referred to the praise and love of the Creator; nor does it sink into night, where the Creator is not forsaken for love of the creature. And when Scripture numbered those days in order, it nowhere put in the name of night. For the knowledge of the creature in itself is more faded than when it is known in the wisdom of God, as in the art by which it was made; therefore it can more fittingly be called evening than night; and yet, when it is referred to the praise and love of the Creator, it returns into morning. And when it does this in the knowledge of itself, it is one day; in the knowledge of the firmament, the second day; in the knowledge of the earth and the sea and of all things that are joined to the earth by roots, the third day; in the knowledge of the lights and the stars, the fourth day; in the knowledge of all the animals that swim and fly, which are from the waters, the fifth day; in the knowledge of all the land animals and of man, the sixth day. Further, when God rests on the seventh day from all His works, the rest of God signifies the rest of those who rest in Him, and whom He makes to rest. For this was signified in the people of the Old Testament by the keeping of the sabbath and the precept of the law.

paras.t: At ubi Scripturæ loquuntur de mundi creatione, non dicitur satis evidenter, utrum aut quo modo seu ordine creati sint angeli ; sed si prætermissi non sunt, significati sunt nomine cœli, quum dictum est, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Vel potius nomine lucis, de qua legitur, Dixit Deus : Fiat lux. Quod autem prætermissi non sunt, hinc puto, quoniam scriptum est, Deum requievisse die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis quæ fecit, quum liber Genesis ita exorsus est, In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram, ita ut ante nil videatur fecisse. Quum ergo a cœlo et terra inceperit, et terra invisibilis et incomposita fuerit, luce quoque nondum facta tenebræ fuerint super faciem abyssi, id est super quamdam indistinctam confusionem terræ et aquæ, deinde si omnia disposita sunt, quæ per sex dies facta narrantur : quomodo angeli prætermitterentur, quasi non essent in operibus Dei, a quibus die septimo requievit ? Si igitur angeli pertinent ad opera Dei horum dierum, ipsi sunt lux quæ dies vocata est : ad cujus diei unitatem commendandam, non est dictum, dies primus, sed, dies unus. Nec alius est dies secundus, vel tertius, aut ceteri ; sed idem unus dies repetitus est, ad implendum senarium aut septenarium numerum, utpote propter senarium operum, et septenarium quietis diei. Quum enim dixit Deus, Fiat lux, et facta est lux. Si in hac luce recte intelligitur angelorum creatio, facti sunt utique participes lucis æternæ, quæ est incommutabilis sapientia et unigenitus Filius Dei, ut ea luce illuminati, qua et creati, sint et ipsi lux, non in se, sed in Deo ; nec prius tempore angeli tenebræ erant, sed simul ut facti sunt, lux facti sunt, ut sapienter beateque viverent. Illi equidem angeli sancti non per verba discunt, sed per ipsam incommutabilis veritatis præsentiam. Melius enim sciunt creaturam in sapientia Dei quam in se ipsa ; imo et se ipsos melius in sapientia et Verbo Dei, quam in se ipsis. Verumtamen et in se ipsis cognoscunt se, quoniam facti sunt. In Deo ergo cognoscunt se tanquam diurna cognitione, in se ipsis vero tanquam notitia vespertina.
paras.en: But where the Scriptures speak of the creation of the world, it is not said clearly enough whether, or in what way or order, the angels were created; but if they were not passed over, they are signified by the name of heaven, where it is said, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]; or rather by the name of light, of which we read, [[1:3|God said: Be light made|Dixit Deus : Fiat lux]]. That they were not passed over I gather from this: it is written that God [[Gen 2:2|rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done|requievisse die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis quæ fecit]], while the book of Genesis begins thus, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram]], so that He seems to have made nothing before. Since, then, He began from heaven and earth, and [[1:2|the earth was void and empty|terra invisibilis et incomposita]] [Augustine's older Latin version: *invisible and unformed*], and, light not yet being made, [[1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|tenebræ fuerint super faciem abyssi]], that is, upon a certain undistinguished confusion of earth and water; and since after that all the things were set in order which are told as made through six days: how should the angels have been passed over, as if they were not among the works of God from which He rested on the seventh day? If, then, the angels belong to the works of God of these days, they are the light which was called Day; and to commend the oneness of this day it is not said, the first day, but [[1:5|one day|dies unus]]. Nor is the second day, or the third, or the rest, another day; but the same one day was repeated to fill up the number six or seven: that is, on account of the six of the works and the seven of the day of rest. For God said, [[1:3|Be light made. And light was made|Fiat lux, et facta est lux]]: if by this light the creation of the angels is rightly understood, they were surely made partakers of the eternal light, which is the unchangeable Wisdom and only-begotten Son of God, so that, enlightened by the light by which they were also created, they too might be light, not in themselves but in God; nor were the angels darkness earlier in time, but as soon as they were made they were made light, so as to live wisely and blessedly. Those holy angels, indeed, learn not through words but through the very presence of the unchangeable Truth. For they know the creature better in the wisdom of God than in itself; indeed they know even themselves better in the wisdom and Word of God than in themselves. Yet they also know themselves in themselves, since they were made. In God, therefore, they know themselves as by daytime knowledge, but in themselves as by evening knowledge.

paras.t: Multum enim differt, an aliquid cognoscatur ea ratione, qua factum est, an in se ipso. Sicque opera sex dierum aliter cognoscuntur ab angelis sanctis in Deo, aliter in se ipsis : quæ opera quum ad laudem venerationemque Creatoris referuntur, tanquam mane lucescit in mentibus contemplantium. Hæc autem opera, propter senarii numeri perfectionem, facta narrantur sex diebus, hoc est eodem die sexies repetito : quoniam per senarium numerum significata est perfectio operum. Numerus enim senarius primus completur, hoc est, sexta parte sui, et tertia atque dimidia, quæ sunt unum et duo ac tria : quæ in summam ducta, sex fiunt. In quo numero perfecit Deus opera sua. Hinc ratio numerorum spernenda non est, qui in multis Scripturarum locis quam magni existimentur, constat intuentibus diligenter, nec frustra in laudibus Dei dictum est, Omnia in mensura et numero et pondere disposuisti. Porro, in septimo die, hoc est eodem die septies repetito, qui etiam numerus alia ratione perfectus est, Dei requies commendatur. In qua ut primo sanctificatio sonat, ita Deus noluit istum diem in ullis suis sanctificare operibus, sed in requie sua, quæ nequaquam vesperam habet, quum non sit res creata. De septenarii quoque numeri perfectione plurima dici possent, de quo sufficiat dicere, quod ternarius est primus numerus totus impar, quaternarius autem totus par, ex quibus duobus septenarius constat, idcirco pro universitate multoties ponitur. Hæc omnia sumpta sunt ex diversis capitulis undecimi libri de Civitate Dei.
paras.en: For it makes a great difference whether a thing is known in the reason by which it was made, or in itself. And so the works of the six days are known by the holy angels in one way in God and in another way in themselves; and when these works are referred to the praise and worship of the Creator, it is as though morning dawns in the minds of those who contemplate them. Now these works are told as made in six days, that is, in the same day six times repeated, on account of the perfection of the number six; for by the number six the perfection of the works is signified. For six is the first number that is made up of its own parts, that is, of its sixth, its third and its half, which are one, two and three, and these added together make six [six is thus a "perfect number", equal to the sum of its divisors]. In this number God perfected His works. Hence the reckoning of numbers is not to be despised: how highly they are esteemed in many places of the Scriptures is plain to those who look carefully; and not in vain was it said in the praises of God, [[Wis 11:21|thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight|Omnia in mensura et numero et pondere disposuisti]]. Further, in the seventh day, that is, in the same day seven times repeated, which number is also perfect for another reason, the rest of God is commended. In this rest, as sanctification is first spoken of [in Gen 2:3, where God sanctified the seventh day], so God willed to sanctify this day not in any of His works but in His rest, which has no evening at all, since it is not a created thing. Of the perfection of the number seven, too, a great deal could be said; let it suffice to say of it that three is the first number wholly odd, and four the first wholly even, and seven is made of these two; and therefore it is often put for the whole. All this is taken from various chapters of the eleventh book of The City of God.

paras.t: Ex quibus patere potest intentio Augustini, et qualiter primum libri Genesis capitulum intelligat : nempe quum dicitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram ; per cœlum intelligit naturam angelicam, seu angelos universos secundum se consideratos, et quasi informes, hoc est ut nondum ad Creatorem conversos. Per terram vero, intelligit materiam primam omnino informem, ab omni forma abstractam, non quod unquam fuerit sic abstracta realiter aut aliquo tempore ante omnem formam, sed solum prioritate naturæ, sicut sonus est prior voce, et vox verbo. Eamdem demum materiam dicit significatam nomine abyssi et aquæ. Et dicit quod Moyses rudi populo loquens expressit materiam illam informem per nomina rerum […] notarum.
paras.en: From these passages Augustine's mind can be seen, and how he understands the first chapter of the book of Genesis: namely, when it is said, [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], by heaven he understands the angelic nature, that is, all the angels considered in themselves and as it were unformed, that is, not yet turned to the Creator. But by earth he understands prime matter [matter considered apart from every form, pure potentiality], wholly unformed and abstracted from every form: not that it was ever really so abstracted, or at any time before all form, but only by priority of nature, as sound is prior to the voice, and the voice to the word. Lastly he says that the same matter is signified by the name of the deep and of the water. And he says that Moses, speaking to an unlearned people, expressed that unformed matter by the names of […] known things.

paras.t: Materiæ etenim competit triplex proprietas. Prima est retinere, et ita designatur per terram. Secunda est recipere, et ita designatur per aquam. Tertia est carere omni perfectione formali et actuali, et ita vocatur abyssus, ab a, quod est sine, et basis, quasi sine base aut fundamento subsistendi. Vel ab a et byssus, quod est genus candidissimi lini, quasi sine candore et perfectione. Hæc quoque materia erat in se inanis, vacua, tenebrosa. Nunquam tamen realiter exstitit sine luce, secundum Augustinum, qui dicit solem in exordio perfecte productum.
paras.en: For a threefold property belongs to matter. The first is to retain, and so it is designated by earth. The second is to receive, and so it is designated by water. The third is to lack all formal and actual perfection, and so it is called abyss [*abyssus*, the Douay-Rheims "deep"], from *a*, which means without, and *basis*, as being without base or foundation on which to subsist; or from *a* and *byssus*, which is a kind of very white linen, as being without whiteness and perfection. This matter, too, was in itself void, empty and dark. Yet according to Augustine it never really existed without light, for he says that the sun was produced complete at the beginning.

paras.t: Deinde quum dicitur, Fiat lux : per lucis productionem, intelligit angelorum formationem, et conversionem ad Creatorem, ut ante expositum est.
paras.en: Then, when it is said, [[1:3|Be light made|Fiat lux]], by the production of light he understands the forming of the angels and their turning to the Creator, as was explained above.

paras.t: Præterea, dum firmamentum scribitur secunda die factum, non intelligitur alia dies secundum istam positionem, quum omnia opera sex dierum simul facta existimet, et omnes dies illi sint unus dies, juxta sensum nunc introductum. Præterea, dum aqua legitur tertia die congregata, apparuisseque arida, non est intelligendum secundum hanc viam, quod aqua unquam operuit totam terram, aut tunc ab elemento terræ remota sit, sed quod tunc informi materiæ impressa est forma substantialis aquæ, per quam aqua suum naturalem motum sortitur ; quod item alteri parti ejusdem materiæ impressa est forma substantialis terræ, per quam competit terræ, esse et videri quod est. Simili modo exponit de firmamento, non quod informitas formationem secundum tempus præcessit.
paras.en: Further, when the firmament is written to have been made on the second day, no other day is understood on this position, since he holds that all the works of the six days were made at once, and that all those days are one day, in the sense now set out. Further, when the water is read to have been gathered together on the third day, and the dry land to have appeared, it is not to be understood, on this way of reading, that the water ever covered the whole earth, or was then taken away from the element of earth; but that the substantial form of water was then impressed on the unformed matter, by which water obtains its natural motion; and likewise that the substantial form of earth was impressed on another part of the same matter, by which it belongs to earth to be, and to be seen to be, what it is. He expounds the firmament in the same way: not that unformedness went before formation in time.

paras.t: Insuper quum tertio die legitur dictum : Producat terra herbam, etc., exponit Augustinus causaliter, ita quod tunc data est terræ virtus propagandi similia ex similibus quum prima die productæ sint plantæ, sicut et aliæ species rerum. Nam et infra habetur : Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ in die quando creata sunt, in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram, et omne virgultum antequam oriretur in terra. Nihilo minus secundum Augustinum, totum istud simul peractum est, quum tertius dies non sit posterior primo per successionem.
paras.en: Moreover, when we read that on the third day it was said, [[1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Producat terra herbam]], etc., Augustine expounds it causally [that is, of the causal or seminal powers then put into things, not of the things themselves coming to be then]: so that the earth was then given the power of propagating like from like, whereas the plants were produced on the first day, as were the other species of things too. For below it is also said: [[Gen 2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth, when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ in die quando creata sunt, in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram]], [[Gen 2:5|every plant of the field before it sprung up in the earth|et omne virgultum antequam oriretur in terra]] [the margin reference here is unreadable; the words are Gen 2:4–5]. Nonetheless, according to Augustine, all this was done at once, since the third day is not later than the first by succession.

paras.t: Deinde quum luminaria et sidera facta narrantur quarto die, intelligit hoc, quantum ad relationem angelicæ cognitionis ad hoc quartum genus operis Dei, quod tamen prima die distincte productum est.
paras.en: Then, when the lights and the stars are told as made on the fourth day, he understands this as to the relation of the angelic knowledge to this fourth kind of God's work, which was nonetheless produced distinctly on the first day.

paras.t: Rursus, dum quinto die pisces et aves facti referuntur ex aqua, exponit causaliter, sicut de productione plantarum ex terra, ita quod juxta Augustinum, quarta die data est aquæ virtus causalis ad productionem præfatam, quod tamen realiter factum est simul secundum eum. Et idem dicendum de opere sextæ diei.
paras.en: Again, when the fishes and birds are related to have been made from the water on the fifth day, he expounds it causally, as with the production of the plants from the earth: so that according to Augustine the causal power for that production was given to the water on the fourth day [so printed; the fifth day seems to be meant], which nonetheless, according to him, was really done at once. And the same must be said of the work of the sixth day.

paras.t: Si autem quis capere nequeat ista, audiat Augustinum super Genesim, sic loquentem : Quum audis tunc omnia facta esse simul, illam senariam repetitionem sine intervallis temporum factam apprehende, si potes ; si vero non potes, relinque hæc apprehendenda eis qui possunt, tu autem profice cum Scriptura, tuæ infirmitati deserviente, atque materno incessu tecum tardius ambulante, quæ sic loquitur, ut superbos altitudine sua irrideat, profunditate sua attentos perterreat, veritate magnos pascat, affabilitate parvos enutriat. Unde secundum Gregorium, Scriptura sacra est fluvius, in quo peditat agnus, natatque elephas.
paras.en: But if anyone cannot take this in, let him hear Augustine on Genesis, speaking thus: When you hear that all things were then made at once, grasp, if you can, that sixfold repetition as made without intervals of time; but if you cannot, leave these things to be grasped by those who can, and do you go forward with the Scripture, which stoops to your weakness and walks more slowly with you at a mother's pace; which speaks so as to mock the proud by its height, to terrify the attentive by its depth, to feed the great with its truth, and to nourish the little ones with its kindliness. Hence, according to Gregory, Holy Scripture is a river in which a lamb may wade and an elephant swim.

paras.t: Verumtamen huic expositioni Augustini non immoror, quoniam propter motiva septimo articulo tacta, ei consentiendum non reor, sed sicut Augustinus multum sobrie, et absque omni incauta assertione ipsam depromsit, sic reverenter tractanda est, non indecenter ab aliquo respuenda ; præsertim quia perutilis est ad defendendum Scripturam ab irrisione perfidorum, in propriis oculis sapientum, quasi sensum Dei cognoscant, quum propriæ præsumptionis excæcati sint tenebris.
paras.en: Still, I do not dwell on this exposition of Augustine, since for the reasons touched on in the seventh article I do not think it is to be agreed with; but as Augustine set it forth very soberly and without any rash assertion, so it is to be treated with reverence, and not unbecomingly rejected by anyone; especially because it is very useful for defending Scripture from the mockery of unbelievers who are wise in their own eyes [the Latin *sapientum* (that is, *sapientium*) seems to go with *perfidorum*; a word such as *qui sunt* may have dropped out before it, but the sense is the same], as though they knew the mind of God, when they are blinded by the darkness of their own presumption.

1.title: De spirituali ac mystica hujus capituli expositione.
1.title_en: On the spiritual and mystical exposition of this chapter.

paras.t: Scriptura sacra fecundissima est, et multiplicem parit sensum; atque historice gesta, spiritualem continent intellectum. Quemadmodum ergo Creator in principio, hoc est in unico Verbo suo, et in exordio sæculorum fecit cœlum et terram, sic in principio fecit angelos electos et sanctos qui designantur per cœlum, et angelos malos qui designantur per terram, quia a summo bono aversi, ad vanitatem ac vilia sunt conversi, et meruerunt sub terra recludi. Unde et Jeremias loquitur Deo: Recedentes a te, in terram scribentur. Et quamvis Deus non fecerit eos malos, sed propria voluntate aversi sint, attamen fecit eos, quantum ad id quod substantialiter sunt. Itaque sicut Deus in principio simul creavit summa et infima, cœlestia et terrena, spiritualia et corporalia: ita in principio simul condidit prædestinatos atque præscitos, electos ac reprobos, vasa misericordiæ, vasaque iræ. Insuper, ab exordio primæ ætatis mundi, creavit homines quosdam electos, spirituales ac virtuosos, qui designantur per cœlum; homines quoque carnales ac reprobos, qui exprimuntur per terram. Ab initio etenim, boni et mali cœperunt esse permixti. Rursus, quemadmodum Deus creavit species universi, videlicet angelos, cœlestia corpora, elementa et mixta, in multiplici varietate ac ordine naturalium perfectionum; ita in angelis primo, deinde in hominibus posuit supernaturalia dona gratiæ ac virtutum, in multiformi gradu, distinctione, et ordine imperscrutabili.
paras.en: Holy Scripture is most fruitful and brings forth a manifold sense; and things done in history contain a spiritual meaning. As, then, the Creator in [[1:1|the beginning|principio]], that is, in his only Word, and at the outset of the ages, made [[1:1|heaven, and earth|cœlum et terram]], so in the beginning he made the elect and holy angels, who are signified by heaven, and the wicked angels, who are signified by earth, because, turned away from the highest good, they were turned to vanity and vile things, and deserved to be shut up beneath the earth. Whence Jeremias too says to God: [[Jer 17:13|they that depart from thee, shall be written in the earth|Recedentes a te, in terram scribentur]]. And although God did not make them wicked, but they turned away by their own will, yet he made them as to what they are in substance. So, as God in the beginning created together the highest things and the lowest, the heavenly and the earthly, the spiritual and the bodily, so in the beginning he founded together the predestined and the foreknown [that is, those foreknown to be lost], the elect and the reprobate, [[Rom 9:23|vessels of mercy|vasa misericordiæ]], and [[Rom 9:22|vessels of wrath|vasaque iræ]]. Moreover, from the outset of the first age of the world he created certain elect men, spiritual and virtuous, who are signified by heaven, and also carnal and reprobate men, who are expressed by earth. For from the beginning the good and the wicked began to be mingled together. Again, as God created the species of the universe, namely the angels, the heavenly bodies, the elements and the compounds, in a manifold variety and order of natural perfections, so, first in the angels and then in men, he placed the supernatural gifts of grace and of the virtues, in manifold degree, distinction, and an unsearchable order.

paras.t: Terra autem erat inanis et vacua. Terra ista, mystice est homo terrenus vel carnalis, qui sibi ipsi relictus, et secundum se consideratus, vanus, deformis, et vacuus est, utpote ornatu virtutum privatus, et spiritualibus gratiis destitutus. Propter quod dixit Christifera Virgo: Divites dimisit inanes. Sapiens quoque: Vani sunt omnes quibus non subest scientia Dei. Et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi: hoc est, ignorantiarum et vitiorum caligo operuit corda humana, quousque Deus ea illuminavit, imo usque ad Christi adventum et evangelicæ legis promulgationem, tenebræ pro maxima parte dominabantur hominibus. Propter quod in Actibus loquitur Paulus: Tempora prioris ignorantiæ despiciens Deus, nunc annuntiat hominibus, ut omnes ubique pœnitentiam agant.
paras.en: [[1:2|And the earth was void and empty|Terra autem erat inanis et vacua]]. This earth, mystically, is the earthly or carnal man, who, left to himself and considered in himself, is vain, misshapen and empty, being deprived of the adornment of the virtues and destitute of spiritual graces. For which reason the Virgin who bore Christ said: [[Luke 1:53|the rich he hath sent empty away|Divites dimisit inanes]] [*inanes*, the same word as *inanis*, "void", here]. And the Wise Man too: [[Wis 13:1|all men are vain, in whom there is not the knowledge of God|Vani sunt omnes quibus non subest scientia Dei]]. [[1:2|and darkness was upon the face of the deep|Et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]]: that is, the gloom of ignorance and of vices covered human hearts until God enlightened them; indeed, until the coming of Christ and the promulgation of the Gospel law, darkness for the most part held sway over men. For which reason Paul says in the Acts: [[Acts 17:30|God indeed having winked at the times of this ignorance, now declareth unto men that all should every where do penance|Tempora prioris ignorantiæ despiciens Deus, nunc annuntiat hominibus, ut omnes ubique pœnitentiam agant]].

paras.t: Et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas. Quemadmodum in Apocalypsi habetur, Aquæ multæ populi multi. Unde et Salomon: Mitte, inquit, panem tuum super transeuntes aquas. Itaque Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas, quando libere quosdam homines gratiose convertit ad se, et instabilia corda eorum, instar aquarum peccando labentia ac defluentia, solidavit per gratiarum charismata. Optimum quippe est gratia stabiliri cor. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Abundantius oportet nos observare ea quæ audivimus, ne forte perefluamus.
paras.en: [[1:2|and the spirit of God moved over the waters|Et Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]] [Denis reads *Spiritus Domini*, "the Spirit of the Lord"]. As we have in the Apocalypse, many waters are many peoples[[Apoc 17:15||]]. Whence Solomon too: [[Eccles 11:1|Cast|Mitte]], he says, [[Eccles 11:1|thy bread upon the running waters|panem tuum super transeuntes aquas]]. So the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters when he freely and graciously turned certain men to himself, and made firm, by the gifts of graces, their unstable hearts, which like waters were slipping and flowing away by sinning. For [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum quippe est gratia stabiliri cor]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Heb 2:1|ought we more diligently to observe the things which we have heard lest perhaps we should let them slip|Abundantius oportet nos observare ea quæ audivimus, ne forte perefluamus]].

paras.t: Dixitque Deus: Fiat lux. Hoc dixit ac adimplevit, quando electorum corda cœpit desuper illustrare, et lucem miserationum suarum multiplicare ac mirificare in eis, quia in omni mundi ætate fuerunt semper aliqui boni. Divisitque lucem a tenebris, hoc est justos a peccatoribus, et electos a reprobis: illos misericorditer vocans, visitans, et informans, istos juste relinquens.
paras.en: [[1:3|And God said: Be light made|Dixitque Deus: Fiat lux]]. This he said and fulfilled when he began to enlighten the hearts of the elect from on high, and to multiply and make wonderful in them the light of his mercies; for in every age of the world there have always been some good men. [[1:4|and he divided the light from the darkness|Divisitque lucem a tenebris]], that is, the just from sinners and the elect from the reprobate: calling, visiting and forming the former in his mercy, justly leaving the latter.

paras.t: Appellavitque Deus lucem diem. Hæc quippe lux gratiæ, fides, seu cognitio propriæ culpæ, infusio quoque doni sapientiæ, et contemplatio divinorum, est pulcherrimus dies mentis, de quo loquitur Paulus: Dies autem appropinquavit. Et Isaias: Erit dies ex die. Et tenebras noctem. Vitia enim, nox cordis sunt. Hinc impiis semper nox est. Omnis enim qui male agit, odit et fugit lucem. Via vero et vita impiorum tenebrosa. Hinc juxta Apostolum, Qui dormiunt, utpote negligentes, nocte dormiunt; et qui ebrii sunt, nocte ebrii sunt. Nisi enim nox ignorantiæ seu inadvertentiæ, aut peccati obfuscaret corda eorum, torporem et immoderantiam penitus abhorrerent ac devitarent.
paras.en: [[1:5|And he called the light Day|Appellavitque Deus lucem diem]]. For this light of grace, faith or the knowledge of one's own guilt, and also the infusion of the gift of wisdom and the contemplation of divine things, is the most beautiful day of the mind, of which Paul says: [[Rom 13:12|And the day is at hand|Dies autem appropinquavit]]. And Isaias: There shall be day from day[[Is 66:23||]] [the margin's verse is unreadable, and these words are not found in Isaias; the nearest is Is 66:23, "there shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath"]. [[1:5|and the darkness Night|Et tenebras noctem]]. For vices are the night of the heart. Hence for the wicked it is always night. For [[John 3:20|every one that doth evil hateth|Omnis enim qui male agit, odit]] and flees the light. But the way and the life of the wicked are dark. Hence, according to the Apostle, [[1 Thess 5:7|they that sleep|Qui dormiunt]], being negligent, [[1 Thess 5:7|sleep in the night; and they that are drunk, are drunk in the night|nocte dormiunt; et qui ebrii sunt, nocte ebrii sunt]]. For unless the night of ignorance or heedlessness, or of sin, darkened their hearts, they would utterly abhor and shun sloth and excess.

paras.t: Factumque est vespere et mane dies unus. Vespera lucis præfatæ, dici potest cessatio ab actu virtutis et gratiæ. Non enim possumus in hac vita sine interruptione Deo vacare, aut actualiter semper virtuosis operibus occupari. Mane vero, est renovatio aut repetitio actus virtuosi, ad tempus intermissi: quod dum agimus, completur in nobis dies unus interior.
paras.en: [[1:5|and there was evening and morning one day|Factumque est vespere et mane dies unus]]. The evening of the light spoken of can be called the ceasing from the act of virtue and grace. For in this life we cannot give ourselves to God without interruption, or be always actually busied with virtuous works. But the morning is the renewal or repetition of a virtuous act broken off for a time: and when we do this, one inner day is completed in us.

paras.t: Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis. Firmamentum istud est Ecclesia electorum, quæ, teste Gregorio, ab Abel justo cœpit, quæ divisit inter aquas et aquas, videlicet inter diversas nationes et gentes, quas dijudicavit et separavit ab invicem, et quosdam convertit, incorporavitque sibi. Divisit quoque inter aquas quæ supra se sunt, et eas quæ infra se sunt, id est inter divinam Scripturam et supernaturalem sapientiam atque angelicam illuminationem, et inter sæculares philosophicasque scientias, seu hæreticorum documenta nefaria, et superstitiosas ac falsas doctrinas. In quibus omnibus separavit pretiosum a vili, verum a falso, amplectens vera atque salubria, et reprobans falsa itemque inania. Unde hortatur Apostolus: Doctrinis variis et peregrinis nolite abduci. Et: Nemo vos seducat per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam. Qui etiam de Ecclesia contestatur ad Timotheum: Quæ est columna et firmamentum veritatis. Ecclesia namque (ut ait Chrysostomus) fortior ac solidior est cœlo et terra. Ipsa enim est domus quam sibi ædificavit Sapientia, et firmavit columnis septem, id est septem donis Spiritus Sancti, vel potius universis donis ac gratiis Dei, quia per septem universitas designatur.
paras.en: [[1:6|And God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters|Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis]]. This firmament is the Church of the elect, which, as Gregory witnesses, began from Abel the just, and which divided between waters and waters, namely between the various nations and peoples, which it judged and separated from one another, and some of which it converted and incorporated into itself. It divided also between the waters that are above it and those that are below it[[1:7||]], that is, between divine Scripture, supernatural wisdom and angelic enlightenment on the one hand, and worldly and philosophical sciences, or the wicked teachings of heretics, and superstitious and false doctrines on the other. In all these it separated the precious from the vile, the true from the false, embracing what is true and wholesome, and condemning what is false and also what is empty. Whence the Apostle exhorts: [[Heb 13:9|Be not led away with various and strange doctrines|Doctrinis variis et peregrinis nolite abduci]]. And: Let no one seduce you [[Col 2:8|by philosophy and vain deceit|per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam]]. He also bears witness of the Church to Timothy: which is [[1 Tim 3:15|the pillar and ground of the truth|columna et firmamentum veritatis]] [*firmamentum*, the same word as "firmament" here]. For the Church (as Chrysostom says) is stronger and more solid than heaven and earth. For she is the house which [[Prov 9:1|Wisdom hath built herself|sibi ædificavit Sapientia]], and made firm with seven pillars, that is, with the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, or rather with all the gifts and graces of God, since by seven the whole is signified.

paras.t: Tunc factus est secundus dies, videlicet confirmatio cordium humanorum in fide catholica, sine qua nemo unquam quivit salvari. Et vocavit Deus firmamentum cœlum. Non solum Ecclesia, sed et quilibet justus, discretus ac sapiens, qui præfato modo inter aquas et aquas discernit, cœlum seu homo cœlestis vocari meretur. Qui enim biberit de aqua quam Christus propinat, de aqua utique sapientiæ salutaris, et intellectum suum defigit in arduis et excelsis, sola cœlestia pensans, atque in lege Dei jugiter meditans, et juxta Apostolum, quæ sursum sunt quærens ac sapiens, talis rite cœlum dignus est appellari, et approbatur a Deo, quemadmodum scriptum est: Vidit Deus quod esset bonum.
paras.en: Then was made [[1:8|the second day|secundus dies]], namely the strengthening of human hearts in the Catholic faith, without which no one has ever been able to be saved. [[1:8|And God called the firmament, Heaven|Et vocavit Deus firmamentum cœlum]]. Not only the Church but also every just, discerning and wise man, who in the way described discerns between waters and waters, deserves to be called heaven, or a heavenly man. For he who has drunk of the water that Christ gives to drink, namely of [[Ecclus 15:3|the water of wholesome wisdom|aqua utique sapientiæ salutaris]], and fixes his understanding on things lofty and high, weighing heavenly things alone and meditating continually on the law of God, and, according to the Apostle, seeking and minding [[Col 3:2|the things that are above|quæ sursum sunt]], such a one is rightly worthy to be called heaven, and is approved by God, as it is written: [[1:10|And God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]] [the Vulgate does not have these words on the second day; they stand at v. 10 and elsewhere in the chapter].

paras.t: Dixit vero Deus: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Aquæ istæ cœlo inferiores, sunt (juxta prætacta) falsæ doctrinæ, errores, curiositates ac vitia, et etiam homines vitiosi ac infideles: quæ omnia sunt ab Ecclesia Dei tollenda, atque in locum unum trudenda, arctanda et coercenda, ut aqua lacrimarum mergantur, et igne pœnitentiæ comburantur, seu cum principe tenebrarum descendant in tartarum. Denique locus aquarum istarum, est ecclesia malignantium, et præsens sæculum nequam. His itaque aquis remotis, apparet arida, hoc est, Ecclesia Dei a vitiorum fluviis desiccata, et ab humore concupiscentiæ arefacta, quæ tunc aliis præbet virtutum exempla. Sic quoque quilibet nostrum debet aquas istas a se toto conatu abjicere, pœnitendo et juste ac timorate vivendo, ne cum perversis pervertatur et erroribus implicetur, quatenus ita appareat arida, id est bona cordis sui terra, in qua semen Dei fructificet, imo ortum, faciat centuplum fructum. Hæc, inquam, appareat, hoc est, exemplaris atque conspicua fiat, et coram Deo irreprehensibilem se præsentet.
paras.en: [[1:9|God also said; Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Dixit vero Deus: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. These waters below heaven are (as touched on above) false doctrines, errors, curiosities and vices, and also vicious and unbelieving men: all of which are to be removed from the Church of God, and thrust, confined and held in check in one place, so that they may be drowned in the water of tears and burnt up in the fire of penance, or go down with the prince of darkness into hell. Lastly, the place of these waters is the church of the malignant, and this present wicked world. These waters being removed, then, there appears [[1:9|the dry land|apparet arida]], that is, the Church of God, dried from the rivers of vices and parched of the moisture of concupiscence, which then offers others examples of the virtues. So too each of us ought to cast these waters from him with all his effort, by doing penance and living justly and in fear of God, lest he be perverted with the perverse[[Ps 17:27||]] and entangled in errors, so that thus the dry land may appear, that is, the good ground of his heart, in which the seed of God may bear fruit, nay, [[Luke 8:8|being sprung up, yielded fruit a hundredfold|ortum, faciat centuplum fructum]] [Denis: "may yield"]. Let this, I say, appear, that is, become an example and conspicuous, and present itself blameless before God.

paras.t: Et vocavit Deus aridam terram. Quemadmodum arida, nuncupata est terra, quasi pedibus trita; ita etiam militans Ecclesia et quilibet justus, rite dicitur terra, quia diversis tribulationibus modo subjicitur, atque ab impiis multoties conculcatur. Congregationes autem aquarum maria sunt vocata, id est, conventicula iniquorum et collectiones errorum ac vitiorum, inquietudine, turbulentia et amaritudine sunt repleta, etiam si ad tempus videantur aliquid suavitatis habere.
paras.en: [[1:10|And God called the dry land, Earth|Et vocavit Deus aridam terram]]. As the dry land was named earth, as it were trodden by feet [*terra* as from *terere*, "to tread"], so too the Church militant and every just man is rightly called earth, because now it is subjected to various tribulations, and is many times trodden underfoot by the wicked. And [[1:10|the gathering together of the waters|Congregationes autem aquarum]] are called [[1:10|Seas|maria]], that is, the conventicles of the wicked and the gatherings of errors and vices are filled with restlessness, turbulence and bitterness, even if for a time they seem to have some sweetness.

paras.t: Et ait: Germinet terra herbam virentem et facientem semen, et lignum pomiferum. Exclusis vitiis, Ecclesia et anima pia producit flores dulcissimos atque virentia gramina, utpote meditationes salubres, virtuosas affectiones et opera bona; virtutes quoque et dona Spiritus Sancti tanquam arbores fecundæ, plantantur et oriuntur in ea. Quumque alios convertit ad Dominum, producit ligna pomifera. Quemadmodum enim injusti sunt arida ligna, sic justi sunt ligna fecunda, quæ plantata sunt juxta decursus aquarum.
paras.en: [[1:11|And he said: let the earth bring forth green herb, and such as may seed, and the fruit tree|Et ait: Germinet terra herbam virentem et facientem semen, et lignum pomiferum]]. When vices are shut out, the Church and the devout soul bring forth the sweetest flowers and green grasses, namely wholesome meditations, virtuous affections and good works; the virtues too and the gifts of the Holy Ghost are planted and spring up in it like fruitful trees. And when it converts others to the Lord, it brings forth fruit trees. For as the unjust are dry trees, so the just are fruitful trees, which are [[Ps 1:3|planted near the running waters|plantata sunt juxta decursus aquarum]].

paras.t: Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli. Luminaria sunt boni prælati, sancti doctores, et omnes contemplativi atque perfecti. Stellæ autem sunt omnes Ecclesiæ filii, qui fide, spe et charitate rutilant. Præsertim vero per duo magna luminaria, intelliguntur duæ potestates Ecclesiæ, puta papalis, quæ est luminare majus: et imperialis sive regalis, quæ est luminare minus, quanquam luminare minus accipi possit episcopalis auctoritas. Extensius quoque loquendo, luminare majus est potestas spiritualis; luminare minus, potestas sæcularis, quæ et per duos gladios designantur. Spiritualis vero potestas præest diei, utpote clero; sæcularis nocti, id est vulgo. Rursus luminare majus est evangelica lex, seu novi Testamenti Scriptura, quæ præest diei, id est plebi ac tempori gratiæ. Luminare minus, est vetus Testamentum, quod præerat nocti, id est populo Synagogæ, in qua omnia erant velata. Unde dixit Apostolus: Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit.
paras.en: [[1:14|Let there be lights made in the firmament of heaven|Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli]]. The lights are good prelates, holy doctors, and all the contemplative and perfect. [[1:16|the stars|Stellæ]], again, are all the sons of the Church, who glow with faith, hope and charity. But above all, by [[1:16|two great lights|duo magna luminaria]] are understood the two powers of the Church: the papal, which is the greater light, and the imperial or royal, which is the lesser light; though by the lesser light the episcopal authority may be taken. Speaking more broadly too, the greater light is the spiritual power, the lesser light the secular power, which are also signified by the two swords [that is, the two swords of Luke 22:38, read as the spiritual and the temporal power]. And the spiritual power rules the day, namely the clergy; the secular, the night, that is, the common people. Again, the greater light is the Gospel law, or the Scripture of the New Testament, which rules the day, that is, the people and the time of grace. The lesser light is the Old Testament, which ruled the night, that is, the people of the Synagogue, in which all things were veiled. Whence the Apostle said: [[Rom 13:12|The night is passed And the day is at hand|Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit]].

paras.t: Denique luminaria ista, præcipue spiritualis ac papalis potestas, sunt in signa; quia insinuant subditis quid agere debeant, et oculi subditorum diriguntur in eos quasi in signum, et positi sunt in signa quibus obediatur, quanquam nunc eis contradicatur a multis. Sunt item in tempora et dies et annos, quoniam multa instituunt, quæ singulis annis, certis diebus, et præfixis temporibus observentur, videlicet festa, jejunia, et consimilia.
paras.en: Lastly, these lights, especially the spiritual and papal power, are [[1:14|for signs|in signa]]: because they make known to those under them what they ought to do, and the eyes of those under them are directed to them as to a sign, and they are set up as signs to be obeyed, though now many speak against them. They are likewise [[1:14|for seasons, and for days and years|in tempora et dies et annos]], since they institute many things to be kept every year, on fixed days and at appointed times, namely feasts, fasts and the like.

paras.t: Quinto die produxit aqua pisces et aves, id est, Ecclesia per fontem Baptismi regeneravit ac peperit Christo homines quosdam, qui in tribulationibus et persecutionibus quasi in aqua natant, et quosdam instar avium ascendentes ad superiora per contemplationem, quorum conversatio est in cœlis. Creavitque Deus cete grandia. Hoc fecit ubertim, dum baptizatis tantam contulit gratiam, quod creverunt in viros sublimes, in omni adversitate tribulationeque patientes, qui in afflictionibus, correptionibus atque jejuniis, quasi in omnibus divitiis gloriantur. His demum benedixit Deus, ut crescant et multiplicentur, id est, gratiam sibi concessam, in alios administrent, et numero ac merito augeantur.
paras.en: On the fifth day the water brought forth fishes and birds[[1:20||]]: that is, the Church through the font of Baptism regenerated and bore to Christ certain men who swim in tribulations and persecutions as in water, and certain others who, like birds, rise to higher things by contemplation, whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]]. [[1:21|And God created the great whales|Creavitque Deus cete grandia]]. This he did abundantly when he conferred on the baptized such grace that they grew into lofty men, patient in every adversity and tribulation, who glory in afflictions, chastisements and fastings as in all riches. Lastly God blessed them, that they might increase and multiply[[1:22||]], that is, minister to others the grace granted them, and grow in number and merit.

paras.t: Sexto die terra produxit jumenta, bestias atque reptilia. Ecclesia quippe non solum parit homines obedientes et obsequiosos, qui per jumenta signantur; sed item feroces, qui signantur per bestias: et avaros, qui tanquam reptilia terrenis adhærent: quos tamen Ecclesia non parit, quantum ad mala hæc. Possunt etiam bestiæ et reptilia exponi in bono, intelligendo per bestias eremitas et anachoretas, qui omnem societatem, præsentiamque humanam vitantes, instar ferarum in latibulis solitudinum et vastitate eremorum sunt commorati. Rursus bestiæ dici possunt homines imperfecti, qui a bestialibus motibus adhuc infestantur, præsertim qui ad iram, impatientiam, indignationem, amaritudinemque proclives sunt. Reptilia vero accipi possunt rudes, indocti et materiales, qui se super se levare non didicerunt, sed in sensibilibus detinentur, quamvis desiderent et conentur Deo placere, qui in statu sunt incipientium. Nihilo minus per reptilia possunt humiles designari, qui se ipsos inaniter non extollunt, sed circa propriæ defectuositatis et conditionis ac culpæ considerationem versantur, quasi in terra repentes.
paras.en: On the sixth day the earth brought forth cattle, beasts and creeping things[[1:24||]]. For the Church brings forth not only obedient and dutiful men, who are signified by the cattle, but also fierce ones, who are signified by the beasts, and covetous ones, who like creeping things cling to earthly things; though the Church does not bring these forth as to these evils. The beasts and creeping things can also be expounded in a good sense, understanding by the beasts the hermits and anchorites, who, shunning all company and human presence, have dwelt like wild beasts in the lairs of the solitudes and the wastes of the deserts. Again, the beasts can be called imperfect men, who are still troubled by beastly impulses, especially those prone to anger, impatience, indignation and bitterness. And by the creeping things can be taken the rude, the unlearned and the material-minded, who have not learned to raise themselves above themselves but are held in things of sense, though they desire and strive to please God: these are in the state of beginners. Nevertheless, by the creeping things the humble can be signified, who do not vainly exalt themselves, but busy themselves with considering their own defectiveness, condition and guilt, as it were creeping on the earth.

1.title: Solutio quarumdam quæstionum circa capitulum istud
1.title_en: Solution of certain questions about this chapter

paras.t: QUAMVIS veraciter scriptum est, Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit? attamen quæri potest, cur Deus non produxit omnia simul distincte, sed per sex dierum successionem. Ad hoc utique possunt causæ rationabiles assignari. Prima est, ut per hoc clarissime demonstraret, quod non necessitate naturæ, sed liberrima voluntate sit rerum causa : unde nec ab æterno condidit mundum. Alia causa est, quoniam sicut Deus creavit omnia corporalia propter hominem sic voluit ut modus creationis eorum esset ad hominum informationem perutilis ; quod potissime factum est per hoc, quod per senariam successionem dierum, res creatæ completæ sunt. Ex hoc namque ostenditur, quod oporteat hominem paulatim proficere, et omnem distinctionem, ornatumque gratiæ ac virtutum expectare a Deo. Denique, ex hoc ipso monstratur, quantum intersit inter animam virtutibus ordinatam, et animam vitiis deordinatam atque confusam. Rursus, per hunc modum producendi hæc omnia, dedit nobis Creator exemplum consulte ac moderate, non repente aut quasi improvise seu præcipitanter agendi. Iterum, ut suo exemplo doceret nos sex diebus operari, et septima die, seu die ei succedente, in Deo quiescere, et solis divinis vacare.
paras.en: Although it is truly written, [[Rom 11:34|who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor?|Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?]] [the margin gives Is. xl, 13; Denis's words are those of Rom 11:34, where the Apostle quotes Isaias], yet it may be asked why God did not produce all things at once and distinctly, but through a succession of six days. To this, reasonable causes can certainly be assigned. The first is, that by this He might show most clearly that He is the cause of things not by necessity of nature but by His most free will: whence neither did He found the world from eternity. Another cause is that, as God created all bodily things for the sake of man, so He willed that the manner of their creation should be most profitable for the instruction of men; and this was done chiefly by this, that the things created were completed through a succession of six days. For by this it is shown that man must advance little by little, and must look to God for all the distinction and adornment of grace and of the virtues [distinction and adornment (distinctio, ornatus): the names the schoolmen give to the works of the six days, the dividing of the elements and their furnishing with lights and living things]. Next, by this very thing it is shown how great a difference there is between a soul set in order by the virtues and a soul thrown into disorder and confusion by the vices. Again, by this manner of producing all these things, the Creator gave us an example of acting with deliberation and measure, not suddenly, or as it were unprepared or headlong. Again, that by His example He might teach us to work for six days, and on the seventh day, or the day that follows them, to rest in God and be free for divine things alone.

paras.t: Secundo quæritur circa hoc, quod circa præsens capitulum communiter dicunt expositores, videlicet quod Plato posuit tria increata rerum principia, scilicet Deum, ideam, et hylen, seu materiam primam ; Aristoteles vero duo, puta materiam, et speciem seu formam, et tertium quod operatorium dicitur seu effectivum, utpote Deum. Et istud in principio secundi Sententiarum habetur. Unde in principio Hexaemeron scribit Ambrosius : Miror tantum opinionis assumpsisse homines, ut quidam eorum ponerent tria principia omnium, ut Deum et exemplar atque materiam, sicut Plato et discipuli ejus, et ea assererent esse increata et incorrupta ; Deum quoque non tanquam creatorem materiæ, sed tanquam artificem, ad exemplar, id est, ideam intendendo fecisse mundum de materia quam hylen appellant. Quæritur ergo, an Plato hæc dixerit. Et apparet quod imo, ex his quæ loquitur in Timæo, et quia sancti Patres atque doctores catholici istud ei imponunt. Sed videtur contrarium, quia in primo Timæi vocat Deum mundi conditorem, et ponit quod unus sit mundus, quia ab uno exemplari conditoris sui profluxit. Præterea doctrina Platonis est, quod quidquid boni est in toto universo, a primo summo et essentialiter bono per participationem manavit. Insuper, decimo de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus : Platonici dixerunt, mundum et deos et animas rationales, Deo coæterna, et tamen ab ipso Deo esse creata, ponentes exemplum : si pes ab æterno stetisset in pulvere, vestigium esset ei coæternum, et tamen ab ipso causatum. Iterum Plato apertissime docuit, omnem multitudinem rerum ab uno esse principio : ergo non posuit nisi unum principium simpliciter primum.
paras.en: Secondly, a question is raised about what the expositors commonly say on the present chapter: namely, that Plato posited three uncreated principles of things, to wit God, the idea, and hyle, or prime matter; while Aristotle posited two, namely matter, and species or form, and a third which is called the operative or effective principle, that is, God. And this is found at the beginning of the second book of the Sentences. Whence Ambrose writes at the beginning of the Hexaemeron: I wonder that men have taken up so great an opinion of themselves, that some of them posited three principles of all things, namely God, the exemplar and matter, as did Plato and his disciples, and asserted that these were uncreated and incorruptible; and that God, not as the creator of matter but as a craftsman, looking to an exemplar, that is, the idea, made the world out of the matter which they call hyle. It is asked, then, whether Plato said this. And it appears that he did, from what he says in the Timaeus, and because the holy Fathers and the catholic doctors lay this to his charge. But the contrary seems to be the case, for in the first part of the Timaeus he calls God the founder of the world, and holds that the world is one because it flowed from the one exemplar of its founder. Moreover, it is Plato's teaching that whatever good there is in the whole universe flowed by participation from the first, the supreme and essentially good.
