Further, in the tenth book of the City of God Augustine asserts: The Platonists said that the world, and the gods, and rational souls are coeternal with God, and yet were created by God Himself; and they gave an example: if a foot had stood from eternity in the dust, the footprint would be coeternal with it, and yet caused by it. Again, Plato taught most plainly that the whole multitude of things is from one principle: therefore he posited only one principle that is first simply.

paras.t: Ad ista arbitror respondendum, quia ut ait Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei, Platonis sententiæ de altis et arduis rebus, non faciliter perspiciuntur seu non clare intelliguntur. Amplius dico, quod Plato posuit unum summum et verum Deum in se ipso æternaliter invariabiliterque perfectum et infinitum, et omnia sapienter agentem secundum exemplares rationes in se ipso contentas, nec respicere ad exemplar ab alio elaboratum, aut extra se positum. Verumtamen verum est, quod ponebat ideas extra mentem divinam; sed qualiter, et quid dixerit eas habere a summo bono, et qualiter intenderit dicere, quod informis illa materia seu elementorum confusio præcesserit eorum formationem, difficile est resolute exprimere. Attamen reor, quod juxta Platonis doctrinam, etiam ipsa hyle seu prima materia, et quidquid est citra summum Deum, ab ipso summo Deo processerit.
paras.en: To these, I think, the answer is that, as Augustine says in the book of the City of God, Plato's views on high and difficult matters are not easily seen through, or are not clearly understood. Further, I say that Plato posited one supreme and true God, eternally and unchangeably perfect and infinite in Himself, and doing all things wisely according to the exemplary reasons [that is, the patterns of all things as they are in the divine mind] contained in Himself, and not looking to an exemplar worked out by another or set outside Himself. Yet it is true that he placed the ideas outside the divine mind; but in what way, and what he said they have from the supreme good, and in what sense he meant to say that that formless matter, or confusion of the elements, preceded their formation, is hard to state decisively. Yet I think that, according to Plato's teaching, even hyle itself, or prime matter, and whatever is below the supreme God, proceeded from the supreme God Himself.

paras.t: Nempe ut Thomas in commento suo super librum de Causis fatetur, Proclus Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica mentem Platonis magistri sui plene expressit. Proclus autem theoremate 34 suæ Elementationis effatur : Omne quod secundum naturam convertitur, ad id facit conversionem, a quo et processum propriæ subsistentiæ habet. Deinde in explanatione propositionis ostendit, quod sicut omnia ad primum principium convertuntur, ita ab ipso esse sortita sunt. Unde ibidem concludit : Ex his itaque manifestum, quod appetibile omnibus est intellectus, et procedunt omnia ab intellectu, et totus mundus ab intellectu substantiam habet, et si perpetuus sit, non propter hoc procedit, quia perpetuus : neque enim propter hoc non est conversus, quoniam semper est ordinatus. Sed et procedit semper, et conversus est semper. Rursus asserit Proclus : Omnis multitudo fecunda est ab uno. Et denuo : Omnia, inquit, qualitercumque participantia bono, præcedit quod primo bonum, et quod nihil aliud est quam bonum. Præterea, quod et prima materia juxta Platonem a Deo manaverit, pandit Proclus theoremate 59, in cujus commento ait : Propter quod extremum entium est simplicissimum, sicut et primum, quia a solo primo processit. Per extremum equidem entium, intellexit primam materiam, quod denuo in alterius propositionis commento fatetur : Ex his, inquiens, manifestum, propter quid materia ex uno subsistens, expers est secundum se speciei entis : materia quidem omnium exsistens subjectum, ex omnium causa ens processit. Præterea de Aristotele certum est, quod dixit, a primo ente omnibus derivatum esse et vivere. Unde in libro de Substantia orbis, apertissime asserit Commentator, quod nunquam fuit intentio Aristotelis, dicere quod Deus esset causa cœli solum quantum ad conservationem aut motum ipsius, sed etiam quoad cœli substantiam.
paras.en: For, as Thomas acknowledges in his commentary on the book On Causes, Proclus the Platonist fully set out the mind of Plato his master in his Elements of Theology. Now Proclus declares in theorem 34 of his Elements: Everything that by nature reverts makes its reversion to that from which it also has the procession of its own subsistence. Then, in explaining the proposition, he shows that as all things revert to the first principle, so they have received their being from it. Whence he concludes in the same place: From these things, then, it is manifest that the intellect is desirable to all things, and that all things proceed from the intellect, and the whole world has its substance from the intellect; and if it be perpetual, it is not for this reason that it proceeds, because it is perpetual [so the print; Proclus's sense is that being perpetual does not keep it from proceeding from the intellect]: nor is it for this reason not reverted, because it is always set in order; but it both proceeds always and is reverted always. Again Proclus asserts: Every fruitful multitude is from the one. And again: All things, he says, that in any way share in the good are preceded by that which is good primarily, and which is nothing else than good. Moreover, that prime matter too, according to Plato, flowed from God, Proclus makes plain in theorem 59, in whose commentary he says: For which reason the last of beings is most simple, as is the first also, because it proceeded from the first alone. By the last of beings, indeed, he meant prime matter, as he again acknowledges in the commentary on another proposition: From these things, he says, it is manifest why matter, subsisting from the one, has of itself no share in the form of being: matter, indeed, being the subject of all things, proceeded from the cause of all things as a being. Moreover, it is certain of Aristotle that he said that being and life are derived to all things from the first being. Whence, in the book On the Substance of the Orb, the Commentator [Averroes] asserts most plainly that it was never Aristotle's intention to say that God was the cause of the heaven only as to its preservation or its motion, but also as to the heaven's substance.

paras.t: Amplius, quia per cœlum quidam intelligunt naturam angelicam seu angelos, breviter quæritur, an angeli sint creati in gratia gratum faciente, et caritate : et item, an fuerunt creati ante mundum sensibilem. Ad primum horum dicendum, quod sicut doctores scribunt super secundum Sententiarum, de hoc sunt duæ opiniones, nec est certitudo quid circa hoc verius sit. Augustinus namque in pluribus locis videtur sentire, quod fuerunt creati in gratia, ita quod Deus simul in eis creavit naturam, et largitus est gratiam. Hinc Albertus in libro de Coæquævis, et Thomas in scripto secundi, ac alii multi tenent, quod fuerunt in caritate et gratia conditi. Magister autem Sententiarum, et Bonaventura, ac alii plures, magis divertunt ad aliam opinionem. Ad secundum dicendum, quod doctores Latini et Augustinus communiter tenent, quod angeli fuerunt simul cum sensibili mundo isto creati. Doctores vero Græcorum dicunt, quod diu ante creationem cœli et terræ fuerunt creati, quos in hoc Hieronymus est secutus. Dicitque Thomas in prima parte, quod positio illa non debeat aspernari aut abjici quasi erronea, potissimum propter reverentiam Gregorii Nazianzeni, qui tantæ auctoritatis exstitit in Scripturis, quod nullus unquam ausus fuit eum negare, sicut nec Athanasium, ut refert Hieronymus.
paras.en: Further, because some understand by heaven the angelic nature, or the angels, it is briefly asked whether the angels were created in sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God] and in charity; and likewise, whether they were created before the sensible world. To the first of these it must be said that, as the doctors write on the second book of the Sentences, there are two opinions about this, and there is no certainty which of them is the truer. For Augustine in many places seems to hold that they were created in grace, so that God at one and the same time created their nature in them and bestowed grace. Hence Albert in the book On the Coeval Things, and Thomas in his writing on the second book [of the Sentences], and many others, hold that they were made in charity and grace. But the Master of the Sentences, and Bonaventure, and many others, rather turn aside to the other opinion. To the second it must be said that the Latin doctors and Augustine commonly hold that the angels were created together with this sensible world. But the doctors of the Greeks say that they were created long before the creation of heaven and earth, and Jerome followed them in this. And Thomas says in the First Part that that position ought not to be spurned or cast aside as erroneous, chiefly out of reverence for Gregory Nazianzen, who was of such authority in the Scriptures that no one ever dared to gainsay him, any more than Athanasius, as Jerome relates.

paras.t: Quæritur quoque, cur Moyses non fecit expressam mentionem de angelorum creatione. Ad hoc communiter respondetur, quod ideo, quoniam rudi populo atque ad idololatriam prono loquebatur, qui invisibilium non fuerunt capaces. Et si cognovissent esse tales intellectuales substantias præclarissimas, fuissent ad earum adorationem proclives. Sed contra hoc objici posset : Quod si sic, ergo Moyses non debuit postea aliquam facere mentionem de angelis, quum tamen in hoc Genesis libro scribat, quod angeli fuerunt obviam Jacob, de quibus ipse tunc dixit : Castra Dei sunt hæc. Hinc alii dicunt, quod Moyses satis expressit angelos nomine cœli. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus affirmat, quod Hebræi dicunt angelos secunda die creatos, quod tamen probabilitatem non habet.
paras.en: It is also asked why Moses made no express mention of the creation of the angels. The common answer to this is: because he was speaking to a rude people, prone to idolatry, who were not capable of invisible things; and if they had known that there are such most glorious intellectual substances, they would have been inclined to worship them. But against this it could be objected: if that is so, then Moses ought not to have made any mention of angels later on; and yet in this book of Genesis he writes that angels met Jacob, of whom Jacob then said: [[Gen 32:2|These are the camps of God|Castra Dei sunt hæc]]. Hence others say that Moses expressed the angels sufficiently by the name of heaven. Yet Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos] affirms that the Hebrews say the angels were created on the second day, which, however, has no probability.

paras.t: Quæritur item circa hoc, quod doctores testantur Moysen innuisse personalem distinctionem in Deo, quum scripsit : In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram.
paras.en: It is likewise asked about what the doctors testify, that Moses hinted at a distinction of Persons in God when he wrote: [[1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth.|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram.]]

paras.t: Quocirca sciendum quod Magister Sententiarum primo libro, distinctione 2, et Nicolaus de Lyra in quadam quæstione, pluresque alii dicunt, quod in exordio Genesis, quo habemus, In principio creavit Deus, Hebraica veritas pro hoc nomine Deus, habet Elohim, quod est plurale hujus nominis El, quod significat Deum, ita quod Elohim significat Deos, ac si Moyses dixerit : In principio Dii creavit cœlum et terram : sic quod pluraliter dicendo Dii, insinuavit distinctionem Personarum in Deo, et earumdem unitatem in essentia, singulariter subdens, creavit. Hanc autem Magistri sententiam approbat Rabbi Paulus, et addit, quod quidam Hebræorum doctores exponunt hoc loco Elohim pluraliter, non tamen ad insinuandum pluralitatem Personarum in simplici Deo, sed diversitatem virtutum seu potestatem procedentium ab eo. Hoc autem Rabbi Paulus sufficienter redarguit. Quum igitur S. Moyses intenderit filios Israel a pluralitate deorum revocare ad cultum unius Dei, non est verisimile, quod in exordio suæ scripturæ pluraliter Deum expresserit sub nomine Elohim, nisi ad insinuandam pluralitatem Personarum in Deo. Verumtamen in Scholastica historia dicitur : Hebræus habet Elohim, quod tam singulare quam plurale est.
paras.en: On this it should be known that the Master of the Sentences, in the first book, distinction 2, and Nicholas of Lyra in a certain question, and many others, say that at the opening of Genesis, where we have [[1:1|In the beginning God created|In principio creavit Deus]], the Hebrew verity has, for this noun God, Elohim, which is the plural of the noun El, which signifies God; so that Elohim signifies Gods, as if Moses had said: In the beginning Gods created heaven and earth [Dii creavit: a plural subject with a singular verb]; so that by saying Gods in the plural he hinted at the distinction of Persons in God, and their unity in essence by adding in the singular, created. This view of the Master Rabbi Paul approves, and he adds that certain doctors of the Hebrews explain Elohim in this place as a plural, yet not as hinting at a plurality of Persons in the simple God, but at a diversity of powers or potencies proceeding from Him. But this Rabbi Paul sufficiently refutes. Since, then, holy Moses intended to call the children of Israel back from a plurality of gods to the worship of the one God, it is not likely that at the opening of his scripture he would have expressed God in the plural under the name Elohim, except to hint at the plurality of Persons in God. Yet in the Scholastic History it is said: The Hebrew has Elohim, which is both singular and plural.

2.title: Elucidatio capituli secundi: Igitur perfecti sunt cœli, usque ad illud: Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: “So the heavens and the earth were finished,” as far as “These are the generations of the heaven and the earth”

paras.t: CAPITULUM istud secundum, conclusio est et declaratio plenior eorum, quæ sunt in primo capitulo contenta. Multa quoque nunc adjiciuntur. Itaque ait : Igitur perfecti sunt cœli et terra. Quemadmodum in exordio primi capituli, quo habetur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram : per cœlum et terram, intelliguntur omnia cœlestia corpora, imo et spirituales et intellectuales substantiæ, quarum habitatio est in cœlo, et omnia elementa ; ita hoc loco per cœlum et terram, eadem intelliguntur, quæ omnia perfecta, id est completa, creata, instituta atque distincta sunt in primis diebus. Nam primo die creata sunt et distingui cœperunt, quæ distinctio die secundo ac tertio consummata describitur, sicut præhabitum est. Et omnis ornatus eorum, supple, perfectus est. Nam ceteris tribus diebus ornata sunt, utpote quarto, quinto et sexto diebus, sicut expositum est.
paras.en: This second chapter is the conclusion and a fuller declaration of what is contained in the first chapter; and many things are now added as well. And so he says: [[2:1|So the heavens and the earth were finished|Igitur perfecti sunt cœli et terra]]. Just as at the beginning of the first chapter, where we read, [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], by heaven and earth are understood all the heavenly bodies, and indeed also the spiritual and intellectual substances whose dwelling is in heaven, and all the elements: so in this place heaven and earth mean the same things, all of which were finished, that is, completed, created, set up and distinguished, in the first days. For on the first day they were created and began to be distinguished, and this distinction is described as completed on the second and third days, as was said before. [[2:1|and all the furniture of them|Et omnis ornatus eorum]] [Latin *ornatus*, "adornment" or "array", which the Douay-Rheims renders "furniture"]: supply, was finished. For on the other three days, namely the fourth, fifth and sixth, they were adorned, as has been expounded.

paras.t: Complevitque Deus die septimo opus suum quod fecerat. Si intra sex dies perfecti sunt cœli et terra, atque omnis eorum ornatus : quomodo septimo die complevit Deus opus suum quod fecerat sex diebus ? Et respondendum, quod septimo die illud complevit, quia perfectioni quam infra sex dies contulit operi suo, addidit aliam septimo die. Unde et alia translatio continet, Complevit Deus sexto die, etc. Nempe per opus Dei, intelligitur hoc loco congeries seu universitas operum sex dierum. Quemadmodum autem unaquæque res dicitur perfici seu perfecta uno modo, quando acquirit aut habet omnia ad suam essentiam ac subsistentiam pertinentia, sicut leo fertur perfectus, dum habet suæ speciei formam substantialem atque materiam, et concomitantia eas ; alio autem modo, quando exercet operationem sibi convenientem, per quam finem suæ institutionis attingit : sic universum seu mundus, qui est opus sex dierum, dicitur uno modo perfectus, quando adeptus est et accepit omnes partes ac species ad suam integritatem spectantes. Et hanc perfectionem sexta die sortitus est. Sicque asseritur Deus sexto die opus suum complesse.
paras.en: [[2:2|And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made|Complevitque Deus die septimo opus suum quod fecerat]]. If within six days [[2:1|the heavens and the earth were finished|perfecti sunt cœli et terra]], and [[2:1|all the furniture of them|omnis eorum ornatus]], how did God on the seventh day complete the work which he had made in six days? The answer must be that he completed it on the seventh day because to the perfection which he gave his work within the six days he added another on the seventh day. Hence another translation also reads: God completed on the sixth day, etc. [this is the reading of the Septuagint]. For by the work of God is understood in this place the whole assemblage or totality of the works of the six days. Now each thing is said to be perfected, or perfect, in one way when it acquires or has everything that belongs to its essence and subsistence, as a lion is called perfect when it has the substantial form and the matter of its species, and what goes with them; and in another way when it exercises the operation suited to it, by which it attains the end for which it was made. So too the universe or world, which is the work of the six days, is called perfect in one way when it has obtained and received all the parts and species that belong to its integrity. This perfection it received on the sixth day; and thus God is said to have completed his work on the sixth day.

paras.t: Alio modo mundus vocatur perfectus, in quantum partes et species ad suam integritatem ac ordinem pertinentes, cœperunt operationes sibi convenientes, propter quas exercendas institutæ fuerant, exercere et exsequi. Sicque dicitur Deus septimo die opus suum complesse, quoniam septimo die cœperunt opera sex dierum generaliter exercere actus congruos sibi, et in invicem agere, atque similia propagare, seu administrari ac gubernari. De quo opere locutus est Christus : Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Hinc paulo post dicitur Deus diei septimo benedixisse, sicut mox exponetur. Sic itaque complevit die septimo opus suum, illud deinceps administrando, movendo ac gubernando, ac secundariis perfectionibus illud ornando. Rursus, tunc illud complevit, id est, consummatum ostendit. Itemque complevit, quoniam plures species rerum non condidit. Et iterum, quoniam septimo die aliquid egit quod ante non fecit. Nam septimo diei benedixit, et eum sanctificavit.
paras.en: In another way the world is called perfect inasmuch as the parts and species belonging to its integrity and order began to exercise and carry out the operations suited to them, for the exercise of which they had been made. And thus God is said to have completed his work on the seventh day, since on the seventh day the works of the six days began, in general, to exercise the acts befitting them, to act upon one another, and to propagate their like, or to be administered and governed. Of this work Christ spoke: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Hence a little further on God is said to have blessed the seventh day, as will shortly be expounded. So then [[2:2|on the seventh day God ended his work|complevit die septimo opus suum]] by thenceforth administering, moving and governing it, and adorning it with secondary perfections. Again, he completed it then, that is, showed it to be consummated. Likewise he completed it in that he made no more species of things. And again, because on the seventh day he did something he had not done before: for [[2:3|he blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it|septimo diei benedixit, et eum sanctificavit]].

paras.t: Et requievit Deus die septimo ab universo opere quod patrarat. Operibus sex dierum ultra prædicta nil addidit, quod ad præfatam mundi integritatem ac ordinem universi spectaret, sicque ab eis requievit, id est, plura creare cessavit, ita quod deinceps nil fecit, quod non aliquo modo in operibus illis præcesserit seu continebatur, utpote virtualiter, materialiter, aut similitudinarie. Denique requievit, non quod operando laboraverit, lassatusve fuerit, quippe qui solo jussu condidit universa. Requievit etiam non a motu, nec requievit in operibus suis, quasi in illis quies, perfectio, aut beatitudo seu finis suus consistat ; sed requievit ab eis in semetipso, tanquam sibi ipsi in se prorsus supersufficientissimus, nec aliquo indigens. Verumtamen in intellectualibus creaturis quievit per gratiam, atque in omnibus fuit per essentiam, præsentiam ac potentiam. Unde et sic exponi potest : Requievit, id est, intellectualem creaturam in se quiescere fecit aut monuit. Præterea per hoc quod dicitur, Ab universo opere quod patrarat, datur intelligi, quod non cessavit alia quædam operari deinceps.
paras.en: [[2:2|and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done|Et requievit Deus die septimo ab universo opere quod patrarat]]. To the works of the six days he added nothing beyond what has been said that would belong to the aforesaid integrity of the world and order of the universe; and so he rested from them, that is, he ceased to create more, so that thereafter he made nothing that had not in some way gone before in those works or been contained in them, namely virtually, materially, or by likeness. Further, he rested, not because he had toiled in working or grown weary, since he made all things by his command alone. Nor did he rest from motion, nor rest in his works, as though his rest, perfection, beatitude or end consisted in them; but he rested from them in himself, as being in himself wholly and more than sufficient to himself, and in need of nothing. Nevertheless in intellectual creatures he rested by grace, and he was in all things by essence, presence and power. Hence it can also be expounded thus: He rested, that is, he made the intellectual creature rest in him, or admonished it to. Moreover, by the words [[2:2|from all his work which he had done|Ab universo opere quod patrarat]] we are given to understand that he did not cease from working certain other things thereafter.

paras.t: Benedixitque Deus diei septimo. Sicut ait Gregorius, Benedictio Dei est collatio munerum ejus, et multiplicatio eorumdem. Quoniam ergo juxta prætacta, Deus septimo die quamdam specialem perfectionem et influentiam ac decorationem contulit, et adjecit operibus sex dierum, recte dicitur septimo benedixisse diei. Diei namque ac tempori solent adscribi ea, quæ fiunt in die ac tempore. Et sanctificavit illum, hoc est, sanctum ac celebrem ordinavit, quia ad opera cultus divini specialiter deputavit diem eumdem : et ipsemet tunc quasi ab aliis cessans, sui ipsius contemplationi vacavit, ideo subditur : Quia in ipso cessaverat ab omni opere suo, quod creavit Deus ut faceret, id est, ne otiosus videretur aut illiberalis a communicatione propriæ voluntatis ad extra. Vel, ut faceret ea ad laudem et gloriam sui ipsius : vel quod creavit in proposito ac præscientia mentis suæ, hoc est, quod creare decrevit ab æterno, ut faceret illud exsecutive in tempore præstituto.
paras.en: [[2:3|And he blessed the seventh day|Benedixitque Deus diei septimo]]. As Gregory says, the blessing of God is the bestowal of his gifts and the multiplying of them. Since, then, as was touched on above, God on the seventh day conferred a certain special perfection, influence and adornment on the works of the six days, and added it to them, he is rightly said to have blessed the seventh day; for the things done in a day or a time are commonly ascribed to that day or time. [[2:3|and sanctified it|Et sanctificavit illum]], that is, he ordained it holy and solemn, because he appointed that same day especially for the works of divine worship; and he himself then, as though ceasing from other things, was at leisure for the contemplation of himself. Therefore it is added: [[2:3|because in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made|Quia in ipso cessaverat ab omni opere suo, quod creavit Deus ut faceret]] [the Latin ends *quod creavit Deus ut faceret*, literally "which God created that he might make"; Denis's glosses take it so], that is, lest he should seem idle, or ungenerous in communicating his own will outwardly. Or: that he might make them for his own praise and glory. Or: which he created in the purpose and foreknowledge of his mind, that is, which he decreed from eternity to create, that he might make it in execution at the time appointed.

paras.t: Circa intellectum textus istius scribit Bonaventura super secundum, distinctione 15 : Aliquid dicitur novum dupliciter. Primo, quasi distinctum contra antiquitatem cursus naturæ, et consuetudinem rationalis creaturæ. Et ita non requievit Deus in illis diebus novas facere creaturas, imo interim multa miraculose et supernaturaliter fecit. Secundo dicitur novum, cujus nulla similitudo præcessit, nec aliquod creatum principium, quod esset seminarium ejus. Et ita fertur Deus cessasse novam facere creaturam. Eorum namque quæ successive producuntur, quædam fuerunt in prima distinctione producta in simili, sed non in ratione seminali, ut animæ rationales, quæ creantur atque in simili productæ sunt, quando creata est anima Adæ. Alia tunc producta sunt in ratione seminali, non autem in simili, ut ea quæ generantur ex putrefactione, et ex diversarum specierum commixtione. Alia vero producta sunt tunc in ratione seminali, et in simili, ut plantæ et animalia quæ producuntur per propagationem. Et ad hæc tria rerum genera possunt reduci cuncta quæ fiunt. Propterea scriptum est: Nihil novum sub sole. Aliter etiam dici potest, quod scilicet cessavit facere novam creaturam, quæ sit de necessitate perfectionis universi.
paras.en: On the understanding of this text Bonaventure writes, on the second book [of the Sentences], distinction 15: A thing is called new in two ways. First, as set against the long-standing course of nature and the custom of the rational creature; and in this sense God did not rest in those days from making new creatures, but rather in the meantime did many things miraculously and supernaturally. Secondly, that is called new of which no likeness went before, nor any created principle that might be its seed-bed; and in this sense God is said to have ceased from making a new creature. For of the things that are produced one after another, some were produced in the first distinction [of things] in their likeness, but not in a seminal reason [*ratio seminalis*: a power placed in created things from the beginning, from which things of a given kind afterwards come forth], as rational souls, which are created, and were produced in their likeness when the soul of Adam was created. Others were then produced in a seminal reason, but not in their likeness, as the things that are generated from putrefaction, and from the mingling of different species. Others again were then produced both in a seminal reason and in their likeness, as the plants and animals that are produced by propagation. And to these three kinds of things everything that comes to be can be reduced. Therefore it is written: [[Eccles 1:10|Nothing under the sun is new|Nihil novum sub sole]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the words are those of Eccles 1:10]. It can also be put another way: that he ceased from making any new creature that is needed for the perfection of the universe.

paras.t: Insuper asserit idem Doctor: Sicut dies dicitur malus non ratione sui, sed quia est mensura malæ actionis, propter quod ait Apostolus. Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt: sic dies dicitur benedictus et sanctus, qui est mensura operationis, in qua est benedictio et sanctificatio. Et nihil aliud est, diem aliquem benedicere et sanctificare, quam diem deputare tali actioni tanquam mensuram. Quoniam ergo Deus omnia fecit propter hominis instructionem, ut hominem non solum verbo, sed et opere erudiret: hinc quemadmodum ipse Deus operatus fuit res sex diebus, sic dedit homini licentiam operandi, et inferioribus intendendi per totidem dies. Et sicut septimo die cessavit ab opere, sic voluit ut homo septimo die ab omni opere vacet, ut ei per contemplationem inhæreat, ac inhærendo quiescat. Et quia in hac adhæsione homo obtinet a Deo amplificationem benedictionis et sanctificationis, ideo septimus dies dicitur a Deo benedictus et sanctificatus.
paras.en: The same Doctor further asserts: Just as a day is called evil not by reason of itself but because it is the measure of an evil action (which is why the Apostle says, [[Eph 5:16|redeeming the time, because the days are evil|Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt]]), so that day is called blessed and holy which is the measure of an operation in which there is blessing and sanctification. And to bless and sanctify a day is nothing else than to appoint that day to such an action as its measure. Since, then, God did all things for man's instruction, to teach man not only by word but also by deed, therefore, just as God himself worked his works in six days, so he gave man leave to work and to attend to lower things for as many days. And just as he ceased from work on the seventh day, so he willed that man on the seventh day be free from all work, so as to cleave to him by contemplation and, cleaving, to rest. And because in this adherence man obtains from God an increase of blessing and sanctification, therefore the seventh day is called blessed and sanctified by God.

paras.t: Dicit quoque Albertus: Cessavit Deus ab omni opere dupliciter. Primo, ex parte operis, quoniam postea nihil novum fecit, cujus principia naturalia in sex diebus non præcesserunt secundum formam vel materiam aut similitudinem. Secundo, ex parte efficientis, puta ipsius Dei, quia in sex diebus Deus per se ipsum naturam in principiis suis instituit: postmodum vero non per se ipsum solus, sed pariter cum natura res naturales propagavit.
paras.en: Albert also says: God ceased [[2:3|from all his work|ab omni opere]] in two ways. First, on the side of the work, since afterwards he made nothing new whose natural principles had not gone before in the six days, as to form, or matter, or likeness. Secondly, on the side of the maker, that is, of God himself: for in the six days God by himself established nature in its principles, but afterwards he propagated natural things, not by himself alone, but together with nature.

paras.t: Præterea Rabbi Paulus scribit hoc loco: Si sanctificatio intelligatur secundum applicationem ad divina obsequia, hoc non pertinet ad sensum litteralem, sed mysticum. Ad quod allegat, quod Magister Sententiarum libro secundo asserit, Deum dotasse septimum diem præ ceteris mystica benedictione et sanctificatione. Et rursus, quia si ex sensu litterali hujus benedictionis et sanctificationis haberetur, quod homo die septimo deberet a terrenis cessare operibus, sequeretur quod sancti Patriarchæ fuissent ad observationem sabbati obligati.
paras.en: Rabbi Paul, moreover, writes on this place [Paul of Burgos, a converted Jew who became bishop of Burgos, author of the Additions to Lyra's Postill]: If the sanctification is understood as the appointing [of the day] to divine services, this does not belong to the literal sense, but to the mystical. In support he alleges that the Master of the Sentences [Peter Lombard] asserts in the second book that God endowed the seventh day above the others with a mystical blessing and sanctification. And again: if it followed from the literal sense of this blessing and sanctification that man ought to cease from earthly works on the seventh day, it would follow that the holy Patriarchs had been bound to keep the sabbath.

paras.t: Verum, ut patuit, dictum hoc Pauli istius non videtur consonare doctoribus, qui super secundum communiter sanctificationem sabbati præfato modo exponunt ad litteram. Denique in libris Moysis sæpissime assignatur ad litteram hæc ratio observantiæ sabbati, quoniam sex diebus operatus est Deus, et septimo requievit. Ex quo constat, quod sanctificatio sabbati litteraliter refertur ad applicationem circa obsequium Dei.
paras.en: But, as has been shown, this saying of this Paul does not seem to agree with the doctors, who on the second book [of the Sentences] commonly expound the sanctification of the sabbath literally in the way given above. Moreover, in the books of Moses this reason for keeping the sabbath is given very often, in the literal sense: that in six days God worked, and on the seventh he rested[[Ex 20:11||]][[Ex 31:16||]][[Ex 31:17||]]. From which it is clear that the sanctification of the sabbath refers, literally, to its being appointed to the service of God.

paras.t: Ad id ergo quod ex verbis Magistri assumit, dicendum, quod mysticum seu spirituale sæpe ad litteram pertinet, ita quod litteralis sensus sæpe est spiritualis et mysticus, ut quum Isaias ait de Christo: Erit justitia cingulum lumborum ejus, et fides cinctorium renum ejus, quod ad litteram intelligendum est de spirituali cingulo et spiritualibus lumbis. Et istud in Prophetis, et maxime in Canticis canticorum, sæpissime locum habet. Conformiter in proposito, spiritualis et mystica sanctificatio, litteraliter pertinet ad sabbati sanctificationem. Ad id quod secundo adducit de Patriarchis, dicendum, quod Deus sabbatum sanctificavit, quoniam deputavit illud operibus cultus divini tempore opportuno, ut scilicet juxta intentionem Legislatoris fieret observatio sabbati.
paras.en: To what he takes from the words of the Master, then, it must be said that the mystical or spiritual often belongs to the letter, so that the literal sense is often spiritual and mystical: as when Isaias says of Christ, [[Is 11:5|justice shall be the girdle of his loins: and faith the girdle of his reins|Erit justitia cingulum lumborum ejus, et fides cinctorium renum ejus]], which is to be understood literally of a spiritual girdle and spiritual loins. And this occurs very often in the Prophets, and above all in the Canticle of Canticles. In the same way in the matter before us, the spiritual and mystical sanctification belongs literally to the sanctification of the sabbath. To what he adduces second, about the Patriarchs, it must be said that God sanctified the sabbath in that he appointed it to the works of divine worship at the fitting time; that is to say, so that the sabbath should be kept according to the intention of the Lawgiver.

paras.t: Amplius, quod ait hic Paulus, sanctificatio competit septimæ diei, in quantum res conditæ et multiplicatæ in Deo requiescunt: non videtur idonee dictum, quoniam in Deo requiescere, non competit proprie nisi intellectualibus creaturis, quæ solæ dicuntur capaces Dei per notitiam et amorem; et si ceteræ creaturæ dicantur aliquo modo requiescere in Deo, in quantum conservatur ab eo, hoc competebat eis a primo momento productionis earum.
paras.en: Further, what this Paul says here, that sanctification belongs to the seventh day inasmuch as the things created and multiplied rest in God, does not seem fitly said. For to rest in God belongs properly only to intellectual creatures, which alone are said to be capable of God by knowledge and love; and if the other creatures are said in some way to rest in God, inasmuch as they are preserved by him, this belonged to them from the first moment of their production.

2.title: Prosequtio expositionis hujus capituli ab eo loco: Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ
2.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this chapter from the place: “These are the generations of the heaven and the earth”

paras.t: Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ. Quum cœlum et terra creata sint, quomodo nunc generata dicuntur? Respondetur, quod generatio sumitur nunc extense pro productione, ut sit sensus: Istæ sunt generationes, id est productiones, creationes seu constitutiones cœli et terræ, id est superiorum et inferiorum ac mediorum, ut sæpe expositum est. Istæ, inquam, generationes, quæ descriptæ sunt in primo capitulo per opera sex dierum. Porro aliqui dicunt cœlestia, inferioraque corpora facta ex communi materia, materia illa præjacente effecta. Quando creata sunt, in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram. Dies nunc sumitur pro tempore, secundum Bedam, non pro uno die dumtaxat. Et alii dicunt, quod juxta morem linguæ Hebrææ, ponitur hic singulare pro plurali, videlicet die pro diebus, quemadmodum primo capitulo dictum est: Germinet terra herbam, Producant aquæ reptile, Producat terra animam viventem. Alii dicunt, quod dies supponit hic confuse pro diversis diebus. Vel sumitur zeugmatice, reddendo singula singulis, quoniam ista per recapitulationem dicuntur. Itaque in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram, fecit et omne virgultum. Sed quum cœlum et terra creata sint ante omnem diem, quomodo nunc facta dicuntur in die? Et respondendum, quod si cœlum et terra accipiantur pro solis cœlestibus corporibus et elementis, facta dicuntur in die, quoniam facta sunt in principio temporis et primæ diei, seu simul cum tempore, quod dicitur unum de quatuor coæquævis. Quod si inter creationem et exordium operis distinctionis, quo facta est lux, non exstitit mora, secundum aliam expositionem, eadem erit responsio.
paras.en: [[2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ]]. Since heaven and earth were created, how are they now said to be generated? The answer is that *generation* is here taken broadly for production, so that the sense is: These are the generations, that is, the productions, creations or establishings, of the heaven and the earth, that is, of the higher, the lower and the middle things, as has often been explained. These generations, I say, which were described in the first chapter through the works of the six days. Some say, moreover, that the heavenly and the lower bodies were made from a common matter, that matter having been made beforehand. [[2:4|when they were created, in the day that|Quando creata sunt, in die quo]] God [[2:4|made the heaven and the earth|fecit Deus cœlum et terram]]. *Day* is here taken for time, according to Bede, and not for one day only. Others say that, after the manner of the Hebrew tongue, the singular is put here for the plural, namely *day* for *days*, as was said in the first chapter: [[Gen 1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Germinet terra herbam]], [[Gen 1:20|let the waters bring forth the creeping creature|Producant aquæ reptile]], [[Gen 1:24|Let the earth bring forth the living creature|Producat terra animam viventem]]. Others say that *day* here stands indistinctly for several days. Or it is taken by zeugma [that is, one word serving for several things], assigning each to each, since these things are told by way of recapitulation. So, in the day that God made the heaven and the earth, he made [[2:5|And every plant|et omne virgultum]] also. But since heaven and earth were created before any day, how are they now said to have been made in the day? The answer must be that if heaven and earth are taken for the heavenly bodies and the elements alone, they are said to have been made in the day because they were made at the beginning of time and of the first day, or together with time, which is said to be one of the four things created together [the empyrean heaven, the angelic nature, unformed matter and time, which in the schoolmen's teaching came into being at once]. And if, according to another explanation, there was no interval between the creation and the beginning of the work of distinction, in which light was made, the answer will be the same.

paras.t: In hoc igitur die fecit Deus omne virgultum, id est arbusta recentia agri, hoc est agrorum ubicumque sunt nata virgulta, omnemque herbam, id est universa gramina aut terræ nascentia, regionis, id est totius orbis terrarum, in quibus tunc orta sunt, priusquam germinaret: id est, tertia die fecit hoc Deus subito sua omnipotente virtute, non per temporum moras, antequam terra naturali ordine et successive cœpit virgulta et herbas producere, ex influentia cœlestium corporum et rationibus seminalibus sibi a principio inditis, ut supra in expositione operis tertiæ diei expressum est: ad quam germinationem in aliquibus terræ nascentibus confert et cooperatur cultura humana. Porro quod iste sit sensus, ex sequentibus elicitur verbis: Non enim pluerat Dominus Deus super terram. Ex quo patet, quod productio illa virgultorum atque herbarum, non fuit naturalis et successiva, ad quam solet irrigatio pluvialis requiri.
paras.en: In this day, then, God made [[2:5|every plant|omne virgultum]], that is, the young shrubs [[2:5|of the field|agri]], that is, of the fields, wherever shrubs have sprung up; [[2:5|and every herb|omnemque herbam]], that is, all grasses or things that grow from the earth, [[2:5|of the ground|regionis]], that is, of the whole world, in the places where they then arose, [[2:5|before it grew|priusquam germinaret]]: that is, God did this on the third day, suddenly, by his almighty power, not through the delays of time, before the earth, in the order of nature and step by step, began to bring forth shrubs and herbs by the influence of the heavenly bodies and by the seminal reasons [that is, the causal powers put into things at their creation, from which they later unfold] placed in it from the beginning, as was set out above in the explanation of the work of the third day: and to this sprouting, in some of the things that grow from the earth, human tillage contributes and cooperates. That this is the sense is drawn from the words that follow: [[2:5|for the Lord God had not rained upon the earth|Non enim pluerat Dominus Deus super terram]]. From which it is plain that that production of shrubs and herbs was not natural and gradual, for which watering by rain is usually required.

paras.t: Et homo non erat qui operaretur terram. Circa hoc dicit quidam, quod homo nondum erat formatus, et tamen ipsemet dicit circa illud quod dictum est, Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ: Istæ scilicet generationes quæ prædictæ sunt in operibus sex dierum, in quibus productio hominis utique continetur. Melius ergo exponitur istud, sumendo singulare pro plurali, sicut in istis capitulis fit frequenter. Eritque sensus: Homo non erat qui operaretur terram, id est, tot homines nondum fuerunt, qui possent colere terram, et cooperari ad ejus naturalem germinationem. Et quod iste sit sensus, hinc innotescit, quod etsi unus homo fuisset dumtaxat, non potuit ad communem illam terræ germinationem notabiliter cooperari.
paras.en: [[2:5|and there was not a man to till the earth|Et homo non erat qui operaretur terram]]. On this a certain writer says that man had not yet been formed; and yet he himself says, on the words [[2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ]]: namely, these generations which were told before in the works of the six days, in which the production of man is certainly contained. It is better, then, to explain this by taking the singular for the plural, as happens often in these chapters. And the sense will be: [[2:5|there was not a man to till the earth|Homo non erat qui operaretur terram]], that is, there were not yet so many men as could till the earth and cooperate in its natural sprouting. And that this is the sense is made known from this, that even if there had been one man only, he could not have cooperated notably in that general sprouting of the earth.

paras.t: Sed fons ascendebat e terra, irrigans universam superficiem terræ. Mirum videtur, qualiter unus fons totam terram poterat irrigare. Denique secunda die discooperta est terra ab aquis, substiteruntque montes et valles. Nec apparet, quod aqua unius fontis potuerit vel montium irrigare cacumina, aut superfluere vallibus ad humectandum loca ultra valles sita. Hinc Glossa et Beda sentire videntur, quod per fontem intelligantur pluraliter fontes, qui in diversis terris hinc inde eruperant. Nec imaginari oportet, quod tota omnino superficies terræ fuerit undique irrigata: sed tota irrigata asseritur, quia in locis et partibus opportunis hoc factum est. Hinc alii dicunt, quod aquæ sub terra latentes, ascendebant ad superficiem terræ, per modum fontis in qualibet parte terræ. Verumtamen quidam dicunt, quod tunc unus fons paulatim totam irrigaverit terram, quemadmodum modo Nilus Ægyptum.
paras.en: [[2:6|But a spring rose out of the earth, watering all the surface of the earth.|sed fons ascendebat e terra, irrigans universam superficiem terræ.]] It seems wonderful how one spring could water the whole earth. For on the second day [so the text; in Gen 1:9–13 the dry land appears on the third day] the earth was uncovered by the waters, and mountains and valleys stood forth. Nor does it appear that the water of one spring could have watered the tops of the mountains, or have flowed over the valleys to moisten the places lying beyond them. Hence the Gloss and Bede seem to hold that by *spring* are meant springs in the plural, which had burst forth here and there in different lands. Nor must we imagine that the whole surface of the earth without exception was watered everywhere: but the whole is said to have been watered because this was done in the fitting places and parts. Hence others say that the waters hidden under the earth rose up to the surface of the earth in the manner of a spring in every part of the earth. Some, however, say that one spring then watered the whole earth little by little, as the Nile now waters Egypt.

paras.t: Præterea quidam dicunt, quod per id quod dictum est, Fons ascendebat e terra, ostenditur modus quo facta est prima illa herbarum ac virgultorum productio, ita quod plantæ illæ et herbæ, factæ sunt divina virtute, aqua taliter concurrente et concausante et disponente sua irrigatione. Sed hoc non apparet provide dictum, quoniam plantæ et herbæ illæ sunt immediate et instantanee a Deo productæ, absque concausalitate secundarum causarum, utpote solo imperio Dei, quemadmodum pisces, aves, et animalia terræ. In tali quoque operatione omnipotentiæ Dei, non requirebatur concursus causæ creatæ, nec irrigatio aquæ, quemadmodum nec influentiæ alicujus cælestis. Et istud ex dictis in expositione præcedentis capituli, atque ex scriptis doctorum super secundum Sententiarum, est manifestum. Refert Lyra quod Hebræi dicunt, quod ista sit littera vera, Ascendit nubes de terra; sed verius reor, sanctissimum Hieronymum transtulisse veraciter. Et quod dictio Hebraica, pro qua Hieronymus transtulit, fons, forsan æquivoca sit ad designandum fontem ac nubem.
paras.en: Some say besides that by the words [[2:6|a spring rose out of the earth|Fons ascendebat e terra]] is shown the manner in which that first production of herbs and shrubs was made, so that those plants and herbs were made by the divine power, with the water concurring in this way, acting as a joint cause and disposing them by its watering. But this does not seem wisely said, since those plants and herbs were produced by God immediately and in an instant, without the joint causality of secondary causes, namely by God's command alone, just as the fishes, the birds and the animals of the earth were. In such a working of God's almightiness neither the concurrence of a created cause was required, nor the watering of water, any more than the influence of any heavenly body. And this is plain from what was said in the explanation of the preceding chapter, and from the writings of the doctors on the second book of the Sentences. Lyra relates that the Hebrews say that the true letter is: *A cloud went up from the earth*; but I think it truer that the most holy Jerome translated truthfully, and that the Hebrew word for which Jerome put *spring* is perhaps ambiguous, meaning both a spring and a cloud.

paras.t: Consequenter Moyses plenius atque distinctius narrat, quod primo capitulo de hominis productione et de utroque sexu, obscure ac breviter scripsit. Formavit igitur Dominus Deus hominem de limo terræ. Hic ponitur pars pro toto, videlicet corpus hominis pro homine. Vel si intelligatur de homine toto, non verificatur de eo, nisi secundum partem ipsius. Formavit itaque hominem, id est corpus primi hominis, seu hominem primum, quantum ad corpus suum de limo terræ, non quod corpus illud non fuerit ex quatuor elementis compositum: sed ideo limum terræ expressit, quoniam terra secundum quantitatem abundat in corpore hominis, deinde aqua: ideo ait, de limo, quoniam limus est terra aquæ mixta. Et inspiravit in faciem ejus. Quemadmodum Deus corpus hominis primi formavit non corporalibus manibus, sic inspiravit in faciem ejus non ore materiali, buccis aut faucibus, imo utrumque fecit intellectualiter, præcipiendo, et solo conceptu practico id volendo: itaque inspiravit, id est, creando immisit seu fudit in faciem ejus, hoc est in totum corpus ipsius, intelligendo per synecdochen totum nomine partis. Et specialiter exprimit faciem hominis, quia in ea potissime ostenduntur operationes vitales, et sensus magis vigent atque apparent in ea. Est item pars hominis quodammodo principalior, et etiam pulchrior. Spiraculum vitæ, hoc est animam vitalem seu spiritum rationalem. Et factus est homo in animam viventem, id est, animam vivam, et corpus suum vivificantem, ac immortalem, accepit a Deo per inspirationem seu creationem præfatam.
paras.en: Next Moses tells more fully and more distinctly what he wrote obscurely and briefly in the first chapter about the production of man and about both sexes. [[2:7|And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit igitur Dominus Deus hominem de limo terræ]]. Here the part is put for the whole, namely the body of man for man. Or if it is understood of the whole man, it is not true of him except as regards a part of him. So he formed man, that is, the body of the first man, or the first man as regards his body, of the slime of the earth: not that that body was not composed of the four elements, but he named the slime of the earth because in quantity earth abounds most in man's body, and after it water; and so he says *of the slime*, since slime is earth mixed with water. [[2:7|and breathed into his face|Et inspiravit in faciem ejus]]. Just as God formed the body of the first man not with bodily hands, so he breathed into his face not with a material mouth, cheeks or throat; rather, he did both in an intellectual way, by commanding, and by willing it with his practical conception alone [that is, the idea in the divine mind that directs the making of a thing]. So he breathed, that is, by creating he sent or poured into his face, that is, into his whole body, the whole being understood by synecdoche under the name of the part. And he names the face of man in particular because the vital operations are shown chiefly in it, and the senses are most vigorous and most apparent in it. It is also in a way the chief part of man, and the fairest. [[2:7|the breath of life|Spiraculum vitæ]], that is, a living soul or rational spirit. [[2:7|and man became a living soul|Et factus est homo in animam viventem]], that is, he received from God, through the breathing or creation spoken of, a soul that is alive, that gives life to its body, and that is immortal.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur primo, quum Deus per se ipsum immediate fecerit corpora irrationabilium animalium in prima rerum institutione, sicut et corpus hominis primi, cur Scriptura nunc utitur speciali modo loquendi, describendo hominis formationem secundum corpus et animam? Nempe de aliis generaliter dictum est, Producat terra, etc., Producant aquæ, etc.: nunc autem sic ait, Formavit Dominus Deus hominem. Sed hujus quæstionis facilis exstat solutio, quia ad insinuandum hominis dignitatem, id factum est. Denique, sicut ceteris formis nobilior valde est anima rationalis, sic corpus ipsius nobilioris est complexionis et cœliformioris æqualitatis, pulchrioris quoque figurationis et organizationis. Estque staturæ erectæ, ad innuendum quod anima ejus creata est ad contemplandum ac diligendum cœlestia et divina. Ad insinuandum quoque, quod anima hominis sit omnino ab extra et a Deo immediate creata, ait Scriptura: Inspiravit in faciem ejus. Alia autem translatio continet: Insufflavit (aut sufflavit) in faciem ejus. Anima etenim in Scripturis flatus vocatur, juxta illud Isaiæ: Hæc dicit Dominus, dans flatum populo qui est super terram. Et rursus per Isaiam Deus testatur: Flatus ego faciam, et spiritus a facie mea egredietur. Eadem vero vocatur anima, et spiraculum vitæ, quia per eam homo spirat et vivit. Quidam tamen spiraculum vitæ, vocant spiritum quemdam corporeum in corpore animalis, qui operatur in eo in quinque sensus, et paulatim in moriente exstinguitur. Quumque animal moritur in aliqua corporis parte, adhuc sentitur spiritus ille, quum in parte alia sit exstinctus.
paras.en: On these words it is asked, first: since God by himself made immediately the bodies of the irrational animals in the first establishing of things, just as he made the body of the first man, why does Scripture now use a special manner of speaking, describing the formation of man according to body and soul? For of the others it was said in general terms: [[Gen 1:24|Let the earth bring forth|Producat terra]], etc., [[Gen 1:20|let the waters bring forth|Producant aquæ]], etc.; but now it says: [[2:7|the Lord God formed man|Formavit Dominus Deus hominem]]. The answer to this question is easy: it was done to suggest the dignity of man. For just as the rational soul is far nobler than the other forms, so its body is of a nobler complexion [that is, temperament, the blend of the elements and humours in a body] and of a more heaven-like evenness, and also of a fairer shape and structure. And it is of upright stature, to signify that its soul was created to contemplate and to love heavenly and divine things. To suggest also that the soul of man is wholly from without and created immediately by God, Scripture says: [[2:7|breathed into his face|Inspiravit in faciem ejus]]. Another translation has: He blew (or, he breathed) into his face. For in the Scriptures the soul is called a breath, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 42:5|Thus saith the Lord|Hæc dicit Dominus]], [[Is 42:5|that giveth breath to the people upon it|dans flatum populo qui est super terram]]. And again God testifies through Isaias: [[Is 57:16|breathings I will make|Flatus ego faciam]], [[Is 57:16|the spirit shall go forth from my face|et spiritus a facie mea egredietur]]. The same soul is called the breath of life because by it man breathes and lives. Some, however, call the breath of life a certain bodily spirit in the body of an animal, which works in it in the five senses and is put out little by little in one who is dying. And when an animal dies in some part of its body, that spirit is still felt in it, although in another part it has been put out.

paras.t: Quæritur, an corpus primi hominis sit immediate a Deo formatum. Ad hoc Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 91, respondet: Corpus primi hominis formari non potuit, nisi immediate à Deo. Quemadmodum enim Deo proprium est creare animam, sic soli Deo convenit producere formam in materia sine adminiculo præcedentis formæ substantialis. Unde nec angeli transmutare possunt corpora ad aliquam formam, nisi adhibendo semina quædam, ut tertio de Trinitate loquitur Augustinus. Sed ante primi hominis productionem non fuit formatum aliquod corpus humanum, cujus virtute formaretur aliud simile in specie per viam generationis. Necessarium igitur fuit, primi hominis corpus a Deo formari immediate. Potuit tamen esse, ut angeli aliquod ministerium circa corpus hoc exhiberent, sicut in finali resurrectione adhibebunt, pulveres suscitandorum corporum colligendo.
paras.en: It is asked whether the body of the first man was formed immediately by God. To this Thomas answers in the First Part, question 91: The body of the first man could not be formed except immediately by God. For just as it belongs to God to create the soul, so it belongs to God alone to produce a form in matter without the help of a preceding substantial form. Hence not even angels can change bodies to any form except by applying certain seeds, as Augustine says in the third book *On the Trinity*. But before the production of the first man no human body had been formed by whose power another like it in species might be formed by way of generation. It was necessary, therefore, that the body of the first man be formed immediately by God. It could be, however, that the angels performed some ministry about this body, as they will at the final resurrection by gathering the dust of the bodies to be raised.

paras.t: Quærit etiam Augustinus, an anima primi hominis facta sit extra corpus. Et videtur supra Genesim sentire, quod imo: doctores tamen nunc super secundum communiter dicunt quod non, nec Augustinus dicit illud simpliciter asserendo. Dicunt ergo doctores, quod sicut in ceteris postea, ita in primo homine anima simul creata est et infusa. Est enim naturaliter corporis forma, parsque compositi. In eodem autem actus seu forma non præcedit corpus.
paras.en: Augustine also asks whether the soul of the first man was made outside the body. And in his work on Genesis he seems to hold that it was; but the doctors now commonly say, on the second book [of the Sentences], that it was not, nor does Augustine say it by way of a plain assertion. The doctors say, then, that as in all others afterwards, so in the first man the soul was created and infused at the same time. For it is by nature the form of the body and a part of the composite; and in the same thing the act or form does not come before the body.

paras.t: Quæri etiam potest, an anima illa infusa sit corpori prius formato et organizato. Et ex textu videtur, quod sic, quum scriptum sit, quod Deus inspiravit in faciem ejus. Sed si hoc concedatur, quæratur qualis forma substantialis fuit in corpore illo ante animæ infusionem: et utrum forma illa fuerit corrupta, anima adveniente. Ad istud arbitror respondendum, quod corpus hominis a Deo formatum est et perfecte organizatum in instanti, quoniam infinitæ virtuti competit instantanee operari, et eodem instanti anima ejus est creata, corporique infusa, quemadmodum etiam dicunt doctores factum in formatione corporis Christi et infusione animæ ejus.
paras.en: It may also be asked whether that soul was infused into a body already formed and organized. And from the text it seems that it was, since it is written that God [[2:7|breathed into his face|inspiravit in faciem ejus]]. But if this is granted, it may be asked what substantial form there was in that body before the infusion of the soul, and whether that form was corrupted when the soul came. To this I think the answer must be that the body of man was formed by God and perfectly organized in an instant, since it belongs to infinite power to work instantaneously, and in the same instant his soul was created and infused into the body, as the doctors say was done also in the forming of Christ's body and the infusion of his soul.

paras.t: Insuper, communiter nunc tenetur, quod primus homo factus est in ætate et robore virili, atque ad generandum idonea. Dei enim opera sunt perfecta, et perfectum dicitur unumquodque, quando potest producere simile sibi in specie. Si vero quæratur: an factus sit mortalis aut potius immortalis: respondetur, quod factus est aliquo modo mortalis, et aliquo modo immortalis: quia sic conditus fuit, quod nequaquam moreretur, si Deo obediens permaneret; sin autem, morti subjiceretur. Immortalitas autem non competebat ei ex sua natura, quoniam habuit corpus mixtum, et ex contrariis compositum, quamvis contrariæ qualitates elementorum, fuerint in eodem ad præcipuam æqualitatem temperiemque redactæ. Hinc tertiodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Fatendum est, primos homines ita fuisse institutos, quod si non peccassent, nullum genus mortis experirentur. In Historia demum scholastica dicitur: Hunc locum non intellexit Plato sane, dicens Deum animam creasse, angelos autem corpus formasse, ibi: O dii deorum! quorum pater opifexque ego. Verumtamen per verba illa in secundo Timæi scripta, Plato per deos deorum litteraliter intelligit orbes cœlestes ac stellas, ut etiam Thomas testatur. Nec dicit ibi aperte, quod dii deorum formaverunt corpus primi hominis, sed quod Opifex summus commisit eis executionem productionis animalium terrenorum mortalium.
paras.en: Further, it is now commonly held that the first man was made in the age and strength of manhood, and fit to beget. For the works of God are perfect, and each thing is called perfect when it can produce what is like itself in species. And if it is asked whether he was made mortal or rather immortal, the answer is that he was made in one way mortal and in another way immortal: for he was so made that he would never die if he remained obedient to God, but if not, he would be subject to death. Immortality did not belong to him by his nature, since he had a mixed body, composed of contraries, although the contrary qualities of the elements had been brought in it to an excellent evenness and balance. Hence Augustine says in the thirteenth book of *The City of God*: It must be confessed that the first men were so established that, if they had not sinned, they would have experienced no kind of death. Lastly, it is said in the *Scholastic History*: Plato did not rightly understand this passage, when he said that God created the soul but the angels formed the body, where he says: O gods of gods, whose father and maker am I! Yet by those words written in the second part of the *Timaeus*, Plato literally understands by *gods of gods* the heavenly spheres and the stars, as Thomas too testifies. Nor does he say there openly that the gods of gods formed the body of the first man, but that the supreme Maker entrusted to them the carrying out of the production of the mortal earthly animals.

paras.t: Plantaverat autem Dominus Deus paradisum voluptatis a principio. Paradisus iste terrestris, est pars terræ elementaris, quæ in principio est creata: et ita paradisus, quantum ad substantiam suam, qua est pars terræ, factus est prima die seu in exordio temporis ac primæ diei: sed quantum ad id quod pertinet ad paradisi distinctionem, videlicet quantum ad herbas, arbusta et fructus ipsius, plantatus est tertio die, in qua aquis in unum collectis, Deus præcepit: Producat terra herbam virentem. Dicitur autem paradisus voluptatis, quoniam amœnissimus atque pulcherrimus locus est, et longa lataque regio. In quo posuit hominem quem formaverat. Ex quo patet quod Deus primum hominem extra paradisum creavit, et quod mulier facta est postea.
paras.en: [[2:8|And the Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning|Plantaverat autem Dominus Deus paradisum voluptatis a principio]]. This earthly paradise is a part of the elemental earth, which was created in the beginning; and so paradise, as to its substance, by which it is a part of the earth, was made on the first day, or at the outset of time and of the first day; but as to what belongs to the distinction [that is, the adorning and setting in order of what was first created] of paradise, namely its herbs, shrubs and fruits, it was planted on the third day, on which, when the waters had been gathered into one, God commanded: [[Gen 1:11|let the earth bring forth green herb|Producat terra herbam virentem]]. It is called a paradise of pleasure because it is a most delightful and most beautiful place, and a long and broad region. [[2:8|wherein he placed man whom he had formed|In quo posuit hominem quem formaverat]]. From this it is plain that God created the first man outside paradise, and that the woman was made afterwards.

paras.t: Circa hæc multa occurrunt quærenda. Primo an paradisus sit locus corporeus. Ad hoc respondet Augustinus super Genesim ad litteram libro octavo: Tres, inquiens sunt sententiæ de paradiso. Una eorum, qui posuerunt paradisum spiritualiter tantum. Et ista fuit Origenis opinio, qui omnia quæ in hoc capitulo de paradiso scribuntur, dixit spiritualiter esse intelligenda, ad designandum quod primus homo conditus fuit in magna opulentia spiritualium gratiarum, delectationumque internarum. Hanc opinionem reprobat Augustinus etiam tertiodecimo de Civitate Dei. Epiphanius quoque episcopus Cypri, in quadam epistola ab Hieronymo translata. Secunda fuit positio dicentium, ea quæ de paradiso dicuntur, corporaliter solum esse accipienda: quod non est satis idonee dictum, quoniam omnia illa spiritualiter etiam exponuntur. Et ipse Adam in spiritualibus voluptatibus exstitit constitutus, prout in sequenti pandetur articulo. Tertia est doctrina eorum, qui paradisum corporaliter spiritualiterque intelligunt, quam approbat Augustinus, imo Ecclesia Dei.
paras.en: On these words many questions arise. First, whether paradise is a bodily place. To this Augustine answers in the eighth book on Genesis according to the letter: There are, he says, three opinions about paradise. One is of those who held paradise to be spiritual only. And this was the opinion of Origen, who said that everything written in this chapter about paradise is to be understood spiritually, to signify that the first man was made in a great wealth of spiritual graces and inward delights. Augustine rejects this opinion also in the thirteenth book of *The City of God*; and so does Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, in a certain letter translated by Jerome. The second was the position of those who said that what is told of paradise is to be taken in a bodily sense only: which is not said fittingly enough, since all those things are also explained spiritually. And Adam himself was set in spiritual delights, as will be shown in the following article. The third is the teaching of those who understand paradise both bodily and spiritually, which Augustine approves, and indeed the Church of God.

paras.t: De hac re ait Bonaventura super secundum, distinctione 17: Sicut refert Magister, tres fuerunt de paradiso sententiæ. Prima, quod solum fuerat corporalis. Alii vero attendentes, quod beatificatio hominis in paradiso spirituali consistit, qui est Dei fruitio, non in corporali amœnitate, dixerunt paradisum, de quo loquitur hæc scriptura, spiritualem esse, non corporalem; et omnia quæ dicuntur de paradiso in littera, esse metaphorice dicta, ita quod homo dicitur positus fuisse in paradiso, non quasi corporaliter illuc translatus aut localiter situs, sed quia in spirituali amœnitate est positus ex Dei amore et cognitione, juxta quod de angelo lapso in Ezechiele habetur: In deliciis paradisi Dei fuisti. Tertia positio est, quod est paradisus corporalis, et est paradisus spiritualis, qui designat statum quietis et spiritualium amœnitatem deliciarum. Et paradisus iste spiritualis est duplex, secundum duplicem statum Ecclesiæ. Est enim status Ecclesiæ militantis, et item status Ecclesiæ triumphantis; sicque unus est spiritualis paradisus in Ecclesia militante, alter in triumphante: et de utroque possunt exponi, quæ de paradiso dicuntur, saltem pro parte. Porro paradisus corporalis, locus est deliciarum et amœnitatis. Et iste etiam duplex est, juxta duplicem hominis statum, puta perfectum et imperfectum. Juxta statum perfectum, paradisus est cœlum empyreum; secundum statum imperfectum, est paradisus terrestris, in quo decuit hominem poni, ut esset facultas perveniendi ad patriam, atque ut Deus ostenderet homini benevolentiam suam, cui paravit ac præstitit tam amœnissimum locum ad habitandum: sicque amœnitas exterioris habitaculi, corresponderet deliciis interioribus, quas habet anima, Dei templum exsistens, et habuit primi hominis anima. Hæc Bonaventura.
paras.en: On this matter Bonaventure says, on the second book [of the Sentences], distinction 17: As the Master [Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences] relates, there were three opinions about paradise. The first, that it was bodily only. Others, considering that man's beatitude consists in the spiritual paradise, which is the enjoyment of God, and not in bodily delightfulness, said that the paradise of which this Scripture speaks is spiritual, not bodily, and that everything said of paradise in the letter is said metaphorically; so that man is said to have been placed in paradise not as though bodily carried there or set in a place, but because he was placed in a spiritual delightfulness by the love and knowledge of God, according to what is said in Ezechiel of the fallen angel: [[Ezech 28:13|Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God|In deliciis paradisi Dei fuisti]]. The third position is that there is a bodily paradise and there is a spiritual paradise, which signifies a state of rest and the delightfulness of spiritual delights. And this spiritual paradise is twofold, according to the twofold state of the Church: for there is the state of the Church militant, and the state of the Church triumphant; and so there is one spiritual paradise in the Church militant, and another in the Church triumphant, and what is said of paradise can be explained of both, at least in part. The bodily paradise, again, is a place of delights and delightfulness. And this too is twofold, according to the twofold state of man, namely the perfect and the imperfect. According to the perfect state, paradise is the empyrean heaven; according to the imperfect state, it is the earthly paradise, in which it was fitting that man should be placed, so that he might have the means of reaching the fatherland, and so that God might show his kindness to man, for whom he prepared and provided so delightful a place to dwell in; and so that the delightfulness of the outward dwelling might answer to the inward delights which the soul has, being the temple of God, and which the soul of the first man had. Thus far Bonaventure.

paras.t: Secundo quæritur, quare primus homo extra paradisum plasmatus est. Ad hoc Thomas respondet in prima parte, quæstione 102: Immortalitas hominis erat supernaturale donum. Paradisus autem competebat homini ratione immortalitatis. Decuit ergo hominem extra paradisum creari, et deinde in illum transferri, ut agnoscatur, quid convenerit homini per naturam, quid item per gratiam; seu ut sciretur, quod paradisus non competebat ei per naturam. Denique, secundum eumdem Doctorem, paradisus fuit conveniens locus habitationi humanæ, quoniam propter temperiem aeris, præservavit hominem ab exteriori corruptivo, et per fructus lignorum suorum valuit homini contra interius corruptivum, quod est per consumptionem humidi radicalis. Competebat etiam homini ratione suæ incorruptibilitatis, quia et corpus ejus incorruptibile fuit, non ex sua natura, sed partim ex virtute animæ ejus. Hæc Thomas. Unde et Bonaventura: Debuit, inquit, homo extra paradisum produci, ut melius cogitaret beneficium Dei, dum videret se illuc abunde adductum. Item ad ostendendum, quod homo non erat factus ad æternaliter ibi habitandum, sed ad temporaliter peregrinandum. Et quoniam Deus præsciebat hominis casum, voluit eum in paradiso locare, quatenus homo per ejectionem suam de loco tam voluptuoso, sensibiliter sciret, quanta spiritualia bona perdidisset per culpam; cognosceret quoque, quanta sit differentia inter eum qui Deo obedit, et eum qui inobediens est eidem.
paras.en: Secondly it is asked why the first man was fashioned outside paradise. To this Thomas answers in the First Part, question 102: The immortality of man was a supernatural gift, and paradise belonged to man by reason of his immortality. It was fitting, therefore, that man should be created outside paradise and afterwards brought into it, so that it might be recognized what belonged to man by nature and what by grace; or so that it might be known that paradise did not belong to him by nature. Further, according to the same Doctor, paradise was a place fitting for man's dwelling, since by the mildness of its air it preserved man from what corrupts from without, and by the fruit of its trees it availed man against what corrupts from within, which comes about through the consuming of the radical moisture [in the medicine of the time, the moisture innate in the body, whose wasting brings age and death]. It belonged to man also by reason of his incorruptibility, because his body too was incorruptible, not by its own nature, but partly by the power of his soul. Thus far Thomas. Hence Bonaventure too says: Man had to be produced outside paradise so that he might better consider God's kindness when he saw himself brought there so bountifully; and also to show that man had not been made to dwell there for ever, but to be a pilgrim for a time. And since God foreknew the fall of man, he willed to place him in paradise so that, by being cast out of so delightful a place, man might know by his senses how great were the spiritual goods he had lost through his fault, and might also know how great is the difference between one who obeys God and one who disobeys him.

paras.t: Insuper, sicut et alii dicunt, homo factus est immortalis quantum ad corpus, non per naturam aut qualitates intrinsecas, quasi non potens mori, sicut post finalem resurrectionem corpora electorum erunt omnino immortalia et impassibilia per dotes, quæ ex animabus gloriosis redundabunt in ea: sed factus fuit immortalis per gratiam, quasi potens non mori, si in innocentia permaneret. Sicque immortalitas ista inerat homini, per remotionem eorum quæ potuerunt eum corruptibilem facere: quorum remotio principaliter fuit a providentia Dei præcavente ab homine extrinseca corruptiva; deinde fuit partim ex virtute animæ, quæ per virtutem divinitus sibi collatam, poterat corpus præservare ab interiori læsivo. Quoniam ergo locus conveniens confert ad vitæ conservationem, quemadmodum locus intoxicatus corruptivus est vitæ, hinc Deus providit homini de loco aptissimo.
paras.en: Moreover, as others also say, man was made immortal as regards the body, not by nature or by inward qualities, as though not able to die (as after the final resurrection the bodies of the elect will be wholly immortal and impassible through the dowries [that is, the endowments of the glorified body, such as impassibility and clarity] which will overflow into them from the glorious souls), but he was made immortal by grace, as able not to die if he remained in innocence. And so this immortality was in man through the removal of the things that could make him corruptible: a removal that came chiefly from the providence of God, guarding man against what corrupts from without, and then partly from the power of the soul, which by a power given it from God could preserve the body from what harms from within. Since, then, a fitting place helps to preserve life, just as a poisoned place destroys life, God therefore provided man with a most fitting place.

paras.t: Tertio quæritur, quid et qualis sit paradisus. Ad hoc Damascenus libro secundo respondet : Quoniam Deus conditurus erat hominem ex visibili invisibilique natura, secundum propriam imaginem et similitudinem, tanquam quemdam regem et principem omnis terræ et eorum quæ sunt in ea, constituit ante eum quasi regiam quamdam, hoc est locum regalem, in qua conversans, beatam et opulentam duceret vitam. Et hic est divinus paradisus, a Deo in Eden plantatus, promptuarium universæ exsultationis ac gaudii, qui est positus in oriente, excelsior omni terra residua, temperatissimo, tenuissimo, atque purissimo aere circumfulgens, plantis ac floribus semper comatus, bono odore ac lumine plenus, excedens intelligentiam pulchritudinis universæ formæ et auræ sensibilis : divina regio et digna conversatione ejus, qui secundum Dei imaginem factus est. Hinc alii dicunt, quod paradisus sit locus in alto situs, et usque circulum seu sphæram lunæ pertingens. Unde nec aquæ diluvii pervenerunt ad eum. Et hoc etiam dicunt Beda et Scholastica historia : quod tamen intelligi non potest quantum ad corporalem altitudinem aut approximationem : sed salvari potest, si intelligatur quantum ad similitudinem, qua convenientiam habet cum proprietatibus cœlestium corporum in temperie, æqualitate, pulchritudine, etc. Imo secundum Thomam in prima parte, paradisus non pertingit usque ad medium interstitium aeris, quia in illo est maxima intemperies aeris. Verumtamen S. Bonaventura affirmat : Tantæ altitudinis est paradisus, ut illuc non conscendant vapores in aere elevati, sed est ibi aer mundus et purus, perpetuitatis statui aptus. Et quia vapores non pertingunt ad paradisum, dicitur pertingere usque ad orbem lunæ. Nam luna dominatur vaporibus.
paras.en: Thirdly it is asked what paradise is, and of what kind. To this Damascene replies in his second book: Since God was about to make man of a visible and an invisible nature, after his own image and likeness, as a kind of king and prince of all the earth and of the things that are in it, he set up for him beforehand a kind of palace, that is, a royal place, dwelling in which he might lead a blessed and plentiful life. And this is the divine paradise, planted by God in Eden, a storehouse of all exultation and joy, which is set in the east, higher than all the rest of the earth, shining with the most temperate, finest and purest air, ever crowned with plants and flowers, full of sweet fragrance and of light, passing all understanding in the beauty of every form and air that the senses perceive: a divine region, and worthy to be the dwelling of him who was made after the image of God. Hence others say that paradise is a place set on high, reaching up to the circle or sphere of the moon; so that the waters of the flood did not reach it. And Bede and the Scholastic History say this too: which, however, cannot be understood of bodily height or nearness; but it can be upheld if it is understood of likeness, in that paradise agrees with the properties of the heavenly bodies in mildness, evenness, beauty, etc. Indeed, according to Thomas in the First Part, paradise does not reach even to the middle region of the air, because in that region is the greatest harshness of the air [the middle region of the air: in the physics of the time, the cold zone where clouds, hail and storms are formed]. Nevertheless St. Bonaventure affirms: Paradise is of such height that the vapours raised in the air do not climb up there, but the air there is clean and pure, suited to a state of perpetuity. And because vapours do not reach to paradise, it is said to reach to the orb of the moon. For the moon rules over vapours.

paras.t: Quarto quæritur ubi sit paradisus. Ad quod respondetur, quod ubi nostra translatio habet, A principio, antiqua translatio habet, Ad orientem.
