Ideo paradisus dicitur esse in oriente, sed in qua parte orientis, diversimode traditur. Aliqui enim dicunt, quod sit in oriente æquinoctiali ; quia secundum istos, inter duos tropicos sub circulo æquinoctiali est temperatissima regio : ad quod auctor de Sphæra, multas rationes adducit. Unde et Bonaventura ait : Quum paradisus sit secus æquinoctialem, est ibi magna temperies temporis ; et propter puritatem aeris, est ibi contemperantia caloris. Sed quoniam Aristoteles dicit in secundo Meteororum, quod inter duos tropicos non potest esse regio habitabilis propter nimiam caliditatem, quia sol bis pertransit ibi in quolibet anno : idcirco qui in hoc sequuntur Philosophum, dicunt quod paradisus sit extra tropicos versus orientem æstivalem aut hiemalem. Et istud sanctus Thomas dicit rationabilius esse. Nam et terræ illi loco vicinæ, sunt intemperatæ propter propinquitatem ad solem. Est autem paradisus a terris habitabilibus remotus atque secretus, montibus, aquis, aut etiam intemperie aeris interpositis in mediis locis, ita ut adiri non possit ; nec notitia ejus poterit haberi, nisi ex revelatione. Idcirco philosophi et historiographi non sunt de eo locuti.
paras.en: Fourthly it is asked where paradise is. To which the answer is that where our translation has, [[2:8|from the beginning|A principio]], the old translation has, Toward the east [the older Latin version, made from the Greek Septuagint]. Therefore paradise is said to be in the east; but in what part of the east is handed down in different ways. For some say that it is in the equinoctial east [that is, in the east under the equator]; because, according to these, between the two tropics, under the equinoctial circle, lies the most temperate region: for which the author of the Sphere [Sacrobosco, in his treatise On the Sphere] brings many reasons. Hence Bonaventure too says: Since paradise is near the equinoctial, there is great mildness of season there; and because of the purity of the air, the heat there is tempered. But since Aristotle says in the second book of the Meteors that between the two tropics there cannot be a habitable region, because of excessive heat, since the sun passes over there twice in every year: therefore those who follow the Philosopher in this say that paradise is outside the tropics, toward the summer or the winter east [that is, toward the point where the sun rises at midsummer or at midwinter]. And St. Thomas says that this is more reasonable. For the lands near that place [under the equator] are intemperate because of their nearness to the sun. Paradise, moreover, is remote and hidden from the habitable lands, with mountains, waters, or even intemperate air lying in the places between, so that it cannot be reached; nor could knowledge of it be had except by revelation. Therefore the philosophers and the writers of history have not spoken of it.

paras.t: Produxitque Dominus Deus de humo, id est humida terra paradisi, omne lignum pulchrum visu, et ad vescendum suave, id est, universas arbores speciosas atque fructiferas, quarum fructus erant dulces ad manducandum. Istud, ut tactum est, fecit Deus tertia die. Nec solum in paradiso erant arbores pulchræ et fructuosæ, sed et ubique terrarum ; sed multo abundantius in paradiso, in quo erant etiam arbores quæ miras ac speciales habebant virtutes. Unde nunc subditur : Lignum etiam vitæ produxit Deus in medio paradisi. De hoc Magister secundo libro sic ait : Lignum vitæ, ut docent Beda et Strabus, sic dictum est, quia accepit divinitus hanc virtutem, ut qui ex ejus fructu comederet, corpus ejus firmaretur stabili sanitate, atque perpetua soliditate, nec ulla infirmitate aut ætatis debilitate in occasum vel in deterius laberetur. Hinc Strabus ait apertius, et habetur in Glossa : Lignum vitæ naturaliter habuit hanc naturam, ut qui ex ejus fructu comederet, perpetua soliditate firmaretur, atque beata immortalitate vestiretur, nulla infirmitate, anxietate, seniive lassitudine, aut imbecillitate fatigandus.
paras.en: [[2:9|And the Lord God brought forth of the ground|Produxitque Dominus Deus de humo]], that is, of the moist earth of paradise [Denis glosses *humus*, ground, as moist earth, *humida terra*], [[2:9|all manner of trees, fair to behold, and pleasant to eat of|omne lignum pulchrum visu, et ad vescendum suave]], that is, all trees comely and fruitful, whose fruits were sweet to eat. This, as was touched on before, God did on the third day. Nor were there fair and fruitful trees in paradise only, but everywhere on earth; but far more abundantly in paradise, in which there were also trees that had wonderful and special powers. Hence it now goes on: [[2:9|the tree of life also|Lignum etiam vitæ]] God brought forth [[2:9|in the midst of paradise|in medio paradisi]]. Of this the Master [Peter Lombard, in the Sentences] says thus in the second book: The tree of life, as Bede and Strabo teach, is so called because it received from God this power, that whoever ate of its fruit, his body would be made firm with stable health and perpetual soundness, and would not slip into decline or into a worse state through any infirmity or the weakness of age. Hence Strabo says more plainly, and it is found in the Gloss: The tree of life had by nature this property, that whoever ate of its fruit would be made firm with perpetual soundness and clothed with blessed immortality, never to be wearied by any infirmity, anxiety, the tiredness of old age, or feebleness.

paras.t: Sed mirum videtur, et quæri potest, qualiter res illa pure corporalis, potuit tantam habere virtutem. Ad quod posset quis breviter respondere, quod multæ gemmæ et herbæ ac consimilia, multas occultissimas habent vires, mirificas et valde mirabiles : quod potissime competit his quæ in paradiso nascuntur. Circa hoc scribit Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 97 : Duo remedia data sunt homini in statu innocentiæ, contra duos defectus ; quorum defectuum unus, est deperditio humidi naturalis ex actione naturalis caloris. Et contra hunc defectum subveniebatur, vel potius subventum fuisset, si non peccasset, homini per esum lignorum paradisi communiter, juxta quod infra habetur : Ex omni ligno paradisi vesceris. Alius defectus est ex admixtione extranei nutrimenti cum valido ac humido naturali, ex cujus admixtione naturalis vigor complexionis debilitatur magis magisque successive, secundum Philosophum libro de Generatione, quemadmodum vinum ex permixtione aquæ, debile redditur tanto plus, quo amplius ei miscetur, ita quod tandem ex lymphatione corrumpitur. Et contra hunc defectum, subventum fuisset homini per esum ligni vitæ. Propter quod quartodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Cibus aderat homini, ne esuriret ; potus, ne sitiret ; lignum vitæ, ne illum senectus dissolveret. Unde infra fertur : Videte ne forte sumat de ligno vitæ, et vivat in æternum. Imo Augustinus testatur, quod homo potuisset post peccatum semper vivere, si ei permissum fuisset de ligno vitæ comedere.
paras.en: But it seems a wonder, and it may be asked, how that purely bodily thing could have so great a power. To which one could briefly answer that many gems and herbs and the like have many most hidden powers, marvellous and very wonderful: and this applies above all to the things that grow in paradise. On this Thomas writes in the First Part, question 97: Two remedies were given to man in the state of innocence, against two defects. One of these defects is the loss of the natural moisture through the action of the natural heat [the *humidum naturale* or *radicale* of medieval physiology, the body's vital moisture, thought to be slowly used up through life]. And against this defect man was helped, or rather would have been helped had he not sinned, by eating of the trees of paradise in general, according to what is found below: [[2:16|Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Ex omni ligno paradisi vesceris]]. The other defect comes from the mixing of foreign nourishment with the strong and natural moisture, through which mixing the natural vigour of the constitution is weakened more and more by degrees, according to the Philosopher in the book On Generation; just as wine, by being mixed with water, is made the weaker the more water is mixed with it, so that at last it is spoiled by the watering. And against this defect man would have been helped by eating of the tree of life. For which reason Augustine says in the fourteenth book of the City of God: Food was at hand for man, lest he hunger; drink, lest he thirst; the tree of life, lest old age should dissolve him. Hence it is said below: See, [[Gen 3:22|lest perhaps he|ne forte]] [[Gen 3:22|take also of the tree of life|sumat de ligno vitæ]], [[Gen 3:22|and live for ever|et vivat in æternum]]. Indeed Augustine testifies that man could have lived for ever even after sin, had he been permitted to eat of the tree of life.

paras.t: Præterea de hac materia scribit Bonaventura super secundum, distinctione 17 : Universitas lignorum paradisi, sub tribus comprehenditur differentiis, secundum quod ad triplicem hominis utilitatem poterant ordinari. Nam poterant ei prodesse, quantum ad corpus, aut quantum ad animam, aut quantum ad utrumque conjunctum. Si primo modo, sic erant ligna fructifera quæ præbebant ei alimenta, quantum ad corporis sustentationem. Si quantum ad animam, sic fuit lignum scientiæ boni et mali, quod ordinabatur ad probationem obedientiæ hominis. Si quantum ad totum compositum, sic fuit lignum vitæ, quod facere potuisset ad humanæ vitæ perpetuationem. Unde hæc duo ligna dumtaxat specialiter nominantur, propter suos speciales effectus, propter quos Deus posuit illa duo in medio paradisi juxta se invicem, ut ex uno, utpote ex ligno vitæ, conciperet affectum amoris : ex alio, affectum timoris. Lignum quoque vitæ sic appellatur, non ab effectu quem habuit, sed ad quem ordinabatur, quem etiam habuisset, si homo stetisset. Hæc Bonaventura.
paras.en: Moreover Bonaventure writes on this matter, on the second book [of the Sentences], distinction 17: The whole of the trees of paradise is comprised under three differences, according as they could be ordered to a threefold use for man. For they could profit him as to the body, or as to the soul, or as to both joined together. If in the first way, such were the fruit-bearing trees, which provided him with food for the sustaining of the body. If as to the soul, such was the tree of knowledge of good and evil, which was ordered to the testing of man's obedience. If as to the whole composite, such was the tree of life, which could have served for the perpetuation of human life. Hence these two trees alone are named specially, because of their special effects; and on account of these God set those two in the midst of paradise next to each other, so that from the one, namely from the tree of life, man might conceive the affection of love, and from the other the affection of fear. The tree of life, too, is so called not from an effect which it had, but from the effect to which it was ordered, which it would also have had if man had stood. Thus far Bonaventure.

paras.t: De alio autem ligno subjungitur : lignumque, id est arborem scientiæ boni et mali. Arbor illa ita vocata est ex eventu, quoniam homo manducando de fructu ligni illius, experimentaliter didicit et cognovit in malum suum, quid sit obedientiæ virtus, quid inobedientiæ vitium, et quantum distant ista ab invicem : quod tamen ante habitualiter scivit notitia simplici, sed non experimentali. Verumtamen in his verbis per bonum et malum, intelligi possunt tam bona et mala corporalia, quam bona et mala spiritualia. Unde in Scholastica historia dicitur : Lignum scientiæ boni et mali, vocatum est ex eo, quod secutum est post comestionem, utpote ex pœna inflicta pro illo peccato. Prius enim homo nesciebat quid esset malum, quia nondum expertus. Bonum dicimus sanitatem et fortitudinem, malum vero ægritudinem et imbecillitatem, quæ nondum senserat. Cognoverat quidem ea per scientiam, quia ex uno contrariorum cognoscitur reliquum, sed non per experientiam, quemadmodum medicus qui nunquam fuit infirmus, scit morbos : sed dum ægrotat, magis eos cognoscit, quia cognoscit et sentit : sicut de puero delicate nutrito dicitur, quod ignorat quid sit malum sive paupertas. Rursus in eadem habetur Historia, quod Plato per lignum vitæ, per lignum quoque scientiæ boni et mali, intellexit hominem ipsum, quia putavit nomina illa non convenire arboribus.
paras.en: Of the other tree it is added: [[2:9|and the tree|lignumque]], that is, the tree [[2:9|of knowledge of good and evil|scientiæ boni et mali]]. That tree was so called from the outcome, since man, by eating of the fruit of that tree, learned and came to know by experience, to his own harm, what the virtue of obedience is, what the vice of disobedience, and how far they stand apart from each other: which he had known before habitually, by simple knowledge, but not by experience. Yet in these words, by good and evil may be understood both bodily goods and evils and spiritual goods and evils. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: The tree of knowledge of good and evil was so named from what followed after the eating, namely from the punishment inflicted for that sin. For before, man did not know what evil was, because he had not yet experienced it. We call good health and strength, and evil sickness and weakness, which he had not yet felt. He had known them indeed by knowledge, since one of two contraries is known from the other, but not by experience; just as a physician who has never been sick knows diseases, but when he falls sick knows them better, because he both knows and feels them: as it is said of a boy delicately brought up that he does not know what evil, or poverty, is. Again it is found in the same History that Plato understood by the tree of life, and also by the tree of knowledge of good and evil, man himself, because he thought those names did not fit trees.

paras.t: Præterea de his lignis ait Damascenus libro secundo : In medio paradisi plantavit Deus lignum vitæ et lignum cognitionis, per experientiam quamdam et approbationem, et exercitium obedientiæ et inobedientiæ hominis : ideo lignum cognitionis boni et mali vocatur. Lignum autem vitæ sic dictum est, vel quasi habens operationem tributivam vitæ, vel quia solum comestibile dignis vitæ, et non subjectis morti. Refert quidam hoc loco, quod Josephus dicit primo Antiquitatum libro, quod fructus arboris scientiæ boni et mali habuit virtutem accelerandi usum rationis : quod ille reprobat, dicens hoc falsum esse, quoniam virtus corporalis non se extendit ad hujusmodi accelerationem. Sed quidquid sit de veritate dicti Josephi, quem Hieronymus dicit fuisse virum doctissimum, ratio reprobationis illius non valet. Nam dato quod virtus corporalis non extenderet se directe ad accelerationem præfatam, quæ est spiritualis effectus, tamen dispositive et cooperative ac instrumentaliter posset se virtus corporalis ad effectum illum extendere. Nam et gemmæ aliquæ habent virtutem influendi et imprimendi in animam rationalem, atque causandi in ea diversas affectiones, imo et inducendi eam ad actus plurimos virtuosos. Legitur quoque in libro Tobiæ, quod fumus cordis piscis cujusdam habeat vim extricandi omne genus dæmoniorum. Denique Damascenus ait libro secundo, quod lignum scientiæ boni et mali, ita vocatum est propter causam expressam, aut quoniam dabat accipientibus virtutem naturæ propriæ cognitivam, quod bonum erat perfectis, malum autem imperfectioribus, quemadmodum solidus cibus, malus est mollibus adhuc et lacte egentibus. Porro verba Josephi sunt hæc : Illa plantatio, scilicet arbor prudentiæ, causa acuminis erat et intellectus, quod juxta prætacta posset ad pium trahi intellectum.
paras.en: Moreover Damascene says of these trees in the second book: In the midst of paradise God planted the tree of life and the tree of knowledge, for a kind of experience and proving, and an exercise of man's obedience and disobedience: therefore it is called the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The tree of life, again, is so called either as having an operation that bestows life, or because it was to be eaten only by those worthy of life, and not by those subject to death. A certain writer relates at this place that Josephus says in the first book of the Antiquities that the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil had the power of hastening the use of reason: which that writer rejects, saying that this is false, since a bodily power does not extend to a hastening of this kind. But whatever be the truth of Josephus's saying (Jerome says that he was a most learned man), the reason given for that rejection does not hold. For granted that a bodily power would not extend directly to the aforesaid hastening, which is a spiritual effect, yet a bodily power could extend to that effect dispositively, co-operatively and instrumentally. For some gems too have the power of flowing into the rational soul and making an impression on it, and of causing various affections in it, and even of inducing it to a great many virtuous acts. We read too in the book of Tobias that the smoke of the heart of a certain fish has power to drive away every kind of devil[[Tob 6:8||]]. Lastly Damascene says in the second book that the tree of knowledge of good and evil was so called for the reason stated, or because it gave to those who took of it a power of knowing their own nature, which was good for the perfect but bad for the less perfect, just as solid food is bad for those who are still tender and in need of milk. Now the words of Josephus are these: That plant, namely the tree of prudence, was a cause of sharpness and of understanding: which, in the light of what was said above, could be drawn to a pious sense.

paras.t: Et fluvius egrediebatur de loco voluptatis ad irrigandum paradisum. Quum locus voluptatis et paradisus sint idem, quomodo fluvius egrediebatur de loco voluptatis, id est de paradiso, ad irrigandum paradisum ? Et respondendum, quod fluvius ille oriebatur in quadam parte paradisi ex redundantissimo fonte, et ita currebat per paradisum, ad irrigandum eumdem et planitiem ac arbusta et virgulta ipsius, quemadmodum Nilus plana loca Ægypti. Porro in Scholastica historia dicitur, quod fons ille potest intelligi vel abyssus, hoc est omnium matrix aquarum, vel pro fontibus pluraliter. Unde et alii dicunt, quod fluvius paradisi oriebatur ibi de fonte vel fontibus. Sic namque Hieronymus ait quod Jordanis habet duos fontes, unum nomine Jor, alium nomine Dan. Verumtamen Damascenus ait libro secundo : Oceanus est velut fluvius quidam, circuiens omnem terram. De quo mihi videtur dixisse Scriptura divina, quoniam fluvius procedit de paradiso. Hic Oceanus in quatuor principia, hoc est in quatuor flumina dividitur. Nomen uni Phison. Ex his Damasceni verbis apparet, quod Oceanus sit fluvius de paradiso egrediens. Ad hoc Thomas super secundum respondet, quod primum principium illorum fluminum, sicut et ceterarum aquarum, est Oceanus; sed principium proximum est fons ille, qui surgit in illa parte terræ. Dicitur ergo Oceanus de paradiso egredi, atque in quatuor capita dividi, in quantum fons ille paradisi et fluvius, quem ibidem producit, ex Oceano primordialiter fluit et exit.
paras.en: [[2:10|And a river went out of the place of pleasure to water paradise|Et fluvius egrediebatur de loco voluptatis ad irrigandum paradisum]]. Since the place of pleasure and paradise are the same, how did a river go out of the place of pleasure, that is, out of paradise, to water paradise? The answer must be that that river rose in a certain part of paradise from a most abundant spring, and so ran through paradise to water it, its plain and its groves and thickets, as the Nile waters the flat lands of Egypt. Further, it is said in the Scholastic History that that spring may be understood either as the abyss, that is, the mother of all waters, or as springs in the plural. Hence others too say that the river of paradise rose there from a spring or springs. For so Jerome says that the Jordan has two springs, one by the name of Jor, the other by the name of Dan. Yet Damascene says in the second book: The Ocean is as it were a certain river going round the whole earth. It seems to me that divine Scripture spoke of it in saying that [[2:10|a river went out|fluvius procedit]] of paradise. This Ocean is divided into four beginnings, that is, into four rivers. [[2:11|The name of the one is Phison|Nomen uni Phison]]. From these words of Damascene it appears that the Ocean is the river going out of paradise. To this Thomas, on the second book [of the Sentences], answers that the first beginning of those rivers, as of the other waters, is the Ocean; but their nearest beginning is that spring which rises in that part of the earth. The Ocean, then, is said to go out of paradise and to be divided into four heads inasmuch as that spring of paradise, and the river which it brings forth there, flows and goes out from the Ocean in the first place.

paras.t: Qui inde dividitur in quatuor capita, hoc est, fluvius ille per paradisum decurrens, tandem per quatuor meatus seu loca se dividit, et currere incipit, sive in paradiso, sive extra et prope eum, incipiat illa divisio. Dividitur ergo in quatuor capita, hoc est in quatuor magna ac principalia flumina, quæ licet habeant unum caput in paradiso, nihilo minus capitalia nuncupantur, per comparationem ad aquas, quæ extra paradisum in diversis regionibus manant ex ipsis.
paras.en: [[2:10|which from thence is divided into four heads|Qui inde dividitur in quatuor capita]], that is, that river, running down through paradise, at length divides itself through four channels or places and begins to run, whether that division begins in paradise or outside it and near it. It is divided, then, into four heads, that is, into four great and principal rivers, which, although they have one head in paradise, are none the less called heads [Latin *capitalia*, “head” or “chief” rivers] by comparison with the waters which flow out from them in various regions outside paradise.

paras.t: Nomen unius Phison. Phison, ut dicitur, in Hebræo fertilitatem seu abundantiam sonat : sicque fluvius ille dicitur Phison, quasi piscibus plenus, vel quoniam terram per quam fluit, fecundat. De hoc in Scholastica historia scribitur : Phison a Gangaro rege, alio nomine dictus est Ganges. Et secundum Isidorum, Phison interpretatur caterva, quoniam decem flumina intra se recipit, quæ scilicet extra paradisum hinc inde fluunt in ipsum : vel mutatio oris, quia mutatur a facie seu dispositione, quam habet in paradiso. Mutatur quippe secundum diversa loca in tribus, videlicet in colore, quoniam alibi clarus est, alibi turbidus ; in quantitate, quia alicubi parvus, alicubi magnus ; in sensu, nam in aliquibus locis est calidus, in aliis frigidus.
paras.en: [[2:11|The name of the one is Phison|Nomen unius Phison]]. Phison, as is said, means in Hebrew fertility or abundance: and so that river is called Phison as if full of fish [the Latin *piscibus*, fish, echoes the name], or because it makes fruitful the land through which it flows. Of this it is written in the Scholastic History: Phison was called by another name Ganges, from King Gangarus. And according to Isidore, Phison is interpreted *a troop*, since it receives into itself ten rivers, which flow into it from this side and that outside paradise; or *change of face*, since it is changed from the face or condition which it has in paradise. For it changes from place to place in three things: in colour, since in one place it is clear, in another muddy; in size, since in some places it is small, in others great; and in feeling, for in some places it is warm, in others cold.

paras.t: Ipse est qui circuit omnem terram Hevilath, id est, Phison hinc inde decurrit per Indiam, quæ dicta est Hevilath, ab Hevila filio Jectan, de quo infra habetur. Quocirca sciendum quod infra legitur de duobus qui dicti sunt Hevila. Et India dicta est Hevilath, ab Hevila illo qui fuit filius Jectan, propter quod ait Glossa : Hevilath regio Indiæ, post diluvium possessa est ab Hevila filio Jectan, filii Heber, patriarchæ Hebræorum. Porro an Phison ita circumeat Indiam, ut faciat eam insulam, certum non habeo. Ubi nascitur aurum. Plinius etenim dicit, quod regiones Indiæ præ ceteris abundent aureis venis, id est subterraneis venis et locis, in quibus nascitur aurum. In Scholastica quoque historia dicitur, quod fluvius iste aureas trahit arenas. Et aurum terræ illius, videlicet Indiæ, optimum est, utpote magis decoctum, purum, pretiosum ac virtuosum in proprietatibus auri, quarum una est exhilarare videntem. Ibique invenitur bdellium. Circa hoc habetur in Glossa : Bdellium, secundum Plinium, est arbor aromatica, magnitudine oleagina, cujus lacrima, id est humor seu gutta, est lucida, gustu amara, ac boni odoris, sed odoratior fit vini infusione. Et lapis onychinus. Onyx, ut ait Glossa, est lapis pretiosus, sic dictus, quia permixtum habet candorem, ad similitudinem unguis humani. Unguis etenim Græce vocatur onyx. Itaque lapis ille coloratus est instar humani unguis. Antiqua translatio habet carbunculum, qui ignei est coloris, et dicitur illustrare tenebras noctis.
paras.en: [[2:11|that is it which compasseth all the land of Hevilath|Ipse est qui circuit omnem terram Hevilath]], that is, Phison runs this way and that through India, which was called Hevilath from Hevila the son of Jectan, of whom we read below[[Gen 10:29||]] [the margin gives Gen. x, 22; Hevila the son of Jectan is named at Gen 10:29]. On this it should be known that below we read of two men who were called Hevila. And India was called Hevilath from that Hevila who was the son of Jectan; for which reason the Gloss says: Hevilath, a region of India, was possessed after the flood by Hevila the son of Jectan, son of Heber, the patriarch of the Hebrews. But whether Phison so goes round India as to make it an island, I do not know for certain. [[2:11|where gold groweth|Ubi nascitur aurum]]. For Pliny says that the regions of India abound beyond others in veins of gold, that is, in underground veins and places in which gold grows. In the Scholastic History too it is said that this river carries golden sands. [[2:12|And the gold of that land|Et aurum terræ illius]], namely of India, [[2:12|is very good|optimum est]], as being more refined, pure, precious and potent in the properties of gold, one of which is to gladden the one who looks on it. [[2:12|there is found bdellium|Ibique invenitur bdellium]]. On this it is found in the Gloss: Bdellium, according to Pliny, is an aromatic tree, of the size of an olive tree, whose tear, that is, its sap or drop, is clear, bitter to the taste and of good odour, but becomes more fragrant when wine is poured on it. [[2:12|and the onyx stone|Et lapis onychinus]]. Onyx, as the Gloss says, is a precious stone so called because it has a whiteness mixed in it, after the likeness of a human nail. For a nail is called *onyx* in Greek. And so that stone is coloured like a human nail. The old translation has *carbuncle*, which is of a fiery colour and is said to light up the darkness of night.

paras.t: Et nomen fluvii secundi est Gehon. Ipse est qui circuit omnem terram Æthiopiæ ; et inde descendit in Ægyptum, et ibi vocatur Nilus, et est turbidus. Nomen vero fluminis tertii, Tigris, qui ita vocatur, quia velocissime currit instar tigridis, quæ est celerrimum animal. Ipse vadit contra Assyrios, id est per terram Assyriorum, deinde per majorem (ut fertur) Armeniam. Et dicitur ire seu currere contra Assyrios, quasi ex opposito Assyriorum, respectu pergentium illuc ex altera parte. Fluvius autem quartus, ipse est Euphrates, qui currit per Chaldæam, et est unus terminus terræ Israel, imo secundum Glossam, in vicino irrigat terram promissionis : ideo Moyses non expressit, per quam terram decurrat, quoniam satis innotuit filiis Israel, quibus hæc scripsit. Currit quoque per minorem Armeniam et Persiam, ut legitur.
paras.en: [[2:13|And the name of the second river is Gehon|Et nomen fluvii secundi est Gehon]]. [[2:13|the same is it that compasseth all the land of Ethiopia|Ipse est qui circuit omnem terram Æthiopiæ]]; and from there it goes down into Egypt, and there it is called the Nile, and it is muddy. [[2:14|And the name of the third river is Tigris|Nomen vero fluminis tertii, Tigris]], which is so called because it runs very swiftly, like the tiger, which is the swiftest of animals. [[2:14|the same passeth along by the Assyrians|Ipse vadit contra Assyrios]], that is, through the land of the Assyrians, and then (as is said) through Greater Armenia. And it is said to go or run *against* the Assyrians [Latin *contra Assyrios*, which the Douay-Rheims renders “along by the Assyrians”], as it were over against the Assyrians, with respect to those travelling there from the other side. [[2:14|And the fourth river is Euphrates|Fluvius autem quartus, ipse est Euphrates]], which runs through Chaldea and is one boundary of the land of Israel; indeed, according to the Gloss, it waters the land of promise near by: and therefore Moses did not state through what land it runs, since it was well enough known to the children of Israel, for whom he wrote these things. It runs also through Lesser Armenia and Persia, as we read.

paras.t: Porro adversarii legis Moysis quidam hæretici atque philosophi, dixerunt hæc omnia quæ de ortu fluviorum istorum recitat Moyses, esse conficta et fabulam falsam, quia ad oculum constat, quod fluvii isti habent ortum extra paradisum, et in terra habitabili. Phison namque oritur in locis Caucasi montis ; Gehon non procul ab Atlante, qui est mons Africæ ad occidentem ; Tigris et Euphrates ex Armenia, ut etiam Beda refert. Ad istud respondetur in Scholastica historia : Quatuor flumina ista ab eodem fonte paradisi emanant, ac separantur. Et quidam eorum iterum inter se commiscentur, et iterum separantur. Sæpe quoque absorbentur a terra, atque in pluribus locis rursus erumpunt. Hinc Augustinus octavo libro super Genesim ait, quod sicut in aliis contingit fluminibus ut alicubi intrent terram, et alibi exeant, ita de fluviis istis credendum. Unde et aliqui dicunt, quod Pison currit per deserta Indiæ quandoque sub terra, aliquando super terram. Hinc ortus fluviorum horum diversi leguntur.
paras.en: Further, certain heretics and philosophers, adversaries of the law of Moses, said that all these things which Moses relates about the source of these rivers are made up and a false fable, because it is plain to the eye that these rivers have their source outside paradise and in the habitable earth. For Phison rises in the region of Mount Caucasus; Gehon not far from Atlas, which is a mountain of Africa toward the west; Tigris and Euphrates in Armenia, as Bede also relates. To this the answer is given in the Scholastic History: These four rivers flow forth from the same spring of paradise and are separated. And some of them mingle again with one another, and are separated again. Often too they are swallowed up by the earth, and break out again in many places. Hence Augustine says in the eighth book on Genesis that, just as it happens with other rivers that they enter the earth in one place and come out in another, so it is to be believed of these rivers. Hence some also say that Pison runs through the deserts of India, sometimes under the earth, sometimes above the earth. Hence different sources are read of for these rivers.

2.title: Elucidatio residuæ partis hujus capituli: Tulit ergo Dominus
2.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this chapter: “And the Lord God took”

paras.t: Tulit ergo Dominus Deus hominem, et posuit eum in paradisum voluptatis. Communiter dicitur, quod Deus formavit primum hominem in agro Damasceno, de terra, limo seu pulvere terræ illius; sed ex quo fundamento procedat hoc dictum, ignoro, nisi forte quis dicat, quod in eo loco formatus est Adam, ad quem post transgressionem suam rejectus est, sicque post expulsionem a paradiso, credatur habitasse in loco illo ac prope. Nam et sepultus creditur in spelunca duplici prope Hebron, sicut in libro Josue legitur: Adam maximus ibi inter Enacim situs est. Sed quæri potest, qualiter Deus tulit hominem de loco suæ formationis, an per se ipsum, utpote solo imperio, an per subjectam creaturam seu famulatu angelico, an forsitan ivit pedester usque ad paradisum, cujus exsistentiam et locum scire non poterat, nisi ex revelatione: ergo nec viam ad paradisum, nisi eodem modo seu ducatu angelico. Et reor probabile, quod obsequio angelico facta sit illa translatio etiam subito, quamvis non in instanti, quemadmodum angelus tulit Habacuc de Judæa in Babylonem. Et infra habetur quod Dominus tulit Enoch, quem etiam in paradisum tunc transtulit.
paras.en: [[2:15|And the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise of pleasure|Tulit ergo Dominus Deus hominem, et posuit eum in paradisum voluptatis]]. It is commonly said that God formed the first man in the Damascene field, out of the earth, the slime or dust of that land; but on what ground this saying rests I do not know, unless perhaps someone were to say that Adam was formed in the place to which he was cast back after his transgression, and so, after his expulsion from paradise, he is believed to have lived in that place or near it. For he is also believed to have been buried in the double cave near Hebron, as we read in the book of Josue: [[Jos 14:15|Adam the greatest among the Enacims was laid there|Adam maximus ibi inter Enacim situs est]] [the margin gives Josue xv, 15; the words are at Jos 14:15. Denis, with the tradition of his time, takes this Adam to be the first man]. But it may be asked how God took man from the place of his formation: whether by himself, that is, by his command alone, or through a creature subject to him, that is, by the service of angels; or whether perhaps man went on foot as far as paradise, whose existence and place he could not know except by revelation, and so could not know the way to paradise either, except in the same manner, that is, under the guidance of an angel. And I think it probable that this removal was made by the ministry of angels, and suddenly too, though not in an instant, as the angel carried Habacuc from Judea into Babylon[[Dan 14:35||]]. And further on we have it that the Lord took Henoch[[Gen 5:24||]], whom he then also removed into paradise.

paras.t: Posuit itaque eum in paradiso voluptatis, propter causas præcedenti articulo tactas. Factus est autem extra paradisum, et deinde constitutus est in eo, ut operaretur, hoc est, ut ipse homo operaretur paradisum, faciendo in eo aliqua opera delectabilia et jucunda per agriculturam, non ex necessitate aut indigentia, sed potius ex abundanti lætitia, ad experientiam et exercitationem naturalis virtutis. Nec tamen operatio talis corporalis exterior, fuit ratio principalis, propter quam in paradiso est positus; imo principaliter constitutus est ibi, ut operaretur actus spirituales interiores divinos, vacando contemplationi ac laudibus Creatoris, quousque peregrinatione completa, transferretur ad vitam perfecte beatam et paradisum cœlestem. Et custodiret illum, id est, ipse primus homo custodiret sibi ipsi paradisum, ne peccando mereretur privari habitatione tam deliciosa, et tam gratiose concessa; non autem indiguit paradisum ab impugnatoribus custodire. Potest et ita intelligi: Posuit eum in paradisum, ut ipse Deus operaretur hominem, id est, exerceret et coleret eum, perficiendo eum in omni virtute et profectu assiduo, et custodiret hominem in paradiso ab omni exteriori læsivo, atque ab omni periculo, quantum in se fuit.
paras.en: So he [[2:15|put him into the paradise of pleasure|Posuit itaque eum in paradiso voluptatis]], for the reasons touched on in the preceding article. Now he was made outside paradise, and then established in it [[2:15|to dress it|ut operaretur]], that is, so that man himself should work paradise, doing in it some delightful and pleasant works by tilling it, not from necessity or need, but rather out of overflowing gladness, to try and exercise his natural powers. Yet such bodily, outward work was not the principal reason for which he was placed in paradise; rather, he was established there principally to perform inward, spiritual and divine acts, giving himself to contemplation and to the praises of the Creator, until, his pilgrimage completed, he should be carried over to the perfectly blessed life and the heavenly paradise. [[2:15|and to keep it|Et custodiret illum]], that is, that the first man himself should keep paradise for himself, lest by sinning he should deserve to be deprived of so delightful a dwelling, so graciously granted; for he had no need to guard paradise against assailants. It may also be understood thus: he [[2:15|put him into the paradise|Posuit eum in paradisum]] so that God himself should work man, that is, exercise and cultivate him, perfecting him in every virtue and in constant progress, and should keep man in paradise from everything outward that could harm him and from every danger, as far as lay with him.

paras.t: Præcepitque ei, dicens: Ex omni ligno paradisi comede, hoc est, de fructibus omnium arborum paradisi manduca, excepto eo quod subditur: De ligno autem scientiæ boni et mali ne comedas.
paras.en: [[2:16|And he commanded him, saying: Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Præcepitque ei, dicens: Ex omni ligno paradisi comede]][[Gen 1:29||]] [the margin refers to Gen 1:29, where God first gave man the trees for food], that is, eat of the fruits of all the trees of paradise, except what is added: [[2:17|But of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat|De ligno autem scientiæ boni et mali ne comedas]].

paras.t: Deus in omnibus agit, quod suam bonitatem, sapientiam et excellentiam decet. Nec ideo omittit id facere, quoniam prævidet creaturas abusuras et ingratas futuras beneficiis suis, præsertim quia ex earum abusione, ingratitudine et peccatis, novit multa bona elicere, et prava per justitiam ordinare. Quemadmodum ergo non omisit angelos reprobos condere, quia prævidit eos mox æternaliter perituros: ita non omisit primo homini dare præceptum, quamvis sciret eum illud protinus transgressurum, et posteritatem suam perditurum. Hinc asserit Augustinus: Oportebat ut homo sub Domino positus, ab aliqua re prohiberetur, ut virtus ei esset promerendi ipsa obedientia, quæ sola verissime virtus est rationali creaturæ sub Dei potestate degenti: quemadmodum primus et maximus tumor est, velle uti ad libitum propria potestate, quod est inobedientia. Nec erat unde homo cogitaret Dominum se habere, nisi aliquid ei juberetur.
paras.en: God does in all things what befits his goodness, wisdom and excellence; nor does he leave off doing it because he foresees that creatures will abuse his benefits and be ungrateful for them, especially since out of their abuse, ingratitude and sins he knows how to draw many goods, and to set wicked things in order by his justice. So, just as he did not leave off creating the reprobate angels because he foresaw that they would soon perish eternally, so he did not leave off giving the first man a precept, though he knew that he would straightway transgress it and ruin his posterity. Hence Augustine asserts: It was fitting that man, placed under the Lord, should be forbidden something, so that obedience itself should be his virtue for meriting, which alone is most truly virtue for a rational creature living under God's power; just as the first and greatest swelling [that is, of pride] is to wish to use one's own power at one's pleasure, which is disobedience. Nor had man anything to make him think that he had a Lord, unless something were commanded him.

paras.t: Denique secundum Bonaventuram, Deus prohibuit homini esum ligni illius, propter meritum obedientiæ acquirendum ex parte hominis, et propter ostendendum jurisdictionis suæ imperium, quod habebat in homine. Et quia prohibuit illud propter obedientiæ meritum, idcirco ut meritum illud esset plenum, a tali re prohibuit hominem, a qua non debuit abstinere, nisi obedientiæ solius intuitu: et ideo prohibuit eum a re in se bona, scilicet a fructu ligni illius, ab actu non malo in se, hoc est ab esu fructus illius. Rursus, quia prohibuit ad ostendendum suæ jurisdictionis dominium, ideo a tali re debuit prohibere, a qua homo non deberet manum retrahere, nisi propter solum Dei imperium: et hoc fuit res bona. Hinc mandatum illud, vocatur mandatum disciplinæ: quia ad hoc homo non obligabatur ex se, aut ex aliquo naturalis rationis dictamine, sed ex sola Dei præceptione. Itaque, sicut prætactum est, decor qui attenditur in operibus Dei secundum regulam divinæ sapientiæ, intermitti non debet propter commodum creaturæ.
paras.en: Again, according to Bonaventure, God forbade man to eat of that tree for the sake of the merit of obedience to be gained on man's part, and to show the sovereignty of his jurisdiction which he had over man. And because he forbade it for the merit of obedience, therefore, so that the merit might be full, he forbade man a thing from which he had no need to abstain except out of regard for obedience alone; and so he forbade him a thing good in itself, namely the fruit of that tree, and an act not evil in itself, namely the eating of that fruit. Again, because he forbade it to show the dominion of his jurisdiction, he had to forbid a thing from which man would not have to withdraw his hand except for God's command alone: and this was a good thing. Hence that commandment is called a commandment of discipline [*mandatum disciplinæ*: a positive precept, binding by God's command alone and not by natural law], because man was not bound to it of himself, or by any dictate of natural reason, but by God's command alone. So, as was touched on above, the comeliness that is looked for in the works of God according to the rule of divine wisdom ought not to be left aside for the creature's convenience.

paras.t: Et quoniam homo timore pœnæ frequenter retrahitur ab iniquitate, Deus comminationem adjecit: In quacumque enim die naturali, quæ noctem includit, comederis ex eo, morte morieris, id est, necessitatem moriendi in corpore mox incurres. Unde alia translatio habet, mortalis eris, atque in anima protinus spiritualiter morieris peccando mortaliter. Nec istud fuit comminatio tantum, sed etiam vera et absoluta prænuntiatio.
paras.en: And since man is often held back from iniquity by fear of punishment, God added a threat: [[2:17|For in what day soever|In quacumque enim die]] (a natural day, that is, which includes the night) [[2:17|thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death|comederis ex eo, morte morieris]], that is, thou shalt straightway incur the necessity of dying in the body (hence another translation has: thou shalt be mortal), and in the soul thou shalt at once die spiritually by sinning mortally. Nor was this a threat only, but also a true and absolute foretelling.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæri potest, cur ait, Morte morieris, quum sufficeret dicere, Morieris. Ad quod respondendum, quod talis replicatio seu ingeminatio, est Hebræi sermonis proprietas, sicut in libris veteris Testamenti uberrime innotescit. Porro Henricus de Hassia circa hoc scribit: Est, inquiens, vita ad mortem, et est mors ad vitam. Quidam enim dum vivunt, moriuntur: et quidam dum moriuntur, vivunt. Fiunt ergo, ut ait Ambrosius, quatuor distinctiones seu combinationes, quæ sunt: Vita vivere, morte mori, vita mori, et morte vivere. Vita vivere, est virtute et gratia vivere, et merita vitæ beatæ habere in hujus corporis vita. Morte mori, est cum morte corporis animam non habere meritum vitæ æternæ. Sed vita moritur, qui vitiose vivendo, mortem damnationis meretur. Morte autem vivunt, qui moriuntur ut vivant, ut martyres sancti.
paras.en: On this it may be asked why he says, [[2:17|thou shalt die the death|Morte morieris]], when it would be enough to say, Thou shalt die. To which the answer is that such repetition or doubling is a property of Hebrew speech, as appears most abundantly in the books of the Old Testament. Further, Henry of Hesse writes on this: There is, he says, a life unto death, and there is a death unto life. For some, while they live, die; and some, while they die, live. There are thus, as Ambrose says, four distinctions or combinations, namely: to live with life, to die with death, to die with life, and to live with death. To live with life is to live by virtue and grace, and to have the merits of the blessed life in the life of this body. To die with death is, with the death of the body, for the soul not to have the merit of eternal life. But he dies with life who, by living viciously, merits the death of damnation. And they live by death who die that they may live, as the holy martyrs.

paras.t: Dixit quoque Dominus Deus: Non est bonum hominem esse solum, id est, virum sine uxore manere non expedit, habendo respectum ad finem conditi hominis et institutionis humanæ, qui est, ut per eum impleatur numerus electorum in patria, ad quod requiritur multiplicatio hominum, quæ sine utriusque sexus commixtione naturaliter fieri nequit. Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi, id est, personam ejusdem speciei, sed alterius sexus producamus, quæ viro cooperetur ad hominum multiplicationem.
paras.en: [[2:18|And the Lord God said: It is not good for man to be alone|Dixit quoque Dominus Deus: Non est bonum hominem esse solum]], that is, it is not expedient for the man to remain without a wife, having regard to the end for which man was made and mankind was instituted, which is that through it the number of the elect in the fatherland should be filled up; and for this the multiplication of men is required, which cannot naturally come about without the union of both sexes. [[2:18|let us make him a help like unto himself|Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi]], that is, let us bring forth a person of the same species but of the other sex, who may work together with the man for the multiplying of mankind.

paras.t: His dictis, adduxit Deus animalia bruta ad Adam, primo, ut Adæ pateret ad oculum, non esse inter animalia aliquod suppositum aptum ad prolificandum ex eo. Secundo, ut animalibus imponeret nomina. Unde subjungitur: Formatis igitur, Dominus Deus, de humo cunctis animantibus terræ, et universis volatilibus cœli, adduxit ea ad Adam, id est, postquam Deus universa animalia terræ et volucres cœli fecit de terra, præsentavit ea oculis Adæ, ut videret quid vocaret ea, hoc est, ut ipse Adam diligenter attenderet quo nomine unumquodque illorum esset vocandum, considerando singulorum naturas et proprietates, ex quibus sunt nomina imponenda.
paras.en: This said, God brought the brute animals to Adam: first, so that it might be plain to Adam's eyes that among the animals there was no individual [*suppositum*, a subsisting individual] fit for begetting offspring with him; secondly, that he might give names to the animals. Hence it is added: [[2:19|And the Lord God having formed out of the ground all the beasts of the earth, and all the fowls of the air, brought them to Adam|Formatis igitur, Dominus Deus, de humo cunctis animantibus terræ, et universis volatilibus cœli, adduxit ea ad Adam]], that is, after God had made all the animals of the earth and the birds of the air from the earth, he presented them to Adam's eyes, [[2:19|to see what he would call them|ut videret quid vocaret ea]], that is, that Adam himself should carefully consider by what name each of them was to be called, considering the natures and properties of each, from which names are to be given.

paras.t: Circa hoc triplex est quæstio. Prima, quemadmodo aves dicuntur nunc factæ de humo, quum capitulo præcedenti productæ legantur de aqua. Secunda, qualiter animalia sunt adducta ad Adam. Tertia, cur voluit Deus ut eis imponeret nomina. Ad primam Augustinus respondet, quod humus seu terra nunc sumitur, prout alia elementa includit, quemadmodum in exordio primi capituli, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Potest et aliter responderi, quod ideo dicuntur aves factæ de terra, quoniam in earum corporibus elementum terræ prædominatur, quantum ad materiæ quantitatem. Ad secundam similiter Augustinus respondet, quod non violentia, nec voce formata in aere, sed ministerio angelorum animalia sint adducta. Alii dicunt, quod solo jussu Omnipotentis. Quidam etiam opinati fuerunt, quod adductio illa animalium fuerit solum spiritualiter facta, ita quod imaginationi Adæ repræsentata fuerunt, ut consideraret per intellectum proprietates ipsorum, et apta cunctis nomina daret. Præterea, quamvis secundum ordinem recitationis textus istius, adductio hæc animalium videatur facta in paradiso, quidam tamen dixerunt quod extra paradisum peracta sit, quia Scriptura frequenter non servat ordinem rerum gestarum in describendo, sed aliqua dicit per recapitulationem, aliqua per anticipationem. Sed magis consonat expositioni Sanctorum ac textui, quod in paradiso adducta sint coram Adam.
paras.en: On this there is a threefold question. First, how the birds are now said to have been made from the ground, when in the preceding chapter they are read to have been brought forth from the water. Second, how the animals were brought to Adam. Third, why God willed that he should give them names. To the first Augustine answers that ground or earth is here taken as including the other elements, as at the opening of the first chapter: [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. It may also be answered otherwise, that the birds are said to have been made from the earth because in their bodies the element of earth predominates, as to the quantity of matter. To the second Augustine likewise answers that the animals were brought not by force, nor by a voice formed in the air, but by the ministry of angels. Others say, by the command of the Almighty alone. Some have even held that this bringing of the animals was done only spiritually, so that they were represented to Adam's imagination, that he might consider their properties with his understanding and give them all fitting names. Moreover, although by the order in which this text tells it the bringing of the animals seems to have been done in paradise, some have said that it took place outside paradise, since Scripture often does not keep the order of events in describing them, but tells some things by recapitulation and some by anticipation. But it agrees better with the exposition of the saints and with the text that they were brought before Adam in paradise.

paras.t: Ad tertiam respondetur, quod appellatio illa animalium, facta est ab Adam ad posterorum informationem. Quemadmodum enim Conditor fecit Adam perfectum, quantum ad corpus in ætate virili ac robore ad prolificandum; ita fecit eum perfectum in anima, quantum ad scientiam naturalem, per quam posset instruere posteros. Sicque Adam imposuit nomina omnibus illis, ut posteros edoceret nomina eorumdem. Denique ante suam transgressionem fuit perspicacioris scientiæ atque majoris dignitatis, ut angelico famulatu fieret coram eo illa adductio. Potest etiam dici, quod ideo ei adducta sunt, quatenus omnium illorum considerando naturas et proprietates, magis incitaretur ad Creatoris reverentiam ac amorem, et ei gratior esset pro excellentia et dominatione, quas ei super irrationabilia contulit. Ex quibus ostenditur, quod Deus concreavit Adæ non solum scientiam rerum, sed et notitiam cujusdam loquelæ. Quod si quæratur, cujus et in quo idiomate Adam imposuit animalibus nomina: respondetur, quod linguæ Hebrææ, et quod in ea imposuit animalibus nomina. Unde Hieronymus: Videtur, inquit, quod lingua Hebræa fuit prima hominibus, quoniam nomina quæ usque ad divisionem linguarum in Genesi legimus, sunt Hebræa.
paras.en: To the third it is answered that this naming of the animals was done by Adam for the instruction of his descendants. For just as the Maker made Adam perfect as to the body, in the age and strength of manhood for begetting offspring, so he made him perfect in soul as to natural knowledge, by which he could instruct his descendants. And so Adam gave names to all of them, to teach his descendants their names. Moreover, before his transgression he was of keener knowledge and greater dignity, so that this bringing was done before him by the service of angels. It may also be said that they were brought to him so that, by considering the natures and properties of all of them, he might be the more stirred to reverence and love of the Creator, and be more grateful to him for the excellence and dominion over irrational things which he had conferred on him. From this it is shown that God created together with Adam not only the knowledge of things but also the knowledge of a certain speech. And if it be asked of what tongue and in what idiom Adam gave the animals names, the answer is: of the Hebrew tongue, and that it was in it that he gave the animals names. Hence Jerome: It seems, he says, that the Hebrew tongue was the first among men, since the names which we read in Genesis up to the division of tongues are Hebrew.

paras.t: Quæri insuper potest, an etiam pisces adducti sint. Et dicunt quidam, quod imo. Verumtamen Augustinus videtur sentire quod non, nam ait: De piscibus non dicitur quod Adam eis imposuit nomina, sed credibile est, quod piscibus paulatim cognitis, juxta gentium diversitatem nomina exstent imposita. Hinc quum auctor Scholasticæ dixisset historiæ, In animantibus terræ, et aeris, intelligenda sunt animantia aquæ; mox addidit, Vel potius pisces postea ab hominibus sunt cogniti et nominati, quia æquivocantur cum animalibus terræ, eo quod deprehensi sunt similes illis esse.
paras.en: It may further be asked whether the fishes also were brought. And some say that indeed they were. Augustine, however, seems to think not, for he says: It is not said of the fishes that Adam gave them names; but it is credible that, as the fishes gradually became known, names were given them according to the diversity of the nations. Hence when the author of the Scholastic History [Peter Comestor] had said, Under the animals of the earth and of the air are to be understood the animals of the water, he at once added: Or rather, the fishes were known and named by men later, because they share names with the animals of the earth, since they were found to be like them.

paras.t: Iterum quæri potest, an universa et singula animalia illa adducta sint. Ad quod respondendum videtur, quod si in qualibet specie per commixtionem sexuum generante, non sunt nisi duo individua primo creata, ut aliqui opinantur, universa et singula sunt adducta. Si vero in eadem specie plura individua simul facta fuerunt, sufficiebat tamen adductio duorum individuorum, quum eadem nomina competerent eis et cæteris suæ naturæ consortibus. Irrationabilibus quippe non videtur imposuisse nomina propria, sed communia solum.
paras.en: Again it may be asked whether all those animals, each and every one, were brought. To this it seems the answer should be that if in every species that begets by the union of the sexes only two individuals were created at first, as some hold, then each and every one was brought. But if in the same species several individuals were made together, the bringing of two individuals was still enough, since the same names would fit them and the other sharers of their nature. For he does not seem to have given proper names to irrational creatures, but only common ones.

paras.t: Omne enim quod vocavit Adam animæ viventis, ipsum est nomen ejus, id est, omne animal vivum, vocatur veraciter nomine illo quod Adam sibi imposuit: quod primo de Hebræis verificatur nominibus, deinde proportionabiliter quoque de aliis. Nam quamvis bestiam, quæ equus vocatur in Latino, non vocaverit hoc nomine, equus: tamen vocavit eam nomine Hebræo, cui correspondet hoc nomen Latinum, equus. Appellavitque Adam nominibus suis cuncta animantia. Si hoc absolute accipiatur, sequeretur quod et piscibus nomina apta imposuit. Si vero accipiatur solum pro his, de quibus in speciali subjungitur, et universa volatilia cœli, et omnes bestias terræ, non teneret consequentia illa.
paras.en: [[2:19|for whatsoever Adam called any living creature the same is its name|Omne enim quod vocavit Adam animæ viventis, ipsum est nomen ejus]], that is, every living animal is truly called by the name which Adam gave it: which is verified first of the Hebrew names, and then proportionately of the others as well. For although he did not call the beast that is called *equus* in Latin by this name, *equus*, yet he called it by the Hebrew name to which this Latin name *equus* corresponds. [[2:20|And Adam called all the beasts by their names|Appellavitque Adam nominibus suis cuncta animantia]]. If this is taken absolutely, it would follow that he gave fitting names to the fishes too. But if it is taken only of those that are specified next, [[2:20|and all the fowls of the air, and all the cattle of the field|et universa volatilia cœli, et omnes bestias terræ]], that consequence would not hold.

paras.t: Adæ vero non inveniebatur adjutor similis ejus, id est, nulla reperiebatur nec fuit persona ejusdem speciei cum Adam, quæ posset ei cooperari in prolificando. Ex hoc vero apertissime sequitur, quod vir fuit prius tempore factus quam mulier.
paras.en: [[2:20|but for Adam there was not found a helper like himself|Adæ vero non inveniebatur adjutor similis ejus]], that is, no person was found, nor was there any, of the same species as Adam, who could work with him in begetting offspring. From this it follows most plainly that the man was made before the woman in time.

paras.t: Immisit ergo Dominus Deus soporem in Adam. Iste sopor secundum doctores catholicos, non fuit somnus naturalis aut corporalis, sed potius obdormitio, quies, ecstasis seu absorptio mentis in Deo, ex profunda ac intensissima contemplatione Dei ac secretorum mysteriorum ipsius. Ex qua obdormitione corpus et vires sensitivæ sopiebantur, atque a vita animali actuali et actibus circa propria objecta suspendebantur, donec mens rediit ad se ipsam. Unde quidam dicunt Adam tunc supernæ curiæ interfuisse: quod tamen intelligendum non est, quasi anima ejus fuerit realiter separata a corpore, aut translata in cœlum, vel quod viderit Deum tunc clare per speciem, sed quod anagogica contemplatione multum sublimi contemplatus sit Deum, et illuminatus ab eo de quibusdam secretis, ut statim dicetur. Cumque obdormisset modo prælato, tulit Dominus […] Hoc factum est supernaturaliter et immediate a Deo, et sine Adæ exvigilatione atque dolore; imo ad se ipsum reversus, non sensit inde dolorem. Verumtamen Augustinus tangit, quod costa potuit ministrari per angelos, id est, ministerio angelorum auferri, Deo jubente.
paras.en: [[2:21|Then the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam|Immisit ergo Dominus Deus soporem in Adam]]. This sleep, according to the Catholic doctors, was not a natural or bodily sleep, but rather a falling asleep, a rest, an ecstasy or absorption of the mind in God, arising from a deep and most intense contemplation of God and of his secret mysteries. By this falling asleep the body and the powers of sense were lulled, and suspended from the actual life of the senses and from their acts about their proper objects, until the mind returned to itself. Hence some say that Adam was then present at the heavenly court; which, however, is not to be understood as though his soul had been really separated from the body, or carried up into heaven, or as though he then saw God clearly by sight [*per speciem*, that is, face to face], but that in a most lofty anagogical contemplation [that is, contemplation that lifts the mind up to heavenly things] he contemplated God and was enlightened by him about certain secrets, as will be said presently. [[2:21|and when he was fast asleep|Cumque obdormisset]] in the manner described, the Lord [[2:21|took|tulit]] […] This was done supernaturally and immediately by God, without Adam's waking and without pain; indeed, when he came back to himself he felt no pain from it. Augustine, however, touches on the point that the rib could have been taken by the angels, that is, removed by the ministry of angels at God's bidding.

paras.t: Et replevit carnem pro ea, id est, loco costæ sublatæ posuit carnem, extendendo seu augendo carnem quæ propinqua fuerat costæ, ita quod locum illum replevit. Et ædificavit Dominus Deus costam, quam tulerat de Adam, in mulierem, id est, de costa illa formavit corpus Evæ per se ipsum immediate, supernaturaliter et instantanee, sicut et corpus Adæ, quorum utrumque fecit solo jussu omnipotentis sapientiæ suæ. In eodem quoque instanti creavit et corpori suo infudit animam Evæ.
paras.en: [[2:21|and filled up flesh for it|Et replevit carnem pro ea]], that is, in place of the rib taken away he put flesh, stretching or increasing the flesh that had been next to the rib, so that it filled that place. [[2:22|And the Lord God built the rib which he took from Adam into a woman|Et ædificavit Dominus Deus costam, quam tulerat de Adam, in mulierem]], that is, from that rib he formed Eve's body himself, immediately, supernaturally and instantaneously, as he did Adam's body too, both of which he made by the sole command of his almighty wisdom. In the same instant also he created Eve's soul and poured it into her body.

paras.t: Et adduxit eam ad Adam, tanquam ad superiorem seu perfectiorem, et tanquam ad caput suum atque principium, et quoniam fuerat ei matrimonialiter et socialiter ac amicabiliter copulanda: in signum quoque, quod femina maritanda, debet duci ad virum.
paras.en: [[2:22|and brought her to Adam|Et adduxit eam ad Adam]], as to one higher or more perfect, and as to her head and beginning, and because she was to be joined to him in marriage, in companionship and in friendship; and also as a sign that a woman who is to be married ought to be led to her husband.

paras.t: Dixitque Adam: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea, id est, persona ista feminea, quæ nomine ossis et carnis significatur, quoniam ex ossibus et carne composita est, est jam formata, quantum ad corpus suum, ex uno de ossibus meis, puta ex costa mea, et etiam de carne mea, quoniam Deus tollendo costam ex Adam, tulit simul cum costa aliquam partem carnis, qua costa fuerat tecta. Hæc vocabitur virago, quoniam de viro sumpta est. Apparet quibusdam quod impropria sit nominatio ista, quia virago magis designat mulierem viriliter agentem, quam de viro sumptam: ideo magis proprie diceretur vira, si sermo Latinus hoc pateretur. Sed ultimum istud non videtur idonee dictum, quia etsi dictio ista, vira, esset in usu, per eam non designaretur mulier facta de viro, sed solum persona feminei sexus, sicut per virum persona sexus virilis. Nam ita haberent se ad invicem vir et vira, sicut dominus et domina. Per dominam autem non designatur, quod res illa qua domina dicitur, sit facta de domino. Unde apparet quod appropriatius diceretur viracta, quasi de viro facta, quam vira; quamvis, in quantum mulier, dicetur proprie vira, quemadmodum in Hebræo dicitur Issa, quod interpretatur mulier. Sumpta est itaque mulier illa de viro quantum ad corpus, non quantum ad animam, quæ nequaquam ex anima viri traducta est, sed immediate a Deo creata. Nec tamen Moyses hoc expressit, quia jam satis dedit illud intelligi, per hoc quod animam viri insinuavit ab extra infusam ac inspiratam. Præterea, sicut dicit Glossa, Theodotion aliam etymologiam suspicatus est, dicens: Hæc vocabitur assumptio, quia de viris sumpta. Issa enim, secundum varietatem accentus, etiam assumptionem designat.
paras.en: [[2:23|And Adam said: This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh|Dixitque Adam: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea]], that is, this female person, who is signified by the name of bone and flesh because she is composed of bones and flesh, is now formed, as to her body, from one of my bones, namely from my rib, and also from my flesh, since God, in taking the rib from Adam, took together with the rib some part of the flesh with which the rib had been covered. [[2:23|she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man|Hæc vocabitur virago, quoniam de viro sumpta est]] [the Latin has *virago*, from *vir*, "man"; the Douay-Rheims has "woman"]. It seems to some that this naming is improper, because *virago* signifies rather a woman who acts manfully than one taken from man; and so she would more properly be called *vira*, if the Latin tongue allowed it. But this last does not seem fitly said, because even if the word *vira* were in use, it would not signify a woman made from man, but only a person of the female sex, as *vir* signifies a person of the male sex. For *vir* and *vira* would stand to each other as *dominus* and *domina* [lord and lady]. But *domina* does not signify that the one who is called *domina* was made from a *dominus*. Hence it appears that she would more aptly be called *viracta*, as though made from man, than *vira*; although, inasmuch as she is a woman, she would properly be called *vira*, as in Hebrew she is called *Issa*, which is interpreted *woman*. So that woman was taken from the man as to the body, not as to the soul, which was in no way derived from the man's soul but created immediately by God. Yet Moses did not express this, because he had already given it to be understood clearly enough by indicating that the man's soul was poured in and breathed in from without. Moreover, as the Gloss says, Theodotion conjectured another etymology, saying: She shall be called assumption [*assumptio*, a taking up], because she was taken from men. For *Issa*, with a different accent, also signifies assumption.

paras.t: Quamobrem, id est, quum tanta sit propinquitas, et quodammodo unitas viri et conjugis suæ, relinquet homo, scilicet vir, patrem suum et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Primo, quod maritus relinquet proprios parentes communiter, quantum ad cohabitationem, mensam et lectum, et uxori suæ adhærebit in his, quia ad prolificandum accipit eam: ideo habet providere sibi ipsi et contorali ac propriæ proli, nec manet sub cura parentum ut ante: sed emancipatus efficitur, et suam accipit portionem. Secundo, quod homo relinquet parentes suos, quantum ad ineundum conjugium, quoniam nunquam licuit filio cum matre sua contrahere, nec filiæ cum proprio patre, quia concubitus est contra reverentiam qua proles suis tenetur parentibus: ceteræ autem personæ, quantumlibet cognatæ, potuerunt aliquando matrimonialiter sociari. Potest et tertio exponi de dilectionis derelictione. Nam vir quum ducit uxorem, quamvis non desinat parentes suos diligere, attamen incipit plus amare conjugem, quam parentes, quantum ad amorem illum zelotypum. Et erunt duo in carne una, id est, tam familiariter ac intime copulabuntur, quasi sint una caro: et iterum erunt duo supposita, utpote vir et uxor, in carne una, hoc est, caro unius erit alterius, et caro uniuscujusque ipsorum, erit ambobus communis, uni ad essendum, alteri ad utendum: vir quippe sui corporis potestatem non habet, sed mulier, et econtra. Erunt quoque duo in carne una, hoc est, in uno carnali opere seu commercio, atque in una prole communicabunt, concurrent, et unum fient, unum, inquam, per communionem, causalitatem, et dilectionem.
paras.en: [[2:24|Wherefore|Quamobrem]], that is, since so great is the nearness, and in a way the oneness, of a man and his wife, [[2:24|a man shall leave|relinquet homo]], that is, the husband, [[2:24|father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife|patrem suum et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ]]. This is explained in two ways. First, that the husband will leave his own parents in the common way, as to living together, table and bed, and will cleave to his wife in these things, because he takes her for begetting offspring: so he must provide for himself, for his bedfellow and for his own offspring, and no longer remains under his parents' care as before, but is made independent [*emancipatus*: released from his father's authority] and receives his own portion. Secondly, that a man will leave his parents as to entering marriage, since it was never lawful for a son to marry his mother, nor a daughter her own father, because such intercourse is against the reverence which offspring owe their parents; but other persons, however closely related, could at one time be joined in marriage. It can also be expounded, thirdly, of a leaving in love. For when a man takes a wife, although he does not cease to love his parents, yet he begins to love his wife more than his parents, as regards that jealous love [*amor zelotypus*, the exclusive love proper to spouses]. [[2:24|and they shall be two in one flesh|Et erunt duo in carne una]], that is, they will be joined so closely and intimately that they are as it were one flesh; and again, they will be two individuals [*supposita*], namely husband and wife, in one flesh, that is, the flesh of the one will be the other's, and the flesh of each of them will be common to both, to the one for being, to the other for use: for the husband [[1 Cor 7:4|hath not power of his own body: but the wife|sui corporis potestatem non habet, sed mulier]], and conversely. They will also be two in one flesh, that is, in one carnal act or intercourse; and they will share in one offspring, concur, and become one: one, I say, by communion, by causality, and by love.

paras.t: Erat autem uterque nudus, Adam scilicet et uxor ejus. Non enim indiguerunt vestitu contra intemperiem aeris, aut aliquam læsionem. Nec erubescebant ex mutuæ nuditatis genitaliumque membrorum intuitu. Erubescentia namque est timor seu pudor de re turpi; turpitudo autem non erat in membris aut corpore ex creatione, aut ipsa originali conditione. Et ideo quoniam non erat in eis aliqua appetitio, aut motio inhonesta, nec suspicabantur sibi tale quid imminere, non erubuerunt, sicut nec glorificati in corpore post diem judicii. Ideo Josephus deliravit, dicendo quod inerubescentia illa priorum parentum, venit ex imperitia et puerili simplicitate. Sic enim status eorum fuisset ex peccato melioratus, utpote majori usu rationis et pleniori scientia decoratus. Jam quoque præhabitum est, quod Adam fuit in naturali scientia perfectus creatus. Nec aliter potuisset animalibus apta imponere nomina. In præfato item sopore fuit mirabiliter illustratus: idcirco nequaquam erant asinina et brutali simplicitate obfuscati, sed magis illuminati ante suam transgressionem, quæ non mediocriter vulneravit in eis naturalia, abstulitque gratuita saltem nonnulla. Itaque nihil putabant celandum, quia nihil senserunt reprimendum, et quoniam membra præfata rationi omnino obediebant: nunc autem præcipue sunt erubescenda, quoniam rationi sunt præsertim rebellia.
paras.en: [[2:25|And they were both naked: to wit, Adam and his wife|Erat autem uterque nudus, Adam scilicet et uxor ejus]]. For they had no need of clothing against the harshness of the weather or any hurt. [[2:25|and were not ashamed|Nec erubescebant]] at the sight of each other's nakedness and of the members of generation. For shame is a fear or bashfulness about something base; but there was no baseness in the members or the body by creation, or by the original condition itself. And so, since there was in them no unseemly desire or movement, nor did they suspect that any such thing threatened them, they were not ashamed, just as those glorified in body after the day of judgment will not be either. Josephus therefore talked nonsense in saying that this freedom from shame in our first parents came from inexperience and childish simplicity. For then their state would have been bettered by sin, as being adorned with a greater use of reason and a fuller knowledge. It has also been shown already that Adam was created perfect in natural knowledge; nor could he otherwise have given the animals fitting names. In the aforesaid sleep, too, he was wonderfully enlightened: so they were by no means darkened with an asinine and brutish simplicity, but were rather enlightened before their transgression, which wounded their natural gifts not a little, and took away at least some of the gratuitous ones [that is, the gifts of grace added to nature]. So they thought nothing needed hiding, because they felt nothing that needed restraining, and because those members obeyed reason entirely; but now they are above all to be blushed for, since they are above all rebellious against reason.

2.title: Introductio et solutio quæstionum, concernentium passum textus istius articulo præcedenti expositum
2.title_en: Introduction and solution of questions concerning the passage of this text expounded in the preceding article

paras.t: QUÆRITUR circa illud. Tulit Dominus Deus hominem, et posuit eum in paradiso : a qua parte terræ tulit eum, hoc est, in qua parte terræ factus est primus homo. Ad hoc respondet Henricus de Hassia : De hoc non est certitudo. Sed Josephus dicit, quod in agro Damasceno, hoc est in agro juxta quem postea est ædificata Damascus urbs Syriæ. Dicitque Josephus, quod ibi factus sit Adam de terra rubra conspersa seu humida. Nam et Adam uno modo interpretatur ac sonat, rubens, vel rubra terra. Alii dicunt, quod factus sit in medio terræ habitabilis, utpote circa Jerusalem, quoniam ibi aut prope nasciturus et conversaturus fuerat Christus. In Elucidario, in quo multa notabilia breviter continentur, quamvis non cuncta authentica sint, dicitur quod Adam in Hebron, id est, agro ubi nunc Hebron est, formatus sit, et illuc post ejectionem suam reversus ac conversatus. Cui dicto apparentiam facit, quod ibidem sepultus describitur.
paras.en: QUESTION is raised concerning the words, [[2:15|the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise|Tulit Dominus Deus hominem, et posuit eum in paradiso]]: from what part of the earth did he take him, that is, in what part of the earth was the first man made? To this Henry of Hesse answers: Of this there is no certainty. But Josephus says that it was in the field of Damascus, that is, in the field beside which Damascus, a city of Syria, was afterwards built. And Josephus says that Adam was made there of red earth, sprinkled or moist. For *Adam*, in one way, is also interpreted and sounds as 'reddish', or 'red earth'. Others say that he was made in the middle of the habitable earth, namely about Jerusalem, since Christ was to be born and to live there or near it. In the Elucidarium, in which many notable things are briefly contained, though not all of them are authentic, it is said that Adam was formed in Hebron, that is, in the field where Hebron now is, and that after his expulsion he returned there and lived there. This saying is made likely by the fact that he is described as buried in the same place[[Jos 14:15||]] [the verse reads: Adam the greatest among the Enacims was laid there; the Adam there is a giant of the Enacims, whom some took for the first man].

paras.t: Secundo quæritur, quum vir sit dignior muliere, cur mulier in paradiso formata est, vir extra paradisum. Respondetur, quod viro extra paradisum plasmato, ad innuendum, quod mansio paradisi sibi naturaliter non deberetur, satis innotuit, quod mulieri mansio illa non debebatur, quum esset imperfectior viro : idcirco ad illud designandum, non oportebat eam extra paradisum formari. Assignantur quoque et aliæ causæ, videlicet quod Deus in hoc honoravit sexum femineum. Unde et de nobiliori materia eam formavit, quam virum, puta de costa viri, de limo formati. Et quia ipse Creator omnipotens prævidit se ex sexu illo incarnandum. Et rursus, ne viri conjuges suas contemnant, sed venerentur.
paras.en: Secondly, it is asked why, since the man is more worthy than the woman, the woman was formed in paradise and the man outside paradise. The answer is that, the man having been fashioned outside paradise to intimate that the dwelling of paradise was not due to him by nature, it was made known clearly enough that that dwelling was not due to the woman, since she was less perfect than the man: therefore, to signify this, there was no need for her to be formed outside paradise. Other reasons too are given, namely that God in this honoured the female sex. Hence he also formed her of a nobler material than the man, to wit, of the rib of the man, who had been formed of slime. And because the almighty Creator himself foresaw that he was to be incarnate of that sex. And again, so that men should not despise their wives, but revere them.

paras.t: Tertio quæritur circa illud. Præcepitque ei, dicens : Ex omni ligno paradisi comede : quot præcepta dedit Deus Adæ in principio seu paradiso. Ad hoc communiter respondetur, quod tria. Unum fuit, Crescite et multiplicamini. Et hoc pertinebat ad conservationem speciei. Verumtamen hoc præceptum, secundum ordinem historiæ textus, datum est Adæ ante translationem suam in paradisum. Secundum præceptum fuit, Ex omni ligno paradisi comede, quod pertinet ad conservationem individui. Et hæc duo præcepta erant affirmativa. Tertium exstitit negativum, videlicet : De ligno scientiæ boni et mali ne comedas.
paras.en: Thirdly, it is asked concerning the words [[2:16|And he commanded him, saying: Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Præcepitque ei, dicens : Ex omni ligno paradisi comede]], how many precepts God gave Adam in the beginning, or in paradise. To this the common answer is: three. One was, [[Gen 1:28|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]]. And this belonged to the preservation of the species. Yet this precept, according to the order of the history of the text, was given to Adam before his removal into paradise. The second precept was, [[2:16|Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat|Ex omni ligno paradisi comede]], which belongs to the preservation of the individual. And these two precepts were affirmative. The third was negative, namely: [[2:17|of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat|De ligno scientiæ boni et mali ne comedas]].

paras.t: Quarto quæritur, an etiam mulieri data sint ista præcepta. Et videtur quod non. Nam in prolatione primi præcepti nondum fuit producta. Porro duo ultima ista præcepta, soli Adæ data leguntur. Oppositum tamen apparet ex eo, quod infra mulier respondet serpenti : De fructu ligni quod est in medio paradisi, præcepit nobis Deus ne comederemus, ne forte moriamur. Ad hoc Augustinus quasi dubitative respondet, quod præcepta ista sic data sunt viro, ut per eum devenirent ad Evam. In Scholastica historia datur ista responsio assertive. Et additur ibi, quod jussio ista dicitur Adæ facta forte per anticipationem, quoniam muliere formata, utrisque est data. Verumtamen hoc non habetur ex textu, nisi forte ex responsione Evæ præallegata : quæ tamen ita intelligi potest, quod jussiones hæ primo et immediate factæ sunt viro, et mulieri per eum.
paras.en: Fourthly, it is asked whether these precepts were given to the woman also. And it seems not. For when the first precept was uttered she had not yet been brought forth. Moreover, the two latter precepts are read as given to Adam alone. Yet the opposite appears from the fact that further on the woman answers the serpent: [[Gen 3:3|of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God hath commanded us that we should not eat|De fructu ligni quod est in medio paradisi, præcepit nobis Deus ne comederemus]], [[Gen 3:3|lest perhaps we die|ne forte moriamur]]. To this Augustine answers, as though in doubt, that these precepts were given to the man in such a way that through him they should come to Eve. In the Scholastic History this answer is given as certain. And it is added there that this command is perhaps said to have been given to Adam by anticipation, since, once the woman had been formed, it was given to both.
